heading: མདོ་སྡེ་ཇི་ལྟར་འཆད་པའི་ཚུལ་དང་པོར་དགོས་པ་དང་བརྗོད་བྱ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Here, one who wishes to explain the sūtra should first state its purpose, in order to engage the listeners in taking it up earnestly and so forth. Without realizing the purpose, intelligent people will not engage in anything at all. Next, in order to show the method for accomplishing the purpose of the sūtra, the subject matter should be stated. A sūtra empty of subject matter does not accomplish the desired purpose, just like words such as 'ten pomegranates'. Next, in order to make that subject matter easy to grasp, the summarized meaning should be stated. Next, in order to understand the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words should be stated. Next, in order to show that the sequence is not contradictory, the connections among the words should be shown. Next, in order to clear away logical contradictions between earlier and later parts, replies to objections should be stated. The procedure is like that. In this regard, the very name of this sūtra, the Diamond Cutter, indicates its subject matter and purpose. Thus, it is the Diamond Cutter in two ways. Because it cuts the subtle afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations that are difficult to destroy like a diamond, this indicates that its purpose is the relinquishing of the two obscurations. Alternatively, 'cutter' means it is like a vajra because it resembles the shape of a vajra. A vajra is made thick at its two ends and thin in the middle. Similarly, this prajñāpāramitā also thoroughly teaches as vast the level of action through aspiration at the beginning, and the level of a buddha at the end. By being thin in the middle, it indicates the level of pure extraordinary resolve. Therefore, this is like the shape of a vajra; this indicates that these three levels are its subject matter.

Here, one who wishes to explain the sūtra should first state its purpose, in order to engage the listeners in taking it up earnestly and so forth. Without realizing the purpose, intelligent people will not engage in anything at all. Next, in order to show the method for accomplishing the purpose of the sūtra, the subject matter should be stated. A sūtra empty of subject matter does not accomplish the desired purpose, just like words such as 'ten pomegranates'. Next, in order to make that subject matter easy to grasp, the summarized meaning should be stated. Next, in order to understand the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words should be stated. Next, in order to show that the sequence is not contradictory, the connections among the words should be shown. Next, in order to clear away logical contradictions between earlier and later parts, replies to objections should be stated. The procedure is like that. In this regard, the very name of this sūtra, the Diamond Cutter, indicates its subject matter and purpose. Thus, it is the Diamond Cutter in two ways. Because it cuts the subtle afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations that are difficult to destroy like a diamond, this indicates that its purpose is the relinquishing of the two obscurations. Alternatively, 'cutter' means it is like a vajra because it resembles the shape of a vajra. A vajra is made thick at its two ends and thin in the middle. Similarly, this prajñāpāramitā also thoroughly teaches as vast the level of action through aspiration at the beginning, and the level of a buddha at the end. By being thin in the middle, it indicates the level of pure extraordinary resolve. Therefore, this is like the shape of a vajra; this indicates that these three levels are its subject matter.

heading: བསྡུས་དོན་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In this regard, the setting is the cause for the sūtra to arise, and that is shown starting from "Thus have I heard" up to "Then the venerable Subhūti". Therefore, it is stated by the authentic compiler in order to inspire trust in himself, and it should be stated for all sūtras. The initiation of the discourse is the connection to the context in order to explain the meaning of the sūtra. Because if spoken out of context, everything would become confused, in order to clear away confusion, the connection to the context should be made in all cases. That is shown by "Then the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat" and so forth. Ensuring the uninterrupted lineage of the buddhas is also shown by that very passage. Since the noble Subhūti knew that this prajñāpāramitā makes the lineage of the buddhas uninterrupted, the elder Subhūti first laid out exactly how the lineage of the buddhas becomes uninterrupted. The characteristics of practice are shown by "How should one who has genuinely entered the bodhisattva vehicle abide?" and so forth. The locus of those characteristics of practice is whichever object a bodhisattva should abide in, practice, and perfectly control the mind in—that is called its locus. That, moreover, is shown starting from "Subhūti, here, one who has genuinely entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus, 'I...'" up to the final verse, "A star, a visual aberration," and so forth. These two, the characteristics of practice and its locus, completely show the entirety of a bodhisattva's activities; this is the summarized meaning for now.

Here, one who wishes to explain the sūtra should first state its purpose, in order to engage the listeners in taking it up earnestly and so forth. Without realizing the purpose, intelligent people will not engage in anything at all. Next, in order to show the method for accomplishing the purpose of the sūtra, the subject matter should be stated. A sūtra empty of subject matter does not accomplish the desired purpose, just like words such as 'ten pomegranates'. Next, in order to make that subject matter easy to grasp, the summarized meaning should be stated. Next, in order to understand the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words should be stated. Next, in order to show that the sequence is not contradictory, the connections among the words should be shown. Next, in order to clear away logical contradictions between earlier and later parts, replies to objections should be stated. The procedure is like that. In this regard, the very name of this sūtra, the Diamond Cutter, indicates its subject matter and purpose. Thus, it is the Diamond Cutter in two ways. Because it cuts the subtle afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations that are difficult to destroy like a diamond, this indicates that its purpose is the relinquishing of the two obscurations. Alternatively, 'cutter' means it is like a vajra because it resembles the shape of a vajra. A vajra is made thick at its two ends and thin in the middle. Similarly, this prajñāpāramitā also thoroughly teaches as vast the level of action through aspiration at the beginning, and the level of a buddha at the end. By being thin in the middle, it indicates the level of pure extraordinary resolve. Therefore, this is like the shape of a vajra; this indicates that these three levels are its subject matter.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: The meaning of the words and so forth should also be stated; those will be stated. In this regard, although the term 'Thus' appears in many meanings such as acceptance and so forth, here, by the power of the context and so forth, it should be understood as a presentation. This presents the entirety of the meaning of the sūtra occurring below. 'By me' excludes others and indicates that the meaning was heard directly. The implication is: 'I heard it myself; it did not come solely through transmission.' 'Heard' negates realization, because other than a buddha, there is no one else who realizes such dharmas by themselves. This clears away lack of trust. 'At one time' means at a single time; it indicates that such rare and supreme dharmas are difficult to hear at all times. Alternatively, it shows that he himself has heard much. It indicates: 'At one time I heard this, but at other times I heard other things as well.' Alternatively, connecting it with what follows as 'at one time the Blessed One was dwelling,' it establishes that for the purpose of benefiting those immeasurable trainees, he was dwelling elsewhere at other times. 'Blessed One' means that because he possesses the conquering of the four māras, which have the characteristics of the afflictions, the aggregates, the lord of death, and the child of the gods, he is called 'Blessed One' by way of etymology.

Here, one who wishes to explain the sūtra should first state its purpose, in order to engage the listeners in taking it up earnestly and so forth. Without realizing the purpose, intelligent people will not engage in anything at all. Next, in order to show the method for accomplishing the purpose of the sūtra, the subject matter should be stated. A sūtra empty of subject matter does not accomplish the desired purpose, just like words such as 'ten pomegranates'. Next, in order to make that subject matter easy to grasp, the summarized meaning should be stated. Next, in order to understand the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words should be stated. Next, in order to show that the sequence is not contradictory, the connections among the words should be shown. Next, in order to clear away logical contradictions between earlier and later parts, replies to objections should be stated. The procedure is like that. In this regard, the very name of this sūtra, the Diamond Cutter, indicates its subject matter and purpose. Thus, it is the Diamond Cutter in two ways. Because it cuts the subtle afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations that are difficult to destroy like a diamond, this indicates that its purpose is the relinquishing of the two obscurations. Alternatively, 'cutter' means it is like a vajra because it resembles the shape of a vajra. A vajra is made thick at its two ends and thin in the middle. Similarly, this prajñāpāramitā also thoroughly teaches as vast the level of action through aspiration at the beginning, and the level of a buddha at the end. By being thin in the middle, it indicates the level of pure extraordinary resolve. Therefore, this is like the shape of a vajra; this indicates that these three levels are its subject matter.

In this regard, the setting is the cause for the sūtra to arise, and that is shown starting from "Thus have I heard" up to "Then the venerable Subhūti". Therefore, it is stated by the authentic compiler in order to inspire trust in himself, and it should be stated for all sūtras. The initiation of the discourse is the connection to the context in order to explain the meaning of the sūtra. Because if spoken out of context, everything would become confused, in order to clear away confusion, the connection to the context should be made in all cases. That is shown by "Then the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat" and so forth. Ensuring the uninterrupted lineage of the buddhas is also shown by that very passage. Since the noble Subhūti knew that this prajñāpāramitā makes the lineage of the buddhas uninterrupted, the elder Subhūti first laid out exactly how the lineage of the buddhas becomes uninterrupted. The characteristics of practice are shown by "How should one who has genuinely entered the bodhisattva vehicle abide?" and so forth. The locus of those characteristics of practice is whichever object a bodhisattva should abide in, practice, and perfectly control the mind in—that is called its locus. That, moreover, is shown starting from "Subhūti, here, one who has genuinely entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus, 'I...'" up to the final verse, "A star, a visual aberration," and so forth. These two, the characteristics of practice and its locus, completely show the entirety of a bodhisattva's activities; this is the summarized meaning for now.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: Alternatively, because he is endowed with sovereignty and so forth, he is called 'Glorious'. As it is said: 'Complete endowment with sovereignty, physical beauty, glory, and renown, wisdom, and diligent exertion—these six are called "glory".' 'Śrāvastī' means that because it is the hermitage of the sage Śrāvasta, it is the city of Śrāvastī; because the particular region characterized by it is jointly connected with it, it is called Śrāvastī. The place is mentioned in order to declare that the place has become a stūpa; thus, even in this very text it is stated, 'that place becomes a stūpa.' Alternatively, the authentic compiler states all these in order to establish that his words are worthy of being grasped. Thus, if they are spoken along with the location, along with the circumstances, and along with the master, for the purpose of inspiring trust in the world, others will grasp the words; otherwise, the words would not be worthy of being grasped. Since the region of Śrāvastī is very vast and it would not be known exactly where he was dwelling, 'the grove of Prince Jeta' is mentioned; because it is the grove of that one called Prince Jeta, it is the grove of Prince Jeta. Since it is possible that even that might not be renowned to anyone at all, 'in Anāthapiṇḍada's park' is mentioned. The householder 'Anāthapiṇḍada' was renowned as such because out of compassion for the protectorless he gave them alms; since he bought the park from Prince Jeta by laying down precious jewels side by side for the sake of the Blessed One, and since Prince Jeta also had some pavilions and so forth adorned for the Blessed One from that, it is renowned as the grove of those two. If only any one of these were mentioned, the desire to express the specific place would not be understood, so all three phrases are mentioned. Alternatively, this mention of 'Śrāvastī' indicates the perfection of benefiting others, because he dwells among the multitudes.

Here, one who wishes to explain the sūtra should first state its purpose, in order to engage the listeners in taking it up earnestly and so forth. Without realizing the purpose, intelligent people will not engage in anything at all. Next, in order to show the method for accomplishing the purpose of the sūtra, the subject matter should be stated. A sūtra empty of subject matter does not accomplish the desired purpose, just like words such as 'ten pomegranates'. Next, in order to make that subject matter easy to grasp, the summarized meaning should be stated. Next, in order to understand the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words should be stated. Next, in order to show that the sequence is not contradictory, the connections among the words should be shown. Next, in order to clear away logical contradictions between earlier and later parts, replies to objections should be stated. The procedure is like that. In this regard, the very name of this sūtra, the Diamond Cutter, indicates its subject matter and purpose. Thus, it is the Diamond Cutter in two ways. Because it cuts the subtle afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations that are difficult to destroy like a diamond, this indicates that its purpose is the relinquishing of the two obscurations. Alternatively, 'cutter' means it is like a vajra because it resembles the shape of a vajra. A vajra is made thick at its two ends and thin in the middle. Similarly, this prajñāpāramitā also thoroughly teaches as vast the level of action through aspiration at the beginning, and the level of a buddha at the end. By being thin in the middle, it indicates the level of pure extraordinary resolve. Therefore, this is like the shape of a vajra; this indicates that these three levels are its subject matter.

In this regard, the setting is the cause for the sūtra to arise, and that is shown starting from "Thus have I heard" up to "Then the venerable Subhūti". Therefore, it is stated by the authentic compiler in order to inspire trust in himself, and it should be stated for all sūtras. The initiation of the discourse is the connection to the context in order to explain the meaning of the sūtra. Because if spoken out of context, everything would become confused, in order to clear away confusion, the connection to the context should be made in all cases. That is shown by "Then the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat" and so forth. Ensuring the uninterrupted lineage of the buddhas is also shown by that very passage. Since the noble Subhūti knew that this prajñāpāramitā makes the lineage of the buddhas uninterrupted, the elder Subhūti first laid out exactly how the lineage of the buddhas becomes uninterrupted. The characteristics of practice are shown by "How should one who has genuinely entered the bodhisattva vehicle abide?" and so forth. The locus of those characteristics of practice is whichever object a bodhisattva should abide in, practice, and perfectly control the mind in—that is called its locus. That, moreover, is shown starting from "Subhūti, here, one who has genuinely entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus, 'I...'" up to the final verse, "A star, a visual aberration," and so forth. These two, the characteristics of practice and its locus, completely show the entirety of a bodhisattva's activities; this is the summarized meaning for now.

source: རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་གྱི་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་དབེན་པ་ན་བཞུགས་པས་རང་གི་དོན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །འདི་ལ་དབང་སུ་ཡོད་སྙམ་པ་ལ། དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བས་དགེ་སློང་དག་གོ། །བདུད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྒོལ་བ་དག་གིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པས་མང་པོ་དེ་དག་ལ་དགེ་འདུན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་ཕལ་ཆེ་བ་དང་མཐུ་གཉིས་ཏེ། དེས་ནི་མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཕལ་ཆེ་བ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་སྙམ་པ་དང་། སྟོང་ཉིས་བརྒྱ་ལྔ་བཅུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེའི་ཚེ་ན་དེ་སྙེད་ཅིག་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རབ་ཏུ་མང་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་ཆེད་དུ་མདོ་སྡེ་འཆད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་དག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སྙིང་སྟོབས་ཆེ་བའི་བསམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་གོ །ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་སྙིང་སྟོབས་ཡོད་པས་དེ་རྣམ་པར་གཅོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཆོས་དང་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། མོས་པ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དང་།ཚོགས་དང་། དུས་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམ་པ་བདུན་དང་ལྡན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དག་གོ། །དེ་ལ་ཆོས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
translation: This mention of 'the grove of Prince Jeta, Anāthapiṇḍada's park' indicates the perfection of benefiting oneself, because he dwells in solitude. Thinking, 'Who possesses mastery in this?', 'a great saṅgha of monks' is mentioned; because they are free from afflictions, they are 'monks'. Because they cannot be divided by opponents such as māras and so forth, those multitudes are called a 'saṅgha'. Those of the 'great saṅgha of monks' have two greatnesses: multitude and power; this indicates greatness in power. Thinking, 'What is the greatness of multitude?', 'one thousand two hundred and fifty' and so forth is mentioned, because at that time there were that many. That the bodhisattvas were exceedingly more numerous than the saṅgha of monks is because the sūtra is taught for their sake. Because they possess intentions with great courage for awakening, they are 'bodhisattvas'. Since śrāvakas also have courage for awakening, in order to exclude them, 'great beings' is mentioned. Because they are endowed with seven kinds of great characteristics—dharma, generation of the mind, inclination, intention, accumulation, time, and perfect accomplishment—they are 'great beings'. In this regard, 'great dharma' is because the teaching of dharma to bodhisattvas, such as the prajñāpāramitā in one hundred thousand lines and so forth, is extensive.

The meaning of the words and so forth should also be stated; those will be stated. In this regard, although the term 'Thus' appears in many meanings such as acceptance and so forth, here, by the power of the context and so forth, it should be understood as a presentation. This presents the entirety of the meaning of the sūtra occurring below. 'By me' excludes others and indicates that the meaning was heard directly. The implication is: 'I heard it myself; it did not come solely through transmission.' 'Heard' negates realization, because other than a buddha, there is no one else who realizes such dharmas by themselves. This clears away lack of trust. 'At one time' means at a single time; it indicates that such rare and supreme dharmas are difficult to hear at all times. Alternatively, it shows that he himself has heard much. It indicates: 'At one time I heard this, but at other times I heard other things as well.' Alternatively, connecting it with what follows as 'at one time the Blessed One was dwelling,' it establishes that for the purpose of benefiting those immeasurable trainees, he was dwelling elsewhere at other times. 'Blessed One' means that because he possesses the conquering of the four māras, which have the characteristics of the afflictions, the aggregates, the lord of death, and the child of the gods, he is called 'Blessed One' by way of etymology.

ཡང་ན་དབང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པས་ལེགས་ལྡན་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཇི་སྐད་དུ། དབང་དང་རབ་ཏུ་ལྡན་པ་དང་། །གཟུགས་དང་དཔལ་དང་གྲགས་པ་དང་། །ཡེ་ཤེས་དང་ནི་ནན་ཏན་དང་། །དྲུག་པོ་དེ་ལ་ལེགས་ཞེས་བྱ། །ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དྲང་སྲོང་མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་བསྟི་གནས་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་མཉན་ཡོད་དེ། དེས་མཚོན་པའི་ཡུལ་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་ཀྱང་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྲེལ་པའི་ཕྱིར་མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །ཡུལ་སྨོས་པ་དེ་ཡང་ཡུལ་དེ་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པར་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་འདི་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཡང་ན་ཡང་དག་པར་སྡུད་པར་བྱེད་པས་བདག་གི་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འོས་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཐམས་ཅད་སྨོས་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཡིད་ཆེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ནི་ས་ཕྱོགས་དང་བཅས་པ་རྣམ་པ་དང་བཅས། དབང་ཕྱུག་དང་བཅས་པས་སྨྲས་ན། གཞན་དག་གིས་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འགྱུར་གྱི། གཞན་དུ་ན་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འོས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཡུལ་མཉན་ཡོད་ཧ་ཅང་རྒྱ་ཆེས་ཏེ་གང་ན་བཞུགས་གཏོལ་མེད་པས་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེ་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དེའི་ཚལ་ཡིན་པས་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཡང་ཇི་སྟེ་ན་སུ་ལ་ཡང་མ་གྲགས་ཀྱང་སྲིད་པས་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་གྱི་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཁྱིམ་བདག་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་ཞེས་པ་མགོན་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་སྟེ་ཟས་སྦྱིན་པས་དེ་ལྟར་གྲགས་པ་དེས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་བཀྲམ་པ་གཤིབས་པས་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ལས་ཀུན་དགའི་ར་བ་ཉོས་པ་དང་། རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལས་ཅུང་ཞིག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་ཁང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བརྒྱན་དུ་བཅུག་པས་དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཚལ་དེ་གྲགས་སོ། །གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་ཞིག་སྨོས་ན་ནི་ཡུལ་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་བརྗོད་པར་འདོད་པ་རྟོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བས་ཚིག་གསུམ་ཆར་སྨོས་སོ། །ཡང་ན་མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་མང་པོའི་ནང་ན་བཞུགས་པས་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །

Alternatively, because he is endowed with sovereignty and so forth, he is called 'Glorious'. As it is said: 'Complete endowment with sovereignty, physical beauty, glory, and renown, wisdom, and diligent exertion—these six are called "glory".' 'Śrāvastī' means that because it is the hermitage of the sage Śrāvasta, it is the city of Śrāvastī; because the particular region characterized by it is jointly connected with it, it is called Śrāvastī. The place is mentioned in order to declare that the place has become a stūpa; thus, even in this very text it is stated, 'that place becomes a stūpa.' Alternatively, the authentic compiler states all these in order to establish that his words are worthy of being grasped. Thus, if they are spoken along with the location, along with the circumstances, and along with the master, for the purpose of inspiring trust in the world, others will grasp the words; otherwise, the words would not be worthy of being grasped. Since the region of Śrāvastī is very vast and it would not be known exactly where he was dwelling, 'the grove of Prince Jeta' is mentioned; because it is the grove of that one called Prince Jeta, it is the grove of Prince Jeta. Since it is possible that even that might not be renowned to anyone at all, 'in Anāthapiṇḍada's park' is mentioned. The householder 'Anāthapiṇḍada' was renowned as such because out of compassion for the protectorless he gave them alms; since he bought the park from Prince Jeta by laying down precious jewels side by side for the sake of the Blessed One, and since Prince Jeta also had some pavilions and so forth adorned for the Blessed One from that, it is renowned as the grove of those two. If only any one of these were mentioned, the desire to express the specific place would not be understood, so all three phrases are mentioned. Alternatively, this mention of 'Śrāvastī' indicates the perfection of benefiting others, because he dwells among the multitudes.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: 'Great generation of the mind' is because they generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Great inclination' is because they themselves are inclined toward the profound and great dharma. 'Great intention' is because they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. 'Great accumulation' is because their accumulations of merit and wisdom are immeasurable. 'Great time' is because they attain awakening over three countless great eons. 'Great perfect accomplishment' is because they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Dwelling' means dwelling by means of the four postures, or rather, dwelling by means of the unsurpassed abodes of Brahmā, the gods, and the noble ones. The particle 'te' indicates that the dwelling was already established. In this regard, having understood that the saṅgha of monks stays right at the feet of the Tathāgata at all times because they have done what was to be done and are objects of compassion, they are mentioned first in order to indicate their constancy. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, not having fully completed the accomplishment of the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, they possess great compassion for those who have not done what is to be done, and roam throughout the worldly realms in order to accomplish the welfare of transmigrators, so they do not stay at the feet of the Blessed One at all times.

The meaning of the words and so forth should also be stated; those will be stated. In this regard, although the term 'Thus' appears in many meanings such as acceptance and so forth, here, by the power of the context and so forth, it should be understood as a presentation. This presents the entirety of the meaning of the sūtra occurring below. 'By me' excludes others and indicates that the meaning was heard directly. The implication is: 'I heard it myself; it did not come solely through transmission.' 'Heard' negates realization, because other than a buddha, there is no one else who realizes such dharmas by themselves. This clears away lack of trust. 'At one time' means at a single time; it indicates that such rare and supreme dharmas are difficult to hear at all times. Alternatively, it shows that he himself has heard much. It indicates: 'At one time I heard this, but at other times I heard other things as well.' Alternatively, connecting it with what follows as 'at one time the Blessed One was dwelling,' it establishes that for the purpose of benefiting those immeasurable trainees, he was dwelling elsewhere at other times. 'Blessed One' means that because he possesses the conquering of the four māras, which have the characteristics of the afflictions, the aggregates, the lord of death, and the child of the gods, he is called 'Blessed One' by way of etymology.

ཡང་ན་དབང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པས་ལེགས་ལྡན་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཇི་སྐད་དུ། དབང་དང་རབ་ཏུ་ལྡན་པ་དང་། །གཟུགས་དང་དཔལ་དང་གྲགས་པ་དང་། །ཡེ་ཤེས་དང་ནི་ནན་ཏན་དང་། །དྲུག་པོ་དེ་ལ་ལེགས་ཞེས་བྱ། །ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དྲང་སྲོང་མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་བསྟི་གནས་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་མཉན་ཡོད་དེ། དེས་མཚོན་པའི་ཡུལ་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་ཀྱང་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྲེལ་པའི་ཕྱིར་མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །ཡུལ་སྨོས་པ་དེ་ཡང་ཡུལ་དེ་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པར་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་འདི་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཡང་ན་ཡང་དག་པར་སྡུད་པར་བྱེད་པས་བདག་གི་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འོས་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཐམས་ཅད་སྨོས་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཡིད་ཆེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ནི་ས་ཕྱོགས་དང་བཅས་པ་རྣམ་པ་དང་བཅས། དབང་ཕྱུག་དང་བཅས་པས་སྨྲས་ན། གཞན་དག་གིས་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འགྱུར་གྱི། གཞན་དུ་ན་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འོས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཡུལ་མཉན་ཡོད་ཧ་ཅང་རྒྱ་ཆེས་ཏེ་གང་ན་བཞུགས་གཏོལ་མེད་པས་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེ་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དེའི་ཚལ་ཡིན་པས་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཡང་ཇི་སྟེ་ན་སུ་ལ་ཡང་མ་གྲགས་ཀྱང་སྲིད་པས་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་གྱི་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཁྱིམ་བདག་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་ཞེས་པ་མགོན་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་སྟེ་ཟས་སྦྱིན་པས་དེ་ལྟར་གྲགས་པ་དེས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་བཀྲམ་པ་གཤིབས་པས་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ལས་ཀུན་དགའི་ར་བ་ཉོས་པ་དང་། རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལས་ཅུང་ཞིག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་ཁང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བརྒྱན་དུ་བཅུག་པས་དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཚལ་དེ་གྲགས་སོ། །གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་ཞིག་སྨོས་ན་ནི་ཡུལ་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་བརྗོད་པར་འདོད་པ་རྟོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བས་ཚིག་གསུམ་ཆར་སྨོས་སོ། །ཡང་ན་མཉན་ཡོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་མང་པོའི་ནང་ན་བཞུགས་པས་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །

Alternatively, because he is endowed with sovereignty and so forth, he is called 'Glorious'. As it is said: 'Complete endowment with sovereignty, physical beauty, glory, and renown, wisdom, and diligent exertion—these six are called "glory".' 'Śrāvastī' means that because it is the hermitage of the sage Śrāvasta, it is the city of Śrāvastī; because the particular region characterized by it is jointly connected with it, it is called Śrāvastī. The place is mentioned in order to declare that the place has become a stūpa; thus, even in this very text it is stated, 'that place becomes a stūpa.' Alternatively, the authentic compiler states all these in order to establish that his words are worthy of being grasped. Thus, if they are spoken along with the location, along with the circumstances, and along with the master, for the purpose of inspiring trust in the world, others will grasp the words; otherwise, the words would not be worthy of being grasped. Since the region of Śrāvastī is very vast and it would not be known exactly where he was dwelling, 'the grove of Prince Jeta' is mentioned; because it is the grove of that one called Prince Jeta, it is the grove of Prince Jeta. Since it is possible that even that might not be renowned to anyone at all, 'in Anāthapiṇḍada's park' is mentioned. The householder 'Anāthapiṇḍada' was renowned as such because out of compassion for the protectorless he gave them alms; since he bought the park from Prince Jeta by laying down precious jewels side by side for the sake of the Blessed One, and since Prince Jeta also had some pavilions and so forth adorned for the Blessed One from that, it is renowned as the grove of those two. If only any one of these were mentioned, the desire to express the specific place would not be understood, so all three phrases are mentioned. Alternatively, this mention of 'Śrāvastī' indicates the perfection of benefiting others, because he dwells among the multitudes.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: Therefore, bodhisattvas are not mentioned in the sūtras of the śrāvakas, because those are not for their sake, and because they are not constant. 'Then' means after that. 'Time' means certainty; this determines the time for food. Determining the time means determining the time as 'at this time one should certainly eat'. Furthermore, not knowing what that is, it is to be explained by mentioning 'morning'; this is compounded as 'it is both the morning and the time of the occasion'. The characteristic of the morning is that it becomes the time for those observing fasting vows and those who have gone forth to obtain food; in order to understand that it was conclusively determined by the Blessed One, 'the time of the occasion' is mentioned. Otherwise, mentioning only 'morning' would not be understood as conclusively determined; because it is possible that the Blessed One might act casually, therefore all three words are mentioned. 'Under-robe' refers to putting on robes in a way conforming to householders; and that is done in order to establish reverence for the trainings among the śrāvakas. Otherwise, how could one who is untamed himself tame others? Regarding 'putting on the dharma robes', putting on the dharma robes should be seen as having the characteristic of donning them; otherwise it is not the context. 'Great city' is a specific region, meaning the specification of Śrāvastī.

This mention of 'the grove of Prince Jeta, Anāthapiṇḍada's park' indicates the perfection of benefiting oneself, because he dwells in solitude. Thinking, 'Who possesses mastery in this?', 'a great saṅgha of monks' is mentioned; because they are free from afflictions, they are 'monks'. Because they cannot be divided by opponents such as māras and so forth, those multitudes are called a 'saṅgha'. Those of the 'great saṅgha of monks' have two greatnesses: multitude and power; this indicates greatness in power. Thinking, 'What is the greatness of multitude?', 'one thousand two hundred and fifty' and so forth is mentioned, because at that time there were that many. That the bodhisattvas were exceedingly more numerous than the saṅgha of monks is because the sūtra is taught for their sake. Because they possess intentions with great courage for awakening, they are 'bodhisattvas'. Since śrāvakas also have courage for awakening, in order to exclude them, 'great beings' is mentioned. Because they are endowed with seven kinds of great characteristics—dharma, generation of the mind, inclination, intention, accumulation, time, and perfect accomplishment—they are 'great beings'. In this regard, 'great dharma' is because the teaching of dharma to bodhisattvas, such as the prajñāpāramitā in one hundred thousand lines and so forth, is extensive.

སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མོས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཟབ་ཅིང་ཆེ་བ་ལ་མོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བསམ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཕན་པ་དང་བདེ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བསམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དུས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་གྲངས་མེད་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བཞུགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་བཞི་པོ་དག་གིས་སམ། ཡང་ན་ཚངས་པ་དང་ལྷའི་དང་། འཕགས་པའི་བཞུགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་དག་གིས་བཞུགས་པའོ། །ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞུགས་ཟིན་པར་བསྟན་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ནི་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་དང་། སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ཉིད་ན་འདུག་པར་རིག་ནས་རྟག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གོང་དུ་སྨོས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་བྱ་བ་མ་བྱས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་ཆེ་བས་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་སུ་རྒྱུ་བས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ན་མི་འདུག་པས་འོག་ཏུ་སྨོས་སོ། །

'Great generation of the mind' is because they generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Great inclination' is because they themselves are inclined toward the profound and great dharma. 'Great intention' is because they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. 'Great accumulation' is because their accumulations of merit and wisdom are immeasurable. 'Great time' is because they attain awakening over three countless great eons. 'Great perfect accomplishment' is because they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Dwelling' means dwelling by means of the four postures, or rather, dwelling by means of the unsurpassed abodes of Brahmā, the gods, and the noble ones. The particle 'te' indicates that the dwelling was already established. In this regard, having understood that the saṅgha of monks stays right at the feet of the Tathāgata at all times because they have done what was to be done and are objects of compassion, they are mentioned first in order to indicate their constancy. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, not having fully completed the accomplishment of the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, they possess great compassion for those who have not done what is to be done, and roam throughout the worldly realms in order to accomplish the welfare of transmigrators, so they do not stay at the feet of the Blessed One at all times.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One enter for alms?': It is to guide the śrāvakas to having few desires, to benefit housewives, the poor, the sick, the elderly, and so forth, to cause the blind and so forth to obtain eyes and so forth, and to generate faith in the Blessed One in others by continually showing various marvelous things; thus one should understand that the purposes are immeasurable. 'Having done the activity of food' means that it is spoken thus regarding one who has done and accomplished the activity of food, such as food and so forth. If even those born from small roots of virtue, such as Brahmā and so forth, do not perform the activity of food because they are free from the attachment of eating food by mouthfuls, would the Blessed One, born from inconceivable roots of virtue, do so? Likewise, it is also said in the noble Dharmasaṃgīti: 'The Tathāgata does not possess hunger and thirst, does not defecate and urinate; His body is not frail.' That is true, but nevertheless, if that body of the Blessed One were not ultimate, then there would be occasion for all criticisms; but when this is the emanation body of the Blessed One, displaying such kinds of behavior and engaging in accordance with the intentions of the sentient beings to be tamed, at that time how could there be occasion for criticism? In order to encourage them by saying, 'Even a human being who exerts effort attains such an unsurpassed state,' He displays a human body to those to be tamed, and thus displays the manner of taking a meal.

This mention of 'the grove of Prince Jeta, Anāthapiṇḍada's park' indicates the perfection of benefiting oneself, because he dwells in solitude. Thinking, 'Who possesses mastery in this?', 'a great saṅgha of monks' is mentioned; because they are free from afflictions, they are 'monks'. Because they cannot be divided by opponents such as māras and so forth, those multitudes are called a 'saṅgha'. Those of the 'great saṅgha of monks' have two greatnesses: multitude and power; this indicates greatness in power. Thinking, 'What is the greatness of multitude?', 'one thousand two hundred and fifty' and so forth is mentioned, because at that time there were that many. That the bodhisattvas were exceedingly more numerous than the saṅgha of monks is because the sūtra is taught for their sake. Because they possess intentions with great courage for awakening, they are 'bodhisattvas'. Since śrāvakas also have courage for awakening, in order to exclude them, 'great beings' is mentioned. Because they are endowed with seven kinds of great characteristics—dharma, generation of the mind, inclination, intention, accumulation, time, and perfect accomplishment—they are 'great beings'. In this regard, 'great dharma' is because the teaching of dharma to bodhisattvas, such as the prajñāpāramitā in one hundred thousand lines and so forth, is extensive.

སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མོས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཟབ་ཅིང་ཆེ་བ་ལ་མོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བསམ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཕན་པ་དང་བདེ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བསམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དུས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་གྲངས་མེད་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བཞུགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་བཞི་པོ་དག་གིས་སམ། ཡང་ན་ཚངས་པ་དང་ལྷའི་དང་། འཕགས་པའི་བཞུགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་དག་གིས་བཞུགས་པའོ། །ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞུགས་ཟིན་པར་བསྟན་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ནི་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་དང་། སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ཉིད་ན་འདུག་པར་རིག་ནས་རྟག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གོང་དུ་སྨོས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་བྱ་བ་མ་བྱས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་ཆེ་བས་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་སུ་རྒྱུ་བས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ན་མི་འདུག་པས་འོག་ཏུ་སྨོས་སོ། །

'Great generation of the mind' is because they generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Great inclination' is because they themselves are inclined toward the profound and great dharma. 'Great intention' is because they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. 'Great accumulation' is because their accumulations of merit and wisdom are immeasurable. 'Great time' is because they attain awakening over three countless great eons. 'Great perfect accomplishment' is because they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Dwelling' means dwelling by means of the four postures, or rather, dwelling by means of the unsurpassed abodes of Brahmā, the gods, and the noble ones. The particle 'te' indicates that the dwelling was already established. In this regard, having understood that the saṅgha of monks stays right at the feet of the Tathāgata at all times because they have done what was to be done and are objects of compassion, they are mentioned first in order to indicate their constancy. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, not having fully completed the accomplishment of the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, they possess great compassion for those who have not done what is to be done, and roam throughout the worldly realms in order to accomplish the welfare of transmigrators, so they do not stay at the feet of the Blessed One at all times.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: By showing the complete purification of alms to whatever donors and benefactors, it generates joy in them; and those who have the fortune but, due to some karmic obscuration, have been born among the hungry ghosts and so forth, if touched by the nectar-like fingernails of the Blessed One's hand, it becomes the supreme taste of the gods, and when they eat the inexhaustible food carried by majestic yakṣas and so forth, their minds become satisfied with supreme happiness, and since they also obtain supreme samādhi, the activity of food of the Blessed One is immeasurable. If one asks, 'With what kind of aspect did He perform the activity of food?', therefore 'at the end' and so forth is mentioned; having received everything, whatever meal is eaten at the end is 'eating the alms meal at the end', and this is preceded by properly taking it up in order to guide the śrāvakas toward the qualities of purification. 'Ate' is a word meaning that He had already eaten. Alternatively, regarding 'at the end', whatever is received a second time is called 'subsequent food'; that subsequent food is compounded in words as 'it is both the food at the end and alms'. Alternatively, whatever alms it is that consists of eating that afternoon food is spoken of in that way. Therefore, because of possessing the qualities of purification and abandoning food at the wrong time, 'ate' is a word meaning that He is free from those two. 'Having put away' means putting away.

སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མོས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཟབ་ཅིང་ཆེ་བ་ལ་མོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བསམ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཕན་པ་དང་བདེ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བསམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དུས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་གྲངས་མེད་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བཞུགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་བཞི་པོ་དག་གིས་སམ། ཡང་ན་ཚངས་པ་དང་ལྷའི་དང་། འཕགས་པའི་བཞུགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་དག་གིས་བཞུགས་པའོ། །ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞུགས་ཟིན་པར་བསྟན་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ནི་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་དང་། སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ཉིད་ན་འདུག་པར་རིག་ནས་རྟག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གོང་དུ་སྨོས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་བྱ་བ་མ་བྱས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་ཆེ་བས་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་སུ་རྒྱུ་བས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ན་མི་འདུག་པས་འོག་ཏུ་སྨོས་སོ། །
[3-4] translation already produced for this document:
'Great generation of the mind' is because they generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Great inclination' is because they themselves are inclined toward the profound and great dharma. 'Great intention' is because they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. 'Great accumulation' is because their accumulations of merit and wisdom are immeasurable. 'Great time' is because they attain awakening over three countless great eons. 'Great perfect accomplishment' is because they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Dwelling' means dwelling by means of the four postures, or rather, dwelling by means of the unsurpassed abodes of Brahmā, the gods, and the noble ones. The particle 'te' indicates that the dwelling was already established. In this regard, having understood that the saṅgha of monks stays right at the feet of the Tathāgata at all times because they have done what was to be done and are objects of compassion, they are mentioned first in order to indicate their constancy. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, not having fully completed the accomplishment of the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, they possess great compassion for those who have not done what is to be done, and roam throughout the worldly realms in order to accomplish the welfare of transmigrators, so they do not stay at the feet of the Blessed One at all times.

དེ་བས་ན་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་མདོ་སྡེ་ལས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མི་སྨོས་ཏེ།དེ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་ཆེད་དུ་མ་ཡིན་པ་དང་། མི་རྟག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེའི་འོག་ཏུའོ། །ཚེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ངེས་པ་སྟེ། འདིས་ནི་ཟས་ཀྱི་དུས་ངེས་པའོ། །དུས་ངེས་པ་ནི་དུས་འདི་ངེས་པར་བཟའ་བར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་དུས་ངེས་པའོ། །དེ་ཡང་གང་ཡིན་པ་མི་ཤེས་ནས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་སྔ་དྲོ་ཞེས་སྨོས་པས་འཆད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་སྔ་དྲོ་ཡང་ཡིན་ལ་དུས་ཀྱི་ཚེ་ཡང་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་བསྡུའོ། །སྔ་དྲོའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ནི་བསྙེན་གནས་གནས་པ་དང་། རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཟས་ཀྱི་དུས་ཕྱིར་འཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གཅིག་ཏུ་འཆད་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུས་ཀྱི་ཚེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །གཞན་དུ་ན་སྔ་དྲོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་པ་ནི་དེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་ཆད་པར་མི་རྟོགས་ཏེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་གྱི་ན་མཛད་ཀྱང་སྲིད་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཚིག་གསུམ་ཆར་སྨོས་སོ། །ཤམ་ཐབས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁྱིམ་དུ་འདུག་པ་དང་མཐུན་པའི་གོས་མནབས་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་བསླབ་པ་དག་ལ་གུས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་མཛད་དོ། །གཞན་དུ་ན་ནི་བདག་མ་དུལ་བས་གཞན་འདུལ་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། ཆོས་གོས་མནབས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་ཆོས་གོས་མནབས་པ་ནི་བགོ་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། གཞན་ནི་སྐབས་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡུལ་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་སྟེ། མཉན་ཡོད་རྣམ་པར་བཅད་པའི་དོན་ཏོ། །

Therefore, bodhisattvas are not mentioned in the sūtras of the śrāvakas, because those are not for their sake, and because they are not constant. 'Then' means after that. 'Time' means certainty; this determines the time for food. Determining the time means determining the time as 'at this time one should certainly eat'. Furthermore, not knowing what that is, it is to be explained by mentioning 'morning'; this is compounded as 'it is both the morning and the time of the occasion'. The characteristic of the morning is that it becomes the time for those observing fasting vows and those who have gone forth to obtain food; in order to understand that it was conclusively determined by the Blessed One, 'the time of the occasion' is mentioned. Otherwise, mentioning only 'morning' would not be understood as conclusively determined; because it is possible that the Blessed One might act casually, therefore all three words are mentioned. 'Under-robe' refers to putting on robes in a way conforming to householders; and that is done in order to establish reverence for the trainings among the śrāvakas. Otherwise, how could one who is untamed himself tame others? Regarding 'putting on the dharma robes', putting on the dharma robes should be seen as having the characteristic of donning them; otherwise it is not the context. 'Great city' is a specific region, meaning the specification of Śrāvastī.

If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One enter for alms?': It is to guide the śrāvakas to having few desires, to benefit housewives, the poor, the sick, the elderly, and so forth, to cause the blind and so forth to obtain eyes and so forth, and to generate faith in the Blessed One in others by continually showing various marvelous things; thus one should understand that the purposes are immeasurable. 'Having done the activity of food' means that it is spoken thus regarding one who has done and accomplished the activity of food, such as food and so forth. If even those born from small roots of virtue, such as Brahmā and so forth, do not perform the activity of food because they are free from the attachment of eating food by mouthfuls, would the Blessed One, born from inconceivable roots of virtue, do so? Likewise, it is also said in the noble Dharmasaṃgīti: 'The Tathāgata does not possess hunger and thirst, does not defecate and urinate; His body is not frail.' That is true, but nevertheless, if that body of the Blessed One were not ultimate, then there would be occasion for all criticisms; but when this is the emanation body of the Blessed One, displaying such kinds of behavior and engaging in accordance with the intentions of the sentient beings to be tamed, at that time how could there be occasion for criticism? In order to encourage them by saying, 'Even a human being who exerts effort attains such an unsurpassed state,' He displays a human body to those to be tamed, and thus displays the manner of taking a meal.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: Furthermore, although those who exert themselves in taking orders, such as Śakra and so forth, constantly remain in the presence of the Blessed One, the Blessed One Himself put away the alms bowl and dharma robes in order to show that those who have gone forth do it themselves. It is also in order to eliminate the mental displeasure of those with small fortune who lack servants. Although the appearance of impurity is constantly abandoned far away and He places His feet upon lotuses, one should regard washing His feet as being in accordance with the intention of sentient beings who are inclined toward the Action Tantras and so forth, or in order to show reverence for the trainings such as 'one with filthy feet should not trample on bedding and seats'. 'On the arranged seat' refers to it being arranged by gods and so forth. 'Straightening the body' is a word meaning that He acts without bending down too much or leaning back too much. If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One dwell in the posture of abandonment at the time of teaching the dharma?': It is in order to guide the world into generating exertion in abandonment, saying, 'Only those of abandonment are capable of teaching, knowing, and hearing this dharma, whereas others are not.' 'Establishing mindfulness in front' is a word meaning that He actualized the mindfulness of the prayer He had made previously when He was a bodhisattva, 'When I attain the unsurpassed state, I shall act in such a way that the lineage of the Buddhas will not be interrupted.' Although the Buddha Blessed Ones constantly rest in equipoise and thus always abide in mindfulness everywhere, mindfulness at the wrong time achieves nothing, whereas mindfulness of the prayer at the right time is accompanied by its result. Since mindfulness at the right time also shows that the Blessed One is constantly resting in equipoise, there is no contradiction.

'Great generation of the mind' is because they generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Great inclination' is because they themselves are inclined toward the profound and great dharma. 'Great intention' is because they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. 'Great accumulation' is because their accumulations of merit and wisdom are immeasurable. 'Great time' is because they attain awakening over three countless great eons. 'Great perfect accomplishment' is because they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. 'Dwelling' means dwelling by means of the four postures, or rather, dwelling by means of the unsurpassed abodes of Brahmā, the gods, and the noble ones. The particle 'te' indicates that the dwelling was already established. In this regard, having understood that the saṅgha of monks stays right at the feet of the Tathāgata at all times because they have done what was to be done and are objects of compassion, they are mentioned first in order to indicate their constancy. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, not having fully completed the accomplishment of the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, they possess great compassion for those who have not done what is to be done, and roam throughout the worldly realms in order to accomplish the welfare of transmigrators, so they do not stay at the feet of the Blessed One at all times.

Therefore, bodhisattvas are not mentioned in the sūtras of the śrāvakas, because those are not for their sake, and because they are not constant. 'Then' means after that. 'Time' means certainty; this determines the time for food. Determining the time means determining the time as 'at this time one should certainly eat'. Furthermore, not knowing what that is, it is to be explained by mentioning 'morning'; this is compounded as 'it is both the morning and the time of the occasion'. The characteristic of the morning is that it becomes the time for those observing fasting vows and those who have gone forth to obtain food; in order to understand that it was conclusively determined by the Blessed One, 'the time of the occasion' is mentioned. Otherwise, mentioning only 'morning' would not be understood as conclusively determined; because it is possible that the Blessed One might act casually, therefore all three words are mentioned. 'Under-robe' refers to putting on robes in a way conforming to householders; and that is done in order to establish reverence for the trainings among the śrāvakas. Otherwise, how could one who is untamed himself tame others? Regarding 'putting on the dharma robes', putting on the dharma robes should be seen as having the characteristic of donning them; otherwise it is not the context. 'Great city' is a specific region, meaning the specification of Śrāvastī.

If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One enter for alms?': It is to guide the śrāvakas to having few desires, to benefit housewives, the poor, the sick, the elderly, and so forth, to cause the blind and so forth to obtain eyes and so forth, and to generate faith in the Blessed One in others by continually showing various marvelous things; thus one should understand that the purposes are immeasurable. 'Having done the activity of food' means that it is spoken thus regarding one who has done and accomplished the activity of food, such as food and so forth. If even those born from small roots of virtue, such as Brahmā and so forth, do not perform the activity of food because they are free from the attachment of eating food by mouthfuls, would the Blessed One, born from inconceivable roots of virtue, do so? Likewise, it is also said in the noble Dharmasaṃgīti: 'The Tathāgata does not possess hunger and thirst, does not defecate and urinate; His body is not frail.' That is true, but nevertheless, if that body of the Blessed One were not ultimate, then there would be occasion for all criticisms; but when this is the emanation body of the Blessed One, displaying such kinds of behavior and engaging in accordance with the intentions of the sentient beings to be tamed, at that time how could there be occasion for criticism? In order to encourage them by saying, 'Even a human being who exerts effort attains such an unsurpassed state,' He displays a human body to those to be tamed, and thus displays the manner of taking a meal.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: If one asks, 'Why is "Then many monks" mentioned?': It is in order to show that, of however many in number the saṅgha of monks with whom the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, not all of them assembled there at the time of teaching the dharma, but rather that 'many'—three or more—assembled there. Furthermore, it was spoken by the compiler in order to generate confidence in others. 'Assembled' merely means drawing near. 'Sat down' refers to sitting on a seat. Because the world mostly establishes the specific preceded by establishing the general, both are mentioned in accordance with worldly convention. Otherwise, by just 'sat down' alone, both would be mentioned. The meaning of the words of the prologue and so forth has been explained.

སྦྱིན་པ་པོ་དང་། སྦྱིན་བདག་གང་ལ་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྦྱོང་བ་བསྟན་པས་དེ་དག་དགའ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། གང་དག་སྐལ་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་འགའ་ཞིག་གིས་ཡི་དགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ནང་དུ་སྐྱེས་པ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཕྱག་གི་སེན་མོ་བདུད་རྩི་ཅན་གྱིས་རེག་ན་ལྷའི་རོ་བྲོ་བ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་ཟད་མི་ཤེས་པ་གནོད་སྦྱིན་གཟི་སྟོབས་ཅན་ལ་སོགས་པས་ཁྱེར་བ་ཟོས་ན། དེ་དག་བདེ་བ་མཆོག་གིས་སེམས་ཚིམ་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་མཆོག་ཀྱང་འཐོབ་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཟས་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་ནི་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་དོ། །རྣམ་པ་ཅི་འདྲ་བས་ཟས་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་བྱས་ཤེ་ན། དེའི་ཕྱིར་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་བླངས་ནས་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཞལ་ཟས་གང་གསོལ་བ་དེ་ནི་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཀྱི་ཞལ་ཟས་མཇུག་ཏུ་གསོལ་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པར་ལེན་པ་སྔོན་དུ་བཏང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གསོལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གསོལ་ཟིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །ཡང་ན་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལན་གཉིས་པ་ལ་བླངས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལ་ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་དེ་ནི་ཟས་མཇུག་ཀྱང་ཡིན་ལ་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཀྱང་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་ཚིག་རྣམ་པར་སྦྱར་རོ། །ཡང་ན་ཕྱི་དྲོའི་ཟས་དེ་ཟ་བ་གང་ཡིན་པའི་བསོད་སྙོམས་དེ་ལ་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཅན་ཡིན་པ་དང་། དུས་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཟས་སྤངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསོལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་གཉིས་དང་བྲལ་ལོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཞག་ནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞག་སྟེའོ། །

By showing the complete purification of alms to whatever donors and benefactors, it generates joy in them; and those who have the fortune but, due to some karmic obscuration, have been born among the hungry ghosts and so forth, if touched by the nectar-like fingernails of the Blessed One's hand, it becomes the supreme taste of the gods, and when they eat the inexhaustible food carried by majestic yakṣas and so forth, their minds become satisfied with supreme happiness, and since they also obtain supreme samādhi, the activity of food of the Blessed One is immeasurable. If one asks, 'With what kind of aspect did He perform the activity of food?', therefore 'at the end' and so forth is mentioned; having received everything, whatever meal is eaten at the end is 'eating the alms meal at the end', and this is preceded by properly taking it up in order to guide the śrāvakas toward the qualities of purification. 'Ate' is a word meaning that He had already eaten. Alternatively, regarding 'at the end', whatever is received a second time is called 'subsequent food'; that subsequent food is compounded in words as 'it is both the food at the end and alms'. Alternatively, whatever alms it is that consists of eating that afternoon food is spoken of in that way. Therefore, because of possessing the qualities of purification and abandoning food at the wrong time, 'ate' is a word meaning that He is free from those two. 'Having put away' means putting away.

དེ་ཡང་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ན་བཀའ་ནོད་པ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་དག་ཀྱང་རྟག་ཏུ་གནས་མོད་ཀྱི་རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་བ་ནི་བདག་ཉིད་བྱེད་པའོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ལྷུང་བཟེད་དང་ཆོས་གོས་བཞག་པ་མཛད་དོ། །སྐལ་བ་ཆུང་ངུ་གཡོག་མི་འབྱོར་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བ་སྤོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་ངོ་། །མི་གཙང་བར་སྣང་བ་རྟག་ཏུ་རིང་དུ་སྤངས་པ་དང་། ཞབས་པདྨ་ལ་འཇོག་མོད་ཀྱི། བྱ་བའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་མོས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་བསམ་པ་དང་མཐུན་པ་འམ། རྐང་པ་རུལ་ཅན་གྱིས་མལ་ཆ་དང་སྟན་ལ་མི་རྫིའོ་ཞེས་བསླབ་པ་དག་ལ་གུས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞབས་འཁྲུ་བར་བལྟའོ། །གདན་བཤམས་པ་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྷ་ལ་སོགས་པས་བཤམས་པའོ། །སྐུ་དྲང་པོར་བསྲང་སྟེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཧ་ཅང་ཡང་མི་དགུ། ཧ་ཅང་ཡང་མི་དགྱེ་བར་མཛད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །ཆོས་སྟོན་པའི་དུས་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སྤོང་བའི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གྱིས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བཞུགས་ཤེ་ན། སྤོང་བ་དག་ཁོ་ནས་ཆོས་འདི་བསྟན་པ་དང་། ཤེས་པ་དང་ཉན་པར་ནུས་ཀྱི་གཞན་དག་གིས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྤོང་བ་ལ་འཇིག་རྟེན་ནན་ཏན་བསྐྱེད་དུ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དྲན་པ་སྔོན་དུ་གཞག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྔོན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་གྱུར་པའི་ཚེ། བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་ཚེ་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་ནས་ཇི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་མི་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་བདག་གིས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྨོན་ལམ་བཏབ་པའི་སྨོན་ལམ་དེ་དྲན་པ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དག་ནི་རྟག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་དྲན་པ་ལ་གནས་མོད་ཀྱི། དུས་མ་ཡིན་པར་དྲན་པ་དེས་ནི་ཅིར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། དུས་སུ་སྨོན་ལམ་དྲན་པ་ནི་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དུས་སུ་དྲན་པས་ཀྱང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྟག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པ་ཉིད་དུ་སྟོན་པས་འགལ་བ་མེད་དོ། །

Furthermore, although those who exert themselves in taking orders, such as Śakra and so forth, constantly remain in the presence of the Blessed One, the Blessed One Himself put away the alms bowl and dharma robes in order to show that those who have gone forth do it themselves. It is also in order to eliminate the mental displeasure of those with small fortune who lack servants. Although the appearance of impurity is constantly abandoned far away and He places His feet upon lotuses, one should regard washing His feet as being in accordance with the intention of sentient beings who are inclined toward the Action Tantras and so forth, or in order to show reverence for the trainings such as 'one with filthy feet should not trample on bedding and seats'. 'On the arranged seat' refers to it being arranged by gods and so forth. 'Straightening the body' is a word meaning that He acts without bending down too much or leaning back too much. If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One dwell in the posture of abandonment at the time of teaching the dharma?': It is in order to guide the world into generating exertion in abandonment, saying, 'Only those of abandonment are capable of teaching, knowing, and hearing this dharma, whereas others are not.' 'Establishing mindfulness in front' is a word meaning that He actualized the mindfulness of the prayer He had made previously when He was a bodhisattva, 'When I attain the unsurpassed state, I shall act in such a way that the lineage of the Buddhas will not be interrupted.' Although the Buddha Blessed Ones constantly rest in equipoise and thus always abide in mindfulness everywhere, mindfulness at the wrong time achieves nothing, whereas mindfulness of the prayer at the right time is accompanied by its result. Since mindfulness at the right time also shows that the Blessed One is constantly resting in equipoise, there is no contradiction.

source: ད་ནི་གླེང་བསླང་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་བྱ་བ་བརྗོད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་བར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ལན་གཉིས་སུ་སྨོས་སོ། །བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བོད་པའོ། །བདག་མེད་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ནས་ཡང་དག་པར་གཤེགས་སོ། །ལེགས་པར་གཤེགས་པས་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་སྟེ། ལེགས་པར་བསྟོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཡང་ན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་བག་ཆགས་དང་བཅས་པ་མ་ལུས་པར་སྤངས་ཏེ། གཤེགས་པས་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་སྟེ། བུམ་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་གང་བ་ བཞིན་ནོ། །ཡང་ན་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་གཤེགས་པས་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་སྟེ། རིམས་ནད་ཤིན་ཏུ་བྱང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཇི་སྙེད་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཕན་གདགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་བྱེ་བྲག་སྟེ། ཕན་གདགས་པ་གང་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱིས་ཕན་གདགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །རྒྱལ་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དག་ཀྱང་འབངས་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྟོན་པ་དག་ལ་ཅི་ནུས་ཀྱིས་རྗེས་སུ་འཛིན་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་འདིར་ངོ་མཚར་བ་ཅི་ཆེ་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པ་ལ་ངོ་མཚར་གྱི་རྒྱུར། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །དངོས་པོའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་གསུངས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའོ། །ཡང་ན་སྔ་མ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་བདག་མེད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ནས་གཤེགས་ཏེ། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་སྤངས་པ་རྙེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར། འདིར་ཡང་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའོ། །
translation: Now, the raising of the topic and making the lineage of the Buddhas uninterrupted will be explained. In order to show that it is extremely wonderful, it is mentioned twice. 'Sugata' is a vocative. He has properly gone via the path of the two kinds of selflessness. Because He has gone well, He is Sugata, just like saying 'well-praised'. Alternatively, having abandoned the afflictive and cognitive obscurations along with their latencies without exception, because He has gone, He is Sugata, just like a completely full vase. Alternatively, because He has gone without returning, He is Sugata, just like a completely cured infectious disease. 'With whatever' is a specific detail of the benefit to be given; it is a word meaning that He has benefited with however many benefits there are. If one suspects, thinking, 'If even kings and so forth care for subjects and so forth who rely on them as much as they are able, what is so wonderful about that here concerning the Blessed One?', as the cause of wonder, 'by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha' is mentioned. Because He has spoken of the reality of entities exactly as it is, He is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, just as previous ones have gone via the path of the two kinds of selflessness and attained the abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, so here too He has gone, therefore He is the Tathāgata.

By showing the complete purification of alms to whatever donors and benefactors, it generates joy in them; and those who have the fortune but, due to some karmic obscuration, have been born among the hungry ghosts and so forth, if touched by the nectar-like fingernails of the Blessed One's hand, it becomes the supreme taste of the gods, and when they eat the inexhaustible food carried by majestic yakṣas and so forth, their minds become satisfied with supreme happiness, and since they also obtain supreme samādhi, the activity of food of the Blessed One is immeasurable. If one asks, 'With what kind of aspect did He perform the activity of food?', therefore 'at the end' and so forth is mentioned; having received everything, whatever meal is eaten at the end is 'eating the alms meal at the end', and this is preceded by properly taking it up in order to guide the śrāvakas toward the qualities of purification. 'Ate' is a word meaning that He had already eaten. Alternatively, regarding 'at the end', whatever is received a second time is called 'subsequent food'; that subsequent food is compounded in words as 'it is both the food at the end and alms'. Alternatively, whatever alms it is that consists of eating that afternoon food is spoken of in that way. Therefore, because of possessing the qualities of purification and abandoning food at the wrong time, 'ate' is a word meaning that He is free from those two. 'Having put away' means putting away.

Furthermore, although those who exert themselves in taking orders, such as Śakra and so forth, constantly remain in the presence of the Blessed One, the Blessed One Himself put away the alms bowl and dharma robes in order to show that those who have gone forth do it themselves. It is also in order to eliminate the mental displeasure of those with small fortune who lack servants. Although the appearance of impurity is constantly abandoned far away and He places His feet upon lotuses, one should regard washing His feet as being in accordance with the intention of sentient beings who are inclined toward the Action Tantras and so forth, or in order to show reverence for the trainings such as 'one with filthy feet should not trample on bedding and seats'. 'On the arranged seat' refers to it being arranged by gods and so forth. 'Straightening the body' is a word meaning that He acts without bending down too much or leaning back too much. If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One dwell in the posture of abandonment at the time of teaching the dharma?': It is in order to guide the world into generating exertion in abandonment, saying, 'Only those of abandonment are capable of teaching, knowing, and hearing this dharma, whereas others are not.' 'Establishing mindfulness in front' is a word meaning that He actualized the mindfulness of the prayer He had made previously when He was a bodhisattva, 'When I attain the unsurpassed state, I shall act in such a way that the lineage of the Buddhas will not be interrupted.' Although the Buddha Blessed Ones constantly rest in equipoise and thus always abide in mindfulness everywhere, mindfulness at the wrong time achieves nothing, whereas mindfulness of the prayer at the right time is accompanied by its result. Since mindfulness at the right time also shows that the Blessed One is constantly resting in equipoise, there is no contradiction.

If one asks, 'Why is "Then many monks" mentioned?': It is in order to show that, of however many in number the saṅgha of monks with whom the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, not all of them assembled there at the time of teaching the dharma, but rather that 'many'—three or more—assembled there. Furthermore, it was spoken by the compiler in order to generate confidence in others. 'Assembled' merely means drawing near. 'Sat down' refers to sitting on a seat. Because the world mostly establishes the specific preceded by establishing the general, both are mentioned in accordance with worldly convention. Otherwise, by just 'sat down' alone, both would be mentioned. The meaning of the words of the prologue and so forth has been explained.

heading: གླེང་བསླང་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་བཤད་པ།
translation: Because He is worthy of being venerated by the entire world, or because He has destroyed the enemies that are the afflictions, He is the Arhat. Because He has properly and thoroughly understood all objects of knowledge, He is the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha. By those words, the complete perfection of all the Blessed One's intrinsic purposes, wisdom and abandonment, is completely shown. By that, it comes to show this: that kings and so forth benefiting subjects and so forth is not very wonderful here, because they benefit others out of desiring their own purposes such as gain and respect, whereas the Blessed One is the Tathāgata; having destroyed the enemies and perfectly and fully awakened, and having attained all complete perfections, whatever benefits He gives, those are shown to be wonderful here. Regarding this benefiting by the Blessed One, since there is no other cause for benefiting whatsoever besides great compassion, this aspect shows the Blessed One to be great compassion itself. 'Benefited' means that, having manifestly and perfectly awakened, at the time the Blessed One turned the wheel of dharma, He caused bodhisattvas whose roots of virtue were completely ripened to enter the bhūmis, in order to make the bodhisattvas thoroughly settle into the dharmatā.

སྦྱིན་པ་པོ་དང་། སྦྱིན་བདག་གང་ལ་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྦྱོང་བ་བསྟན་པས་དེ་དག་དགའ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། གང་དག་སྐལ་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་ལས་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་འགའ་ཞིག་གིས་ཡི་དགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ནང་དུ་སྐྱེས་པ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཕྱག་གི་སེན་མོ་བདུད་རྩི་ཅན་གྱིས་རེག་ན་ལྷའི་རོ་བྲོ་བ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་ཟད་མི་ཤེས་པ་གནོད་སྦྱིན་གཟི་སྟོབས་ཅན་ལ་སོགས་པས་ཁྱེར་བ་ཟོས་ན། དེ་དག་བདེ་བ་མཆོག་གིས་སེམས་ཚིམ་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་མཆོག་ཀྱང་འཐོབ་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཟས་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་ནི་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་དོ། །རྣམ་པ་ཅི་འདྲ་བས་ཟས་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་བྱས་ཤེ་ན། དེའི་ཕྱིར་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་བླངས་ནས་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཞལ་ཟས་གང་གསོལ་བ་དེ་ནི་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཀྱི་ཞལ་ཟས་མཇུག་ཏུ་གསོལ་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པར་ལེན་པ་སྔོན་དུ་བཏང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གསོལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གསོལ་ཟིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །ཡང་ན་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལན་གཉིས་པ་ལ་བླངས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལ་ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་དེ་ནི་ཟས་མཇུག་ཀྱང་ཡིན་ལ་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཀྱང་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་ཚིག་རྣམ་པར་སྦྱར་རོ། །ཡང་ན་ཕྱི་དྲོའི་ཟས་དེ་ཟ་བ་གང་ཡིན་པའི་བསོད་སྙོམས་དེ་ལ་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཅན་ཡིན་པ་དང་། དུས་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཟས་སྤངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསོལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་གཉིས་དང་བྲལ་ལོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཞག་ནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞག་སྟེའོ། །

By showing the complete purification of alms to whatever donors and benefactors, it generates joy in them; and those who have the fortune but, due to some karmic obscuration, have been born among the hungry ghosts and so forth, if touched by the nectar-like fingernails of the Blessed One's hand, it becomes the supreme taste of the gods, and when they eat the inexhaustible food carried by majestic yakṣas and so forth, their minds become satisfied with supreme happiness, and since they also obtain supreme samādhi, the activity of food of the Blessed One is immeasurable. If one asks, 'With what kind of aspect did He perform the activity of food?', therefore 'at the end' and so forth is mentioned; having received everything, whatever meal is eaten at the end is 'eating the alms meal at the end', and this is preceded by properly taking it up in order to guide the śrāvakas toward the qualities of purification. 'Ate' is a word meaning that He had already eaten. Alternatively, regarding 'at the end', whatever is received a second time is called 'subsequent food'; that subsequent food is compounded in words as 'it is both the food at the end and alms'. Alternatively, whatever alms it is that consists of eating that afternoon food is spoken of in that way. Therefore, because of possessing the qualities of purification and abandoning food at the wrong time, 'ate' is a word meaning that He is free from those two. 'Having put away' means putting away.

དེ་ཡང་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ན་བཀའ་ནོད་པ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་དག་ཀྱང་རྟག་ཏུ་གནས་མོད་ཀྱི་རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་བ་ནི་བདག་ཉིད་བྱེད་པའོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ལྷུང་བཟེད་དང་ཆོས་གོས་བཞག་པ་མཛད་དོ། །སྐལ་བ་ཆུང་ངུ་གཡོག་མི་འབྱོར་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བ་སྤོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་ངོ་། །མི་གཙང་བར་སྣང་བ་རྟག་ཏུ་རིང་དུ་སྤངས་པ་དང་། ཞབས་པདྨ་ལ་འཇོག་མོད་ཀྱི། བྱ་བའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་མོས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་བསམ་པ་དང་མཐུན་པ་འམ། རྐང་པ་རུལ་ཅན་གྱིས་མལ་ཆ་དང་སྟན་ལ་མི་རྫིའོ་ཞེས་བསླབ་པ་དག་ལ་གུས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞབས་འཁྲུ་བར་བལྟའོ། །གདན་བཤམས་པ་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྷ་ལ་སོགས་པས་བཤམས་པའོ། །སྐུ་དྲང་པོར་བསྲང་སྟེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཧ་ཅང་ཡང་མི་དགུ། ཧ་ཅང་ཡང་མི་དགྱེ་བར་མཛད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །ཆོས་སྟོན་པའི་དུས་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སྤོང་བའི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་གྱིས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བཞུགས་ཤེ་ན། སྤོང་བ་དག་ཁོ་ནས་ཆོས་འདི་བསྟན་པ་དང་། ཤེས་པ་དང་ཉན་པར་ནུས་ཀྱི་གཞན་དག་གིས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྤོང་བ་ལ་འཇིག་རྟེན་ནན་ཏན་བསྐྱེད་དུ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དྲན་པ་སྔོན་དུ་གཞག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྔོན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་གྱུར་པའི་ཚེ། བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་ཚེ་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་ནས་ཇི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་མི་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་བདག་གིས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྨོན་ལམ་བཏབ་པའི་སྨོན་ལམ་དེ་དྲན་པ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དག་ནི་རྟག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་དྲན་པ་ལ་གནས་མོད་ཀྱི། དུས་མ་ཡིན་པར་དྲན་པ་དེས་ནི་ཅིར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། དུས་སུ་སྨོན་ལམ་དྲན་པ་ནི་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དུས་སུ་དྲན་པས་ཀྱང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྟག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་གཞག་པ་ཉིད་དུ་སྟོན་པས་འགལ་བ་མེད་དོ། །

Furthermore, although those who exert themselves in taking orders, such as Śakra and so forth, constantly remain in the presence of the Blessed One, the Blessed One Himself put away the alms bowl and dharma robes in order to show that those who have gone forth do it themselves. It is also in order to eliminate the mental displeasure of those with small fortune who lack servants. Although the appearance of impurity is constantly abandoned far away and He places His feet upon lotuses, one should regard washing His feet as being in accordance with the intention of sentient beings who are inclined toward the Action Tantras and so forth, or in order to show reverence for the trainings such as 'one with filthy feet should not trample on bedding and seats'. 'On the arranged seat' refers to it being arranged by gods and so forth. 'Straightening the body' is a word meaning that He acts without bending down too much or leaning back too much. If one asks, 'Why did the Blessed One dwell in the posture of abandonment at the time of teaching the dharma?': It is in order to guide the world into generating exertion in abandonment, saying, 'Only those of abandonment are capable of teaching, knowing, and hearing this dharma, whereas others are not.' 'Establishing mindfulness in front' is a word meaning that He actualized the mindfulness of the prayer He had made previously when He was a bodhisattva, 'When I attain the unsurpassed state, I shall act in such a way that the lineage of the Buddhas will not be interrupted.' Although the Buddha Blessed Ones constantly rest in equipoise and thus always abide in mindfulness everywhere, mindfulness at the wrong time achieves nothing, whereas mindfulness of the prayer at the right time is accompanied by its result. Since mindfulness at the right time also shows that the Blessed One is constantly resting in equipoise, there is no contradiction.

དེ་ནས་དགེ་སློང་མང་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་སྨོས་ཤེ་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མཉན་ཡོད་ན་དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཚད་ཇི་སྙེད་དང་བཞུགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཆོས་སྟོན་པའི་དུས་ན་དེར་མ་འདུས་ཀྱི། མང་པོ་གསུམ་ཡན་ཆད་དེར་འདུས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་ཡང་དག་པར་སྡུད་པར་བྱེད་པས་གཞན་དག་ཡིད་ཆེས་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྨྲས་སོ། །འདུས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཉེ་བ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་དོ། །འདུག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྟན་ལ་འདུག་པའོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ནི་ཕལ་ཆེར་སྤྱིར་གཞག་པ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་ཅན་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་འཇོག་པས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་གྲགས་པ་དང་མཐུན་པར་གཉིས་ཀ་སྨོས་སོ། །གཞན་དུ་ན་ནི་འདུག་གོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཙམ་ཁོ་ནས་གཉིས་ཀ་སྨོས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །གླེང་གཞིའི་ཚིག་གི་དོན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །

heading: གླེང་བསླང་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་བཤད་པ།
source: ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པ་ནི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་དག་ཕན་བཏགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ལ་གཏད་པ་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་འཇོག་ཏུ་གཞུག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ང་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ནི་ཁྱེད་ཀྱིས་ཅི་ནས་དེ་དག་ཡོན་ཏན་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་། ཐོབ་པ་དག་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཉམས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་གྱིས་ཤིག་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཕན་བཏགས་པ་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་བཏགས་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ལྔས་དམ་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དུས་དང་། ཁྱད་པར་དང་། རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་དང་། བསྟན་པ་དང་། ཁྱབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་དུས་ནི་ཚེ་རབས་གཞན་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ནི་ཕྱི་རོལ་པ་དང་། ཉན་ཐོས་དང་། རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་དག་པས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ནི་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་དེ་དག་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བསྟན་པ་ནི་གཏན་དུ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཁྱབ་པ་ནི་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་དེ་བདག་དང་གཞན་གྱི་རྒྱུད་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་དམ་པར་བལྟ་སྟེ། གནས་དང་ཆོས་ཉིད་རབ་ཏུ་འཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཀར་གདགས་པའོ། །
translation: 'Entrusted' means that beginners whose roots of virtue are not completely ripened are entrusted to those very ones who have been benefited, in order to make the bodhisattvas thoroughly settle into the dharmatā. Showing 'I pass into complete nirvāṇa' means saying, 'Whatever you do, act such that those who have not attained qualities will attain them, and that they will not completely decline from those they have attained.' Thus, by both 'benefited' and 'entrusted', making the lineage of the Buddhas uninterrupted is completely shown. Benefiting the bodhisattvas should be understood as supreme through five aspects: time, distinction, expansiveness, stability, and pervasiveness. Regarding that, time: because it is in other lifetimes. Distinction: because it is especially exalted above the benefiting done by non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. Expansiveness: because those benefits are unsurpassed. Stability: because it is permanent. Pervasiveness: because that benefit benefits the mind-streams of oneself and others. 'Entrusted' should also be seen as supreme through three aspects: the basis, the thorough attainment of the dharmatā, and the giving of the command.
