By way of application to the perfections, he spoke the words 'Moreover' and so forth. That too should be seen as the nature of two phrases having the nature of a general rule and an exception: this is the meaning of saying that a bodhisattva should indeed give a gift, but not by abiding in entities. By this term 'gift,' through the medium of the three types of giving, all six perfections are taught, not just giving alone. Herein, the giving of material things teaches the perfection of giving. The giving of fearlessness teaches the perfections of moral discipline and patience. The giving of Dharma teaches the perfections of effort, concentration, and wisdom: if there is no effort, one becomes thoroughly weary of retaining and teaching the Dharma, and thus will not teach the Dharma; if there is no concentration, because one desires what is more than faith, one will become an afflicted teacher; if there is no wisdom, one will teach it erroneously. Therefore, if all three are absent, the giving of Dharma will not be accomplished. Others explain that effort goes everywhere. By saying 'should give a gift,' it teaches how to abide in the six perfections through aspiration and prayer.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: It is also illogical for it to be exactly multiple, because a single consciousness is not established, since there is no experience of a consciousness apprehending just a single atom. If that is not established, multiplicity is also not established, because multiplicity has the nature of a collection of singles. Because consciousnesses are bodiless, it is also impossible for them to arise apprehending by remaining covering the object, by which the conceptualization that multiple consciousnesses arise for the sake of forming the structure of the aspect of the painting would become sound. Furthermore, would they be similar in their entire nature, or in one part? For a start, it is not in their entire nature, because, just like the object, the consciousness would become the nature of inert matter. It is also not by a part, because a single thing has no parts. Even if one thoroughly conceptualizes it as a part by way of particular exclusions, since things such as being an entity exist in all similar dharmas, it would absurdly follow that everything would be known by everything. But if one posits that it is known by the two—arising from it and being similar to it—then it would absurdly follow that it also apprehends the immediately preceding condition that corresponds in object. Even granting that there is similarity, ultimately an external object is not established by direct perception, because the consciousness knows the aspect of blue and so forth that exists in itself. There is no second knowing of the aspect of blue and so forth, by which the object too would become an object of direct perception.

Imputing the convention of non-existence to a rabbit's horn and so forth is also due to the cause of merely lacking the capacity to perform a function. By implication, the object to which the convention of existence is imputed is exactly what is capable of performing a function, because existence and non-existence have the characteristic of abiding by mutually excluding each other. If one imputes the name 'entity' even to that which is empty of all capacities of such a kind and is no different from a rabbit's horn and so forth, there is no dispute about names. However, those endowed with understanding of the meaningless assertion state that it is illogical to impute the convention of entity to such a kind of unobservable nature, which is no different from the son of a barren woman and so forth. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished. Because it would absurdly follow that space and so forth are also agents, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in what is harmonious with the position, it is also not contradictory. Because there is also no other characteristic of the self, therefore it is similar to the son of a barren woman. As for persons, too, if they perish, it would absurdly follow that they are included exactly within the aggregates, because the aggregates include all conditioned things. But if they do not perish, then at that time, by being dissimilar to the dharmas belonging to the aggregates, they would become exactly another entity from them, and the faults of that have already been stated. Therefore, there is no entity whatsoever that is called inexpressible. Therefore, the lion's roar of the Bhagavan, 'all dharmas are selfless,' terrifies all the herds of tīrthika elephants and is invincible, so there is no need for much.

By way of application to the perfections, he spoke the words 'Moreover' and so forth. That too should be seen as the nature of two phrases having the nature of a general rule and an exception: this is the meaning of saying that a bodhisattva should indeed give a gift, but not by abiding in entities. By this term 'gift,' through the medium of the three types of giving, all six perfections are taught, not just giving alone. Herein, the giving of material things teaches the perfection of giving. The giving of fearlessness teaches the perfections of moral discipline and patience. The giving of Dharma teaches the perfections of effort, concentration, and wisdom: if there is no effort, one becomes thoroughly weary of retaining and teaching the Dharma, and thus will not teach the Dharma; if there is no concentration, because one desires what is more than faith, one will become an afflicted teacher; if there is no wisdom, one will teach it erroneously. Therefore, if all three are absent, the giving of Dharma will not be accomplished. Others explain that effort goes everywhere. By saying 'should give a gift,' it teaches how to abide in the six perfections through aspiration and prayer.

By "not abiding in entities" and so forth, it is taught how this is to be accomplished by entering into yogic equipoise. By "a bodhisattva should thus give a gift" and so forth, it is taught how, having annihilated distraction, the mind should be thoroughly apprehended. Herein, by "not abiding in entities," the reality of the application to the perfections is taught. Adhering as reality to entities such as the gift to be given, the giver, and the receiver is "abiding"; therefore, if a bodhisattva applies to the perfections after adhering to entities, it will become a wrong application, because they erroneously adhere while ultimately there is no entity whatsoever to which adherence would occur. This is because there is no valid cognition that establishes that, and because there is that which subverts it. Thus, that others ultimately assert the entity of an object as different from consciousness is, for a start, not established by direct perception, because it is illogical for an object that is other to be apprehended by consciousness. If the apprehension of an object by consciousness were to become one of three positions—with an aspect, without an aspect, or with another's aspect—for a start, it is not "with an aspect," because when seeing a multicolored mat and so forth, since they are not different from the single consciousness, it would absurdly follow that the aspects too have the nature of being single; or, since the consciousness too is not different from the aspects, it would absurdly follow that it has the nature of being multiple, just like the nature of the aspects.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If one says, "That consciousness of whatever it may be is exactly what apprehends the object," it is so by way of imputation, but ultimately there is no knowing of it, because it knows exactly the aspect that exists in itself. Because the object is utterly hidden, how could there be such a thing as saying that it is exclusively the aspect of that consciousness? A cause is certainly not established as being a producer merely by engendering its own nature, because an illusion appears. Atoms are not the object of a consciousness in which a gross form appears, because they are subtle. They are also not a collection, because it is not an entity other than them. Also, because the object of conceptualization is nonexistent. If the collection is another entity, it is illogical for it to be single, because it appears in different directions, and because it possesses the incompatible properties of being obstructed and unobstructed. Even if the collection were multiple, it would be exactly those atoms themselves, but it is not another entity. It is also not the position called "without an aspect," because it does not do anything whatsoever to blue and so forth. If it knew merely by existing, then all consciousnesses would know everything, because there is also no difference in all of them. Therefore, it could not be posited that "this is the knowing of blue, but not of yellow," because there is no particular cause for a positing whatsoever.

རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་མེད་པར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་ཡང་དོན་བྱེད་པའི་ནུས་པ་མེད་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་རྒྱུའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ན་ཡོད་པར་ཐ་སྙད་གདགས་པ་དོན་བྱེད་ནུས་པའི་ཡུལ་ཉིད་དེ། ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་ནི་ཕན་ཚུན་སྤངས་ཏེ་གནས་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ནུས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་སྟོང་པ་རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་བྱེ་བྲག་མེད་པ་ལ་ཡང་དངོས་པོ་ཞེས་མིང་དུ་འདོགས་ན་ནི་མིང་ལ་ནི་བརྩད་པ་མེད་དོ། །འོན་ཀྱང་དོན་མེད་པའི་འདོད་པ་རྟོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དག་ནི་རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་མི་དམིགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མོ་གཤམ་གྱི་བུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་བྱེ་བྲག་མེད་པ་ལ་དངོས་པོར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་རིགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྨྲའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གཏན་ཚིགས་མ་གྲུབ་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ཡང་བྱེད་པ་པོར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བས་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཕྱོགས་དང་མཐུན་པ་ལ་ཡོད་པས་འགལ་བ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བདག་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་གཞན་ཡང་མེད་པས་དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་མོ་གཤམ་གྱི་བུ་དང་འདྲའོ། །གང་ཟག་དག་ཀྱང་གལ་ཏེ་འཇིག་ན་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ཁོ་ནའི་ནང་དུ་འདུས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་སྟེ། ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་འདུས་བྱས་མཐའ་དག་བསྡུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འོན་ཏེ་མི་འཇིག་ན་དེའི་ཚེ་ཕུང་པོར་གཏོགས་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་དང་མི་འདྲ་བས་དེ་ལས་དོན་གཞན་པ་ཁོ་ནར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེའི་ཉེས་པ་ནི་བརྗོད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བརྗོད་དུ་མི་རུང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དངོས་པོ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་དེ། དེས་ན་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདག་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་སེང་གེའི་སྒྲ་ནི་མུ་སྟེགས་བྱེད་གླང་པོ་ཆེའི་ཁྱུ་མཐའ་དག་སྐྲག་པར་མཛད་ཅིང་བརྫི་བ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་པས་མང་དུ་མི་དགོས་སོ། །

Imputing the convention of non-existence to a rabbit's horn and so forth is also due to the cause of merely lacking the capacity to perform a function. By implication, the object to which the convention of existence is imputed is exactly what is capable of performing a function, because existence and non-existence have the characteristic of abiding by mutually excluding each other. If one imputes the name 'entity' even to that which is empty of all capacities of such a kind and is no different from a rabbit's horn and so forth, there is no dispute about names. However, those endowed with understanding of the meaningless assertion state that it is illogical to impute the convention of entity to such a kind of unobservable nature, which is no different from the son of a barren woman and so forth. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished. Because it would absurdly follow that space and so forth are also agents, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in what is harmonious with the position, it is also not contradictory. Because there is also no other characteristic of the self, therefore it is similar to the son of a barren woman. As for persons, too, if they perish, it would absurdly follow that they are included exactly within the aggregates, because the aggregates include all conditioned things. But if they do not perish, then at that time, by being dissimilar to the dharmas belonging to the aggregates, they would become exactly another entity from them, and the faults of that have already been stated. Therefore, there is no entity whatsoever that is called inexpressible. Therefore, the lion's roar of the Bhagavan, 'all dharmas are selfless,' terrifies all the herds of tīrthika elephants and is invincible, so there is no need for much.

ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། ཡང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ཡང་སྤྱིར་བཏང་བ་དང་དམིགས་ཀྱིས་བསལ་བའི་རང་བཞིན་ཚིག་གཉིས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་ནི་བྱ་མོད་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སྦྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་སྦྱིན་པ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ཅར་བསྟན་གྱི་སྦྱིན་པ་འབའ་ཞིག་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལ་ཟང་ཟིང་སྦྱིན་པ་ནི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་བསྟན་ནོ། །མི་འཇིགས་པ་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ། །ཆོས་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྣམས་ཏེ། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་མེད་ན་ཆོས་བཟུང་བ་དང་བསྟན་པ་ལ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྐྱོ་སྟེ་ཆོས་མི་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བསམ་གཏན་མེད་ན་དད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་འདོད་པས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་གྱི་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཤེས་རབ་མེད་ན་དེ་ནི་དེ་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གསུམ་ཆར་མེད་ན་ཆོས་སྦྱིན་པ་འགྲུབ་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །གཞན་དག་ནི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀུན་དུ་འགྲོའོ་ཞེས་འཆད་དོ། །སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་དག་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

By way of application to the perfections, he spoke the words 'Moreover' and so forth. That too should be seen as the nature of two phrases having the nature of a general rule and an exception: this is the meaning of saying that a bodhisattva should indeed give a gift, but not by abiding in entities. By this term 'gift,' through the medium of the three types of giving, all six perfections are taught, not just giving alone. Herein, the giving of material things teaches the perfection of giving. The giving of fearlessness teaches the perfections of moral discipline and patience. The giving of Dharma teaches the perfections of effort, concentration, and wisdom: if there is no effort, one becomes thoroughly weary of retaining and teaching the Dharma, and thus will not teach the Dharma; if there is no concentration, because one desires what is more than faith, one will become an afflicted teacher; if there is no wisdom, one will teach it erroneously. Therefore, if all three are absent, the giving of Dharma will not be accomplished. Others explain that effort goes everywhere. By saying 'should give a gift,' it teaches how to abide in the six perfections through aspiration and prayer.

By "not abiding in entities" and so forth, it is taught how this is to be accomplished by entering into yogic equipoise. By "a bodhisattva should thus give a gift" and so forth, it is taught how, having annihilated distraction, the mind should be thoroughly apprehended. Herein, by "not abiding in entities," the reality of the application to the perfections is taught. Adhering as reality to entities such as the gift to be given, the giver, and the receiver is "abiding"; therefore, if a bodhisattva applies to the perfections after adhering to entities, it will become a wrong application, because they erroneously adhere while ultimately there is no entity whatsoever to which adherence would occur. This is because there is no valid cognition that establishes that, and because there is that which subverts it. Thus, that others ultimately assert the entity of an object as different from consciousness is, for a start, not established by direct perception, because it is illogical for an object that is other to be apprehended by consciousness. If the apprehension of an object by consciousness were to become one of three positions—with an aspect, without an aspect, or with another's aspect—for a start, it is not "with an aspect," because when seeing a multicolored mat and so forth, since they are not different from the single consciousness, it would absurdly follow that the aspects too have the nature of being single; or, since the consciousness too is not different from the aspects, it would absurdly follow that it has the nature of being multiple, just like the nature of the aspects.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If one accepts a single difference, that itself would be accepted as being with an aspect, because for the nature of consciousness, which has no difference in merely being the nature of conceptualization, there is no other difference apart from the aspect. It is also not the position called "with another's aspect," because it would absurdly follow too far. If that were so, then a consciousness of an aspect would also be conceptualized as possessing the object of form. Therefore, the object is established by direct perception. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that that object, which has not become an object of direct perception, is connected together with any mark such as consciousness. If one infers merely a cause in general that is different from the effect of consciousness, the assertion is not established, because there is also another cause, the other immediately preceding condition. There is also no other valid cognition. Therefore, for a start, an external object is not established. The ultimate nature of consciousness is also not established by direct perception, because there is no individual knowing of a non-dual nature. If it were not so in that regard, then everyone would not see reality. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that any mark is connected together with such an aspect. If one asks, "How would there be thorough affliction and complete purification?" It is not so, because, according to you, it is not established that those two and any of that are connected.

It is also illogical for it to be exactly multiple, because a single consciousness is not established, since there is no experience of a consciousness apprehending just a single atom. If that is not established, multiplicity is also not established, because multiplicity has the nature of a collection of singles. Because consciousnesses are bodiless, it is also impossible for them to arise apprehending by remaining covering the object, by which the conceptualization that multiple consciousnesses arise for the sake of forming the structure of the aspect of the painting would become sound. Furthermore, would they be similar in their entire nature, or in one part? For a start, it is not in their entire nature, because, just like the object, the consciousness would become the nature of inert matter. It is also not by a part, because a single thing has no parts. Even if one thoroughly conceptualizes it as a part by way of particular exclusions, since things such as being an entity exist in all similar dharmas, it would absurdly follow that everything would be known by everything. But if one posits that it is known by the two—arising from it and being similar to it—then it would absurdly follow that it also apprehends the immediately preceding condition that corresponds in object. Even granting that there is similarity, ultimately an external object is not established by direct perception, because the consciousness knows the aspect of blue and so forth that exists in itself. There is no second knowing of the aspect of blue and so forth, by which the object too would become an object of direct perception.

If one says, "That consciousness of whatever it may be is exactly what apprehends the object," it is so by way of imputation, but ultimately there is no knowing of it, because it knows exactly the aspect that exists in itself. Because the object is utterly hidden, how could there be such a thing as saying that it is exclusively the aspect of that consciousness? A cause is certainly not established as being a producer merely by engendering its own nature, because an illusion appears. Atoms are not the object of a consciousness in which a gross form appears, because they are subtle. They are also not a collection, because it is not an entity other than them. Also, because the object of conceptualization is nonexistent. If the collection is another entity, it is illogical for it to be single, because it appears in different directions, and because it possesses the incompatible properties of being obstructed and unobstructed. Even if the collection were multiple, it would be exactly those atoms themselves, but it is not another entity. It is also not the position called "without an aspect," because it does not do anything whatsoever to blue and so forth. If it knew merely by existing, then all consciousnesses would know everything, because there is also no difference in all of them. Therefore, it could not be posited that "this is the knowing of blue, but not of yellow," because there is no particular cause for a positing whatsoever.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Because it is not established that those two are connected with the ultimate entity in any way. It is not established as connected by the characteristic of arising from that, because that is entirely hidden. A connection with what is hidden cannot be apprehended by anyone who sees this side. When ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when not examined, are not contradictory as the root of thorough affliction, and when ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when examined, are reversed, complete purification is also viable as solely agreeable when not examined, possessing the characteristic of arising as a state incompatible with that; at that time, since there is ultimately no entity, how could it absurdly follow that those two also do not exist? This absurd consequence arises for someone who accepts those two as definitively single and causeless, but it does not for one who speaks of dependent arising conventionally. Therefore, there is not even the slightest valid cognition establishing the nature of an ultimate entity. There is indeed that which subverts it: thus, whatever is devoid of a nature of one and multiple, that ultimately has no nature, just like a lotus in the sky; and the entire aspect of entities of the nature of consciousness and objects of knowledge, as asserted by others, is also empty of a nature of one and multiple. This by implication is the non-apprehension of the pervader, because one and multiple pervade the nature.

By "not abiding in entities" and so forth, it is taught how this is to be accomplished by entering into yogic equipoise. By "a bodhisattva should thus give a gift" and so forth, it is taught how, having annihilated distraction, the mind should be thoroughly apprehended. Herein, by "not abiding in entities," the reality of the application to the perfections is taught. Adhering as reality to entities such as the gift to be given, the giver, and the receiver is "abiding"; therefore, if a bodhisattva applies to the perfections after adhering to entities, it will become a wrong application, because they erroneously adhere while ultimately there is no entity whatsoever to which adherence would occur. This is because there is no valid cognition that establishes that, and because there is that which subverts it. Thus, that others ultimately assert the entity of an object as different from consciousness is, for a start, not established by direct perception, because it is illogical for an object that is other to be apprehended by consciousness. If the apprehension of an object by consciousness were to become one of three positions—with an aspect, without an aspect, or with another's aspect—for a start, it is not "with an aspect," because when seeing a multicolored mat and so forth, since they are not different from the single consciousness, it would absurdly follow that the aspects too have the nature of being single; or, since the consciousness too is not different from the aspects, it would absurdly follow that it has the nature of being multiple, just like the nature of the aspects.

It is also illogical for it to be exactly multiple, because a single consciousness is not established, since there is no experience of a consciousness apprehending just a single atom. If that is not established, multiplicity is also not established, because multiplicity has the nature of a collection of singles. Because consciousnesses are bodiless, it is also impossible for them to arise apprehending by remaining covering the object, by which the conceptualization that multiple consciousnesses arise for the sake of forming the structure of the aspect of the painting would become sound. Furthermore, would they be similar in their entire nature, or in one part? For a start, it is not in their entire nature, because, just like the object, the consciousness would become the nature of inert matter. It is also not by a part, because a single thing has no parts. Even if one thoroughly conceptualizes it as a part by way of particular exclusions, since things such as being an entity exist in all similar dharmas, it would absurdly follow that everything would be known by everything. But if one posits that it is known by the two—arising from it and being similar to it—then it would absurdly follow that it also apprehends the immediately preceding condition that corresponds in object. Even granting that there is similarity, ultimately an external object is not established by direct perception, because the consciousness knows the aspect of blue and so forth that exists in itself. If one says, "That consciousness of whatever it may be is exactly what apprehends the object," it is so by way of imputation, but ultimately there is no knowing of it, because it knows exactly the aspect that exists in itself. Because the object is utterly hidden, how could there be such a thing as saying that it is exclusively the aspect of that consciousness? A cause is certainly not established as being a producer merely by engendering its own nature, because an illusion appears. Atoms are not the object of a consciousness in which a gross form appears, because they are subtle. They are also not a collection, because it is not an entity other than them. Also, because the object of conceptualization is nonexistent. If the collection is another entity, it is illogical for it to be single, because it appears in different directions, and because it possesses the incompatible properties of being obstructed and unobstructed. Even if the collection were multiple, it would be exactly those atoms themselves, but it is not another entity. It is also not the position called "without an aspect," because it does not do anything whatsoever to blue and so forth. If it knew merely by existing, then all consciousnesses would know everything, because there is also no difference in all of them. Therefore, it could not be posited that "this is the knowing of blue, but not of yellow," because there is no particular cause for a positing whatsoever.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Those two also do not exist in it. Thus, for a start, that external entity of the sense-spheres of form and so forth is not single, because one apprehends contradictory properties, such as being obstructed and unobstructed. If, while possessing contradictory properties, it were still exactly single, then everything would become a single substance, and therefore they would arise and be destroyed together. It is also not multiple, because thus, if it is broken down into multiplicity, it would be differentiated into atoms, and the atoms, too, having no parts, do not abide on a far side and a near side, just like mind and mental factors. Therefore, they would not appear to abide pervading a direction; if they were to do so, therefore one must accept them as having different directional parts. If one accepts that, how could it be single? Therefore, thus, for a start, an external object is established as exactly devoid of a nature of one and multiple. A consciousness in which blue and so forth appears is also not of a single nature, because it appears to apprehend the aspect of a painting, just like multiple moments of consciousness existing in different continuums. It is also unsuitable to express that consciousnesses arise simultaneously in accordance with an enumeration of multiplicity, because for things without parts and without a body, it is illogical to abide on a near side and a far side.

If one accepts a single difference, that itself would be accepted as being with an aspect, because for the nature of consciousness, which has no difference in merely being the nature of conceptualization, there is no other difference apart from the aspect. It is also not the position called "with another's aspect," because it would absurdly follow too far. If that were so, then a consciousness of an aspect would also be conceptualized as possessing the object of form. Therefore, the object is established by direct perception. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that that object, which has not become an object of direct perception, is connected together with any mark such as consciousness. If one infers merely a cause in general that is different from the effect of consciousness, the assertion is not established, because there is also another cause, the other immediately preceding condition. There is also no other valid cognition. Therefore, for a start, an external object is not established. The ultimate nature of consciousness is also not established by direct perception, because there is no individual knowing of a non-dual nature. If it were not so in that regard, then everyone would not see reality. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that any mark is connected together with such an aspect. If one asks, "How would there be thorough affliction and complete purification?" It is not so, because, according to you, it is not established that those two and any of that are connected.

Because it is not established that those two are connected with the ultimate entity in any way. It is not established as connected by the characteristic of arising from that, because that is entirely hidden. A connection with what is hidden cannot be apprehended by anyone who sees this side. When ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when not examined, are not contradictory as the root of thorough affliction, and when ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when examined, are reversed, complete purification is also viable as solely agreeable when not examined, possessing the characteristic of arising as a state incompatible with that; at that time, since there is ultimately no entity, how could it absurdly follow that those two also do not exist? This absurd consequence arises for someone who accepts those two as definitively single and causeless, but it does not for one who speaks of dependent arising conventionally. Therefore, there is not even the slightest valid cognition establishing the nature of an ultimate entity. There is indeed that which subverts it: thus, whatever is devoid of a nature of one and multiple, that ultimately has no nature, just like a lotus in the sky; and the entire aspect of entities of the nature of consciousness and objects of knowledge, as asserted by others, is also empty of a nature of one and multiple. This by implication is the non-apprehension of the pervader, because one and multiple pervade the nature.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If they do not abide like that, they would not appear like that. If one says, "However, consciousness is exclusively single, and because false aspects appear to it, it does not have the fault of multiplicity," if that were so, then how would those false things appear to it? That which is called "appearing" refers to the nature of clarity. If it is a property belonging to the nature of consciousness, how could that which is false appear if it is utterly nonexistent, just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth? Therefore, if one accepts the aspects of the clear nature as exactly false, what other nature of consciousness is left over that would be true for you? There is no consciousness whatsoever called "the nature of clarity," because with reference to the exclusion of others, general designations are applied only to particulars. If the particulars are false, it would become utterly clear that everything is also false. As for aspects that do not exist, they have no connection with that true nature of consciousness by which they would definitively appear to it, either by the characteristic of being its nature or by the characteristic of arising from it. If there is no connection, it is illogical for them to appear, because it would absurdly follow too far. Therefore, the reason is also not unestablished.

གལ་ཏེ་གང་དེའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དོན་འཛིན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེ་ན། བརྟགས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་ནི་ཡིན་གྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་རིག་པ་ནི་མེད་དེ། བདག་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཉིད་རིག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དོན་ཤིན་ཏུ་ལྐོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཤེས་པ་དེའི་རྣམ་པ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ག་ལ་ཡོད། རྒྱུ་ནི་ངེས་པར་བདག་གི་ངོ་བོ་བསྐྲུན་པ་ཁོ་ནས་སྐྱེད་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དེ་འཁྲུལ་པ་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རགས་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཤེས་པའི་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ཕྲ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་དག་འདུས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ལས་དོན་གཞན་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པའི་ཡུལ་ཡང་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདུས་པའི་དོན་གཞན་ན་ནི་ཕྱོགས་ཐ་དད་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། བསྒྲིབས་པ་དང་མ་བསྒྲིབས་པ་ཆོས་མི་མཐུན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཅིག་པུར་མི་རིགས་སོ། །འདུས་པ་དུ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཡང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཡིན་པར་འགྱུར་གྱི། དེ་དོན་གཞན་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྣམ་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་སྔོན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ཅི་ཡང་མི་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡོད་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་རིག་ན་ནི་ཤེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཐམས་ཅད་རིག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཡང་བྱེ་བྲག་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་འདི་ནི་སྔོན་པོ་རིག་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་སེར་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པའི་རྒྱུའི་བྱེ་བྲག་གང་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

If one says, "That consciousness of whatever it may be is exactly what apprehends the object," it is so by way of imputation, but ultimately there is no knowing of it, because it knows exactly the aspect that exists in itself. Because the object is utterly hidden, how could there be such a thing as saying that it is exclusively the aspect of that consciousness? A cause is certainly not established as being a producer merely by engendering its own nature, because an illusion appears. Atoms are not the object of a consciousness in which a gross form appears, because they are subtle. They are also not a collection, because it is not an entity other than them. Also, because the object of conceptualization is nonexistent. If the collection is another entity, it is illogical for it to be single, because it appears in different directions, and because it possesses the incompatible properties of being obstructed and unobstructed. Even if the collection were multiple, it would be exactly those atoms themselves, but it is not another entity. It is also not the position called "without an aspect," because it does not do anything whatsoever to blue and so forth. If it knew merely by existing, then all consciousnesses would know everything, because there is also no difference in all of them. Therefore, it could not be posited that "this is the knowing of blue, but not of yellow," because there is no particular cause for a positing whatsoever.

བྱེ་བྲག་གཅིག་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་དེ་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ།རྟོག་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཙམ་དུ་བྱེ་བྲག་མེད་པའི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་ལ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་མ་གཏོགས་པར་ཐ་དད་པ་གཞན་མེད་དོ། །གཞན་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་རྣམ་པའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་ཅན་དུ་བརྟག་པར་བྱ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དོན་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་འགྲུབ་པོ། །རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པས་ཀྱང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མ་གྱུར་པའི་དོན་དེ་དང་ཤེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྟགས་གང་དང་ཡང་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྲེལ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཤེས་པ་འབྲས་བུ་དང་ཐ་དད་པ་ཞིག་སྤྱིར་རྒྱུ་ཙམ་དུ་རྗེས་སུ་དཔོག་ན་ནི་འདོད་པ་མི་འགྲུབ་སྟེ། རྒྱུ་གཞན་དེ་མ་ཐག་པའི་རྐྱེན་གཞན་ཡང་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཚད་མ་གཞན་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དོན་ནི་མི་འགྲུབ་པོ། །ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པ་ཡང་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མི་འགྲུབ་སྟེ་གཉིས་སུ་མེད་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་སོ་སོར་རིག་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་དེ་ཁོ་ན་མཐོང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པས་ཀྱང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྟགས་གང་ཡང་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྲེལ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་རྣམ་པར་བྱང་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་ལྟར་ན་དེ་གཉིས་དང་དེ་གང་ཡང་འབྲེལ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

If one accepts a single difference, that itself would be accepted as being with an aspect, because for the nature of consciousness, which has no difference in merely being the nature of conceptualization, there is no other difference apart from the aspect. It is also not the position called "with another's aspect," because it would absurdly follow too far. If that were so, then a consciousness of an aspect would also be conceptualized as possessing the object of form. Therefore, the object is established by direct perception. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that that object, which has not become an object of direct perception, is connected together with any mark such as consciousness. If one infers merely a cause in general that is different from the effect of consciousness, the assertion is not established, because there is also another cause, the other immediately preceding condition. There is also no other valid cognition. Therefore, for a start, an external object is not established. The ultimate nature of consciousness is also not established by direct perception, because there is no individual knowing of a non-dual nature. If it were not so in that regard, then everyone would not see reality. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that any mark is connected together with such an aspect. If one asks, "How would there be thorough affliction and complete purification?" It is not so, because, according to you, it is not established that those two and any of that are connected.

Because it is not established that those two are connected with the ultimate entity in any way. It is not established as connected by the characteristic of arising from that, because that is entirely hidden. A connection with what is hidden cannot be apprehended by anyone who sees this side. When ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when not examined, are not contradictory as the root of thorough affliction, and when ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when examined, are reversed, complete purification is also viable as solely agreeable when not examined, possessing the characteristic of arising as a state incompatible with that; at that time, since there is ultimately no entity, how could it absurdly follow that those two also do not exist? This absurd consequence arises for someone who accepts those two as definitively single and causeless, but it does not for one who speaks of dependent arising conventionally. Therefore, there is not even the slightest valid cognition establishing the nature of an ultimate entity. There is indeed that which subverts it: thus, whatever is devoid of a nature of one and multiple, that ultimately has no nature, just like a lotus in the sky; and the entire aspect of entities of the nature of consciousness and objects of knowledge, as asserted by others, is also empty of a nature of one and multiple. This by implication is the non-apprehension of the pervader, because one and multiple pervade the nature.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in the homologous class, it is also not contradictory. Therefore, in whatever way entities are conceptualized, in that way they unravel. For that very reason, it is explained: "However entities are conceptually examined, their nature does not exist truly. Thus they do not exist in the nature of one and multiple." The Bhagavat also stated in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: "Just as forms appear in a mirror, although utterly devoid of being one and other, yet they do not exist there; likewise, if the nature of entities is taken apart by the intellect, the nature is unapprehendable. Therefore, they are inexpressible, and are explained as also having no nature." Similarly, it is also stated in the noble Samādhirājasūtra: "For example, just as a wet trunk of a banana tree, when taken apart layer by layer by someone desiring its core, has no core inside or outside; know all dharmas to be like that."

If one says, "That consciousness of whatever it may be is exactly what apprehends the object," it is so by way of imputation, but ultimately there is no knowing of it, because it knows exactly the aspect that exists in itself. Because the object is utterly hidden, how could there be such a thing as saying that it is exclusively the aspect of that consciousness? A cause is certainly not established as being a producer merely by engendering its own nature, because an illusion appears. Atoms are not the object of a consciousness in which a gross form appears, because they are subtle. They are also not a collection, because it is not an entity other than them. Also, because the object of conceptualization is nonexistent. If the collection is another entity, it is illogical for it to be single, because it appears in different directions, and because it possesses the incompatible properties of being obstructed and unobstructed. Even if the collection were multiple, it would be exactly those atoms themselves, but it is not another entity. It is also not the position called "without an aspect," because it does not do anything whatsoever to blue and so forth. If it knew merely by existing, then all consciousnesses would know everything, because there is also no difference in all of them. Therefore, it could not be posited that "this is the knowing of blue, but not of yellow," because there is no particular cause for a positing whatsoever.

If one accepts a single difference, that itself would be accepted as being with an aspect, because for the nature of consciousness, which has no difference in merely being the nature of conceptualization, there is no other difference apart from the aspect. It is also not the position called "with another's aspect," because it would absurdly follow too far. If that were so, then a consciousness of an aspect would also be conceptualized as possessing the object of form. Therefore, the object is established by direct perception. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that that object, which has not become an object of direct perception, is connected together with any mark such as consciousness. If one infers merely a cause in general that is different from the effect of consciousness, the assertion is not established, because there is also another cause, the other immediately preceding condition. There is also no other valid cognition. Therefore, for a start, an external object is not established. The ultimate nature of consciousness is also not established by direct perception, because there is no individual knowing of a non-dual nature. If it were not so in that regard, then everyone would not see reality. It is also not by inference, because it is not established that any mark is connected together with such an aspect. If one asks, "How would there be thorough affliction and complete purification?" It is not so, because, according to you, it is not established that those two and any of that are connected.

Because it is not established that those two are connected with the ultimate entity in any way. It is not established as connected by the characteristic of arising from that, because that is entirely hidden. A connection with what is hidden cannot be apprehended by anyone who sees this side. When ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when not examined, are not contradictory as the root of thorough affliction, and when ignorance and so forth, which are agreeable when examined, are reversed, complete purification is also viable as solely agreeable when not examined, possessing the characteristic of arising as a state incompatible with that; at that time, since there is ultimately no entity, how could it absurdly follow that those two also do not exist? This absurd consequence arises for someone who accepts those two as definitively single and causeless, but it does not for one who speaks of dependent arising conventionally. Therefore, there is not even the slightest valid cognition establishing the nature of an ultimate entity. There is indeed that which subverts it: thus, whatever is devoid of a nature of one and multiple, that ultimately has no nature, just like a lotus in the sky; and the entire aspect of entities of the nature of consciousness and objects of knowledge, as asserted by others, is also empty of a nature of one and multiple. This by implication is the non-apprehension of the pervader, because one and multiple pervade the nature.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Therefore, since all entities are like an illusion, pleasant when unexamined, one should thus give gifts without being attached. The meaning that "it is not by abiding in entities" is logical here. That being so, the application to giving and so forth is fully taught as it truly exists, but not otherwise. Lest one think, "If, because there are no entities whatsoever ultimately, one should not give gifts by abiding in entities, one should surely give gifts with attachment to non-entities," it is stated: "without abiding in anything whatsoever." A bodhisattva should also abandon the conceptualization of non-entities, because if there is no apprehension of entities, that does not exist. Conventionally, what is to be given, the giver, and so forth exist; therefore, the intention is that attachment to non-entities is also illogical.

དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་མེད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་གང་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་དེ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བསྒྲིབས་པ་དང་མ་བསྒྲིབས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཆོས་འགལ་བ་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཆོས་འགལ་བ་དང་ལྡན་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་གཅིག་པ་ཉིད་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རྫས་གཅིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྱུང་བ་དང་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དུ་མ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་དུ་མར་བཤིག་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཏུ་ཐ་དད་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཆ་ཤས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུལ་རོལ་ན་གནས་པ་ནི་མེད་དེ་སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཁྱབ་པར་གནས་པར་སྣང་བར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ཞིག་ན་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་བླང་བར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་གཅིག་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དེ་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དོན་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་བོ། །སྔོན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་རི་མོའི་རྣམ་པ་འཛིན་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་གཅིག་པུའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐ་དད་པའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་དུ་མ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དུ་མ་རྣམ་གྲངས་བཞིན་དུ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཅིག་ཅར་འབྱུང་ངོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དུ་ཡང་མི་རུང་སྟེ། ཆ་ཤས་མེད་པ་དང་ལུས་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ནི། ཚུ་རོལ་དང་ཕ་རོལ་ན་གནས་པ་མི་རིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Those two also do not exist in it. Thus, for a start, that external entity of the sense-spheres of form and so forth is not single, because one apprehends contradictory properties, such as being obstructed and unobstructed. If, while possessing contradictory properties, it were still exactly single, then everything would become a single substance, and therefore they would arise and be destroyed together. It is also not multiple, because thus, if it is broken down into multiplicity, it would be differentiated into atoms, and the atoms, too, having no parts, do not abide on a far side and a near side, just like mind and mental factors. Therefore, they would not appear to abide pervading a direction; if they were to do so, therefore one must accept them as having different directional parts. If one accepts that, how could it be single? Therefore, thus, for a start, an external object is established as exactly devoid of a nature of one and multiple. A consciousness in which blue and so forth appears is also not of a single nature, because it appears to apprehend the aspect of a painting, just like multiple moments of consciousness existing in different continuums. It is also unsuitable to express that consciousnesses arise simultaneously in accordance with an enumeration of multiplicity, because for things without parts and without a body, it is illogical to abide on a near side and a far side.

དེ་ལྟར་གནས་པ་མེད་ན་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་སྣང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འོན་ཏེ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་ལ། རྣམ་པ་བརྫུན་པ་རྣམས་དེ་ལ་སྣང་བས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་གོ་བརྫུན་པ་དེ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་དེ་ལ་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར། སྣང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ལ་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དུ་གཏོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཡིན་ན་བརྫུན་བ་རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བར་ཤིན་དུ་མེད་ན་གོ་སྣང་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པ་རྣམས་བརྫུན་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་བདེན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་གཞན་ཅི་ཞིག་ལུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གཞན་རྣམ་པར་བཅད་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་བྱེ་བྲག་རྣམས་ཁོ་ན་ལ་སྤྱིར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བྱེ་བྲག་རྣམས་བརྫུན་ན་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་བརྫུན་པར་ཤིན་དུ་གསལ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པའི་ངོ་བོའི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དེ་ལ་གང་གིས་ན་དེ་ལ་ངེས་པར་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ། དེ་ལས་འབྱུང་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འབྲེལ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །འབྲེལ་པ་མེད་ན་ནི་སྣང་བར་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གཏན་ཚིགས་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

If they do not abide like that, they would not appear like that. If one says, "However, consciousness is exclusively single, and because false aspects appear to it, it does not have the fault of multiplicity," if that were so, then how would those false things appear to it? That which is called "appearing" refers to the nature of clarity. If it is a property belonging to the nature of consciousness, how could that which is false appear if it is utterly nonexistent, just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth? Therefore, if one accepts the aspects of the clear nature as exactly false, what other nature of consciousness is left over that would be true for you? There is no consciousness whatsoever called "the nature of clarity," because with reference to the exclusion of others, general designations are applied only to particulars. If the particulars are false, it would become utterly clear that everything is also false. As for aspects that do not exist, they have no connection with that true nature of consciousness by which they would definitively appear to it, either by the characteristic of being its nature or by the characteristic of arising from it. If there is no connection, it is illogical for them to appear, because it would absurdly follow too far. Therefore, the reason is also not unestablished.

དངོས་པོའི་རྣམ་པ་གཞན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འགལ་བ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟ་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་བརྟགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་དེ་ལྟར་འབྲེལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་བརྟགས་ན། །བདེན་པར་དེ་ཡི་ངོ་བོ་མེད། །འདི་ལྟར་དེ་དག་གཅིག་པུ་དང་། །དུ་མའི་ངོ་བོར་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འཕགས་པ་ལང་ཀར་གཤེགས་པ་ལས། ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མེ་ལོང་ལ། །གཅིག་དང་གཞན་ཡང་རྣམ་སྤངས་པར། །སྣང་ཡང་དེ་ན་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །དེ་ལྟར་དངོས་པོའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད། །བློ་ཡིས་རྣམ་པར་གཞིགས་ན་གོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ནི་གཟུང་དུ་མེད། །དེ་ཕྱིར་དེ་དག་བརྗོད་མེད་ཅིང་། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བཤད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་པོའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། དཔེར་ན་ཆུ་ཤིང་རློན་པའི་སྡོང་པོ་ལ། །སྙིང་པོ་འདོད་མིས་རིམ་པར་བཤིག་བྱས་ཀྱང་། །ཕྱི་དང་ནང་ན་སྙིང་པོ་ཡོད་མིན་པ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །

Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in the homologous class, it is also not contradictory. Therefore, in whatever way entities are conceptualized, in that way they unravel. For that very reason, it is explained: "However entities are conceptually examined, their nature does not exist truly. Thus they do not exist in the nature of one and multiple." The Bhagavat also stated in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: "Just as forms appear in a mirror, although utterly devoid of being one and other, yet they do not exist there; likewise, if the nature of entities is taken apart by the intellect, the nature is unapprehendable. Therefore, they are inexpressible, and are explained as also having no nature." Similarly, it is also stated in the noble Samādhirājasūtra: "For example, just as a wet trunk of a banana tree, when taken apart layer by layer by someone desiring its core, has no core inside or outside; know all dharmas to be like that."

translation: By "without abiding in form" and so forth, it extensively demonstrates exactly what a bodhisattva should not abide in when giving gifts. By the word "dharmas," the sense-sphere of dharmas is encompassed. Since they are illustrated by elaborating upon this sense-sphere, therefore the internal sense-spheres such as the eye are not mentioned. In order to teach that one should also not conceptualize things as non-arising and so forth, "Subhūti, however..." and so forth is stated; "sign" refers to an entity's own defining characteristic, that is, a mark. That, too, refers to being unarisen and so forth. Apprehending that is perception. Not conceptualizing that is not abiding in it.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

[3-40] source:
དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་མེད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་གང་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་དེ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བསྒྲིབས་པ་དང་མ་བསྒྲིབས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཆོས་འགལ་བ་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཆོས་འགལ་བ་དང་ལྡན་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་གཅིག་པ་ཉིད་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རྫས་གཅིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྱུང་བ་དང་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དུ་མ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་དུ་མར་བཤིག་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཏུ་ཐ་དད་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཆ་ཤས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུལ་རོལ་ན་གནས་པ་ནི་མེད་དེ་སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཁྱབ་པར་གནས་པར་སྣང་བར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ཞིག་ན་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་བླང་བར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་གཅིག་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དེ་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དོན་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་བོ། །སྔོན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་རི་མོའི་རྣམ་པ་འཛིན་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་གཅིག་པུའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐ་དད་པའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་དུ་མ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དུ་མ་རྣམ་གྲངས་བཞིན་དུ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཅིག་ཅར་འབྱུང་ངོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དུ་ཡང་མི་རུང་སྟེ། ཆ་ཤས་མེད་པ་དང་ལུས་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ནི། ཚུ་རོལ་དང་ཕ་རོལ་ན་གནས་པ་མི་རིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-40] translation already produced for this document:
Those two also do not exist in it. Thus, for a start, that external entity of the sense-spheres of form and so forth is not single, because one apprehends contradictory properties, such as being obstructed and unobstructed. If, while possessing contradictory properties, it were still exactly single, then everything would become a single substance, and therefore they would arise and be destroyed together. It is also not multiple, because thus, if it is broken down into multiplicity, it would be differentiated into atoms, and the atoms, too, having no parts, do not abide on a far side and a near side, just like mind and mental factors. Therefore, they would not appear to abide pervading a direction; if they were to do so, therefore one must accept them as having different directional parts. If one accepts that, how could it be single? Therefore, thus, for a start, an external object is established as exactly devoid of a nature of one and multiple. A consciousness in which blue and so forth appears is also not of a single nature, because it appears to apprehend the aspect of a painting, just like multiple moments of consciousness existing in different continuums. It is also unsuitable to express that consciousnesses arise simultaneously in accordance with an enumeration of multiplicity, because for things without parts and without a body, it is illogical to abide on a near side and a far side.

[3-41] source:
དེ་ལྟར་གནས་པ་མེད་ན་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་སྣང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འོན་ཏེ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་ལ། རྣམ་པ་བརྫུན་པ་རྣམས་དེ་ལ་སྣང་བས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་གོ་བརྫུན་པ་དེ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་དེ་ལ་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར། སྣང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ལ་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དུ་གཏོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཡིན་ན་བརྫུན་བ་རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བར་ཤིན་དུ་མེད་ན་གོ་སྣང་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པ་རྣམས་བརྫུན་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་བདེན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་གཞན་ཅི་ཞིག་ལུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གཞན་རྣམ་པར་བཅད་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་བྱེ་བྲག་རྣམས་ཁོ་ན་ལ་སྤྱིར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བྱེ་བྲག་རྣམས་བརྫུན་ན་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་བརྫུན་པར་ཤིན་དུ་གསལ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པའི་ངོ་བོའི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དེ་ལ་གང་གིས་ན་དེ་ལ་ངེས་པར་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ། དེ་ལས་འབྱུང་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འབྲེལ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །འབྲེལ་པ་མེད་ན་ནི་སྣང་བར་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གཏན་ཚིགས་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-41] translation already produced for this document:
If they do not abide like that, they would not appear like that. If one says, "However, consciousness is exclusively single, and because false aspects appear to it, it does not have the fault of multiplicity," if that were so, then how would those false things appear to it? That which is called "appearing" refers to the nature of clarity. If it is a property belonging to the nature of consciousness, how could that which is false appear if it is utterly nonexistent, just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth? Therefore, if one accepts the aspects of the clear nature as exactly false, what other nature of consciousness is left over that would be true for you? There is no consciousness whatsoever called "the nature of clarity," because with reference to the exclusion of others, general designations are applied only to particulars. If the particulars are false, it would become utterly clear that everything is also false. As for aspects that do not exist, they have no connection with that true nature of consciousness by which they would definitively appear to it, either by the characteristic of being its nature or by the characteristic of arising from it. If there is no connection, it is illogical for them to appear, because it would absurdly follow too far. Therefore, the reason is also not unestablished.

དངོས་པོའི་རྣམ་པ་གཞན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འགལ་བ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟ་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་བརྟགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་དེ་ལྟར་འབྲེལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་བརྟགས་ན། །བདེན་པར་དེ་ཡི་ངོ་བོ་མེད། །འདི་ལྟར་དེ་དག་གཅིག་པུ་དང་། །དུ་མའི་ངོ་བོར་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འཕགས་པ་ལང་ཀར་གཤེགས་པ་ལས། ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མེ་ལོང་ལ། །གཅིག་དང་གཞན་ཡང་རྣམ་སྤངས་པར། །སྣང་ཡང་དེ་ན་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །དེ་ལྟར་དངོས་པོའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད། །བློ་ཡིས་རྣམ་པར་གཞིགས་ན་གོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ནི་གཟུང་དུ་མེད། །དེ་ཕྱིར་དེ་དག་བརྗོད་མེད་ཅིང་། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བཤད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་པོའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། དཔེར་ན་ཆུ་ཤིང་རློན་པའི་སྡོང་པོ་ལ། །སྙིང་པོ་འདོད་མིས་རིམ་པར་བཤིག་བྱས་ཀྱང་། །ཕྱི་དང་ནང་ན་སྙིང་པོ་ཡོད་མིན་པ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །

Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in the homologous class, it is also not contradictory. Therefore, in whatever way entities are conceptualized, in that way they unravel. For that very reason, it is explained: "However entities are conceptually examined, their nature does not exist truly. Thus they do not exist in the nature of one and multiple." The Bhagavat also stated in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: "Just as forms appear in a mirror, although utterly devoid of being one and other, yet they do not exist there; likewise, if the nature of entities is taken apart by the intellect, the nature is unapprehendable. Therefore, they are inexpressible, and are explained as also having no nature." Similarly, it is also stated in the noble Samādhirājasūtra: "For example, just as a wet trunk of a banana tree, when taken apart layer by layer by someone desiring its core, has no core inside or outside; know all dharmas to be like that."

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: By that, the statement "without abiding in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, by all of this, profundity is also taught, and the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and deprecation is also taught. For the view of those who have apprehension, the suitability of completely perfecting the accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom is refuted; thus, whatever is given out of a desire to make offerings and to benefit generates extreme faith, but not by abiding in the non-apprehension of what is to be given, the giver, and the recipient. Thus, are what is to be given and so forth unapprehended because they do not exist, or because there is no object? In the first position, since no one gives anything whatsoever, it would absurdly follow that there is no merit. Because sentient beings would not exist, the great pains taken by bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, they are not entirely nonexistent. Because the Bhagavat sees the entities of what is to be given and so forth, it is not the case that there is no object.

Those two also do not exist in it. Thus, for a start, that external entity of the sense-spheres of form and so forth is not single, because one apprehends contradictory properties, such as being obstructed and unobstructed. If, while possessing contradictory properties, it were still exactly single, then everything would become a single substance, and therefore they would arise and be destroyed together. It is also not multiple, because thus, if it is broken down into multiplicity, it would be differentiated into atoms, and the atoms, too, having no parts, do not abide on a far side and a near side, just like mind and mental factors. Therefore, they would not appear to abide pervading a direction; if they were to do so, therefore one must accept them as having different directional parts. If one accepts that, how could it be single? Therefore, thus, for a start, an external object is established as exactly devoid of a nature of one and multiple. A consciousness in which blue and so forth appears is also not of a single nature, because it appears to apprehend the aspect of a painting, just like multiple moments of consciousness existing in different continuums. It is also unsuitable to express that consciousnesses arise simultaneously in accordance with an enumeration of multiplicity, because for things without parts and without a body, it is illogical to abide on a near side and a far side.

If they do not abide like that, they would not appear like that. If one says, "However, consciousness is exclusively single, and because false aspects appear to it, it does not have the fault of multiplicity," if that were so, then how would those false things appear to it? That which is called "appearing" refers to the nature of clarity. If it is a property belonging to the nature of consciousness, how could that which is false appear if it is utterly nonexistent, just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth? Therefore, if one accepts the aspects of the clear nature as exactly false, what other nature of consciousness is left over that would be true for you? There is no consciousness whatsoever called "the nature of clarity," because with reference to the exclusion of others, general designations are applied only to particulars. If the particulars are false, it would become utterly clear that everything is also false. As for aspects that do not exist, they have no connection with that true nature of consciousness by which they would definitively appear to it, either by the characteristic of being its nature or by the characteristic of arising from it. If there is no connection, it is illogical for them to appear, because it would absurdly follow too far. Therefore, the reason is also not unestablished.

Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in the homologous class, it is also not contradictory. Therefore, in whatever way entities are conceptualized, in that way they unravel. For that very reason, it is explained: "However entities are conceptually examined, their nature does not exist truly. Thus they do not exist in the nature of one and multiple." The Bhagavat also stated in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: "Just as forms appear in a mirror, although utterly devoid of being one and other, yet they do not exist there; likewise, if the nature of entities is taken apart by the intellect, the nature is unapprehendable. Therefore, they are inexpressible, and are explained as also having no nature." Similarly, it is also stated in the noble Samādhirājasūtra: "For example, just as a wet trunk of a banana tree, when taken apart layer by layer by someone desiring its core, has no core inside or outside; know all dharmas to be like that."

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Keeping all those objections in mind—such as, "If that were not so, how could the Bhagavat have given away his son and so forth to those who desired them?"—it was asked, "Why is that?" and in reply, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth was stated. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from correct view, because they are completely pure, accomplish an agreeable and particularly noble result, but not that arising from error. It is like the branches of ethical discipline and so forth arising from wrong view. Because the entities of what is to be given and so forth do not exist whatsoever in the manner just mentioned, apprehending them is solely an error, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the modes of the perfections arising from that are of little power because they arise from impure causes, like giving and so forth arising from the error of self and what is mine. The non-apprehension of what have become objects of apprehension, such as what is to be given, is unmistaken because its object is genuine reality, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, because it arises from extensive causes, giving and so forth from that have a great result, like a sprout and so forth manifesting from a viable seed.

Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in the homologous class, it is also not contradictory. Therefore, in whatever way entities are conceptualized, in that way they unravel. For that very reason, it is explained: "However entities are conceptually examined, their nature does not exist truly. Thus they do not exist in the nature of one and multiple." The Bhagavat also stated in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: "Just as forms appear in a mirror, although utterly devoid of being one and other, yet they do not exist there; likewise, if the nature of entities is taken apart by the intellect, the nature is unapprehendable. Therefore, they are inexpressible, and are explained as also having no nature." Similarly, it is also stated in the noble Samādhirājasūtra: "For example, just as a wet trunk of a banana tree, when taken apart layer by layer by someone desiring its core, has no core inside or outside; know all dharmas to be like that."

Therefore, since all entities are like an illusion, pleasant when unexamined, one should thus give gifts without being attached. The meaning that "it is not by abiding in entities" is logical here. That being so, the application to giving and so forth is fully taught as it truly exists, but not otherwise. Lest one think, "If, because there are no entities whatsoever ultimately, one should not give gifts by abiding in entities, one should surely give gifts with attachment to non-entities," it is stated: "without abiding in anything whatsoever." A bodhisattva should also abandon the conceptualization of non-entities, because if there is no apprehension of entities, that does not exist. Conventionally, what is to be given, the giver, and so forth exist; therefore, the intention is that attachment to non-entities is also illogical.

By "without abiding in form" and so forth, it extensively demonstrates exactly what a bodhisattva should not abide in when giving gifts. By the word "dharmas," the sense-sphere of dharmas is encompassed. Since they are illustrated by elaborating upon this sense-sphere, therefore the internal sense-spheres such as the eye are not mentioned. In order to teach that one should also not conceptualize things as non-arising and so forth, "Subhūti, however..." and so forth is stated; "sign" refers to an entity's own defining characteristic, that is, a mark. That, too, refers to being unarisen and so forth. Apprehending that is perception. Not conceptualizing that is not abiding in it.

དེས་ནི་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་འདིས་ཟབ་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ལ། སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པ་དང་སྐུར་བ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་དགག་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དམིགས་པ་ཅན་རྣམས་ལྟ་བ་འདི་ལ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་བྱ་བར་རུང་བ་བཀག་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་མཆོད་པ་དང་ཕན་གདགས་པར་འདོད་པས་གང་བྱིན་པ་དེ་ཤིན་དུ་དང་བ་བསྐྱེད་ཀྱི། སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ་པོ་དང་། ལེན་པ་པོ་མི་དམིགས་པ་ལ་གནས་པས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལྟར་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མི་དམིགས་སམ་འོན་ཏེ་ཡུལ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་སུས་ཅི་ཡང་བྱིན་པ་མེད་པས་བསོད་ནམས་མེད་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་ཅན་དག་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་ཡོངས་སུ་ངལ་བར་བྱས་པ་དེ་ཡང་དོན་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་གཟིགས་པས་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-45] translation already produced for this document:
By that, the statement "without abiding in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, by all of this, profundity is also taught, and the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and deprecation is also taught. For the view of those who have apprehension, the suitability of completely perfecting the accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom is refuted; thus, whatever is given out of a desire to make offerings and to benefit generates extreme faith, but not by abiding in the non-apprehension of what is to be given, the giver, and the recipient. Thus, are what is to be given and so forth unapprehended because they do not exist, or because there is no object? In the first position, since no one gives anything whatsoever, it would absurdly follow that there is no merit. Because sentient beings would not exist, the great pains taken by bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, they are not entirely nonexistent. Because the Bhagavat sees the entities of what is to be given and so forth, it is not the case that there is no object.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Therefore, giving and so forth that abide in non-apprehension, because they arise from correct view, generate extreme faith for the wise, but not otherwise. It is also not asserted that what is to be given and so forth are completely nonexistent—whereby, because of not engaging in giving and so forth, there would be no merit—because they are accepted to exist conventionally. In the state of not being in meditative equipoise, because they are apprehended as illusion-like, it is also not the case that there is no apprehension in all respects. At that time as well, it is posited as non-apprehension arising from resolve. In the state of meditative equipoise, there is solely complete non-apprehension; at that time, engaging in giving and so forth is not accepted, but because actions are performed in the state of initial application or by those who have arisen from equipoise, objections are inappropriate. Because of its great result, this states the extensiveness of the application to the perfections. Because the entities of cause and result are presented conventionally, the extreme of deprecation is also thereby refuted. In three ways, merit is equal to space: because of being all-pervasive, being extensive, and being inexhaustible. Because it generates mundane and supramundane merit, it is all-pervasive; mundane merit is generated by the state of not being in meditative equipoise. Supramundane merit is generated by the state of meditative equipoise. Because it becomes distinguished with superior qualities, it is extensive. Because it will not be completely depleted as long as saṃsāra lasts, it is inexhaustible.

དངོས་པོའི་རྣམ་པ་གཞན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འགལ་བ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟ་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་བརྟགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་དེ་ལྟར་འབྲེལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་བརྟགས་ན། །བདེན་པར་དེ་ཡི་ངོ་བོ་མེད། །འདི་ལྟར་དེ་དག་གཅིག་པུ་དང་། །དུ་མའི་ངོ་བོར་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འཕགས་པ་ལང་ཀར་གཤེགས་པ་ལས། ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མེ་ལོང་ལ། །གཅིག་དང་གཞན་ཡང་རྣམ་སྤངས་པར། །སྣང་ཡང་དེ་ན་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །དེ་ལྟར་དངོས་པོའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད། །བློ་ཡིས་རྣམ་པར་གཞིགས་ན་གོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ནི་གཟུང་དུ་མེད། །དེ་ཕྱིར་དེ་དག་བརྗོད་མེད་ཅིང་། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བཤད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་པོའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། དཔེར་ན་ཆུ་ཤིང་རློན་པའི་སྡོང་པོ་ལ། །སྙིང་པོ་འདོད་མིས་རིམ་པར་བཤིག་བྱས་ཀྱང་། །ཕྱི་དང་ནང་ན་སྙིང་པོ་ཡོད་མིན་པ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །
[3-42] translation already produced for this document:
Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is also not inconclusive. Because it exists in the homologous class, it is also not contradictory. Therefore, in whatever way entities are conceptualized, in that way they unravel. For that very reason, it is explained: "However entities are conceptually examined, their nature does not exist truly. Thus they do not exist in the nature of one and multiple." The Bhagavat also stated in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: "Just as forms appear in a mirror, although utterly devoid of being one and other, yet they do not exist there; likewise, if the nature of entities is taken apart by the intellect, the nature is unapprehendable. Therefore, they are inexpressible, and are explained as also having no nature." Similarly, it is also stated in the noble Samādhirājasūtra: "For example, just as a wet trunk of a banana tree, when taken apart layer by layer by someone desiring its core, has no core inside or outside; know all dharmas to be like that."

[3-43] source:
དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དངོས་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྒྱུ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་མ་བརྟགས་ན་དགའ་བ་ཡིན་པས་དེ་ལྟར་མངོན་པར་མ་ཞེན་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ། །དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་འདི་འདིར་རིགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་གཞན་དུ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དོན་དམ་པར་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ཡང་མེད་པས་དངོས་པོ་ལ་གནས་པས་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་མི་བྱ་ན་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལྟ་ཞིག་སྙམ་པ་ལས། ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པར་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་ཡང་སྤང་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོར་འཛིན་པ་མེད་ན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ནི་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡོད་དེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ཡང་མི་རིགས་པར་དགོངས་པའོ། །
[3-43] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, since all entities are like an illusion, pleasant when unexamined, one should thus give gifts without being attached. The meaning that "it is not by abiding in entities" is logical here. That being so, the application to giving and so forth is fully taught as it truly exists, but not otherwise. Lest one think, "If, because there are no entities whatsoever ultimately, one should not give gifts by abiding in entities, one should surely give gifts with attachment to non-entities," it is stated: "without abiding in anything whatsoever." A bodhisattva should also abandon the conceptualization of non-entities, because if there is no apprehension of entities, that does not exist. Conventionally, what is to be given, the giver, and so forth exist; therefore, the intention is that attachment to non-entities is also illogical.

By that, the statement "without abiding in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, by all of this, profundity is also taught, and the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and deprecation is also taught. For the view of those who have apprehension, the suitability of completely perfecting the accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom is refuted; thus, whatever is given out of a desire to make offerings and to benefit generates extreme faith, but not by abiding in the non-apprehension of what is to be given, the giver, and the recipient. Thus, are what is to be given and so forth unapprehended because they do not exist, or because there is no object? In the first position, since no one gives anything whatsoever, it would absurdly follow that there is no merit. Because sentient beings would not exist, the great pains taken by bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, they are not entirely nonexistent. Because the Bhagavat sees the entities of what is to be given and so forth, it is not the case that there is no object.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Fearing the objection, "If, because it does not exist, giving is to be given without abiding in form, then how should a bodhisattva who desires to obtain the form body of the Tathāgata engage in giving and so forth?", the passage beginning, "Subhūti, what do you think?" teaches the basis for aspiring to obtain the form body; here, by implication, it clears away the discordant class characterized by the pride of manifesting as a Tathāgata with respect to the form body.
