དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་འདོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སྲས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་བར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་རྒོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་མཐའ་དག་སེམས་ལ་བཞག་ནས། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་ལན་དུ། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དགོངས་པ་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཡང་དག་པའི་ལྟ་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིད་དུ་འོང་བ་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་མངོན་པར་འགྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ནས་འབྱུང་བས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ལོག་པར་ལྟ་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་སྨོས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ན་གང་ཡང་མེད་པས་དེར་དམིགས་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། སྨིག་རྒྱུ་ལ་ཆུར་དམིགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་བས་ན་དེ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཚུལ་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་བདག་དང་བདག་གིར་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་རྒྱུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་སྟོབས་ཆུང་བའོ། །སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དམིགས་པའི་རིག་བྱར་གྱུར་པ་མི་དམིགས་པ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་གྱིས་ཡུལ་ཡིན་པས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པ་སྟེ། སྨིག་རྒྱུ་ལ་ཆུར་དམིགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རྒྱས་པའི་རྒྱུ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ལས་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ས་བོན་གྲུང་པོ་ལས་མངོན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་མྱུ་གུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
[3-46] translation already produced for this document:
Keeping all those objections in mind—such as, "If that were not so, how could the Bhagavat have given away his son and so forth to those who desired them?"—it was asked, "Why is that?" and in reply, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth was stated. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from correct view, because they are completely pure, accomplish an agreeable and particularly noble result, but not that arising from error. It is like the branches of ethical discipline and so forth arising from wrong view. Because the entities of what is to be given and so forth do not exist whatsoever in the manner just mentioned, apprehending them is solely an error, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the modes of the perfections arising from that are of little power because they arise from impure causes, like giving and so forth arising from the error of self and what is mine. The non-apprehension of what have become objects of apprehension, such as what is to be given, is unmistaken because its object is genuine reality, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, because it arises from extensive causes, giving and so forth from that have a great result, like a sprout and so forth manifesting from a viable seed.

[3-47] source:
དེ་བས་ན་མི་དམིགས་པ་ལ་གནས་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའི་ལྟ་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཤིན་དུ་དང་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གང་གིས་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་མི་འཇུག་པའི་ཕྱིར་བསོད་ནམས་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་འདོད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡོད་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཉམ་པར་མ་བཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཚེ་ན་ཡང་མོས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་མི་དམིགས་པར་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་གོ། །མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་ནི་ཤིན་ཏུ་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། དེའི་ཚེ་ན་ནི་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པར་འཇུག་པར་ཁས་མི་ལེན་གྱི། དང་པོ་སྦྱོར་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་སམ། །ལངས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་བྱ་བས་ཀླན་ཀར་མི་རུང་ངོ་། །འདིས་ནི་འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་དངོས་པོ་ཉེ་བར་སྟོན་པས་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་བཀག་པར་ཡང་གྱུར་ཏོ། །རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་ན་བསོད་ནམས་ནམ་མཁའ་དང་མཚུངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་སོང་བ་དང་། རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་དང་། མི་ཟད་པས་སོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་དང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་བསྐྱེད་པས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་སོང་བ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ནི་མཉམ་པར་མ་གཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་བསྐྱེད་དོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པ་ནི་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་སོ། །ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པར་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །འཁོར་བ་ཇི་སྲིད་ཀྱི་བར་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏུགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བས་མི་ཟད་པའོ། །
[3-47] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, giving and so forth that abide in non-apprehension, because they arise from correct view, generate extreme faith for the wise, but not otherwise. It is also not asserted that what is to be given and so forth are completely nonexistent—whereby, because of not engaging in giving and so forth, there would be no merit—because they are accepted to exist conventionally. In the state of not being in meditative equipoise, because they are apprehended as illusion-like, it is also not the case that there is no apprehension in all respects. At that time as well, it is posited as non-apprehension arising from resolve. In the state of meditative equipoise, there is solely complete non-apprehension; at that time, engaging in giving and so forth is not accepted, but because actions are performed in the state of initial application or by those who have arisen from equipoise, objections are inappropriate. Because of its great result, this states the extensiveness of the application to the perfections. Because the entities of cause and result are presented conventionally, the extreme of deprecation is also thereby refuted. In three ways, merit is equal to space: because of being all-pervasive, being extensive, and being inexhaustible. Because it generates mundane and supramundane merit, it is all-pervasive; mundane merit is generated by the state of not being in meditative equipoise. Supramundane merit is generated by the state of meditative equipoise. Because it becomes distinguished with superior qualities, it is extensive. Because it will not be completely depleted as long as saṃsāra lasts, it is inexhaustible.

source: མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཚན་དང་དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོས་བརྒྱན་པ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་མཚན་རྣམས་ནི་ཕྱག་དང་ཞབས་ལ་འཁོར་ལོ་མངའ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ཏེ། ཚིག་མངས་ཀྱིས་དོགས་པས་མ་བྲིས་ཀྱི་མདོ་ལས་ཇི་སྐད་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །དེ་དག་ཀྱང་ཡུལ་ན་གནས་པ་དང་། གསལ་བ་དང་། རྫོགས་པས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོ་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་དག་ནི་སེན་མོ་ཟངས་ཀྱི་མདོག་འདྲ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། མདོ་ལས་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །མཚན་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་བཞིན་དུ་བརྫུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་ཏོ། །འདི་ལྟར་མཚན་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་བསགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དམ། དེས་བརྩམས་པ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་གྱི་གཟུགས་ཞིག་ཏུ་གྱུར་གྲང་ན། རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་སྔར་བཤིག་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཉིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་པ་མེད་ན་དེས་ན་བརྩམས་པ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། སྒྲིབ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འགལ་བའི་ཆོས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་དག་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་སྨྲས་པ་ལས་དགོངས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས། དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་ཏེ་ཞེས་གསལ་ཏོ། །གལ་ཏེ་མཚན་རྣམས་བརྫུན་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན་འོ་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མདོ་སྡེ་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ལས་མཚན་རྣམས་གསུངས་སྙམ་དུ་བསམས་ཤིང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། དེ་ཉིད་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨྲས་ཏེ། མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་དོན་དམ་པར་གསུངས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་བཞིན་དུ་དེས་བརྫུན་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཁོ་ནར་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་སྨྲས་པའི་དོན་དེ་ཉིད་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བསྐང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཇི་ཙམ་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །
translation: By completely stating merely the marks as "the excellence of the marks," the entirety of the Tathāgata's form body adorned with the marks and excellent signs is completely taught. In that regard, the marks are the thirty-two, such as having a wheel on the hands and feet; fearing wordiness they are not written here, but you should understand them just as they appear in the sūtra. Those are also excellent because they abide in their domain, are clear, and are complete. The eighty excellent signs are the nails being like the color of copper and so forth; you should know them as they appear in the sūtra. Those marks and so forth are also false, like the marks of a magically emanated Buddha. Therefore, it is taught that one should abide by aspiration and prayer for such a form body. Thus, if one wonders whether those marks are the very nature of accumulated subtle particles, or have become a whole form composed by them: first, the first position is not the case, because the subtle particles have already been dismantled earlier. The second is also not the case. If there is no composer, then there is no whole form composed by it, and because contradictory phenomena explained earlier, such as obscuration, are apprehended. Therefore, based on what was said, the intention was stated; examining that, Subhūti clarified, "It is not." Thinking, "If the marks are solely false, then the Bhagavat spoke of the marks in various sūtras," and having asked, "Why is that?", he said, "Because that itself is without the excellence of the marks"; the meaning of these words is that the excellence of the marks was not spoken of ultimately, but like a magically emanated Buddha, he spoke of them solely as a false nature. By that, the statement "without abiding in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, by all of this, profundity is also taught, and the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and deprecation is also taught. For the view of those who have apprehension, the suitability of completely perfecting the accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom is refuted; thus, whatever is given out of a desire to make offerings and to benefit generates extreme faith, but not by abiding in the non-apprehension of what is to be given, the giver, and the recipient. Thus, are what is to be given and so forth unapprehended because they do not exist, or because there is no object? In the first position, since no one gives anything whatsoever, it would absurdly follow that there is no merit. Because sentient beings would not exist, the great pains taken by bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, they are not entirely nonexistent. Because the Bhagavat sees the entities of what is to be given and so forth, it is not the case that there is no object.

Keeping all those objections in mind—such as, "If that were not so, how could the Bhagavat have given away his son and so forth to those who desired them?"—it was asked, "Why is that?" and in reply, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth was stated. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from correct view, because they are completely pure, accomplish an agreeable and particularly noble result, but not that arising from error. It is like the branches of ethical discipline and so forth arising from wrong view. Because the entities of what is to be given and so forth do not exist whatsoever in the manner just mentioned, apprehending them is solely an error, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the modes of the perfections arising from that are of little power because they arise from impure causes, like giving and so forth arising from the error of self and what is mine. The non-apprehension of what have become objects of apprehension, such as what is to be given, is unmistaken because its object is genuine reality, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, because it arises from extensive causes, giving and so forth from that have a great result, like a sprout and so forth manifesting from a viable seed.

དེ་བས་ན་མི་དམིགས་པ་ལ་གནས་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའི་ལྟ་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཤིན་དུ་དང་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གང་གིས་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་མི་འཇུག་པའི་ཕྱིར་བསོད་ནམས་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་འདོད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡོད་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཉམ་པར་མ་བཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཚེ་ན་ཡང་མོས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་མི་དམིགས་པར་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་གོ། །མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་ནི་ཤིན་ཏུ་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། དེའི་ཚེ་ན་ནི་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པར་འཇུག་པར་ཁས་མི་ལེན་གྱི། དང་པོ་སྦྱོར་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་སམ། །ལངས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་བྱ་བས་ཀླན་ཀར་མི་རུང་ངོ་། །འདིས་ནི་འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་དངོས་པོ་ཉེ་བར་སྟོན་པས་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་བཀག་པར་ཡང་གྱུར་ཏོ། །རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་ན་བསོད་ནམས་ནམ་མཁའ་དང་མཚུངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་སོང་བ་དང་། རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་དང་། མི་ཟད་པས་སོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་དང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་བསྐྱེད་པས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་སོང་བ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ནི་མཉམ་པར་མ་གཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་བསྐྱེད་དོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པ་ནི་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་སོ། །ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པར་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །འཁོར་བ་ཇི་སྲིད་ཀྱི་བར་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏུགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བས་མི་ཟད་པའོ། །

Therefore, giving and so forth that abide in non-apprehension, because they arise from correct view, generate extreme faith for the wise, but not otherwise. It is also not asserted that what is to be given and so forth are completely nonexistent—whereby, because of not engaging in giving and so forth, there would be no merit—because they are accepted to exist conventionally. In the state of not being in meditative equipoise, because they are apprehended as illusion-like, it is also not the case that there is no apprehension in all respects. At that time as well, it is posited as non-apprehension arising from resolve. In the state of meditative equipoise, there is solely complete non-apprehension; at that time, engaging in giving and so forth is not accepted, but because actions are performed in the state of initial application or by those who have arisen from equipoise, objections are inappropriate. Because of its great result, this states the extensiveness of the application to the perfections. Because the entities of cause and result are presented conventionally, the extreme of deprecation is also thereby refuted. In three ways, merit is equal to space: because of being all-pervasive, being extensive, and being inexhaustible. Because it generates mundane and supramundane merit, it is all-pervasive; mundane merit is generated by the state of not being in meditative equipoise. Supramundane merit is generated by the state of meditative equipoise. Because it becomes distinguished with superior qualities, it is extensive. Because it will not be completely depleted as long as saṃsāra lasts, it is inexhaustible.

By that, the statement "without abiding in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, by all of this, profundity is also taught, and the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and deprecation is also taught. For the view of those who have apprehension, the suitability of completely perfecting the accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom is refuted; thus, whatever is given out of a desire to make offerings and to benefit generates extreme faith, but not by abiding in the non-apprehension of what is to be given, the giver, and the recipient. Thus, are what is to be given and so forth unapprehended because they do not exist, or because there is no object? In the first position, since no one gives anything whatsoever, it would absurdly follow that there is no merit. Because sentient beings would not exist, the great pains taken by bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, they are not entirely nonexistent. Because the Bhagavat sees the entities of what is to be given and so forth, it is not the case that there is no object.

Keeping all those objections in mind—such as, "If that were not so, how could the Bhagavat have given away his son and so forth to those who desired them?"—it was asked, "Why is that?" and in reply, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth was stated. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from correct view, because they are completely pure, accomplish an agreeable and particularly noble result, but not that arising from error. It is like the branches of ethical discipline and so forth arising from wrong view. Because the entities of what is to be given and so forth do not exist whatsoever in the manner just mentioned, apprehending them is solely an error, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the modes of the perfections arising from that are of little power because they arise from impure causes, like giving and so forth arising from the error of self and what is mine. The non-apprehension of what have become objects of apprehension, such as what is to be given, is unmistaken because its object is genuine reality, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, because it arises from extensive causes, giving and so forth from that have a great result, like a sprout and so forth manifesting from a viable seed.

Therefore, giving and so forth that abide in non-apprehension, because they arise from correct view, generate extreme faith for the wise, but not otherwise. It is also not asserted that what is to be given and so forth are completely nonexistent—whereby, because of not engaging in giving and so forth, there would be no merit—because they are accepted to exist conventionally. In the state of not being in meditative equipoise, because they are apprehended as illusion-like, it is also not the case that there is no apprehension in all respects. At that time as well, it is posited as non-apprehension arising from resolve. In the state of meditative equipoise, there is solely complete non-apprehension; at that time, engaging in giving and so forth is not accepted, but because actions are performed in the state of initial application or by those who have arisen from equipoise, objections are inappropriate. Because of its great result, this states the extensiveness of the application to the perfections. Because the entities of cause and result are presented conventionally, the extreme of deprecation is also thereby refuted. In three ways, merit is equal to space: because of being all-pervasive, being extensive, and being inexhaustible. Because it generates mundane and supramundane merit, it is all-pervasive; mundane merit is generated by the state of not being in meditative equipoise. Supramundane merit is generated by the state of meditative equipoise. Because it becomes distinguished with superior qualities, it is extensive. Because it will not be completely depleted as long as saṃsāra lasts, it is inexhaustible.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: "As many as are without the excellence of the marks" should be understood as being explained by reversing that. By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. This shows how, having abandoned the two extremes, the mind should be firmly held here: "Thus" means that the Tathāgata should be viewed by the marks like a magically emanated Buddha. This clears away the extreme of deprecation, because the Bhagavat's form body is not deprecated conventionally. "Without marks" is to be viewed ultimately, because no marks whatsoever are established. This clears away the extreme of superimposition. By offering prayers in order to obtain the Tathāgata's form body, extensiveness is stated. Because of not apprehending that, it is profound. The basis for aspiring to obtain the form body has been explained.

By that, the statement "without abiding in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, by all of this, profundity is also taught, and the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and deprecation is also taught. For the view of those who have apprehension, the suitability of completely perfecting the accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom is refuted; thus, whatever is given out of a desire to make offerings and to benefit generates extreme faith, but not by abiding in the non-apprehension of what is to be given, the giver, and the recipient. Thus, are what is to be given and so forth unapprehended because they do not exist, or because there is no object? In the first position, since no one gives anything whatsoever, it would absurdly follow that there is no merit. Because sentient beings would not exist, the great pains taken by bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, they are not entirely nonexistent. Because the Bhagavat sees the entities of what is to be given and so forth, it is not the case that there is no object.

Keeping all those objections in mind—such as, "If that were not so, how could the Bhagavat have given away his son and so forth to those who desired them?"—it was asked, "Why is that?" and in reply, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth was stated. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from correct view, because they are completely pure, accomplish an agreeable and particularly noble result, but not that arising from error. It is like the branches of ethical discipline and so forth arising from wrong view. Because the entities of what is to be given and so forth do not exist whatsoever in the manner just mentioned, apprehending them is solely an error, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the modes of the perfections arising from that are of little power because they arise from impure causes, like giving and so forth arising from the error of self and what is mine. The non-apprehension of what have become objects of apprehension, such as what is to be given, is unmistaken because its object is genuine reality, like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, because it arises from extensive causes, giving and so forth from that have a great result, like a sprout and so forth manifesting from a viable seed.

Therefore, giving and so forth that abide in non-apprehension, because they arise from correct view, generate extreme faith for the wise, but not otherwise. It is also not asserted that what is to be given and so forth are completely nonexistent—whereby, because of not engaging in giving and so forth, there would be no merit—because they are accepted to exist conventionally. In the state of not being in meditative equipoise, because they are apprehended as illusion-like, it is also not the case that there is no apprehension in all respects. At that time as well, it is posited as non-apprehension arising from resolve. In the state of meditative equipoise, there is solely complete non-apprehension; at that time, engaging in giving and so forth is not accepted, but because actions are performed in the state of initial application or by those who have arisen from equipoise, objections are inappropriate. Because of its great result, this states the extensiveness of the application to the perfections. Because the entities of cause and result are presented conventionally, the extreme of deprecation is also thereby refuted. In three ways, merit is equal to space: because of being all-pervasive, being extensive, and being inexhaustible. Because it generates mundane and supramundane merit, it is all-pervasive; mundane merit is generated by the state of not being in meditative equipoise. Supramundane merit is generated by the state of meditative equipoise. Because it becomes distinguished with superior qualities, it is extensive. Because it will not be completely depleted as long as saṃsāra lasts, it is inexhaustible.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The dharma body is of two types: the dharma body of teaching and the dharma body of realization. The dharma body of realization is also of two types: that which has gnosis as its cause and that which has merit as its cause.

"As many as are without the excellence of the marks" should be understood as being explained by reversing that. By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. This shows how, having abandoned the two extremes, the mind should be firmly held here: "Thus" means that the Tathāgata should be viewed by the marks like a magically emanated Buddha. This clears away the extreme of deprecation, because the Bhagavat's form body is not deprecated conventionally. "Without marks" is to be viewed ultimately, because no marks whatsoever are established. This clears away the extreme of superimposition. By offering prayers in order to obtain the Tathāgata's form body, extensiveness is stated. Because of not apprehending that, it is profound. The basis for aspiring to obtain the form body has been explained.

translation: In that regard, fearing that future beings would not believe in the dharma body of teaching because the five degenerations would be predominant and because a jewel of dharma such as this has an extremely profound and extensive result, he asked, "Are there...?" The words "Are there..." should be connected with the meaning of the words "will there appear any sentient beings whatsoever who will produce a true perception with respect to the teaching of the dharma of a sūtra such as this?" As for "the last five hundred," a collection of five hundreds is five hundred; since it is renowned that the Bhagavat's teaching will remain for five periods of five hundred years, he specified "the last," because at that time the five degenerations will be predominant.

By completely stating merely the marks as "the excellence of the marks," the entirety of the Tathāgata's form body adorned with the marks and excellent signs is completely taught. In that regard, the marks are the thirty-two, such as having a wheel on the hands and feet; fearing wordiness they are not written here, but you should understand them just as they appear in the sūtra. Those are also excellent because they abide in their domain, are clear, and are complete. The eighty excellent signs are the nails being like the color of copper and so forth; you should know them as they appear in the sūtra. Those marks and so forth are also false, like the marks of a magically emanated Buddha. Therefore, it is taught that one should abide by aspiration and prayer for such a form body. Thus, if one wonders whether those marks are the very nature of accumulated subtle particles, or have become a whole form composed by them: first, the first position is not the case, because the subtle particles have already been dismantled earlier. The second is also not the case. If there is no composer, then there is no whole form composed by it, and because contradictory phenomena explained earlier, such as obscuration, are apprehended. Therefore, based on what was said, the intention was stated; examining that, Subhūti clarified, "It is not." Thinking, "If the marks are solely false, then the Bhagavat spoke of the marks in various sūtras," and having asked, "Why is that?", he said, "Because that itself is without the excellence of the marks"; the meaning of these words is that the excellence of the marks was not spoken of ultimately, but like a magically emanated Buddha, he spoke of them solely as a false nature. In order to fulfill that very meaning spoken by the noble Subhūti, the Bhagavat stated the passage beginning, "As many as..."

"As many as are without the excellence of the marks" should be understood as being explained by reversing that. By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. This shows how, having abandoned the two extremes, the mind should be firmly held here: "Thus" means that the Tathāgata should be viewed by the marks like a magically emanated Buddha. This clears away the extreme of deprecation, because the Bhagavat's form body is not deprecated conventionally. "Without marks" is to be viewed ultimately, because no marks whatsoever are established. This clears away the extreme of superimposition. By offering prayers in order to obtain the Tathāgata's form body, extensiveness is stated. Because of not apprehending that, it is profound. The basis for aspiring to obtain the form body has been explained.

source: དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པ་ནི་མོས་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ལུང་ནོད་པ་དང་། འཆད་པ་དང་།ཉན་པ་དང་། སེམས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉམས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མདོ་སྡེ་བསྟན་པའི་ངག་རྣམས་ཏེ། འདི་དག་གིས་དོན་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་དག་ནི་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཤད་པ་འདིར་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །བཤད་པ་དག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དང་པོ་ལྟར་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནི་དོན་སྟོན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འདིར་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་འདི་ཡང་དག་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མི་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྲུབ་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཐོགས་པ་མེད་པར་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གཟིགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱི་དོགས་པ་དེ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་སོ། །
translation: "The thorough destruction of the true dharma" is the decline of devotion, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, explaining, listening, thinking, and so forth. "Such as this" means the profound and extensive meaning. "The words of the sūtra" are the statements that teach the sūtra, because by these the meaning is realized and made known. This complete statement of merely a sign completely teaches the entirety of the dharma body of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" refers to what is to be expressed. As for "the teaching" here, it is connected to "such as this," meaning profound and extensive. "Upon the teachings" means "upon the expressions" according to the first. For the second, it means "upon those which teach the meaning." Conceiving the meaning unmistakably is here "true perception," but it does not apply to perceiving "this is true" by adhering to it literally. By this, if the meaning is established, it clears away untrue perception. Because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects, the Bhagavat sees those who will appear as if directly; in order to clear away Subhūti's doubt, he said, "they will appear." "Great beings" was said in order to truly teach their bodhisattva qualities.

Fearing the objection, "If, because it does not exist, giving is to be given without abiding in form, then how should a bodhisattva who desires to obtain the form body of the Tathāgata engage in giving and so forth?", the passage beginning, "Subhūti, what do you think?" teaches the basis for aspiring to obtain the form body; here, by implication, it clears away the discordant class characterized by the pride of manifesting as a Tathāgata with respect to the form body.

མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཚན་དང་དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོས་བརྒྱན་པ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་མཚན་རྣམས་ནི་ཕྱག་དང་ཞབས་ལ་འཁོར་ལོ་མངའ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ཏེ། ཚིག་མངས་ཀྱིས་དོགས་པས་མ་བྲིས་ཀྱི་མདོ་ལས་ཇི་སྐད་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །དེ་དག་ཀྱང་ཡུལ་ན་གནས་པ་དང་། གསལ་བ་དང་། རྫོགས་པས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོ་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་དག་ནི་སེན་མོ་ཟངས་ཀྱི་མདོག་འདྲ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། མདོ་ལས་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །མཚན་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་བཞིན་དུ་བརྫུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་ཏོ། །འདི་ལྟར་མཚན་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་བསགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དམ། དེས་བརྩམས་པ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་གྱི་གཟུགས་ཞིག་ཏུ་གྱུར་གྲང་ན། རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་སྔར་བཤིག་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཉིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་པ་མེད་ན་དེས་ན་བརྩམས་པ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། སྒྲིབ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འགལ་བའི་ཆོས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་དག་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་སྨྲས་པ་ལས་དགོངས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས། དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་ཏེ་ཞེས་གསལ་ཏོ། །གལ་ཏེ་མཚན་རྣམས་བརྫུན་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན་འོ་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མདོ་སྡེ་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ལས་མཚན་རྣམས་གསུངས་སྙམ་དུ་བསམས་ཤིང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། དེ་ཉིད་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨྲས་ཏེ། མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་དོན་དམ་པར་གསུངས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་བཞིན་དུ་དེས་བརྫུན་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཁོ་ནར་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་སྨྲས་པའི་དོན་དེ་ཉིད་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བསྐང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཇི་ཙམ་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །
[3-49] translation already produced for this document:
By completely stating merely the marks as "the excellence of the marks," the entirety of the Tathāgata's form body adorned with the marks and excellent signs is completely taught. In that regard, the marks are the thirty-two, such as having a wheel on the hands and feet; fearing wordiness they are not written here, but you should understand them just as they appear in the sūtra. Those are also excellent because they abide in their domain, are clear, and are complete. The eighty excellent signs are the nails being like the color of copper and so forth; you should know them as they appear in the sūtra. Those marks and so forth are also false, like the marks of a magically emanated Buddha. Therefore, it is taught that one should abide by aspiration and prayer for such a form body. Thus, if one wonders whether those marks are the very nature of accumulated subtle particles, or have become a whole form composed by them: first, the first position is not the case, because the subtle particles have already been dismantled earlier. The second is also not the case. If there is no composer, then there is no whole form composed by it, and because contradictory phenomena explained earlier, such as obscuration, are apprehended. Therefore, based on what was said, the intention was stated; examining that, Subhūti clarified, "It is not." Thinking, "If the marks are solely false, then the Bhagavat spoke of the marks in various sūtras," and having asked, "Why is that?", he said, "Because that itself is without the excellence of the marks"; the meaning of these words is that the excellence of the marks was not spoken of ultimately, but like a magically emanated Buddha, he spoke of them solely as a false nature. In order to fulfill that very meaning spoken by the noble Subhūti, the Bhagavat stated the passage beginning, "As many as..."

ཇི་ཙམ་དུ་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཟློག་སྟེ་བཤད་པར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་འདི་ལ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐའ་གཉིས་སྤངས་ནས་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་བཞིན་དུ་མཚན་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་སེལ་ཏེ། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་སྐུར་པ་མི་འདེབས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་མེད་པ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། མཚན་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པའི་མཐའ་བསལ་ཏོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་སྨོན་ལམ་འདེབས་པས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །དེ་མི་དམིགས་པས་ནི་ཟབ་པའོ། །གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་གནས་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །
[3-51] translation already produced for this document:
"As many as are without the excellence of the marks" should be understood as being explained by reversing that. By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. This shows how, having abandoned the two extremes, the mind should be firmly held here: "Thus" means that the Tathāgata should be viewed by the marks like a magically emanated Buddha. This clears away the extreme of deprecation, because the Bhagavat's form body is not deprecated conventionally. "Without marks" is to be viewed ultimately, because no marks whatsoever are established. This clears away the extreme of superimposition. By offering prayers in order to obtain the Tathāgata's form body, extensiveness is stated. Because of not apprehending that, it is profound. The basis for aspiring to obtain the form body has been explained.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
source: དེ་དག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་། རྒྱུ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་འདུ་ཤེས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ལྷག་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་སེམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་ཏེ། བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ལོགས་ཤིག་དུ་སྨོས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི་འདིར་བསམ་གཏན་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཟུང་སྟེ། བ་ལང་དང་གླང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་དུའོ། །ཕྱི་མའི་དུས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་ནི་ན་བཟའ་དང་ཞལ་ཟས་ལ་སོགས་པས་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་དང་། གདུགས་དང་རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་བ་དན་ལ་སོགས་པས་མཆོད་པའོ། །
translation: What kind of accomplishment they have, by what kind of causes they truly accomplish it, what kind of being embraced by spiritual friends they possess, and by what kind of true perception they will perceive, the Bhagavat completely teaches: by this passage "possessing discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom," it is taught that they possess the accomplishment of the three trainings, in order, as higher discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The reason discipline and wisdom are mentioned separately is that "qualities" here takes up those arising from concentration, in the manner of saying "cows and bulls". If one wonders how such possessors of qualities like discipline will appear in that afflicted later time, the passage beginning "Subhūti..." was spoken. "Having venerated" is to have venerated with robes, food, and so forth, and to have made offerings with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. This shows how, having abandoned the two extremes, the mind should be firmly held here: "Thus" means that the Tathāgata should be viewed by the marks like a magically emanated Buddha. "Without marks" is to be viewed ultimately, because no marks whatsoever are established. This clears away the extreme of superimposition. The basis for aspiring to obtain the form body has been explained.

translation: "Planting roots of virtue" should be viewed in terms of earnestly practicing the excellence of qualities such as discipline, having received instructions and teachings on the crown of the head. By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. By completely stating merely the marks as "the excellence of the marks," the entirety of the Tathāgata's form body adorned with the marks and excellent signs is completely taught. In that regard, the marks are the thirty-two, such as having a wheel on the hands and feet; fearing wordiness they are not written here, but you should understand them just as they appear in the sūtra. Those are also excellent because they abide in their domain, are clear, and are complete. The eighty excellent signs are the nails being like the color of copper and so forth; you should know them as they appear in the sūtra. Those marks and so forth are also false, like the marks of a magically emanated Buddha. Therefore, it is taught that one should abide by aspiration and prayer for such a form body. Thus, if one wonders whether those marks are the very nature of accumulated subtle particles, or have become a whole form composed by them: first, the first position is not the case, because the subtle particles have already been dismantled earlier. The second is also not the case. If there is no composer, then there is no whole form composed by it, and because contradictory phenomena explained earlier, such as obscuration, are apprehended. Therefore, based on what was said, the intention was stated; examining that, Subhūti clarified, "It is not." Thinking, "If the marks are solely false, then the Bhagavat spoke of the marks in various sūtras," and having asked, "Why is that?", he said, "Because that itself is without the excellence of the marks"; the meaning of these words is that the excellence of the marks was not spoken of ultimately, but like a magically emanated Buddha, he spoke of them solely as a false nature. In order to fulfill that very meaning spoken by the noble Subhūti, the Bhagavat stated the passage beginning, "As many as..."

"As many as are without the excellence of the marks" should be understood as being explained by reversing that. By this, how one who enters meditative equipoise in yoga should accomplish this is taught. This shows how, having abandoned the two extremes, the mind should be firmly held here: "Thus" means that the Tathāgata should be viewed by the marks like a magically emanated Buddha. This clears away the extreme of deprecation, because the Bhagavat's form body is not deprecated conventionally. "Without marks" is to be viewed ultimately, because no marks whatsoever are established. This clears away the extreme of superimposition. By offering prayers in order to obtain the Tathāgata's form body, extensiveness is stated. Because of not apprehending that, it is profound. The basis for aspiring to obtain the form body has been explained.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "Those, the Tathāgata sees" refers to the body. By this, being embraced by spiritual friends is taught. That, too, was said in order to encourage those who have entered correctly and to generate shame in those who have entered wrongly. Were it otherwise, since the Bhagavat is omniscient, what difference would there be from teaching "he knows all"? Alternatively, this should be seen as principally teaching that they possess good fortune, meaning "he knows they possess good fortune."

"The thorough destruction of the true dharma" is the decline of devotion, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, explaining, listening, thinking, and so forth. "Such as this" means the profound and extensive meaning. "The words of the sūtra" are the statements that teach the sūtra, because by these the meaning is realized and made known. This complete statement of merely a sign completely teaches the entirety of the dharma body of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" refers to what is to be expressed. As for "the teaching" here, it is connected to "such as this," meaning profound and extensive. "Upon the teachings" means "upon the expressions" according to the first. For the second, it means "upon those which teach the meaning." Conceiving the meaning unmistakably is here "true perception," but it does not apply to perceiving "this is true" by adhering to it literally. By this, if the meaning is established, it clears away untrue perception. Because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects, the Bhagavat sees those who will appear as if directly; in order to clear away Subhūti's doubt, he said, "they will appear." "Great beings" was said in order to truly teach their bodhisattva qualities.

What kind of accomplishment they have, by what kind of causes they truly accomplish it, what kind of being embraced by spiritual friends they possess, and by what kind of true perception they will perceive, the Bhagavat completely teaches: by this passage "possessing discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom," it is taught that they possess the accomplishment of the three trainings, in order, as higher discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The reason discipline and wisdom are mentioned separately is that "qualities" here takes up those arising from concentration, in the manner of saying "cows and bulls". If one wonders how such possessors of qualities like discipline will appear in that afflicted later time, the passage beginning "Subhūti..." was spoken. "Having venerated" is to have venerated with robes, food, and so forth, and to have made offerings with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, in order to teach the complete accumulation of their heap of merit, he said, "all those sentient beings..." "Will produce" refers to the time when merit arises. "Will completely accumulate" refers to completely apprehending its latencies at the time of cessation. By all this, having cleared away untrue perception, he taught that one should abide by both the aspiration and the prayer to produce true perception, and he completely taught the extensiveness of this point.

དེ་ལ་མ་འོངས་པའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིགས་མ་ལྔ་ཤས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཆོས་དཀོན་མཆོག་འདི་འདྲ་བ་ཡང་འབྲས་བུ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་ཡིད་མི་ཆེས་སུ་དོགས་ནས་མཆིས་ལགས་སམ་ཞེས་ཞུས་ཏེ། མཆིས་ལགས་སམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་ནི་ཅི་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ལ་ལ་དག་འདི་ལྟ་བུའི་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཆོས་བཤད་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འབྱུང་བ་དག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་གི་དོན་དེ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་ པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱེ་བྲག་ཏུ་མཛད་དེ། དེའི་ཚེ་སྙིགས་མ་ལྔ་པོ་དག་ནི་ཤས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-53] translation already produced for this document:
In that regard, fearing that future beings would not believe in the dharma body of teaching because the five degenerations would be predominant and because a jewel of dharma such as this has an extremely profound and extensive result, he asked, "Are there...?" The words "Are there..." should be connected with the meaning of the words "will there appear any sentient beings whatsoever who will produce a true perception with respect to the teaching of the dharma of a sūtra such as this?" As for "the last five hundred," a collection of five hundreds is five hundred; since it is renowned that the Bhagavat's teaching will remain for five periods of five hundred years, he specified "the last," because at that time the five degenerations will be predominant.

[3-54] source:
དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པ་ནི་མོས་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ལུང་ནོད་པ་དང་། འཆད་པ་དང་།ཉན་པ་དང་། སེམས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉམས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མདོ་སྡེ་བསྟན་པའི་ངག་རྣམས་ཏེ། འདི་དག་གིས་དོན་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་དག་ནི་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཤད་པ་འདིར་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །བཤད་པ་དག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དང་པོ་ལྟར་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནི་དོན་སྟོན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འདིར་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་འདི་ཡང་དག་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མི་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྲུབ་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཐོགས་པ་མེད་པར་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གཟིགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱི་དོགས་པ་དེ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་སོ། །
[3-54] translation already produced for this document:
"The thorough destruction of the true dharma" is the decline of devotion, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, explaining, listening, thinking, and so forth. "Such as this" means the profound and extensive meaning. "The words of the sūtra" are the statements that teach the sūtra, because by these the meaning is realized and made known. This complete statement of merely a sign completely teaches the entirety of the dharma body of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" refers to what is to be expressed. As for "the teaching" here, it is connected to "such as this," meaning profound and extensive. "Upon the teachings" means "upon the expressions" according to the first. For the second, it means "upon those which teach the meaning." Conceiving the meaning unmistakably is here "true perception," but it does not apply to perceiving "this is true" by adhering to it literally. By this, if the meaning is established, it clears away untrue perception. Because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects, the Bhagavat sees those who will appear as if directly; in order to clear away Subhūti's doubt, he said, "they will appear." "Great beings" was said in order to truly teach their bodhisattva qualities.

[3-55] source:
དེ་དག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་། རྒྱུ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་འདུ་ཤེས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ལྷག་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་སེམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་ཏེ། བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ལོགས་ཤིག་དུ་སྨོས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི་འདིར་བསམ་གཏན་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཟུང་སྟེ། བ་ལང་དང་གླང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་དུའོ། །ཕྱི་མའི་དུས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་ནི་ན་བཟའ་དང་ཞལ་ཟས་ལ་སོགས་པས་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་དང་། གདུགས་དང་རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་བ་དན་ལ་སོགས་པས་མཆོད་པའོ། །
[3-55] translation already produced for this document:
What kind of accomplishment they have, by what kind of causes they truly accomplish it, what kind of being embraced by spiritual friends they possess, and by what kind of true perception they will perceive, the Bhagavat completely teaches: by this passage "possessing discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom," it is taught that they possess the accomplishment of the three trainings, in order, as higher discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The reason discipline and wisdom are mentioned separately is that "qualities" here takes up those arising from concentration, in the manner of saying "cows and bulls". If one wonders how such possessors of qualities like discipline will appear in that afflicted later time, the passage beginning "Subhūti..." was spoken. "Having venerated" is to have venerated with robes, food, and so forth, and to have made offerings with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

[3-56] source:
དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནི་གདམས་ངག་དང་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་སྤྱི་བོས་བླངས་ནས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་ནན་ཏན་བྱེད་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །དེ་བས་ཀྱང་དེ་དག་ཆེས་དགེ་བ་མང་དུ་སྩོགས་པས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། སངས་རྒྱས་འབུམ་ཕྲག་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། འདིས་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་རྒྱུ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-56] translation already produced for this document:
"Planting roots of virtue" should be viewed in terms of earnestly practicing the excellence of qualities such as discipline, having received instructions and teachings on the crown of the head. Furthermore, in order to state that they accumulate virtue in much greater abundance than that, "and a hundred thousand Buddhas" is mentioned; by this, the true accomplishment of their causes is taught.

[3-57] source:
དེ་དག་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མཁྱེན་ཏོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསམ་པ་དང་མིང་ངོ་། །

"Those, the Tathāgata knows" refers to their intentions and names.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "Why is that?" completely requests the reason making it known how they will have venerated many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and here, he said, "those bodhisattva great beings..." and so forth. This completely teaches how one should accomplish meditative absorption in yoga. It also expresses profundity. Apprehending that a self exists by thinking "I am" is the perception of a self.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-52] source:
ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དང་། རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུའོ། །རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་དང་། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་ནོ། །
[3-52] translation already produced for this document:
The dharma body is of two types: the dharma body of teaching and the dharma body of realization. The dharma body of realization is also of two types: that which has gnosis as its cause and that which has merit as its cause.

[3-53] source:
དེ་ལ་མ་འོངས་པའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིགས་མ་ལྔ་ཤས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཆོས་དཀོན་མཆོག་འདི་འདྲ་བ་ཡང་འབྲས་བུ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་ཡིད་མི་ཆེས་སུ་དོགས་ནས་མཆིས་ལགས་སམ་ཞེས་ཞུས་ཏེ། མཆིས་ལགས་སམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་ནི་ཅི་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ལ་ལ་དག་འདི་ལྟ་བུའི་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཆོས་བཤད་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འབྱུང་བ་དག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་གི་དོན་དེ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་ པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱེ་བྲག་ཏུ་མཛད་དེ། དེའི་ཚེ་སྙིགས་མ་ལྔ་པོ་དག་ནི་ཤས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-53] translation already produced for this document:
In that regard, fearing that future beings would not believe in the dharma body of teaching because the five degenerations would be predominant and because a jewel of dharma such as this has an extremely profound and extensive result, he asked, "Are there...?" The words "Are there..." should be connected with the meaning of the words "will there appear any sentient beings whatsoever who will produce a true perception with respect to the teaching of the dharma of a sūtra such as this?" As for "the last five hundred," a collection of five hundreds is five hundred; since it is renowned that the Bhagavat's teaching will remain for five periods of five hundred years, he specified "the last," because at that time the five degenerations will be predominant.

[3-54] source:
དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པ་ནི་མོས་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ལུང་ནོད་པ་དང་། འཆད་པ་དང་།ཉན་པ་དང་། སེམས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉམས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མདོ་སྡེ་བསྟན་པའི་ངག་རྣམས་ཏེ། འདི་དག་གིས་དོན་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་དག་ནི་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཤད་པ་འདིར་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །བཤད་པ་དག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དང་པོ་ལྟར་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནི་དོན་སྟོན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འདིར་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་འདི་ཡང་དག་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མི་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྲུབ་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཐོགས་པ་མེད་པར་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གཟིགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱི་དོགས་པ་དེ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་སོ། །
[3-54] translation already produced for this document:
"The thorough destruction of the true dharma" is the decline of devotion, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, explaining, listening, thinking, and so forth. "Such as this" means the profound and extensive meaning. "The words of the sūtra" are the statements that teach the sūtra, because by these the meaning is realized and made known. This complete statement of merely a sign completely teaches the entirety of the dharma body of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" refers to what is to be expressed. As for "the teaching" here, it is connected to "such as this," meaning profound and extensive. "Upon the teachings" means "upon the expressions" according to the first. For the second, it means "upon those which teach the meaning." Conceiving the meaning unmistakably is here "true perception," but it does not apply to perceiving "this is true" by adhering to it literally. By this, if the meaning is established, it clears away untrue perception. Because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects, the Bhagavat sees those who will appear as if directly; in order to clear away Subhūti's doubt, he said, "they will appear." "Great beings" was said in order to truly teach their bodhisattva qualities.

[3-55] source:
དེ་དག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་། རྒྱུ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་འདུ་ཤེས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ལྷག་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་སེམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་ཏེ། བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ལོགས་ཤིག་དུ་སྨོས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི་འདིར་བསམ་གཏན་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཟུང་སྟེ། བ་ལང་དང་གླང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་དུའོ། །ཕྱི་མའི་དུས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་ནི་ན་བཟའ་དང་ཞལ་ཟས་ལ་སོགས་པས་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་དང་། གདུགས་དང་རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་བ་དན་ལ་སོགས་པས་མཆོད་པའོ། །
[3-55] translation already produced for this document:
What kind of accomplishment they have, by what kind of causes they truly accomplish it, what kind of being embraced by spiritual friends they possess, and by what kind of true perception they will perceive, the Bhagavat completely teaches: by this passage "possessing discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom," it is taught that they possess the accomplishment of the three trainings, in order, as higher discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The reason discipline and wisdom are mentioned separately is that "qualities" here takes up those arising from concentration, in the manner of saying "cows and bulls". If one wonders how such possessors of qualities like discipline will appear in that afflicted later time, the passage beginning "Subhūti..." was spoken. "Having venerated" is to have venerated with robes, food, and so forth, and to have made offerings with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

[3-56] source:
དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནི་གདམས་ངག་དང་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་སྤྱི་བོས་བླངས་ནས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་ནན་ཏན་བྱེད་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །དེ་བས་ཀྱང་དེ་དག་ཆེས་དགེ་བ་མང་དུ་སྩོགས་པས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། སངས་རྒྱས་འབུམ་ཕྲག་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། འདིས་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་རྒྱུ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-56] translation already produced for this document:
"Planting roots of virtue" should be viewed in terms of earnestly practicing the excellence of qualities such as discipline, having received instructions and teachings on the crown of the head. Furthermore, in order to state that they accumulate virtue in much greater abundance than that, "and a hundred thousand Buddhas" is mentioned; by this, the true accomplishment of their causes is taught.

[3-57] source:
དེ་དག་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མཁྱེན་ཏོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསམ་པ་དང་མིང་ངོ་། །
[3-57] translation already produced for this document:
"Those, the Tathāgata knows" refers to their intentions and names.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Apprehending that "mine" exists is the perception of a sentient being. Completely apprehending that that very self remains as long as its lifespan is the perception of a living being. Apprehending it as going again and again into migrations is the perception of a person.

[3-54] translation already produced for this document:
"The thorough destruction of the true dharma" is the decline of devotion, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, explaining, listening, thinking, and so forth. "Such as this" means the profound and extensive meaning. "The words of the sūtra" are the statements that teach the sūtra, because by these the meaning is realized and made known. This complete statement of merely a sign completely teaches the entirety of the dharma body of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" refers to what is to be expressed. As for "the teaching" here, it is connected to "such as this," meaning profound and extensive. "Upon the teachings" means "upon the expressions" according to the first. For the second, it means "upon those which teach the meaning." Conceiving the meaning unmistakably is here "true perception," but it does not apply to perceiving "this is true" by adhering to it literally. By this, if the meaning is established, it clears away untrue perception. Because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects, the Bhagavat sees those who will appear as if directly; in order to clear away Subhūti's doubt, he said, "they will appear." "Great beings" was said in order to truly teach their bodhisattva qualities.

What kind of accomplishment they have, by what kind of causes they truly accomplish it, what kind of being embraced by spiritual friends they possess, and by what kind of true perception they will perceive, the Bhagavat completely teaches: by this passage "possessing discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom," it is taught that they possess the accomplishment of the three trainings, in order, as higher discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The reason discipline and wisdom are mentioned separately is that "qualities" here takes up those arising from concentration, in the manner of saying "cows and bulls". If one wonders how such possessors of qualities like discipline will appear in that afflicted later time, the passage beginning "Subhūti..." was spoken. "Having venerated" is to have venerated with robes, food, and so forth, and to have made offerings with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one wonders whether, in the absence of the perception of a self and so forth, there is the perception of dharmas such as form as there is for the śrāvakas and so forth, he said, "neither is it the perception of a dharma," intending that it is because ultimately no dharma whatsoever exists. If one wonders, in that case, is there a perception of non-existence like that of the nihilists, he said, "neither does a perception of no dharma engage." Because, conventionally, dharmas exist as pleasant when unanalyzed, for those abiding on the conventional path for the time being, the perception of no dharma is not endowed with reasoning. Neither is it for those abiding in ultimate gnosis, because at that time, no dharma whatsoever is observed which, by being negated, would cause the perception of no dharma to engage. That is because it does not exist if there is no apprehending as a dharma. It is impossible anywhere for there to be a negation without an object. Regarding that, for example, even though "mere representation" is true, if one conceptualizes "this is mere representation," one is abiding in mere representation itself; similarly, even though the non-existence of dharmas is true, if one conceptualizes the non-existence of dharmas, it is impossible to abide in that, so they are entirely equivalent. If one wonders whether, if a self and so forth do not exist, they do not engage in the perception of those, but they will have a perception adhering to names, thinking "this self is also only merely a name like form and so forth," he said "and perception," because names belong to the form aggregate, so like form and so forth they are entirely false, and even what is unassociated exists imputedly. Therefore, he intended that perceiving names is also just adhering mistakenly.

In that regard, fearing that future beings would not believe in the dharma body of teaching because the five degenerations would be predominant and because a jewel of dharma such as this has an extremely profound and extensive result, he asked, "Are there...?" The words "Are there..." should be connected with the meaning of the words "will there appear any sentient beings whatsoever who will produce a true perception with respect to the teaching of the dharma of a sūtra such as this?" As for "the last five hundred," a collection of five hundreds is five hundred; since it is renowned that the Bhagavat's teaching will remain for five periods of five hundred years, he specified "the last," because at that time the five degenerations will be predominant.

དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པ་ནི་མོས་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ལུང་ནོད་པ་དང་། འཆད་པ་དང་།ཉན་པ་དང་། སེམས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉམས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མདོ་སྡེ་བསྟན་པའི་ངག་རྣམས་ཏེ། འདི་དག་གིས་དོན་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་དག་ནི་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཤད་པ་འདིར་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །བཤད་པ་དག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དང་པོ་ལྟར་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནི་དོན་སྟོན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འདིར་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་འདི་ཡང་དག་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མི་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྲུབ་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཐོགས་པ་མེད་པར་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གཟིགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱི་དོགས་པ་དེ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་སོ། །
[3-54] translation already produced for this document:
"The thorough destruction of the true dharma" is the decline of devotion, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, explaining, listening, thinking, and so forth. "Such as this" means the profound and extensive meaning. "The words of the sūtra" are the statements that teach the sūtra, because by these the meaning is realized and made known. This complete statement of merely a sign completely teaches the entirety of the dharma body of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" refers to what is to be expressed. As for "the teaching" here, it is connected to "such as this," meaning profound and extensive. "Upon the teachings" means "upon the expressions" according to the first. For the second, it means "upon those which teach the meaning." Conceiving the meaning unmistakably is here "true perception," but it does not apply to perceiving "this is true" by adhering to it literally. By this, if the meaning is established, it clears away untrue perception. Because his knowledge is unimpeded in all respects, the Bhagavat sees those who will appear as if directly; in order to clear away Subhūti's doubt, he said, "they will appear." "Great beings" was said in order to truly teach their bodhisattva qualities.

[3-55] source:
དེ་དག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་། རྒྱུ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་འདུ་ཤེས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ལྷག་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་སེམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་ཏེ། བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ལོགས་ཤིག་དུ་སྨོས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི་འདིར་བསམ་གཏན་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཟུང་སྟེ། བ་ལང་དང་གླང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་དུའོ། །ཕྱི་མའི་དུས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་ནི་ན་བཟའ་དང་ཞལ་ཟས་ལ་སོགས་པས་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་དང་། གདུགས་དང་རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་བ་དན་ལ་སོགས་པས་མཆོད་པའོ། །
[3-55] translation already produced for this document:
What kind of accomplishment they have, by what kind of causes they truly accomplish it, what kind of being embraced by spiritual friends they possess, and by what kind of true perception they will perceive, the Bhagavat completely teaches: by this passage "possessing discipline, possessing qualities, possessing wisdom," it is taught that they possess the accomplishment of the three trainings, in order, as higher discipline, higher mind, and higher wisdom. The reason discipline and wisdom are mentioned separately is that "qualities" here takes up those arising from concentration, in the manner of saying "cows and bulls". If one wonders how such possessors of qualities like discipline will appear in that afflicted later time, the passage beginning "Subhūti..." was spoken. "Having venerated" is to have venerated with robes, food, and so forth, and to have made offerings with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one wonders whether, if that were so, since in that state one is free from all perception, the yogi would become completely non-existent like a dead person or a person who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation, he said, "neither will no perception engage." At that time, there exists the very nature of correct conventional yogic gnosis, by which they become yogis. When rising from that, pure mundane gnosis arises from it. Were it otherwise, it would become entirely causeless. If one asks, "Who understands that very conventional nature of yogic gnosis?", [it is understood] by that very same reasoning: just as the realization of the selflessness of a person realizes the selflessness of the person present in oneself through self-awareness, similarly, it is entirely equivalent here as well. It is not that gnosis and awareness are not accepted even conventionally. The yogi does not observe the selflessness present in phenomena by having individually actualized their specific characteristics, because at that time, past things and so forth are not proximate and are infinite. If one wonders what it is like, then: through analysis that they have no inherent nature, all dharmas that become objects are generally subsumed as selfless, and whatever is thus posited is observed simultaneously. Although their gnosis has no object ultimately, it is posited as a valid cognition because it is non-deceptive, like the consciousness of a true dream. Since its own intrinsic nature is also subsumed within that generality, there is no observer of it separately in that. Therefore, from the realization of both as selfless, it is evident that they have venerated many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Those who have not venerated Buddhas, like the non-Buddhists, cannot possibly realize it. He intended, thinking, "This is not something one is familiar with in saṃsāra." By this, he completely taught how one should accomplish this through meditative absorption in yoga, and by what sort of true perception it becomes their perception, and he also completely taught profundity.

[3-62] translation already produced for this document:
If one wonders whether, in the absence of the perception of a self and so forth, there is the perception of dharmas such as form as there is for the śrāvakas and so forth, he said, "neither is it the perception of a dharma," intending that it is because ultimately no dharma whatsoever exists. If one wonders, in that case, is there a perception of non-existence like that of the nihilists, he said, "neither does a perception of no dharma engage." Because, conventionally, dharmas exist as pleasant when unanalyzed, for those abiding on the conventional path for the time being, the perception of no dharma is not endowed with reasoning. Neither is it for those abiding in ultimate gnosis, because at that time, no dharma whatsoever is observed which, by being negated, would cause the perception of no dharma to engage. That is because it does not exist if there is no apprehending as a dharma. It is impossible anywhere for there to be a negation without an object. Regarding that, for example, even though "mere representation" is true, if one conceptualizes "this is mere representation," one is abiding in mere representation itself; similarly, even though the non-existence of dharmas is true, if one conceptualizes the non-existence of dharmas, it is impossible to abide in that, so they are entirely equivalent. If one wonders whether, if a self and so forth do not exist, they do not engage in the perception of those, but they will have a perception adhering to names, thinking "this self is also only merely a name like form and so forth," he said "and perception," because names belong to the form aggregate, so like form and so forth they are entirely false, and even what is unassociated exists imputedly. Therefore, he intended that perceiving names is also just adhering mistakenly.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Even if they do not have the perception of a self and so forth because a self and so forth do not exist, does not the perception of dharmas and non-dharmas, characterized as well-spoken and poorly explained, whose nature is collections of words and so forth, definitely arise for them? It is not so. Regarding the doubt: if bodhisattvas do not perceive them, having abandoned the dharmas of non-Buddhists generated by incorrect reasoning, how will they generate the aspiration to master the dharmas spoken by the Bhagavan? he requested, "Why is that?" and in reply, he said, "Subhūti, if..." The intention is this: just as dharmas characterized as form and so forth do not exist when individually analyzed as having a singular or plural nature, the explained dharmas are also like that. Whoever has the perception of a dharma has also definitely not abandoned the perception of a self and so forth, because its root is apprehending a dharma as a sign. Because mental engagement endowed with apprehending a dharma as a sign is mental engagement of just that, as love and so forth are not mental engagement of reality, it does not abandon the view of a self. Because of that very fact, there is only one vehicle; thus he said, "that is, the Great Vehicle." Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who has the perception of a dharma has definitely not generated the path of seeing, how will one who is like that abandon the perception of a self and so forth? Because that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing. Therefore, having analyzed all that, he said, "that very thing would become their apprehending of a self." He intended, thinking it is because that is the cause of it, and because its latent tendencies have not been abandoned. Were it otherwise, since those very things are of different types, how would the very perception of a dharma become the apprehending of a self? Dharmas here are asserted as characterized by scriptures generated by reasoning. The opposite of that are non-dharmas. If one wonders, if that is so, how is it that the Bhagavan taught bodhisattvas in various sūtras to completely apprehend the true dharma, having analyzed that, he requested "Why is that?" and in reply, he said "Subhūti..." and so forth.

If one wonders whether, in the absence of the perception of a self and so forth, there is the perception of dharmas such as form as there is for the śrāvakas and so forth, he said, "neither is it the perception of a dharma," intending that it is because ultimately no dharma whatsoever exists. If one wonders, in that case, is there a perception of non-existence like that of the nihilists, he said, "neither does a perception of no dharma engage." Because, conventionally, dharmas exist as pleasant when unanalyzed, for those abiding on the conventional path for the time being, the perception of no dharma is not endowed with reasoning. Neither is it for those abiding in ultimate gnosis, because at that time, no dharma whatsoever is observed which, by being negated, would cause the perception of no dharma to engage. That is because it does not exist if there is no apprehending as a dharma. It is impossible anywhere for there to be a negation without an object. Regarding that, for example, even though "mere representation" is true, if one conceptualizes "this is mere representation," one is abiding in mere representation itself; similarly, even though the non-existence of dharmas is true, if one conceptualizes the non-existence of dharmas, it is impossible to abide in that, so they are entirely equivalent. If one wonders whether, if a self and so forth do not exist, they do not engage in the perception of those, but they will have a perception adhering to names, thinking "this self is also only merely a name like form and so forth," he said "and perception," because names belong to the form aggregate, so like form and so forth they are entirely false, and even what is unassociated exists imputedly. Therefore, he intended that perceiving names is also just adhering mistakenly.

If one wonders whether, if that were so, since in that state one is free from all perception, the yogi would become completely non-existent like a dead person or a person who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation, he said, "neither will no perception engage." At that time, there exists the very nature of correct conventional yogic gnosis, by which they become yogis. When rising from that, pure mundane gnosis arises from it. Were it otherwise, it would become entirely causeless. If one asks, "Who understands that very conventional nature of yogic gnosis?", [it is understood] by that very same reasoning: just as the realization of the selflessness of a person realizes the selflessness of the person present in oneself through self-awareness, similarly, it is entirely equivalent here as well. It is not that gnosis and awareness are not accepted even conventionally. The yogi does not observe the selflessness present in phenomena by having individually actualized their specific characteristics, because at that time, past things and so forth are not proximate and are infinite. If one wonders what it is like, then: through analysis that they have no inherent nature, all dharmas that become objects are generally subsumed as selfless, and whatever is thus posited is observed simultaneously. Although their gnosis has no object ultimately, it is posited as a valid cognition because it is non-deceptive, like the consciousness of a true dream. Since its own intrinsic nature is also subsumed within that generality, there is no observer of it separately in that. Therefore, from the realization of both as selfless, it is evident that they have venerated many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Those who have not venerated Buddhas, like the non-Buddhists, cannot possibly realize it. He intended, thinking, "This is not something one is familiar with in saṃsāra." By this, he completely taught how one should accomplish this through meditative absorption in yoga, and by what sort of true perception it becomes their perception, and he also completely taught profundity.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The statement "should not be wrongly apprehended" means that one should not apprehend it with the characteristic of perverse attachment through an erroneous path; the meaning of the words is that one should not become attached thinking it to be true. He intended, thinking, "It does not refute apprehending the characteristics taught as being like a raft for the purpose of accomplishing the intention." With "Therefore," and so forth, he connects that very meaning with other words. Because attachment to all dharmas and non-dharmas, thinking them to be true, is wrong attachment, if even those raft-like collections of scriptures generated by reasoning, which are spoken for the sake of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra, are to be abandoned because they are not needed after reaching the other shore, what need is there to mention those non-dharmas generated by incorrect reasoning, like the non-Buddhists? The Tathāgata spoke thus, saying, "I have not permitted relying on them even out of necessity." It is not so. If dharmas and non-dharmas and so forth were true in nature, then at that time, because attachment to them has an object ultimately, it would become solely of a reasonable nature even for those who have crossed over to the other shore of saṃsāra, so why would the Tathāgata refute that? This is the summarized meaning.
