Regarding the thought, "Even if all entities cannot be apprehended and cannot be expressed, nevertheless, because they uphold their own characteristics, the entity of dharmas ultimately solely abides," he stated, "that is also not a dharma." Because it is impossible for all entities to uphold their own characteristics, being naturally passed beyond sorrow ultimately. Regarding the thought, "If that is so, then did the Bhagavan manifestly and completely awaken to non-existence?" he stated, "nor is it a non-dharma." That has the nature of refuting non-existence. By this, he teaches entering meditative equipoise in yoga, and he also refutes the extremes of superimposition and deprecation. With "Why is that?", he completely requests the justification here, and in reply here, he stated, "because it is distinguished by the unconditioned." The unconditioned is the ultimate nature of dharmas. Furthermore, when analyzed by reasoning, that abides solely in the characteristic of non-arising, just as analyzed before. As explained by the Bhagavan in the Buddhasaṃgīti: "Ānanda, whatever is the non-arising, non-disintegration, non-abiding, and non-alteration of dharmas is called a noble truth."

ཀུན་དགའ་བོ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་འདི་ལ་དགོངས་ནས་འཕགས་པ་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ནི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱིས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱེ་བའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་ཏོ་ཞེས་ཇི་སྐད་གསུངས་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །འདི་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་བྱུང་ཡང་རུང་མ་བྱུང་ཡང་རུང་རྟག་པར་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོད་པ་དང་། འགྱུར་བ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འདུས་མ་བྱས་སོ། །དེ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཕགས་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་དེས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱེ་བ་སྟེ། འཕགས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་རྟོགས་པས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཞན་དེ་ཁོ་ནའི་ངོ་བོར་མི་རིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདུས་མ་བྱས་དེ་ནི་མེད་པར་དགག་པའི་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ནི་འཕགས་པ་དག་གིས་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་མ་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར། དེ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ངོ་བོ་གཞན་རྟོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོར་འཛིན་པ་མེད་ན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོར་འཛིན་པ་ཁོ་ནར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་འཕགས་པ་དགོངས་པ་ངེས་པར་འགྲེལ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་མདོ་ལས་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ནི་དངོས་པོ་ལས་དོན་གཞན་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཇི་སྐད་ཉེས་པ་བརྗོད་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་དངོས་པོའི་ངོ་བོར་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དངོས་པོའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་གང་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དངོས་པོའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་ཉིད་དུ་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ནི་མེད་པ་ལས་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཁོ་ན་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ངོ་བོར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ངོ་བོ་བཞིན་དུ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་རྟོགས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཉིད་དུ་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡང་བཟློག་པ་དཀའོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་འཕགས་པ་དགོངས་པ་ངེས་པར་འགྲེལ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ལས་དེ་ཁོ་ནའི་དངོས་པོ་ལས་དོན་གཞན་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མ་ལགས་ཆོས་མ་མཆིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ལགས་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་དངོས་པོ་དང་།དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་དང་། ཡོད་པ་དང་། མེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དགག་པའི་ངོ་བོ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་དེ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ནི་གནས་པ་འདིའི་ཟབ་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །གལ་ཏེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ། ཆོས་བསྟན་པའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་མེད་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པས་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཡོངས་སུ་གཟུང་བ་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

As is stated: "Ānanda, intending this, the Tathāgata teaches that noble śrāvakas are distinguished by the unconditioned." This is unconditioned because, whether Tathāgatas appear or do not appear, it permanently exists in that way and has no alteration. Because of realizing it, noble persons are distinguished by it, because the nobles are distinguished by realizing the suchness of dharmas. Because it is illogical for another to be the nature of suchness. That unconditioned is not non-existent in the nature of a non-affirming negation, because it is the entity of the nature of entities. Were it otherwise, the nobles would not realize the nature of entities, because they would realize another entity that is not it. Because it would be absent if the apprehension of an entity were absent, it would absurdly follow that it is solely the apprehension of an entity. Therefore, in sūtras such as the noble Saṃdhinirmocana, it is taught, "Suchness is not a different object from entities," for the faults stated would absurdly follow. It does not ultimately exist as the entity of entities, because no entity of entities whatsoever is established. Like the entity of entities, it would absurdly follow that it is conditioned. Therefore, because it exists in dharmas rather than being non-existent, it would become a nature that is not suchness. It would absurdly follow that everyone would realize it like the entity of the nature of entities. It would also be difficult to reverse the absurd consequence that it would become the very cause of thorough affliction. For that very reason, in those very sūtras such as the noble Saṃdhinirmocana, it is stated, "Suchness is not a different object from entities." Because of that, he stated, "Ultimately it is not a dharma, nor is it a non-dharma." By this, he teaches the nature that refutes entities and non-entities, existence and non-existence, and so forth. By this, he also teaches cutting off distraction. By all this, he also teaches the very profundity of this abiding. Having analyzed the thought, "If there is no dharma whatsoever that the Bhagavan manifestly and completely awakened to or taught as dharma, how should a bodhisattva who desires to obtain the dharma body whose cause is merit engage in completely grasping the true dharma?", it is in order to generate the aspiration to obtain the dharma body whose cause is merit.

རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་ནི་གསེར་དང་། དངུལ་དང་། ཤེལ་དང་། བཻ་ཌཱུརྱ་དང་། རྡོའི་སྙིང་པོ་དང་། སྤུག་དང་། མུ་ཏིག་དམར་པོའོ། །འཕགས་པ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་པདྨ་དཀར་པོ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་རྣམས་སོ། །གླིང་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟོང་ལ་སྟོང་གི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སོ། །དེ་སྟོང་ལ་སྟོང་གཉིས་སོ། །

"From that basis" means that this merit arises from that basis of giving precious substances; the meaning is that it arises from that cause. By stating "much" twice, it describes it as extremely much.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
source: འདི་ཅི་ཡིད་ཆེས་པར་བྱ་བར་ཟད་དམ། འོན་ཏེ་རིགས་པས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡང་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཤིང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། འདིར་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ནི་འདི་ལས་བྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་རིགས་པ་བཀའ་སྩལ་ཏོ། །འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བསོད་ནམས་ཆེས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡང་འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བསོད་ནམས་ཆེ་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། དེ་ལ་ལུས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། རིན་པོ་ཆེ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་བསོད་ནམས་དེ་ནི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འཁོར་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཕལ་པ་འཐོབ་སྟེ། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོའི་འབྲས་བུ་འཐོབ་ཀྱི་དེ་དག་ཉི་ཚེས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གོ་འཕང་དཔེ་མེད་ཅིང་ཟད་མི་ཤེས་པ་ཐོབ་པས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་མི་མངོན། ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་བཏགས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟར་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་གཞན་ལ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་གཞན་དག་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་བསྟན་པའི་རིམ་གྱིས་ཆོས་འདི་ལས་མྱུར་བ་ཁོ་ནར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་འཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་གྱི་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་རྣམས་ལས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གཞན་དག་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པའི་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པས་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྦྱིན་པ་ལས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པ་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་སོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལས་འབྱུང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་གྲུབ་པ་སྟེ། སྤྱད་པ་བཅུ་རྣམས་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་གཅིག་ནས་གཅིག་ཏུ་བརྒྱུད་དེ་ཐོབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སྤྱད་པ་བཅུ་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་ཡི་གེར་འདྲི་བ་དང་། མཆོད་པ་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ་དང་། བཀླག་པ་དང་། མཉན་པ་དང་། གཟུང་བ་དང་། ལུང་ཕོག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་དུ་བྱ་བ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དང་། བསྒོམ་པའོ། །
translation: Regarding the thought, "Is this merely something to be believed, or is it also something to be known through reasoning?", having asked "Why is that?", here he spoke the reasoning: "Subhūti, the unexcelled completely perfect awakening of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the completely perfect Buddhas, has arisen from this." Thinking this, the expression "greater merit" also means it is great merit because its fruit is great, but because it has no body, it is not so by its own nature. That merit arisen from precious substances attains ordinary fruits of cyclic existence, such as great resources; if embraced by wisdom, giving and so forth attain the fruit of great awakening, but not merely by themselves alone. Since by the gift of dharma one attains the state of a Tathāgata, which is without comparison and inexhaustible, why would it not manifest as being great? Just as one is benefited by dharma, precious substances will not greatly benefit others in the same way; for in this way, through the gradual process of teaching it properly to others, from this dharma alone one will quickly attain the state of Buddhahood itself, but not from precious substances. Because of that, he intended, "Since it becomes the supreme benefit for others, the giving of dharma is exceptionally superior to the giving of precious substances." "Arises from this" means properly established; relying on the ten practices, one subsequently attains it by being passed down from one to another—that is the meaning. Those ten practices are writing, offering, giving, reading, listening, grasping, transmitting, reciting, contemplating, and meditating.

[3-75] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If ultimately everything is unarisen, how does the accumulation of merit arise from that basis?", having stated "Why is that?", knowing his own intention, he stated in reply, "because it is not an accumulation." "Ultimately" is to be supplied. Because accumulations exist imputedly, the accumulation of merit does not exist as an entity. Merit is also imputed upon particular instances of the nature of latent tendencies. A bodhisattva also solely exists imputedly, because entities, being unmoving, do not engage in the manner of conditioning. Even when analyzed individually as the nature of one or many, they solely have a false nature. Because of that, ultimately there is no accumulation of merit. By this, he completely teaches entering meditative equipoise in yoga. He also refutes the extreme of superimposition.

Conventionally, the accumulation of merit does abide. Because of that, the Tathāgata stated, "it is called the accumulation of merit." Were it otherwise, if that accumulation of merit existed ultimately, it would not be expressed, because the ultimate is not the object of words. Even if he did not state it, since it would be known as such, stating it would become entirely meaningless; therefore, because he stated it, it is known to be solely conventional. By this, he teaches the refutation of the extreme of deprecation. In that way, after noble Subhūti refuted the two extremes, subsequently, because the retinue became worthy of listening to the extensive dharma and because he also stated that the merit was much greater, the Bhagavan spoke the words "Subhūti, by whoever," and so forth.

[3-77] translation already produced for this document:
By this, because the dharma body whose cause is merit, realized by the Tathāgatas, definitely arises from the dharma body that is taught, it teaches in this way: "If, just for a while, teaching merely a four-line verse from that becomes an origin of merit like that, what need is there to mention the dharma body whose cause is merit, realized by the Tathāgatas?" Although this is not the literal meaning of the words, because it is realized by implication, there is no fault in this meaning. Therefore, it is the intention of thinking, "Although ultimately there is no dharma taught or manifestly and completely awakened to, because conventionally the teaching of the body of merit exists, a bodhisattva should engage in order to obtain merit." By this teaching that the merit is distinguished, he teaches its extensiveness. He also teaches the aspiration to generate it and the making of prayers. Because there are also verses with six lines, he makes the particularization "a four-line verse." This "verse" is not composed, but from prose even merely the words of a four-line verse are grasped. "Having grasped" means having recited it. "Explains" is the words. "Properly teaches" is the meaning. "Incalculable" is because it is extremely much. "Immeasurable" is because it is not an object of comparison. By this, in meaning, he completely dispels the discordant side of not generating merit. By expressing merely the name "merit", he teaches the entire collection of merit of the Tathāgata.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "The Buddha Bhagavans are also born from this" means that conventionally Buddhas are imputed in dependence on that; this is the meaning. Ultimately, there is no difference between awakening and Buddhas. By this teaching that the merit is exceptionally superior, he teaches the aspiration to generate it and abiding by prayer.

A thousand of those is a third-order great thousand-fold world system. "From that basis" means that this merit arises from that basis of giving precious substances; the meaning is that it arises from that cause. [3-75] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If ultimately everything is unarisen, how does the accumulation of merit arise from that basis?", having stated "Why is that?", knowing his own intention, he stated in reply, "because it is not an accumulation." "Ultimately" is to be supplied. Because accumulations exist imputedly, the accumulation of merit does not exist as an entity. Merit is also imputed upon particular instances of the nature of latent tendencies. A bodhisattva also solely exists imputedly, because entities, being unmoving, do not engage in the manner of conditioning. Even when analyzed individually as the nature of one or many, they solely have a false nature. Because of that, ultimately there is no accumulation of merit. By this, he completely teaches entering meditative equipoise in yoga. He also refutes the extreme of superimposition.

[3-76] translation already produced for this document:
Conventionally, the accumulation of merit does abide. Because of that, the Tathāgata stated, "it is called the accumulation of merit." Were it otherwise, if that accumulation of merit existed ultimately, it would not be expressed, because the ultimate is not the object of words. Even if he did not state it, since it would be known as such, stating it would become entirely meaningless; therefore, because he stated it, it is known to be solely conventional. By this, he teaches the refutation of the extreme of deprecation. In that way, after noble Subhūti refuted the two extremes, subsequently, because the retinue became worthy of listening to the extensive dharma and because he also stated that the merit was much greater, the Bhagavan spoke the words "Subhūti, by whoever," and so forth.

[3-77] translation already produced for this document:
By this, because the dharma body whose cause is merit, realized by the Tathāgatas, definitely arises from the dharma body that is taught, it teaches in this way: "If, just for a while, teaching merely a four-line verse from that becomes an origin of merit like that, what need is there to mention the dharma body whose cause is merit, realized by the Tathāgatas?" Although this is not the literal meaning of the words, because it is realized by implication, there is no fault in this meaning. Therefore, it is the intention of thinking, "Although ultimately there is no dharma taught or manifestly and completely awakened to, because conventionally the teaching of the body of merit exists, a bodhisattva should engage in order to obtain merit." By this teaching that the merit is distinguished, he teaches its extensiveness. He also teaches the aspiration to generate it and the making of prayers. Because there are also verses with six lines, he makes the particularization "a four-line verse." This "verse" is not composed, but from prose even merely the words of a four-line verse are grasped. "Having grasped" means having recited it. "Explains" is the words. "Properly teaches" is the meaning. "Incalculable" is because it is extremely much. "Immeasurable" is because it is not an object of comparison. By this, in meaning, he completely dispels the discordant side of not generating merit. By expressing merely the name "merit", he teaches the entire collection of merit of the Tathāgata.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Regarding the thought, "If ultimately all dharmas are solely unarisen, then at that time all qualities of a Buddha would also be solely unarisen; how then does the unexcelled completely perfect awakening arise from this? Buddhas are not different from awakening," having asked "Why is that?", here he stated in reply, "qualities of a Buddha." The dharmas that have the characteristics of unexcelled completely perfect awakening and so forth, which are the cause of imputing a Buddha, are the qualities of a Buddha. Therefore, the intention is: "Although Buddhas ultimately are not different from awakening, because it becomes the cause of imputing them, it is stated that Buddhas are born from this." Because they too are ultimately unarisen, even though qualities of a Buddha do not exist, the Tathāgata stated "the unexcelled completely perfect awakening of the Tathāgatas has arisen from this" and so forth in reliance on the conventional; but not ultimately.

"From that basis" means that this merit arises from that basis of giving precious substances; the meaning is that it arises from that cause. Regarding the thought, "If ultimately everything is unarisen, how does the accumulation of merit arise from that basis?", having stated "Why is that?", knowing his own intention, he stated in reply, "because it is not an accumulation." "Ultimately" is to be supplied. Because accumulations exist imputedly, the accumulation of merit does not exist as an entity. Merit is also imputed upon particular instances of the nature of latent tendencies. A bodhisattva also solely exists imputedly, because entities, being unmoving, do not engage in the manner of conditioning. Even when analyzed individually as the nature of one or many, they solely have a false nature. Because of that, ultimately there is no accumulation of merit. By this, he completely teaches entering meditative equipoise in yoga. He also refutes the extreme of superimposition.

[3-76] translation already produced for this document:
Conventionally, the accumulation of merit does abide. Because of that, the Tathāgata stated, "it is called the accumulation of merit." Were it otherwise, if that accumulation of merit existed ultimately, it would not be expressed, because the ultimate is not the object of words. Even if he did not state it, since it would be known as such, stating it would become entirely meaningless; therefore, because he stated it, it is known to be solely conventional. By this, he teaches the refutation of the extreme of deprecation. In that way, after noble Subhūti refuted the two extremes, subsequently, because the retinue became worthy of listening to the extensive dharma and because he also stated that the merit was much greater, the Bhagavan spoke the words "Subhūti, by whoever," and so forth.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: For that very reason, he intended: "From various other standpoints, 'qualities of a Buddha' cannot be expressed ultimately; because they are to be individually and personally realized, they are inexpressible." By this he teaches entering into yogic meditative equipoise and subduing distraction, and he also teaches the profound. Here, some say: "Since the dharma body has no differentiation, how can there be these three different types of bodies? But if you say that because one will attain the dharma body, and because they are effects corresponding to the cause of the dharma body, the nature of merit and the nature of the teaching are called the 'dharma body' through imputation, then in that case the form body too would become the dharma body, because it is an effect corresponding to the cause of attaining it and because it is the cause of attaining it." That is not true. The dharma body of the Buddha Bhagavans is posited as the nature of completely pure exalted wisdom and whatever is its general dharmatā. This is neither a differentiation of its maturation, nor is it taught as "dharma" here by imputing upon the teaching and merit. What is it like then? It is solely the entity; because it is renowned as such by itself, as in "teaches the dharma", "accumulates the dharma" and so forth.

Regarding the thought, "Is this merely something to be believed, or is it also something to be known through reasoning?", having asked "Why is that?", here he spoke the reasoning: "Subhūti, the unexcelled completely perfect awakening of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the completely perfect Buddhas, has arisen from this." Thinking this, the expression "greater merit" also means it is great merit because its fruit is great, but because it has no body, it is not so by its own nature. That merit arisen from precious substances attains ordinary fruits of cyclic existence, such as great resources; if embraced by wisdom, giving and so forth attain the fruit of great awakening, but not merely by themselves alone. Since by the gift of dharma one attains the state of a Tathāgata, which is without comparison and inexhaustible, why would it not manifest as being great? Just as one is benefited by dharma, precious substances will not greatly benefit others in the same way; for in this way, through the gradual process of teaching it properly to others, from this dharma alone one will quickly attain the state of Buddhahood itself, but not from precious substances. Because of that, he intended, "Since it becomes the supreme benefit for others, the giving of dharma is exceptionally superior to the giving of precious substances." "Arises from this" means properly established; relying on the ten practices, one subsequently attains it by being passed down from one to another—that is the meaning. Those ten practices are writing, offering, giving, reading, listening, grasping, transmitting, reciting, contemplating, and meditating.

Regarding the thought, "If ultimately all dharmas are solely unarisen, then at that time all qualities of a Buddha would also be solely unarisen; how then does the unexcelled completely perfect awakening arise from this? Buddhas are not different from awakening," having asked "Why is that?", here he stated in reply, "qualities of a Buddha." The dharmas that have the characteristics of unexcelled completely perfect awakening and so forth, which are the cause of imputing a Buddha, are the qualities of a Buddha. Therefore, the intention is: "Although Buddhas ultimately are not different from awakening, because it becomes the cause of imputing them, it is stated that Buddhas are born from this." Because they too are ultimately unarisen, even though qualities of a Buddha do not exist, the Tathāgata stated "the unexcelled completely perfect awakening of the Tathāgatas has arisen from this" and so forth in reliance on the conventional; but not ultimately.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Whatever is taught as "dharmas" because they hold their own and general characteristics, that is common to all entities, so the form body is not taught as the Tathāgata, because it is not that which makes known. Even though it is taught by imputation, the form body does not absurdly follow to be the dharma body, because it is an effect corresponding to the cause of merit. As it is said: "In short, the dharma body of the Victors arises from the collection of exalted wisdom, while the form body of the Buddhas arises from the collection of merit." Therefore, because only the collection of exalted wisdom is the cause of attaining it, it is impossible that it will be attained by the form body; because there is no cause for imputing it, the form body is not called the dharma body. The body of the teaching is the fruit of perfectly pure exalted wisdom, and the body of merit, having the characteristic of a collection, is also the cause of attaining it; thus it is indeed reasonable to teach it as the "collection of dharma" by imputation, so there is no need for a lot of words. Thinking that other bad objections might be distinguished as reasonable or unreasonable by those with wisdom, I have not written them, fearing verbosity. The topic of the aspiration to attain the dharma body has been explained.

By this, because the dharma body whose cause is merit, realized by the Tathāgatas, definitely arises from the dharma body that is taught, it teaches in this way: "If, just for a while, teaching merely a four-line verse from that becomes an origin of merit like that, what need is there to mention the dharma body whose cause is merit, realized by the Tathāgatas?" Although this is not the literal meaning of the words, because it is realized by implication, there is no fault in this meaning. Therefore, it is the intention of thinking, "Although ultimately there is no dharma taught or manifestly and completely awakened to, because conventionally the teaching of the body of merit exists, a bodhisattva should engage in order to obtain merit." By this teaching that the merit is distinguished, he teaches its extensiveness. He also teaches the aspiration to generate it and the making of prayers. Because there are also verses with six lines, he makes the particularization "a four-line verse." This "verse" is not composed, but from prose even merely the words of a four-line verse are grasped. "Having grasped" means having recited it. "Explains" is the words. "Properly teaches" is the meaning. "Incalculable" is because it is extremely much. "Immeasurable" is because it is not an object of comparison. By this, in meaning, he completely dispels the discordant side of not generating merit. By expressing merely the name "merit", he teaches the entire collection of merit of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the thought, "Is this merely something to be believed, or is it also something to be known through reasoning?", having asked "Why is that?", here he spoke the reasoning: "Subhūti, the unexcelled completely perfect awakening of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the completely perfect Buddhas, has arisen from this." Thinking this, the expression "greater merit" also means it is great merit because its fruit is great, but because it has no body, it is not so by its own nature. That merit arisen from precious substances attains ordinary fruits of cyclic existence, such as great resources; if embraced by wisdom, giving and so forth attain the fruit of great awakening, but not merely by themselves alone. Since by the gift of dharma one attains the state of a Tathāgata, which is without comparison and inexhaustible, why would it not manifest as being great? Just as one is benefited by dharma, precious substances will not greatly benefit others in the same way; for in this way, through the gradual process of teaching it properly to others, from this dharma alone one will quickly attain the state of Buddhahood itself, but not from precious substances. Because of that, he intended, "Since it becomes the supreme benefit for others, the giving of dharma is exceptionally superior to the giving of precious substances." "Arises from this" means properly established; relying on the ten practices, one subsequently attains it by being passed down from one to another—that is the meaning. Those ten practices are writing, offering, giving, reading, listening, grasping, transmitting, reciting, contemplating, and meditating.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: From here onwards, the twelve topics should be known as the remedies for the twelve types of discordant factors, respectively. Those twelve types of discordant factors are: overweening pride; even if without overweening pride, having little learning; even if having much learning, cultivating mental engagement on a small object; even if cultivating mental engagement on an object that is not small, forsaking sentient beings; even if not forsaking them, engaging with attachment to outer treatises; even if not engaging in them, lacking skill in means to overcome the signs of entities; even if skilled in means for that, not having accumulated the collection of merit; even if having accumulated the collection of merit, experiencing indolence and partaking of alms through gain and respect; even if not experiencing that, being unable to bear suffering; even if unconcerned about suffering, not having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom; even if having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom, thoroughly grasping at a self; and even if lacking thorough grasping at a self, not possessing the instructions. Regarding that, although the Bhagavan has extensively taught the selflessness of persons and dharmas, by the force of having firmly accumulated manifest adherence to a self since beginningless time, thinking, "If whoever engages in the perception of a sentient being and so forth is not called a bodhisattva, if that is so, then how is it that the Bhagavan said: 'At that time, in that period, I became the king named Śūradatta'?"

For that very reason, he intended: "From various other standpoints, 'qualities of a Buddha' cannot be expressed ultimately; because they are to be individually and personally realized, they are inexpressible." By this he teaches entering into yogic meditative equipoise and subduing distraction, and he also teaches the profound. Here, some say: "Since the dharma body has no differentiation, how can there be these three different types of bodies? But if you say that because one will attain the dharma body, and because they are effects corresponding to the cause of the dharma body, the nature of merit and the nature of the teaching are called the 'dharma body' through imputation, then in that case the form body too would become the dharma body, because it is an effect corresponding to the cause of attaining it and because it is the cause of attaining it." That is not true. The dharma body of the Buddha Bhagavans is posited as the nature of completely pure exalted wisdom and whatever is its general dharmatā. This is neither a differentiation of its maturation, nor is it taught as "dharma" here by imputing upon the teaching and merit. What is it like then? It is solely the entity; because it is renowned as such by itself, as in "teaches the dharma", "accumulates the dharma" and so forth.

Whatever is taught as "dharmas" because they hold their own and general characteristics, that is common to all entities, so the form body is not taught as the Tathāgata, because it is not that which makes known. Even though it is taught by imputation, the form body does not absurdly follow to be the dharma body, because it is an effect corresponding to the cause of merit. As it is said: "In short, the dharma body of the Victors arises from the collection of exalted wisdom, while the form body of the Buddhas arises from the collection of merit." Therefore, because only the collection of exalted wisdom is the cause of attaining it, it is impossible that it will be attained by the form body; because there is no cause for imputing it, the form body is not called the dharma body. The body of the teaching is the fruit of perfectly pure exalted wisdom, and the body of merit, having the characteristic of a collection, is also the cause of attaining it; thus it is indeed reasonable to teach it as the "collection of dharma" by imputation, so there is no need for a lot of words. Thinking that other bad objections might be distinguished as reasonable or unreasonable by those with wisdom, I have not written them, fearing verbosity. The topic of the aspiration to attain the dharma body has been explained.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: It would become "I shall teach the dharma to you" and so forth. Thinking, "One who does not have the perception of a sentient being and so forth would not intend in that way", in order to be free from that which becomes an obstruction of overweening pride, making it regarding the fifth topic, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Regarding this, the outer meaning is this: "If even my lowest śrāvakas, the stream-enterers and so forth, who have arrived but not attained nirvāṇa in order to realize the selflessness of dharmas, have no manifest adherence to 'I' and 'mine', what need is there to mention one who has realized both selflessnesses and abandoned obscurations without exception?" Whatever is "At that time I" and so forth, that is merely eliminating [other possibilities] regarding the continuums of others for those who desire to know for the purpose of designating worldly conventions; it is equivalent to conventions such as 'army' and 'forest', but is not due to manifest adherence to it being singular and permanent. Those abiding in the exalted wisdom of suchness cannot express conventions together with the world. Therefore, in order to be free from what becomes a basis for overweening pride, he caused them to grasp it perfectly, saying, "You too should not have manifest adherence to a self." Regarding that, the 'stream' has the characteristic of the path of seeing that goes to the great city of nirvāṇa. 'Entered' means attained; and one who has abandoned all the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is called a 'stream-enterer'. Furthermore, because by having abandoned manifest adherence to the agent, the action, and the activity, one realizes this mere conditionality itself, this teaches realizing selflessness. 'My' refers to manifest adherence to the agent. 'Fruit' refers to manifest adherence to the action. 'Attained' refers to manifest adherence to the activity. By this, in meaning, thinking "I have attained" is thoroughly taught to be a discordant factor.

For that very reason, he intended: "From various other standpoints, 'qualities of a Buddha' cannot be expressed ultimately; because they are to be individually and personally realized, they are inexpressible." By this he teaches entering into yogic meditative equipoise and subduing distraction, and he also teaches the profound. Here, some say: "Since the dharma body has no differentiation, how can there be these three different types of bodies? But if you say that because one will attain the dharma body, and because they are effects corresponding to the cause of the dharma body, the nature of merit and the nature of the teaching are called the 'dharma body' through imputation, then in that case the form body too would become the dharma body, because it is an effect corresponding to the cause of attaining it and because it is the cause of attaining it." That is not true. The dharma body of the Buddha Bhagavans is posited as the nature of completely pure exalted wisdom and whatever is its general dharmatā. This is neither a differentiation of its maturation, nor is it taught as "dharma" here by imputing upon the teaching and merit. What is it like then? It is solely the entity; because it is renowned as such by itself, as in "teaches the dharma", "accumulates the dharma" and so forth.

གང་ཡང་རང་དང་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་འཛིན་པས་ཆོས་རྣམས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་ཐུན་མོང་ཡིན་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མ་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བཏགས་ནས་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་ཐལ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱིས་རྒྱུ་མཐུན་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་སྐད་དུ། མདོར་ན་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཆོས་སྐུ་ནི། །ཡེ་ཤེས་ཚོགས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་སྟེ། །སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་ནི། །བསོད་ནམས་ཚོགས་ལས་བྱུང་བའོ། །ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ་ཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུས་ནི་དེ་འཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མི་སྲིད་དེ། དེའི་གདགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་མེད་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ། །བཤད་པའི་སྐུ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་ལ། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དེ་འཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པས་བཏགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བསྟན་པར་རིགས་པ་ཉིད་དེ་མང་དུ་ནི་མི་དགོས་སོ། །ཀླན་ཀ་ངན་པ་གཞན་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཅན་དག་གིས་རིགས་སམ་མི་རིགས་འབྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་གྲང་སྙམ་དུ་སྟེ་ཚིག་མངས་ཀྱིས་དོགས་ནས་མ་བྲིས་སོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་གནས་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །

Whatever is taught as "dharmas" because they hold their own and general characteristics, that is common to all entities, so the form body is not taught as the Tathāgata, because it is not that which makes known. Even though it is taught by imputation, the form body does not absurdly follow to be the dharma body, because it is an effect corresponding to the cause of merit. As it is said: "In short, the dharma body of the Victors arises from the collection of exalted wisdom, while the form body of the Buddhas arises from the collection of merit." Therefore, because only the collection of exalted wisdom is the cause of attaining it, it is impossible that it will be attained by the form body; because there is no cause for imputing it, the form body is not called the dharma body. The body of the teaching is the fruit of perfectly pure exalted wisdom, and the body of merit, having the characteristic of a collection, is also the cause of attaining it; thus it is indeed reasonable to teach it as the "collection of dharma" by imputation, so there is no need for a lot of words. Thinking that other bad objections might be distinguished as reasonable or unreasonable by those with wisdom, I have not written them, fearing verbosity. The topic of the aspiration to attain the dharma body has been explained.

འདི་མན་ཆད་གནས་བཅུ་གཉིས་ནི་མི་མཐུན་པ་རྣམ་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་གཉེན་པོར་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་དུ་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །མི་མཐུན་པ་རྣམ་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་དང་། མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐོས་པ་ཉུང་བ་དང་། ཐོས་པ་མང་བ་ཡང་དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་དང་། དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བ་དང་། དེ་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་དང་། དེར་མི་འཇུག་ཀྱང་དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་དང་། དེ་ལ་ཐབས་མཁས་ཀྱང་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པ་དང་། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསགས་ཀྱང་ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། དེ་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་མི་བྱེད་ཀྱང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པ་དང་། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་ཇི་མི་སྙམ་ཡང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པ་དང་། ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསགས་ཀྱང་བདག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་དང་།བདག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་མེད་ཀྱང་གདམས་ངག་དང་མི་ལྡན་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེར་བསྟན་ཀྱང་། གང་ཐོག་མ་མེད་པའི་དུས་ནས་བདག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་བརྟན་པོར་བསགས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གལ་ཏེ་སུ་སེམས་ཅན་ ལ་སོགས་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པ་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་ན། དེ་ལྟ་ན་གོ་ཇི་ལྟར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་འདི་སྐད་དུ་ང་དེའི་ཚེ་དེའི་དུས་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་དཔའ་བས་བྱིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་གྱུར་ཏོ།

Those twelve types of discordant factors are: overweening pride; even if without overweening pride, having little learning; even if having much learning, cultivating mental engagement on a small object; even if cultivating mental engagement on an object that is not small, forsaking sentient beings; even if not forsaking them, engaging with attachment to outer treatises; even if not engaging in them, lacking skill in means to overcome the signs of entities; even if skilled in means for that, not having accumulated the collection of merit; even if having accumulated the collection of merit, experiencing indolence and partaking of alms through gain and respect; even if not experiencing that, being unable to bear suffering; even if unconcerned about suffering, not having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom; even if having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom, thoroughly grasping at a self; and even if lacking thorough grasping at a self, not possessing the instructions. heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By thoroughly expressing just a mere sign, saying, 'The stream-enterer does not think thus: "I have attained"', it thoroughly teaches abandoning all overweening pride. Regarding that, it also teaches aspiration and making prayers.

It would become "I shall teach the dharma to you" and so forth. Thinking, "One who does not have the perception of a sentient being and so forth would not intend in that way", in order to be free from that which becomes an obstruction of overweening pride, making it regarding the fifth topic, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Regarding this, the outer meaning is this: "If even my lowest śrāvakas, the stream-enterers and so forth, who have arrived but not attained nirvāṇa in order to realize the selflessness of dharmas, have no manifest adherence to 'I' and 'mine', what need is there to mention one who has realized both selflessnesses and abandoned obscurations without exception?" Whatever is "At that time I" and so forth, that is merely eliminating [other possibilities] regarding the continuums of others for those who desire to know for the purpose of designating worldly conventions; it is equivalent to conventions such as 'army' and 'forest', but is not due to manifest adherence to it being singular and permanent. Those abiding in the exalted wisdom of suchness cannot express conventions together with the world. Therefore, in order to be free from what becomes a basis for overweening pride, he caused them to grasp it perfectly, saying, "You too should not have manifest adherence to a self." Regarding that, the 'stream' has the characteristic of the path of seeing that goes to the great city of nirvāṇa. 'Entered' means attained; and one who has abandoned all the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is called a 'stream-enterer'. Furthermore, because by having abandoned manifest adherence to the agent, the action, and the activity, one realizes this mere conditionality itself, this teaches realizing selflessness. 'My' refers to manifest adherence to the agent. 'Fruit' refers to manifest adherence to the action. 'Attained' refers to manifest adherence to the activity. By this, in meaning, thinking "I have attained" is thoroughly taught to be a discordant factor.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The Noble Subhūti, too, by closely expressing the intention of the Bhagavan, in order to establish it ultimately and to lead into meditative absorption in yoga regarding that, said, "Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything." To the thought, "Why is that?", he said, "He has not entered into form," and so forth. By this, it teaches that ultimately both types of fruits are not to be attained. Thus, if the entity to be attained were to become a fruit, would it become conditioned or unconditioned? Regarding that, first, the unconditioned is just unarisen; because it is non-existent, being similar to a rabbit's horn, it is not suitable to be attained, because there is no difference from the state of not being attained. The conditioned is momentary, being destroyed immediately upon arising; because it does not abide, it will not be attained by anyone in any way. In whatever continuum, due to the active cause characterized by the selfless path having become present, a fruit characterized as a state completely discordant with the arising of afflictions has arisen, regarding that it is merely taught that "he attains the fruit," but ultimately it is not so. Furthermore, would the entities of that which is to be attained and that which attains be of different times or of the same time? First, the first position is not the case; because both must abide, if they are of different times, at the time when one is present the other is non-existent, so how could both of them abide? Neither is it from being of the same time; because, once both are established, there is no benefiting of one another.

Those twelve types of discordant factors are: overweening pride; even if without overweening pride, having little learning; even if having much learning, cultivating mental engagement on a small object; even if cultivating mental engagement on an object that is not small, forsaking sentient beings; even if not forsaking them, engaging with attachment to outer treatises; even if not engaging in them, lacking skill in means to overcome the signs of entities; even if skilled in means for that, not having accumulated the collection of merit; even if having accumulated the collection of merit, experiencing indolence and partaking of alms through gain and respect; even if not experiencing that, being unable to bear suffering; even if unconcerned about suffering, not having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom; even if having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom, thoroughly grasping at a self; and even if lacking thorough grasping at a self, not possessing the instructions. It would become "I shall teach the dharma to you" and so forth. Thinking, "One who does not have the perception of a sentient being and so forth would not intend in that way", in order to be free from that which becomes an obstruction of overweening pride, making it regarding the fifth topic, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Regarding this, the outer meaning is this: "If even my lowest śrāvakas, the stream-enterers and so forth, who have arrived but not attained nirvāṇa in order to realize the selflessness of dharmas, have no manifest adherence to 'I' and 'mine', what need is there to mention one who has realized both selflessnesses and abandoned obscurations without exception?" Whatever is "At that time I" and so forth, that is merely eliminating [other possibilities] regarding the continuums of others for those who desire to know for the purpose of designating worldly conventions; it is equivalent to conventions such as 'army' and 'forest', but is not due to manifest adherence to it being singular and permanent. Those abiding in the exalted wisdom of suchness cannot express conventions together with the world. Therefore, in order to be free from what becomes a basis for overweening pride, he caused them to grasp it perfectly, saying, "You too should not have manifest adherence to a self." Regarding that, the 'stream' has the characteristic of the path of seeing that goes to the great city of nirvāṇa. 'Entered' means attained; and one who has abandoned all the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is called a 'stream-enterer'. Furthermore, because by having abandoned manifest adherence to the agent, the action, and the activity, one realizes this mere conditionality itself, this teaches realizing selflessness. 'My' refers to manifest adherence to the agent. 'Fruit' refers to manifest adherence to the action. 'Attained' refers to manifest adherence to the activity. By this, in meaning, thinking "I have attained" is thoroughly taught to be a discordant factor.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If there is no benefiting, it is not logical to ascertain the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not logical for the characteristics of what is to be attained and what attains it to be simultaneously related through the characteristic of generating mutual association. Thus, first, those entities which are bodiless do not abide in a locus, so they have no association. They do not become the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it merely by being at the same time, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not merely from a single cause, because since that is common to both, there would be no certainty that 'this is what is to be attained, and this is what attains it.' For those that possess bodies, if they are associated with each other by their entire nature, it would entail the absurd consequence of them being one. If by one part, it would entail the absurd consequence of them possessing limbs. Neither is attainment from abiding without interval, because being common to both, without difference, there is no certainty. Therefore, this is merely superimposed by conceptualization. By this, all conventions such as agent and action should be clearly understood. 'Dharmas' refers to the dharmāyatana. By this, the unconditioned is also included, because the dharmāyatana has the nature of seven substances. The remainder, form and so forth, and a portion of the dharmāyatana, teach the conditioned. This is an illustration; therefore, the eye and so forth should also be grasped.

From here onwards, the twelve topics should be known as the remedies for the twelve types of discordant factors, respectively. Those twelve types of discordant factors are: overweening pride; even if without overweening pride, having little learning; even if having much learning, cultivating mental engagement on a small object; even if cultivating mental engagement on an object that is not small, forsaking sentient beings; even if not forsaking them, engaging with attachment to outer treatises; even if not engaging in them, lacking skill in means to overcome the signs of entities; even if skilled in means for that, not having accumulated the collection of merit; even if having accumulated the collection of merit, experiencing indolence and partaking of alms through gain and respect; even if not experiencing that, being unable to bear suffering; even if unconcerned about suffering, not having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom; even if having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom, thoroughly grasping at a self; and even if lacking thorough grasping at a self, not possessing the instructions. Regarding that, although the Bhagavan has extensively taught the selflessness of persons and dharmas, by the force of having firmly accumulated manifest adherence to a self since beginningless time, thinking, "If whoever engages in the perception of a sentient being and so forth is not called a bodhisattva, if that is so, then how is it that the Bhagavan said: 'At that time, in that period, I became the king named Śūradatta'?"

It would become "I shall teach the dharma to you" and so forth. Thinking, "One who does not have the perception of a sentient being and so forth would not intend in that way", in order to be free from that which becomes an obstruction of overweening pride, making it regarding the fifth topic, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Regarding this, the outer meaning is this: "If even my lowest śrāvakas, the stream-enterers and so forth, who have arrived but not attained nirvāṇa in order to realize the selflessness of dharmas, have no manifest adherence to 'I' and 'mine', what need is there to mention one who has realized both selflessnesses and abandoned obscurations without exception?" Whatever is "At that time I" and so forth, that is merely eliminating [other possibilities] regarding the continuums of others for those who desire to know for the purpose of designating worldly conventions; it is equivalent to conventions such as 'army' and 'forest', but is not due to manifest adherence to it being singular and permanent. Those abiding in the exalted wisdom of suchness cannot express conventions together with the world. Therefore, in order to be free from what becomes a basis for overweening pride, he caused them to grasp it perfectly, saying, "You too should not have manifest adherence to a self." Regarding that, the 'stream' has the characteristic of the path of seeing that goes to the great city of nirvāṇa. 'Entered' means attained; and one who has abandoned all the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is called a 'stream-enterer'. Furthermore, because by having abandoned manifest adherence to the agent, the action, and the activity, one realizes this mere conditionality itself, this teaches realizing selflessness. 'My' refers to manifest adherence to the agent. 'Fruit' refers to manifest adherence to the action. 'Attained' refers to manifest adherence to the activity. By this, in meaning, thinking "I have attained" is thoroughly taught to be a discordant factor.

Those twelve types of discordant factors are: overweening pride; even if without overweening pride, having little learning; even if having much learning, cultivating mental engagement on a small object; even if cultivating mental engagement on an object that is not small, forsaking sentient beings; even if not forsaking them, engaging with attachment to outer treatises; even if not engaging in them, lacking skill in means to overcome the signs of entities; even if skilled in means for that, not having accumulated the collection of merit; even if having accumulated the collection of merit, experiencing indolence and partaking of alms through gain and respect; even if not experiencing that, being unable to bear suffering; even if unconcerned about suffering, not having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom; even if having accumulated the collection of exalted wisdom, thoroughly grasping at a self; and even if lacking thorough grasping at a self, not possessing the instructions. Regarding that, although the Bhagavan has extensively taught the selflessness of persons and dharmas, by the force of having firmly accumulated manifest adherence to a self since beginningless time, thinking, "If whoever engages in the perception of a sentient being and so forth is not called a bodhisattva, if that is so, then how is it that the Bhagavan said: 'At that time, in that period, I became the king named Śūradatta'?"

It would become "I shall teach the dharma to you" and so forth. Thinking, "One who does not have the perception of a sentient being and so forth would not intend in that way", in order to be free from that which becomes an obstruction of overweening pride, making it regarding the fifth topic, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Regarding this, the outer meaning is this: "If even my lowest śrāvakas, the stream-enterers and so forth, who have arrived but not attained nirvāṇa in order to realize the selflessness of dharmas, have no manifest adherence to 'I' and 'mine', what need is there to mention one who has realized both selflessnesses and abandoned obscurations without exception?" Whatever is "At that time I" and so forth, that is merely eliminating [other possibilities] regarding the continuums of others for those who desire to know for the purpose of designating worldly conventions; it is equivalent to conventions such as 'army' and 'forest', but is not due to manifest adherence to it being singular and permanent. Those abiding in the exalted wisdom of suchness cannot express conventions together with the world. Therefore, in order to be free from what becomes a basis for overweening pride, he caused them to grasp it perfectly, saying, "You too should not have manifest adherence to a self." Regarding that, the 'stream' has the characteristic of the path of seeing that goes to the great city of nirvāṇa. 'Entered' means attained; and one who has abandoned all the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is called a 'stream-enterer'. Furthermore, because by having abandoned manifest adherence to the agent, the action, and the activity, one realizes this mere conditionality itself, this teaches realizing selflessness. 'My' refers to manifest adherence to the agent. 'Fruit' refers to manifest adherence to the action. 'Attained' refers to manifest adherence to the activity. translation: To the thought, "If one becomes thus attached, thinking 'I have attained', why at that time is he not called a stream-enterer?", he said, "Bhagavan, if," and so forth. If someone becomes attached, thinking "I" as in "by me", they have not abandoned the view of self. He thought, "For whoever has not abandoned the view of self, the noble path has not arisen. Whoever has not had the noble path arise is an ordinary being, so how could they become a stream-enterer?" Thus, whoever becomes attached saying "by me", the view of self completely arises for them. By this, the thorough holding of the mind is taught. By all this, the profoundness of this point is expressed.

The Noble Subhūti, too, by closely expressing the intention of the Bhagavan, in order to establish it ultimately and to lead into meditative absorption in yoga regarding that, said, "Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything." To the thought, "Why is that?", he said, "He has not entered into form," and so forth. By this, it teaches that ultimately both types of fruits are not to be attained. Thus, if the entity to be attained were to become a fruit, would it become conditioned or unconditioned? Regarding that, first, the unconditioned is just unarisen; because it is non-existent, being similar to a rabbit's horn, it is not suitable to be attained, because there is no difference from the state of not being attained. The conditioned is momentary, being destroyed immediately upon arising; because it does not abide, it will not be attained by anyone in any way. In whatever continuum, due to the active cause characterized by the selfless path having become present, a fruit characterized as a state completely discordant with the arising of afflictions has arisen, regarding that it is merely taught that "he attains the fruit," but ultimately it is not so. Furthermore, would the entities of that which is to be attained and that which attains be of different times or of the same time? First, the first position is not the case; because both must abide, if they are of different times, at the time when one is present the other is non-existent, so how could both of them abide? Neither is it from being of the same time; because, once both are established, there is no benefiting of one another.

If there is no benefiting, it is not logical to ascertain the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not logical for the characteristics of what is to be attained and what attains it to be simultaneously related through the characteristic of generating mutual association. Thus, first, those entities which are bodiless do not abide in a locus, so they have no association. They do not become the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it merely by being at the same time, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not merely from a single cause, because since that is common to both, there would be no certainty that 'this is what is to be attained, and this is what attains it.' For those that possess bodies, if they are associated with each other by their entire nature, it would entail the absurd consequence of them being one. If by one part, it would entail the absurd consequence of them possessing limbs. Neither is attainment from abiding without interval, because being common to both, without difference, there is no certainty. Therefore, this is merely superimposed by conceptualization. By this, all conventions such as agent and action should be clearly understood. 'Dharmas' refers to the dharmāyatana. By this, the unconditioned is also included, because the dharmāyatana has the nature of seven substances. The remainder, form and so forth, and a portion of the dharmāyatana, teach the conditioned. The Noble Subhūti, too, by closely expressing the intention of the Bhagavan, in order to establish it ultimately and to lead into meditative absorption in yoga regarding that, said, "Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything." To the thought, "Why is that?", he said, "He has not entered into form," and so forth. By this, it teaches that ultimately both types of fruits are not to be attained. Thus, if the entity to be attained were to become a fruit, would it become conditioned or unconditioned? Regarding that, first, the unconditioned is just unarisen; because it is non-existent, being similar to a rabbit's horn, it is not suitable to be attained, because there is no difference from the state of not being attained. The conditioned is momentary, being destroyed immediately upon arising; because it does not abide, it will not be attained by anyone in any way. In whatever continuum, due to the active cause characterized by the selfless path having become present, a fruit characterized as a state completely discordant with the arising of afflictions has arisen, regarding that it is merely taught that "he attains the fruit," but ultimately it is not so. Furthermore, would the entities of that which is to be attained and that which attains be of different times or of the same time? First, the first position is not the case; because both must abide, if they are of different times, at the time when one is present the other is non-existent, so how could both of them abide? Neither is it from being of the same time; because, once both are established, there is no benefiting of one another.

If there is no benefiting, it is not logical to ascertain the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not logical for the characteristics of what is to be attained and what attains it to be simultaneously related through the characteristic of generating mutual association. Thus, first, those entities which are bodiless do not abide in a locus, so they have no association. They do not become the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it merely by being at the same time, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not merely from a single cause, because since that is common to both, there would be no certainty that 'this is what is to be attained, and this is what attains it.' For those that possess bodies, if they are associated with each other by their entire nature, it would entail the absurd consequence of them being one. If by one part, it would entail the absurd consequence of them possessing limbs. Neither is attainment from abiding without interval, because being common to both, without difference, there is no certainty. Therefore, this is merely superimposed by conceptualization. By this, all conventions such as agent and action should be clearly understood. 'Dharmas' refers to the dharmāyatana. By this, the unconditioned is also included, because the dharmāyatana has the nature of seven substances. The remainder, form and so forth, and a portion of the dharmāyatana, teach the conditioned. This is an illustration; therefore, the eye and so forth should also be grasped.

translation: One who has abandoned the six aspects of afflictions operating in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by meditation is exactly the noble 'once-returner', because they will return once to the desire realm. One who has abandoned all afflictions operating in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by meditation is exactly called a 'non-returner', because they will not return again to the desire realm. At the time when one has abandoned all stains of the afflictions operating in the three realms, at that time, being worthy of being venerated by the entire world, they are called an 'arhat'.

The Noble Subhūti, too, by closely expressing the intention of the Bhagavan, in order to establish it ultimately and to lead into meditative absorption in yoga regarding that, said, "Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything." To the thought, "Why is that?", he said, "He has not entered into form," and so forth. By this, it teaches that ultimately both types of fruits are not to be attained. Thus, if the entity to be attained were to become a fruit, would it become conditioned or unconditioned? Regarding that, first, the unconditioned is just unarisen; because it is non-existent, being similar to a rabbit's horn, it is not suitable to be attained, because there is no difference from the state of not being attained. The conditioned is momentary, being destroyed immediately upon arising; because it does not abide, it will not be attained by anyone in any way. In whatever continuum, due to the active cause characterized by the selfless path having become present, a fruit characterized as a state completely discordant with the arising of afflictions has arisen, regarding that it is merely taught that "he attains the fruit," but ultimately it is not so. Furthermore, would the entities of that which is to be attained and that which attains be of different times or of the same time? First, the first position is not the case; because both must abide, if they are of different times, at the time when one is present the other is non-existent, so how could both of them abide? Neither is it from being of the same time; because, once both are established, there is no benefiting of one another.

If there is no benefiting, it is not logical to ascertain the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not logical for the characteristics of what is to be attained and what attains it to be simultaneously related through the characteristic of generating mutual association. Thus, first, those entities which are bodiless do not abide in a locus, so they have no association. They do not become the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it merely by being at the same time, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not merely from a single cause, because since that is common to both, there would be no certainty that 'this is what is to be attained, and this is what attains it.' For those that possess bodies, if they are associated with each other by their entire nature, it would entail the absurd consequence of them being one. If by one part, it would entail the absurd consequence of them possessing limbs. Neither is attainment from abiding without interval, because being common to both, without difference, there is no certainty. Therefore, this is merely superimposed by conceptualization. By this, all conventions such as agent and action should be clearly understood. 'Dharmas' refers to the dharmāyatana. By this, the unconditioned is also included, because the dharmāyatana has the nature of seven substances. The remainder, form and so forth, and a portion of the dharmāyatana, teach the conditioned. This is an illustration; therefore, the eye and so forth should also be grasped.

translation: "There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

[3-86] translation already produced for this document:
The Noble Subhūti, too, by closely expressing the intention of the Bhagavan, in order to establish it ultimately and to lead into meditative absorption in yoga regarding that, said, "Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything." To the thought, "Why is that?", he said, "He has not entered into form," and so forth. By this, it teaches that ultimately both types of fruits are not to be attained. Thus, if the entity to be attained were to become a fruit, would it become conditioned or unconditioned? Regarding that, first, the unconditioned is just unarisen; because it is non-existent, being similar to a rabbit's horn, it is not suitable to be attained, because there is no difference from the state of not being attained. The conditioned is momentary, being destroyed immediately upon arising; because it does not abide, it will not be attained by anyone in any way. In whatever continuum, due to the active cause characterized by the selfless path having become present, a fruit characterized as a state completely discordant with the arising of afflictions has arisen, regarding that it is merely taught that "he attains the fruit," but ultimately it is not so. Furthermore, would the entities of that which is to be attained and that which attains be of different times or of the same time? First, the first position is not the case; because both must abide, if they are of different times, at the time when one is present the other is non-existent, so how could both of them abide? Neither is it from being of the same time; because, once both are established, there is no benefiting of one another.

[3-87] translation already produced for this document:
If there is no benefiting, it is not logical to ascertain the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not logical for the characteristics of what is to be attained and what attains it to be simultaneously related through the characteristic of generating mutual association. Thus, first, those entities which are bodiless do not abide in a locus, so they have no association. They do not become the entities of what is to be attained and what attains it merely by being at the same time, because it would entail an absurd consequence. It is also not merely from a single cause, because since that is common to both, there would be no certainty that 'this is what is to be attained, and this is what attains it.' For those that possess bodies, if they are associated with each other by their entire nature, it would entail the absurd consequence of them being one. If by one part, it would entail the absurd consequence of them possessing limbs. Neither is attainment from abiding without interval, because being common to both, without difference, there is no certainty. Therefore, this is merely superimposed by conceptualization. By this, all conventions such as agent and action should be clearly understood. 'Dharmas' refers to the dharmāyatana. By this, the unconditioned is also included, because the dharmāyatana has the nature of seven substances. The remainder, form and so forth, and a portion of the dharmāyatana, teach the conditioned. This is an illustration; therefore, the eye and so forth should also be grasped.

If someone becomes attached, thinking "I" as in "by me", they have not abandoned the view of self. He thought, "For whoever has not abandoned the view of self, the noble path has not arisen. Whoever has not had the noble path arise is an ordinary being, so how could they become a stream-enterer?" Thus, whoever becomes attached saying "by me", the view of self completely arises for them. [3-92] translation already produced for this document:
"There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐོས་པ་ཉུང་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "Bhagavan, although I am an arhat free from attachment" means it is not due to being attached to a self. Well then, how is it? It is due to being attached to mere convention, and I have already explained that.

To the thought, "If one becomes thus attached, thinking 'I have attained', why at that time is he not called a stream-enterer?", he said, "Bhagavan, if," and so forth. If someone becomes attached, thinking "I" as in "by me", they have not abandoned the view of self. He thought, "For whoever has not abandoned the view of self, the noble path has not arisen. Whoever has not had the noble path arise is an ordinary being, so how could they become a stream-enterer?" Thus, whoever becomes attached saying "by me", the view of self completely arises for them. By this, the thorough holding of the mind is taught. By all this, the profoundness of this point is expressed.

[3-92] translation already produced for this document:
"There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐོས་པ་ཉུང་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

To the thought, "If one becomes thus attached, thinking 'I have attained', why at that time is he not called a stream-enterer?", he said, "Bhagavan, if," and so forth. If someone becomes attached, thinking "I" as in "by me", they have not abandoned the view of self. He thought, "For whoever has not abandoned the view of self, the noble path has not arisen. Whoever has not had the noble path arise is an ordinary being, so how could they become a stream-enterer?" Thus, whoever becomes attached saying "by me", the view of self completely arises for them. By this, the thorough holding of the mind is taught. By all this, the profoundness of this point is expressed.

འདོད་པ་ན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་བསྒོམ་པས་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བ་རྣམ་པ་དྲུག་སྤངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་འཕགས་པ་ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བ་སྟེ། འདོད་པའི་ཁམས་སུ་ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདོད་པའི་ཁམས་ན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་བསྒོམ་པས་སྤང་པར་བྱ་བ་མཐའ་དག་སྤངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། འདོད་པའི་ཁམས་སུ་ཡང་མི་འོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གང་གི་ཚེ་ཁམས་གསུམ་ན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་དྲི་མ་མཐའ་དག་སྤངས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་དེ་ཉིད་འཇིག་རྟེན་མཐའ་དག་གིས་མཆོད་པར་འོས་པས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །

One who has abandoned the six aspects of afflictions operating in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by meditation is exactly the noble 'once-returner', because they will return once to the desire realm. One who has abandoned all afflictions operating in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by meditation is exactly called a 'non-returner', because they will not return again to the desire realm. At the time when one has abandoned all stains of the afflictions operating in the three realms, at that time, being worthy of being venerated by the entire world, they are called an 'arhat'.
