[3-92] translation already produced for this document:
"There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

heading: ཐོས་པ་མང་ཡང་དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In order to free those who think, "If karma and agents and so forth are indeed ultimately non-existent, then how should bodhisattvas make aspirations in order to accomplish thoroughly pure buddha-fields?", from the hindrance of cultivating mental engagements with small objects, he spoke by way of the seventh point: "Whichever bodhisattva," and so forth. "Untrue" means false. Thinking, "If that is so, how did the Bhagavan speak in various places of the excellent thorough purity of the fields of bodhisattvas?", and asking, "Why is that?", in response, he said, "The arrays of fields," and so forth. Many fields are "the arrays of fields." "Without those arrays" means because ultimately there is no array whatsoever as an essence possessing parts or as an accumulation of subtle particles.

དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཞེས་བགྱི་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མ་མཆིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་སྤངས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད་ལ་དེ་བཏགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ལ། རྒྱུད་ཀྱང་བཏགས་པར་ཡོད་པའི་དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་དེ། དེ་ནི་སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །ད་ནི་འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བདག་ཉིད་དཔང་ཡིན་པས་བདག་གི་ཚིག་གཟུང་བར་འོས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཡོན་ཏན་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པ་དང་། ཡོན་ཏན་ཐུན་མོང་བ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བདག་ཉིད་རྗོད་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་ཉིད་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར། བདག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་བྱེ་བྲག་གོ། །དེ་ཡང་གཉི་གའི་ཆ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བའི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཁོ་ན་བདག་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་གཞན་དག་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་སྐྱེ་བར་མི་རུང་ངོ་སྙམ་ནས་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་ཅིང་། དེ་ལས་ལངས་པ་དེ་དག་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་གཞན་དག་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་སྐྱེ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་སྟེ། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པ་དེས་གནས་པའི་ངང་ཚུལ་ཅན་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་ལ་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །རྣམ་པར་དབྱེ་བ་འདི་ནི་དགའ་བའོ། །བདག་ལ་ལུང་མི་བསྟན་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེའི་ཚེ་བདག་ཏུ་ལྟ་བ་མ་སྤངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་གིས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡང་རྙེད་པར་དཀའ་ན། གང་གཉི་གའི་ཆ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བའི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པས་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པ་ཉིད་ལྟ་སྨོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་དགོས་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བདག་གིས་འབྲས་བུ་འདུས་བྱས་སམ་འདུས་མ་བྱས་འགའ་ཞིག་ཐོབ་པོ་སྙམ་དུ་དེ་ལྟར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་སུ་ཞིག་མི་གནས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པ་ཞེས་ཕྱོགས་དག་ཏུ་གསུངས་ཏེ། གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །
[3-92] translation already produced for this document:
"There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

གལ་ཏེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཅི་ཡང་མེད་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་གྱུར་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་ཆོས་ཇི་ལྟར་བླངས། འོན་ཏེ་མ་བླངས་ན་ནི་དེའི་ཚེ་བདག་ཅག་ཆོས་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་བྱུང་བ་ལ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་མཉེས་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་དུ་གང་དག་དེ་ལྟར་རྟོགས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་ཐོས་པ་ཉུང་བ་གགས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་དྲུག་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་གང་བླངས་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་དགོངས་པ་སྔ་མ་ཉིད་བཟུང་ནས། དེ་ནི་མ་མཆིས་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་དངོས་པོས་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་བླངས་པ་མེད་པ་དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་སྔར་བཤད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ཞི་བའི་ཡང་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མོད་ཀྱི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་དབང་ གིས་ཚིག་གི་ཚོགས་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྣང་བའི་ཤེས་པ་བྱུང་བ་ཙམ་ལ་བླངས་པ་ཞེས་གདགས་ཏེ། དེས་ན་ཐོས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བར་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྱིས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐོས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཚོལ་བའི་དུས་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་བྱུང་བ་མཉེས་པར་བྱའོ། །དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་བླང་བར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་སྤང་བ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡང་སྟོན་ཏོ། །མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་བླངས་སམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཕྱོགས་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་ཆོས་བླང་བའི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཟློག་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །བླངས་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མ་མཆིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པ་གཟུང་དུ་མེད་པར་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་། དེ་ལ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་ཡང་སྟོན་ཏོ། །གནས་འདིའི་ཟབ་པ་ཡང་བརྗོད་དོ། །
[3-95] translation already produced for this document:
In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

heading: ཐོས་པ་མང་ཡང་དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Although those arrays are indeed entirely non-existent, nevertheless, like the arrays of fields apprehended in a dream, they are taught to exist conventionally as merely pleasant when unexamined; therefore, they are called "the arrays of fields". He thought, "Were it not so, since the ultimate nature cannot be expressed, it would not be expressed." Although non-abiding has been explained above, in order to benefit those of a forgetful disposition, to make them remember by means of summarizing at the end, he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Thus" means: because no entity whatsoever is established in the ways stated, one should generate the mind without abiding in that—this is the meaning of the words. The remainder is as before. By this saying, "He speaks untruly of that," implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "I will accomplish the arrays of fields ultimately," is the discordant class. By stating just a sign, "The arrays of fields," it thoroughly shows freedom from all cultivation of mental engagements with small objects. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers regarding the cultivation of mental engagement with small objects. By this saying, "The Tathāgata spoke of them as without those arrays," since it posits the ultimate, it introduces entering into meditative absorption in yoga, and teaches profundity.

[3-92] translation already produced for this document:
"There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

[3-92] translation already produced for this document:
"There is not any dharma called an 'arhat'" means that because it is designated upon the continuum of pristine wisdom that has abandoned such aspects of afflictive obscuration, and because the continuum also exists imputedly, ultimately it does not exist at all; he thought, "It is because it is a superimposition." Now, the noble Subhūti, being a witness himself, in order to make his words worthy of being grasped, expresses himself by way of abiding without afflictions, which is an extraordinary quality, and being an arhat, which is a common quality, and in order to teach exactly the thorough holding of the mind, he said, "I", and so forth. "Without afflictions" is a particular meditative absorption. Furthermore, only arhats who are liberated in both ways enter into meditative absorption in yoga, thinking, "It is not suitable for others to have afflictions arise by focusing on me," and for those who have risen from that, others will not have afflictions arise by focusing on them; those who have the character of abiding by that absence of afflictions are spoken of in this way. This detailed explanation is pleasing. "He would not have prophesied of me" means he thought, "Because the view of self would not have been abandoned at that time, even the fruit of a stream-enterer would be difficult for me to find; so what need is there to even mention abiding without afflictions, which is to be attained by an arhat liberated in both ways?" To the thought, "How should one abide without afflictions?", he said, "He does not abide in anything." "Whoever does not abide by becoming attached in that way, thinking, 'I have attained some conditioned or unconditioned fruit', that very one is said in the tenets to abide without afflictions, and it is not anyone else"—this is the meaning of the words.

[3-95] translation already produced for this document:
In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

heading: དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In order to free those who think, "Although sentient beings do not exist apart from the aggregates, is there not indeed something non-different? Otherwise, how would a bodhisattva engage in thoroughly ripening sentient beings?", from the hindrance characterized by forsaking sentient beings, he spoke by way of the eighth point: "Suppose, for example..." "A man" refers to Rāhu, the lord of the asuras; his body in the desire realm is the size of Mount Meru. Although it is indeed large, it is large pointlessly. Desiring to express the intention behind why the Bhagavan taught this, he asked, "Why is that?", and in order to express that very intention, he said, "There is no entity." Because it is ultimately devoid of the nature of one or many, it is entirely without an essence; like a dreamed body in a dream, the Tathāgata spoke of it conventionally, but not ultimately. Saying, "Therefore it is called a body," expresses the reasoning here. He thought, "Thus, this is merely conventional; therefore it is called that. Were it not so, because no dharma whatsoever is established ultimately, it would not be called that." In order to refute the Rgyaldpogpas and so forth who assert the non-existent as an entity, he said, "Because it has no entity." Since non-entity is the defining characteristic of abiding having abandoned entity, how could it not become an essence discordant with that? Therefore, it is called a body. Were it not so, since no body whatsoever is established ultimately, what would be called a body here? Therefore, this teaching of non-entity thoroughly shows this: even whatever body is the size of Mount Meru, when it is ultimately not a body of a self because of having no essence, then how could the bodies of others possess an essence or possess a self? By this, implicitly, it teaches that for a bodhisattva who strives in thoroughly ripening sentient beings, being attached to sentient beings ultimately is the discordant class. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers to abandon that. By stating just a sign, "a man", it is stated to include all various distinct bodies, such as those born from eggs and so forth.

In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

In order to free those who think, "If karma and agents and so forth are indeed ultimately non-existent, then how should bodhisattvas make aspirations in order to accomplish thoroughly pure buddha-fields?", from the hindrance of cultivating mental engagements with small objects, he spoke by way of the seventh point: "Whichever bodhisattva," and so forth. "Untrue" means false. Thinking, "If that is so, how did the Bhagavan speak in various places of the excellent thorough purity of the fields of bodhisattvas?", and asking, "Why is that?", in response, he said, "The arrays of fields," and so forth. Although those arrays are indeed entirely non-existent, nevertheless, like the arrays of fields apprehended in a dream, they are taught to exist conventionally as merely pleasant when unexamined; therefore, they are called "the arrays of fields". He thought, "Were it not so, since the ultimate nature cannot be expressed, it would not be expressed." Although non-abiding has been explained above, in order to benefit those of a forgetful disposition, to make them remember by means of summarizing at the end, he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Thus" means: because no entity whatsoever is established in the ways stated, one should generate the mind without abiding in that—this is the meaning of the words. The remainder is as before. By this saying, "He speaks untruly of that," implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "I will accomplish the arrays of fields ultimately," is the discordant class. By stating just a sign, "The arrays of fields," it thoroughly shows freedom from all cultivation of mental engagements with small objects. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers regarding the cultivation of mental engagement with small objects. By this saying, "The Tathāgata spoke of them as without those arrays," since it posits the ultimate, it introduces entering into meditative absorption in yoga, and teaches profundity.

In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

Although those arrays are indeed entirely non-existent, nevertheless, like the arrays of fields apprehended in a dream, they are taught to exist conventionally as merely pleasant when unexamined; therefore, they are called "the arrays of fields". He thought, "Were it not so, since the ultimate nature cannot be expressed, it would not be expressed." Although non-abiding has been explained above, in order to benefit those of a forgetful disposition, to make them remember by means of summarizing at the end, he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Thus" means: because no entity whatsoever is established in the ways stated, one should generate the mind without abiding in that—this is the meaning of the words. The remainder is as before. By this saying, "He speaks untruly of that," implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "I will accomplish the arrays of fields ultimately," is the discordant class. By stating just a sign, "The arrays of fields," it thoroughly shows freedom from all cultivation of mental engagements with small objects. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers regarding the cultivation of mental engagement with small objects. By this saying, "The Tathāgata spoke of them as without those arrays," since it posits the ultimate, it introduces entering into meditative absorption in yoga, and teaches profundity.

In order to free those who came to understand thus, thinking, "If ultimately there is nothing to be attained and no attainer, how did the Bhagavan, when he became a bodhisattva, obtain the dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? But if he did not obtain it, then why should those of us who desire to obtain the dharma please the Tathāgatas when they appear?", from the hindrance of having little hearing, he spoke by way of the sixth point: "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata obtained from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly completely awakened Buddha Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti also, having grasped the previous intention, said, "There is not." That there is no dharma whatsoever obtained as an entity of something to be attained and an attainer ultimately, is just as explained before. It is also because all dharmas are peaceful by nature. Although that is so, it is designated as "obtained" merely with respect to the arising of knowledge in which various collections of words and so forth appear by the power of the Tathāgata. Therefore, thoroughly seeking hearing is fruitful. By this, implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "When a bodhisattva thoroughly seeks hearing, they should please Buddhas who have appeared, and after that I will obtain the dharmas of a Buddha," is the discordant class. It also teaches abiding with aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating just a portion, "Did he obtain any dharma from Dīpaṃkara?", it turns away all signs of obtaining dharma. By this saying, "There is not any dharma that was obtained," it posits the ultimate of dharmas as ungraspable, and it also teaches entering into meditative absorption in yoga on that and eradicating distraction. It also expresses the profoundness of this point.

In order to free those who think, "If karma and agents and so forth are indeed ultimately non-existent, then how should bodhisattvas make aspirations in order to accomplish thoroughly pure buddha-fields?", from the hindrance of cultivating mental engagements with small objects, he spoke by way of the seventh point: "Whichever bodhisattva," and so forth. "Untrue" means false. Thinking, "If that is so, how did the Bhagavan speak in various places of the excellent thorough purity of the fields of bodhisattvas?", and asking, "Why is that?", in response, he said, "The arrays of fields," and so forth. translation: Now, by expressing that this dharma discourse is extremely meaningful, in order to free those who are attached to outer treatises from the distraction of being attached to them, he spoke by way of the ninth point: 'Subhūti, what do you think?' By this, it thoroughly shows the preeminence of this dharma discourse through four aspects: completely gathering merit, being revered by gods and so forth, doing what is difficult to do, and making equivalent to the Tathāgata and so forth.

In order to free those who think, "Although sentient beings do not exist apart from the aggregates, is there not indeed something non-different? Otherwise, how would a bodhisattva engage in thoroughly ripening sentient beings?", from the hindrance characterized by forsaking sentient beings, he spoke by way of the eighth point: "Suppose, for example..." "A man" refers to Rāhu, the lord of the asuras; his body in the desire realm is the size of Mount Meru. Although it is indeed large, it is large pointlessly. Desiring to express the intention behind why the Bhagavan taught this, he asked, "Why is that?", and in order to express that very intention, he said, "There is no entity." Because it is ultimately devoid of the nature of one or many, it is entirely without an essence; like a dreamed body in a dream, the Tathāgata spoke of it conventionally, but not ultimately. Saying, "Therefore it is called a body," expresses the reasoning here. He thought, "Thus, this is merely conventional; therefore it is called that. Were it not so, because no dharma whatsoever is established ultimately, it would not be called that." In order to refute the Rgyaldpogpas and so forth who assert the non-existent as an entity, he said, "Because it has no entity." Since non-entity is the defining characteristic of abiding having abandoned entity, how could it not become an essence discordant with that? Therefore, it is called a body. Were it not so, since no body whatsoever is established ultimately, what would be called a body here? Therefore, this teaching of non-entity thoroughly shows this: even whatever body is the size of Mount Meru, when it is ultimately not a body of a self because of having no essence, then how could the bodies of others possess an essence or possess a self? By this, implicitly, it teaches that for a bodhisattva who strives in thoroughly ripening sentient beings, being attached to sentient beings ultimately is the discordant class. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers to abandon that. By stating just a sign, "a man", it is stated to include all various distinct bodies, such as those born from eggs and so forth.

translation: Herein, completely gathering merit is what was spoken as 'begets much merit on that basis.' Being revered by gods and so forth is what was spoken as 'that place becomes a stūpa.' Doing what is difficult to do is what was spoken as 'they will be endowed with supreme wonder.' Making equivalent to the Tathāgata and so forth is what was spoken as 'in that place dwells the Teacher or whoever is like a guru.' Herein, expressing the merit of the gift of precious things thoroughly shows it to be preeminent through two distinguishing aspects: the distinction of the entity and the distinction of the field. The preeminence in the distinction of the entity also consists of vastness and excellence. Herein, vastness is being extremely abundant through the particularity of the basis, which is what was spoken as 'as many world systems as those.'

Although those arrays are indeed entirely non-existent, nevertheless, like the arrays of fields apprehended in a dream, they are taught to exist conventionally as merely pleasant when unexamined; therefore, they are called "the arrays of fields". He thought, "Were it not so, since the ultimate nature cannot be expressed, it would not be expressed." Although non-abiding has been explained above, in order to benefit those of a forgetful disposition, to make them remember by means of summarizing at the end, he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Thus" means: because no entity whatsoever is established in the ways stated, one should generate the mind without abiding in that—this is the meaning of the words. The remainder is as before. By this saying, "He speaks untruly of that," implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "I will accomplish the arrays of fields ultimately," is the discordant class. By stating just a sign, "The arrays of fields," it thoroughly shows freedom from all cultivation of mental engagements with small objects. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers regarding the cultivation of mental engagement with small objects. By this saying, "The Tathāgata spoke of them as without those arrays," since it posits the ultimate, it introduces entering into meditative absorption in yoga, and teaches profundity.

ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ལས་སེམས་ཅན་གུད་ན་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཐ་མི་དད་པ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པ་ཁོ་ན་མ་ཡིན་ནམ་གཞན་དུ་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཇི་ལྟར་འཇུག་སྙམ་དུ་གང་སེམས་པ་དེ་སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་གགས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དབྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བརྒྱད་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྷ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི་དབང་པོ་སྒྲ་གཅན་ཟིན་ཏེ། དེའི་ལུས་ནི་འདོད་པའི་ཁམས་ན་རི་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚད་ཙམ་མོ། །དེ་ཆེར་ཟིན་ཀྱང་དོན་མེད་པར་དེའི་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བསྟན་པའི་དགོངས་པ་བརྗོད་པར་འདོད་པས། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། དགོངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་པོ་མ་མཆིས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། རྨི་ལམ་དག་ན་རྨིས་པའི་ལུས་བཞིན་དུ་དེ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བཞིན་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་ལུས་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདིར་འཐད་པ་སྨྲས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟར་འདི་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཉིད་དེ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱའི་དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་སྐད་མི་བརྗོད་དོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་པའོ། །རྒྱལ་དཔོག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་དག་མེད་པ་ལ་དངོས་པོར་ཁས་ལེན་པ་དེ་དག་དགག་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་དངོས་པོ་མ་མཆིས་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་སྤངས་ཏེ་གནས་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་དེ་དང་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ངོ་བོར་མི་འགྱུར། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ལུས་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པས་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིར་ཅི་ཞིག་བརྗོད་དེ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པ་འདིས་ནི་འདི་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ལུས་ཀྱི་ཚད་རི་རབ་ཙམ་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཡང་གང་གི་ཚེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པས་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ལུས་མ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཇི་ལྟར་གཞན་དག་གི་ལུས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དང་བཅས་པའམ་བདག་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར། འདི་ལ་དོན་གྱིས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བའི་འདུན་པ་དང་།སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལུས་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟུང་བར་བརྗོད་དོ། །

In order to free those who think, "Although sentient beings do not exist apart from the aggregates, is there not indeed something non-different? Otherwise, how would a bodhisattva engage in thoroughly ripening sentient beings?", from the hindrance characterized by forsaking sentient beings, he spoke by way of the eighth point: "Suppose, for example..." "A man" refers to Rāhu, the lord of the asuras; his body in the desire realm is the size of Mount Meru. Although it is indeed large, it is large pointlessly. Desiring to express the intention behind why the Bhagavan taught this, he asked, "Why is that?", and in order to express that very intention, he said, "There is no entity." Because it is ultimately devoid of the nature of one or many, it is entirely without an essence; like a dreamed body in a dream, the Tathāgata spoke of it conventionally, but not ultimately. Saying, "Therefore it is called a body," expresses the reasoning here. He thought, "Thus, this is merely conventional; therefore it is called that. Were it not so, because no dharma whatsoever is established ultimately, it would not be called that." In order to refute the Rgyaldpogpas and so forth who assert the non-existent as an entity, he said, "Because it has no entity." Since non-entity is the defining characteristic of abiding having abandoned entity, how could it not become an essence discordant with that? Therefore, it is called a body. Were it not so, since no body whatsoever is established ultimately, what would be called a body here? Therefore, this teaching of non-entity thoroughly shows this: even whatever body is the size of Mount Meru, when it is ultimately not a body of a self because of having no essence, then how could the bodies of others possess an essence or possess a self? By this, implicitly, it teaches that for a bodhisattva who strives in thoroughly ripening sentient beings, being attached to sentient beings ultimately is the discordant class. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers to abandon that. By stating just a sign, "a man", it is stated to include all various distinct bodies, such as those born from eggs and so forth.

translation: Excellence is being renowned as extremely rare in the world, which is what was spoken as 'having completely filled with the seven precious things.' The field is preeminent because it is endowed with the perfection of one's own and others' benefit. Herein, the perfection of others' benefit is because it teaches others unerringly the objects to be abandoned and to be adopted, which was spoken as 'by the Tathāgata.' Because he spoke exactly in accordance with that suchness of entities, as an etymology, he is called 'one who speaks thus.' The perfection of one's own benefit has two aspects because the perfection of pristine wisdom and the perfection of abandonment are distinct. Herein, this saying 'arhat' teaches the perfection of abandonment; because he has conquered the enemies of the afflictions, as an etymology, he is called 'arhat'.

Although those arrays are indeed entirely non-existent, nevertheless, like the arrays of fields apprehended in a dream, they are taught to exist conventionally as merely pleasant when unexamined; therefore, they are called "the arrays of fields". He thought, "Were it not so, since the ultimate nature cannot be expressed, it would not be expressed." Although non-abiding has been explained above, in order to benefit those of a forgetful disposition, to make them remember by means of summarizing at the end, he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Thus" means: because no entity whatsoever is established in the ways stated, one should generate the mind without abiding in that—this is the meaning of the words. The remainder is as before. By this saying, "He speaks untruly of that," implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "I will accomplish the arrays of fields ultimately," is the discordant class. By stating just a sign, "The arrays of fields," it thoroughly shows freedom from all cultivation of mental engagements with small objects. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers regarding the cultivation of mental engagement with small objects. By this saying, "The Tathāgata spoke of them as without those arrays," since it posits the ultimate, it introduces entering into meditative absorption in yoga, and teaches profundity.

In order to free those who think, "Although sentient beings do not exist apart from the aggregates, is there not indeed something non-different? Otherwise, how would a bodhisattva engage in thoroughly ripening sentient beings?", from the hindrance characterized by forsaking sentient beings, he spoke by way of the eighth point: "Suppose, for example..." "A man" refers to Rāhu, the lord of the asuras; his body in the desire realm is the size of Mount Meru. Although it is indeed large, it is large pointlessly. Desiring to express the intention behind why the Bhagavan taught this, he asked, "Why is that?", and in order to express that very intention, he said, "There is no entity." Because it is ultimately devoid of the nature of one or many, it is entirely without an essence; like a dreamed body in a dream, the Tathāgata spoke of it conventionally, but not ultimately. Saying, "Therefore it is called a body," expresses the reasoning here. He thought, "Thus, this is merely conventional; therefore it is called that. Were it not so, because no dharma whatsoever is established ultimately, it would not be called that." In order to refute the Rgyaldpogpas and so forth who assert the non-existent as an entity, he said, "Because it has no entity." Since non-entity is the defining characteristic of abiding having abandoned entity, how could it not become an essence discordant with that? Therefore, it is called a body. Were it not so, since no body whatsoever is established ultimately, what would be called a body here? Therefore, this teaching of non-entity thoroughly shows this: even whatever body is the size of Mount Meru, when it is ultimately not a body of a self because of having no essence, then how could the bodies of others possess an essence or possess a self? By this, implicitly, it teaches that for a bodhisattva who strives in thoroughly ripening sentient beings, being attached to sentient beings ultimately is the discordant class. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers to abandon that. By stating just a sign, "a man", it is stated to include all various distinct bodies, such as those born from eggs and so forth.

translation: By this saying 'perfectly completely awakened one,' it teaches the perfection of pristine wisdom. Therefore, stating the three words is the meaning of a general summary: 'it is endowed with the fruit.' Saying 'should trust' means aspiring; saying 'should generate trust, should realize' means one should understand, that is, generate wisdom—this is the meaning of the words. Herein, the former is the fruit of the latter. Alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. 'Explained' refers to the words. 'Perfectly shown' means aspiring, which is the meaning of generating trust. 'Innumerable' is because it cannot be completely determined by counting. 'Immeasurable' is because its power cannot be measured or because it is without peer. 'Recites' means one recites the syllables oneself. 'Teaches' means perfectly teaching the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, 'reciting' is the words; 'teaching' is the meaning. 'Becomes a stūpa' means worthy of homage. Being a stūpa itself is 'becoming a stūpa'; for example, like saying 'becoming an authority.'

Although those arrays are indeed entirely non-existent, nevertheless, like the arrays of fields apprehended in a dream, they are taught to exist conventionally as merely pleasant when unexamined; therefore, they are called "the arrays of fields". He thought, "Were it not so, since the ultimate nature cannot be expressed, it would not be expressed." Although non-abiding has been explained above, in order to benefit those of a forgetful disposition, to make them remember by means of summarizing at the end, he said, "Therefore," and so forth. "Thus" means: because no entity whatsoever is established in the ways stated, one should generate the mind without abiding in that—this is the meaning of the words. The remainder is as before. By this saying, "He speaks untruly of that," implicitly, it thoroughly shows that being attached, thinking, "I will accomplish the arrays of fields ultimately," is the discordant class. By stating just a sign, "The arrays of fields," it thoroughly shows freedom from all cultivation of mental engagements with small objects. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers regarding the cultivation of mental engagement with small objects. By this saying, "The Tathāgata spoke of them as without those arrays," since it posits the ultimate, it introduces entering into meditative absorption in yoga, and teaches profundity.

ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ལས་སེམས་ཅན་གུད་ན་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཐ་མི་དད་པ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པ་ཁོ་ན་མ་ཡིན་ནམ་གཞན་དུ་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཇི་ལྟར་འཇུག་སྙམ་དུ་གང་སེམས་པ་དེ་སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་གགས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དབྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བརྒྱད་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྷ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི་དབང་པོ་སྒྲ་གཅན་ཟིན་ཏེ། དེའི་ལུས་ནི་འདོད་པའི་ཁམས་ན་རི་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚད་ཙམ་མོ། །དེ་ཆེར་ཟིན་ཀྱང་དོན་མེད་པར་དེའི་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བསྟན་པའི་དགོངས་པ་བརྗོད་པར་འདོད་པས། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། དགོངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་པོ་མ་མཆིས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། རྨི་ལམ་དག་ན་རྨིས་པའི་ལུས་བཞིན་དུ་དེ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བཞིན་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་ལུས་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདིར་འཐད་པ་སྨྲས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟར་འདི་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཉིད་དེ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱའི་དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་སྐད་མི་བརྗོད་དོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་པའོ། །རྒྱལ་དཔོག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་དག་མེད་པ་ལ་དངོས་པོར་ཁས་ལེན་པ་དེ་དག་དགག་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་དངོས་པོ་མ་མཆིས་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་སྤངས་ཏེ་གནས་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་དེ་དང་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ངོ་བོར་མི་འགྱུར། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ལུས་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པས་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིར་ཅི་ཞིག་བརྗོད་དེ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པ་འདིས་ནི་འདི་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ལུས་ཀྱི་ཚད་རི་རབ་ཙམ་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཡང་གང་གི་ཚེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པས་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ལུས་མ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཇི་ལྟར་གཞན་དག་གི་ལུས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དང་བཅས་པའམ་བདག་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར། འདི་ལ་དོན་གྱིས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བའི་འདུན་པ་དང་།སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལུས་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟུང་བར་བརྗོད་དོ། །

In order to free those who think, "Although sentient beings do not exist apart from the aggregates, is there not indeed something non-different? Otherwise, how would a bodhisattva engage in thoroughly ripening sentient beings?", from the hindrance characterized by forsaking sentient beings, he spoke by way of the eighth point: "Suppose, for example..." "A man" refers to Rāhu, the lord of the asuras; his body in the desire realm is the size of Mount Meru. Although it is indeed large, it is large pointlessly. Desiring to express the intention behind why the Bhagavan taught this, he asked, "Why is that?", and in order to express that very intention, he said, "There is no entity." Because it is ultimately devoid of the nature of one or many, it is entirely without an essence; like a dreamed body in a dream, the Tathāgata spoke of it conventionally, but not ultimately. Saying, "Therefore it is called a body," expresses the reasoning here. He thought, "Thus, this is merely conventional; therefore it is called that. Were it not so, because no dharma whatsoever is established ultimately, it would not be called that." In order to refute the Rgyaldpogpas and so forth who assert the non-existent as an entity, he said, "Because it has no entity." Since non-entity is the defining characteristic of abiding having abandoned entity, how could it not become an essence discordant with that? Therefore, it is called a body. Were it not so, since no body whatsoever is established ultimately, what would be called a body here? Therefore, this teaching of non-entity thoroughly shows this: even whatever body is the size of Mount Meru, when it is ultimately not a body of a self because of having no essence, then how could the bodies of others possess an essence or possess a self? By this, implicitly, it teaches that for a bodhisattva who strives in thoroughly ripening sentient beings, being attached to sentient beings ultimately is the discordant class. It also teaches aspiration and making prayers to abandon that. By stating just a sign, "a man", it is stated to include all various distinct bodies, such as those born from eggs and so forth.

translation: He intended: "If it becomes a stūpa even by teaching a verse merely on the selflessness of persons, what need is there to mention teaching both kinds of selflessness?" 'Taking up' refers to the words. 'Retaining' means not forgetting. 'Reading' means making it into a volume. 'Mastering' refers to the meaning. By this, it teaches retaining through the wisdom arisen from hearing. Because one also retains through reflecting and the wisdom arisen from reflecting, he spoke of 'properly', which means understanding the meaning unerringly—this is the meaning of the words. In some texts, only the single word 'retaining' appears; herein, 'retaining' should be viewed as both the words and the meaning. 'Supreme wonder' is because of understanding a profound and vast dharma of such a kind. 'The Teacher dwells' refers to the dharma preacher, because he performs the deeds of the Teacher; this means it is like the Lord Buddha himself dwelling in actuality. 'Whoever is like a guru' means whoever it may be, such as noble Mañjughoṣa and so forth; because he accomplishes his deeds, one should view that dharma preacher as dwelling there.

The field is preeminent because it is endowed with the perfection of one's own and others' benefit. Herein, the perfection of others' benefit is because it teaches others unerringly the objects to be abandoned and to be adopted, which was spoken as 'by the Tathāgata.' Because he spoke exactly in accordance with that suchness of entities, as an etymology, he is called 'one who speaks thus.' The perfection of one's own benefit has two aspects because the perfection of pristine wisdom and the perfection of abandonment are distinct. By this saying 'perfectly completely awakened one,' it teaches the perfection of pristine wisdom. Therefore, stating the three words is the meaning of a general summary: 'it is endowed with the fruit.' Saying 'should trust' means aspiring; saying 'should generate trust, should realize' means one should understand, that is, generate wisdom—this is the meaning of the words. Herein, the former is the fruit of the latter. Alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. 'Explained' refers to the words. 'Perfectly shown' means aspiring, which is the meaning of generating trust. 'Innumerable' is because it cannot be completely determined by counting. 'Immeasurable' is because its power cannot be measured or because it is without peer. 'Recites' means one recites the syllables oneself. 'Teaches' means perfectly teaching the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, 'reciting' is the words; 'teaching' is the meaning. 'Becomes a stūpa' means worthy of homage. Being a stūpa itself is 'becoming a stūpa'; for example, like saying 'becoming an authority.'

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In some texts, the two words 'another' and 'others' appear; that is a synonym for all of 'whoever is like a guru', because it teaches 'dwells there'. By all this, it teaches the vastness of this topic. Meaningfully, it thoroughly teaches that abandoning the thorough upholding of the true dharma and being attached to outer treatises is the discordant class; it teaches that, having completely abandoned attachment to them, one gives rise to aspiration and prayer toward striving in the dharma. By stating merely the sign 'from this dharma discourse', it thoroughly shows: "Having abandoned attachment to outer treatises, one should strive in all true dharma." Because this dharma discourse is endowed with inconceivable power, in order to benefit others, he expresses that merit is produced for sentient beings merely by hearing its name; therefore, noble Subhūti requested: "What is its name?"

Herein, the perfection of others' benefit is because it teaches others unerringly the objects to be abandoned and to be adopted, which was spoken as 'by the Tathāgata.' Because he spoke exactly in accordance with that suchness of entities, as an etymology, he is called 'one who speaks thus.' The perfection of one's own benefit has two aspects because the perfection of pristine wisdom and the perfection of abandonment are distinct. Herein, this saying 'arhat' teaches the perfection of abandonment; because he has conquered the enemies of the afflictions, as an etymology, he is called 'arhat'.

By this saying 'perfectly completely awakened one,' it teaches the perfection of pristine wisdom. Therefore, stating the three words is the meaning of a general summary: 'it is endowed with the fruit.' Saying 'should trust' means aspiring; saying 'should generate trust, should realize' means one should understand, that is, generate wisdom—this is the meaning of the words. Herein, the former is the fruit of the latter. Alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. 'Explained' refers to the words. 'Perfectly shown' means aspiring, which is the meaning of generating trust. 'Innumerable' is because it cannot be completely determined by counting. 'Immeasurable' is because its power cannot be measured or because it is without peer. 'Recites' means one recites the syllables oneself. 'Teaches' means perfectly teaching the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, 'reciting' is the words; 'teaching' is the meaning. 'Becomes a stūpa' means worthy of homage. Being a stūpa itself is 'becoming a stūpa'; for example, like saying 'becoming an authority.'

Excellence is being renowned as extremely rare in the world, which is what was spoken as 'having completely filled with the seven precious things.' Herein, the perfection of others' benefit is because it teaches others unerringly the objects to be abandoned and to be adopted, which was spoken as 'by the Tathāgata.' Because he spoke exactly in accordance with that suchness of entities, as an etymology, he is called 'one who speaks thus.' The perfection of one's own benefit has two aspects because the perfection of pristine wisdom and the perfection of abandonment are distinct. Herein, this saying 'arhat' teaches the perfection of abandonment; because he has conquered the enemies of the afflictions, as an etymology, he is called 'arhat'.

By this saying 'perfectly completely awakened one,' it teaches the perfection of pristine wisdom. Therefore, stating the three words is the meaning of a general summary: 'it is endowed with the fruit.' Saying 'should trust' means aspiring; saying 'should generate trust, should realize' means one should understand, that is, generate wisdom—this is the meaning of the words. Herein, the former is the fruit of the latter. Alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. 'Explained' refers to the words. 'Perfectly shown' means aspiring, which is the meaning of generating trust. 'Innumerable' is because it cannot be completely determined by counting. 'Immeasurable' is because its power cannot be measured or because it is without peer. 'Recites' means one recites the syllables oneself. 'Teaches' means perfectly teaching the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, 'reciting' is the words; 'teaching' is the meaning. 'Becomes a stūpa' means worthy of homage. Being a stūpa itself is 'becoming a stūpa'; for example, like saying 'becoming an authority.'

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "Prajñāpāramitā": that which is its name is called such. By this, it is wisdom, and because it realizes and thoroughly cuts through the beyond, it goes beyond. That is a compound: "It is wisdom and also going beyond." Alternatively, the beyond of wisdom is the beyond of wisdom; because by this one realizes and thoroughly cuts through it, it is called such. That, moreover, by implication, is the Tathāgata's wisdom, which is endowed with the supreme of all aspects; by other wisdoms, the beyond cannot be gauged. Alternatively, "prajñāpāramitā" is exactly this word meaning "reached." That is solely the wisdom spoken of; because others cannot possibly go to its beyond. By this, the perfection of generosity and so forth are also explained. Because it will express that, this dharma discourse is also called such; just like poetic compositions such as Rol rnyed ma phrogs pa.

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Examining from the thought, "Since it is to be known individually by the Lord himself, it is unshared, and since it is ultimately unarisen, it cannot possibly be expressed by words," he asked, "Why is that?" and in reply he stated, "Subhūti, that which was taught by the Tathāgata as prajñāpāramitā..." Because ultimately it is to be known individually by oneself and is therefore unshared, and because ultimately all dharmas are utterly unarisen, it is indeed inappropriate to express it by words; nevertheless, one imputes externally onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and since that conceptualization is inherently mistaken, the aspect imputed by it is also false itself. Therefore, whatever prajñāpāramitā that has become a conceptual image was taught by the Tathāgata and made understood by words is itself not a perfection, but the Tathāgata's wisdom is not so, because in the true relative it has reached the beyond of the knowable. If it were not so, how would the Lord become omniscient? Because the cognizer is mistaken, it does not understand it and what has become a conceptual image as distinct. Therefore, it is said that in the nature of knowing, that very ultimate wisdom is taught by the Tathāgata. Thus, he intended: "There is no contradiction in teaching it like that." Alternatively, whatever is the Tathāgata's wisdom, that very thing taught by the Tathāgata in the nature of causing realization is ultimately solely non-existent, because ultimately there is no going beyond. The word 'itself' should be viewed as placed after 'is not a perfection'. By this, it thoroughly shows how one should practice by positing it ultimately and entering into meditative equipoise in it.

He intended: "If it becomes a stūpa even by teaching a verse merely on the selflessness of persons, what need is there to mention teaching both kinds of selflessness?" 'Taking up' refers to the words. 'Retaining' means not forgetting. 'Reading' means making it into a volume. 'Mastering' refers to the meaning. By this, it teaches retaining through the wisdom arisen from hearing. Because one also retains through reflecting and the wisdom arisen from reflecting, he spoke of 'properly', which means understanding the meaning unerringly—this is the meaning of the words. In some texts, only the single word 'retaining' appears; herein, 'retaining' should be viewed as both the words and the meaning. 'Supreme wonder' is because of understanding a profound and vast dharma of such a kind. 'The Teacher dwells' refers to the dharma preacher, because he performs the deeds of the Teacher; this means it is like the Lord Buddha himself dwelling in actuality. 'Whoever is like a guru' means whoever it may be, such as noble Mañjughoṣa and so forth; because he accomplishes his deeds, one should view that dharma preacher as dwelling there.

"Prajñāpāramitā": that which is its name is called such. By this, it is wisdom, and because it realizes and thoroughly cuts through the beyond, it goes beyond. That is a compound: "It is wisdom and also going beyond." Alternatively, the beyond of wisdom is the beyond of wisdom; because by this one realizes and thoroughly cuts through it, it is called such. That, moreover, by implication, is the Tathāgata's wisdom, which is endowed with the supreme of all aspects; by other wisdoms, the beyond cannot be gauged. Alternatively, "prajñāpāramitā" is exactly this word meaning "reached." That is solely the wisdom spoken of; because others cannot possibly go to its beyond. By this, the perfection of generosity and so forth are also explained. Because it will express that, this dharma discourse is also called such; just like poetic compositions such as Rol rnyed ma phrogs pa.

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In order to teach that just as prajñāpāramitā is taught by the Lord by imputing externally solely onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and not otherwise, likewise all dharmas are also taught by the Tathāgata, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" because ultimately all dharmas are unestablished. Even if they were established, because specific characteristics are unshared, conventions cannot be designated for them. Because general characteristics are imputed. Apart from specific characteristics and general characteristics, there is no other expressible thing, because those two have the characteristic of abiding in mutual exclusion.

ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཚིག་གསུམ་སྨོས་པ་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྤྱིར་བསྡུ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །མོས་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ན་འདོད་པ་སྟེ། མོས་པ་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ཤེས་རབ་བསྐྱེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདི་ལ་སྔ་མ་ནི་ཕྱི་མའི་འབྲས་བུའོ། །ཡང་ན་ཕྱི་མ་ནི་སྔ་མའི་བཤད་པའོ། །བཤད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྒྲའོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདོད་པ་སྟེ་མོས་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་དོན་ཏོ། །གྲངས་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གྲངས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་གཅད་པར་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཐུ་དཔག་པར་མི་ནུས་པའམ་དཔེ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདོན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བདག་ཉིད་ཡི་གེ་ཁ་ཏོན་དུ་བྱེད་པའོ། །སྟོན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་དག་ལ་ཚིག་གི་དོན་ཡང་དག་པར་སྟོན་པའོ། །ཡང་ན་འདོན་པ་ནི་ཚིག་གོ། །སྟོན་པ་ནི་དོན་ཏོ། །མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཕྱག་བྱ་བར་འོས་པའོ། །མཆོད་རྟེན་ཉིད་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་དབང་དུ་གྱུར་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
[3-105] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying 'perfectly completely awakened one,' it teaches the perfection of pristine wisdom. Therefore, stating the three words is the meaning of a general summary: 'it is endowed with the fruit.' Saying 'should trust' means aspiring; saying 'should generate trust, should realize' means one should understand, that is, generate wisdom—this is the meaning of the words. Herein, the former is the fruit of the latter. Alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. 'Explained' refers to the words. 'Perfectly shown' means aspiring, which is the meaning of generating trust. 'Innumerable' is because it cannot be completely determined by counting. 'Immeasurable' is because its power cannot be measured or because it is without peer. 'Recites' means one recites the syllables oneself. 'Teaches' means perfectly teaching the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, 'reciting' is the words; 'teaching' is the meaning. 'Becomes a stūpa' means worthy of homage. Being a stūpa itself is 'becoming a stūpa'; for example, like saying 'becoming an authority.'

འདི་ལྟར་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་བསྟན་པས་ཀྱང་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ན་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉི་ག་བསྟན་པ་ལྟ་སྨོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་དགོས་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །ལེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཚིག་གོ། །འཛིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མི་བརྗེད་པའོ། །ཀློག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གླེགས་བམ་དུ་བྱས་པའོ། །ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཏོ། འདིས་ནི་ཐོས་པ་ལ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་འཛིན་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བསམ་པ་དང་བསམ་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འཛིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་ཏེ། དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །ཁ་ཅིག་ལས་ནི་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་གཅིག་པོ་འབྱུང་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཚིག་དང་དོན་གཉི་གར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ངོ་མཚར་རབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་རྣམ་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྟོན་པ་གནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་སྟེ། སྟོན་པའི་མཛད་པ་མཛད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་བཞུགས་པ་དང་འདྲའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བླ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འཕགས་པ་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་སྟེ། དེའི་མཛད་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་དེ་གནས་པར་བལྟའོ། །
[3-106] translation already produced for this document:
He intended: "If it becomes a stūpa even by teaching a verse merely on the selflessness of persons, what need is there to mention teaching both kinds of selflessness?" 'Taking up' refers to the words. 'Retaining' means not forgetting. 'Reading' means making it into a volume. 'Mastering' refers to the meaning. By this, it teaches retaining through the wisdom arisen from hearing. Because one also retains through reflecting and the wisdom arisen from reflecting, he spoke of 'properly', which means understanding the meaning unerringly—this is the meaning of the words. In some texts, only the single word 'retaining' appears; herein, 'retaining' should be viewed as both the words and the meaning. 'Supreme wonder' is because of understanding a profound and vast dharma of such a kind. 'The Teacher dwells' refers to the dharma preacher, because he performs the deeds of the Teacher; this means it is like the Lord Buddha himself dwelling in actuality. 'Whoever is like a guru' means whoever it may be, such as noble Mañjughoṣa and so forth; because he accomplishes his deeds, one should view that dharma preacher as dwelling there.

ཁ་ཅིག་ལས་ནི་གཞན་དང་གཞན་དག་ཅེས་ཚིག་གཉིས་འབྱུང་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་བླ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་གང་ཡང་རུང་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཏེ། དེ་ན་གནས་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ནི་གནས་འདིའི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དོན་གྱིས་ན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟུང་བ་བཏང་ནས་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་ལ་ཆོས་ལ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་བཏང་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྨོས་པས་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པ་སྤངས་ཏེ། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ནུས་པ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པས་གཞན་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་མིང་ཐོས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བསོད་ནམས་སྐྱེ་བར་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་འདིའི་མིང་ཅི་ལགས་ཞེས་ཞུས་སོ། །
[3-107] translation already produced for this document:
In some texts, the two words 'another' and 'others' appear; that is a synonym for all of 'whoever is like a guru', because it teaches 'dwells there'. By all this, it teaches the vastness of this topic. Meaningfully, it thoroughly teaches that abandoning the thorough upholding of the true dharma and being attached to outer treatises is the discordant class; it teaches that, having completely abandoned attachment to them, one gives rise to aspiration and prayer toward striving in the dharma. By stating merely the sign 'from this dharma discourse', it thoroughly shows: "Having abandoned attachment to outer treatises, one should strive in all true dharma." Because this dharma discourse is endowed with inconceivable power, in order to benefit others, he expresses that merit is produced for sentient beings merely by hearing its name; therefore, noble Subhūti requested: "What is its name?"

"Prajñāpāramitā": that which is its name is called such. By this, it is wisdom, and because it realizes and thoroughly cuts through the beyond, it goes beyond. That is a compound: "It is wisdom and also going beyond." Alternatively, the beyond of wisdom is the beyond of wisdom; because by this one realizes and thoroughly cuts through it, it is called such. That, moreover, by implication, is the Tathāgata's wisdom, which is endowed with the supreme of all aspects; by other wisdoms, the beyond cannot be gauged. Alternatively, "prajñāpāramitā" is exactly this word meaning "reached." That is solely the wisdom spoken of; because others cannot possibly go to its beyond. By this, the perfection of generosity and so forth are also explained. Because it will express that, this dharma discourse is also called such; just like poetic compositions such as Rol rnyed ma phrogs pa.

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Therefore, the elder Subhūti, intending that ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever taught by the Tathāgata, said, "Lord, there is no dharma whatsoever taught by the Tathāgata." By this, it teaches the subduing of distraction and profundity.

[3-105] translation already produced for this document:
By this saying 'perfectly completely awakened one,' it teaches the perfection of pristine wisdom. Therefore, stating the three words is the meaning of a general summary: 'it is endowed with the fruit.' Saying 'should trust' means aspiring; saying 'should generate trust, should realize' means one should understand, that is, generate wisdom—this is the meaning of the words. Herein, the former is the fruit of the latter. Alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. 'Explained' refers to the words. 'Perfectly shown' means aspiring, which is the meaning of generating trust. 'Innumerable' is because it cannot be completely determined by counting. 'Immeasurable' is because its power cannot be measured or because it is without peer. 'Recites' means one recites the syllables oneself. 'Teaches' means perfectly teaching the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, 'reciting' is the words; 'teaching' is the meaning. 'Becomes a stūpa' means worthy of homage. Being a stūpa itself is 'becoming a stūpa'; for example, like saying 'becoming an authority.'

འདི་ལྟར་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་བསྟན་པས་ཀྱང་མཆོད་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ན་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉི་ག་བསྟན་པ་ལྟ་སྨོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་དགོས་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །ལེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཚིག་གོ། །འཛིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མི་བརྗེད་པའོ། །ཀློག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གླེགས་བམ་དུ་བྱས་པའོ། །ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཏོ། འདིས་ནི་ཐོས་པ་ལ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་འཛིན་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བསམ་པ་དང་བསམ་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འཛིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་ཏེ། དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །ཁ་ཅིག་ལས་ནི་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་གཅིག་པོ་འབྱུང་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཚིག་དང་དོན་གཉི་གར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ངོ་མཚར་རབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་རྣམ་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྟོན་པ་གནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་སྟེ། སྟོན་པའི་མཛད་པ་མཛད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་བཞུགས་པ་དང་འདྲའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བླ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འཕགས་པ་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་སྟེ། དེའི་མཛད་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་དེ་གནས་པར་བལྟའོ། །
[3-106] translation already produced for this document:
He intended: "If it becomes a stūpa even by teaching a verse merely on the selflessness of persons, what need is there to mention teaching both kinds of selflessness?" 'Taking up' refers to the words. 'Retaining' means not forgetting. 'Reading' means making it into a volume. 'Mastering' refers to the meaning. By this, it teaches retaining through the wisdom arisen from hearing. Because one also retains through reflecting and the wisdom arisen from reflecting, he spoke of 'properly', which means understanding the meaning unerringly—this is the meaning of the words. In some texts, only the single word 'retaining' appears; herein, 'retaining' should be viewed as both the words and the meaning. 'Supreme wonder' is because of understanding a profound and vast dharma of such a kind. 'The Teacher dwells' refers to the dharma preacher, because he performs the deeds of the Teacher; this means it is like the Lord Buddha himself dwelling in actuality. 'Whoever is like a guru' means whoever it may be, such as noble Mañjughoṣa and so forth; because he accomplishes his deeds, one should view that dharma preacher as dwelling there.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Although it has thus been extensively taught that all dharmas are selfless, in order to free those beginners who think, "How should one meditate on all dharmas as selfless?" from a lack of skill in means for overcoming the signs of entities, concerning the tenth topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here it teaches that by realizing them to be free from the nature of one and many through two kinds of means, one should meditate on all dharmas as selfless. Among those, the two kinds of means are the means of attenuating and the means of making unapparent. Regarding that, by saying "however many particles of earth there are," it teaches that if one realizes it to be free from a singular nature, it is the means of attenuating. This world system is not logically singular, because it is endowed with distinct dharmas such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Therefore, if it is broken down into many, one should accept breaking it down into subtle particles. Therefore, it teaches that if one meditates on it as subtle particles, singularity itself will be abandoned.

[3-110] translation already produced for this document:
Examining from the thought, "Since it is to be known individually by the Lord himself, it is unshared, and since it is ultimately unarisen, it cannot possibly be expressed by words," he asked, "Why is that?" and in reply he stated, "Subhūti, that which was taught by the Tathāgata as prajñāpāramitā..." Because ultimately it is to be known individually by oneself and is therefore unshared, and because ultimately all dharmas are utterly unarisen, it is indeed inappropriate to express it by words; nevertheless, one imputes externally onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and since that conceptualization is inherently mistaken, the aspect imputed by it is also false itself. Therefore, whatever prajñāpāramitā that has become a conceptual image was taught by the Tathāgata and made understood by words is itself not a perfection, but the Tathāgata's wisdom is not so, because in the true relative it has reached the beyond of the knowable. If it were not so, how would the Lord become omniscient? Because the cognizer is mistaken, it does not understand it and what has become a conceptual image as distinct. Therefore, it is said that in the nature of knowing, that very ultimate wisdom is taught by the Tathāgata. Thus, he intended: "There is no contradiction in teaching it like that." Alternatively, whatever is the Tathāgata's wisdom, that very thing taught by the Tathāgata in the nature of causing realization is ultimately solely non-existent, because ultimately there is no going beyond. The word 'itself' should be viewed as placed after 'is not a perfection'. By this, it thoroughly shows how one should practice by positing it ultimately and entering into meditative equipoise in it.

In order to teach that just as prajñāpāramitā is taught by the Lord by imputing externally solely onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and not otherwise, likewise all dharmas are also taught by the Tathāgata, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" because ultimately all dharmas are unestablished. Examining from the thought, "Since it is to be known individually by the Lord himself, it is unshared, and since it is ultimately unarisen, it cannot possibly be expressed by words," he asked, "Why is that?" and in reply he stated, "Subhūti, that which was taught by the Tathāgata as prajñāpāramitā..." Because ultimately it is to be known individually by oneself and is therefore unshared, and because ultimately all dharmas are utterly unarisen, it is indeed inappropriate to express it by words; nevertheless, one imputes externally onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and since that conceptualization is inherently mistaken, the aspect imputed by it is also false itself. Therefore, whatever prajñāpāramitā that has become a conceptual image was taught by the Tathāgata and made understood by words is itself not a perfection, but the Tathāgata's wisdom is not so, because in the true relative it has reached the beyond of the knowable. If it were not so, how would the Lord become omniscient? Because the cognizer is mistaken, it does not understand it and what has become a conceptual image as distinct. Therefore, it is said that in the nature of knowing, that very ultimate wisdom is taught by the Tathāgata. Thus, he intended: "There is no contradiction in teaching it like that." Alternatively, whatever is the Tathāgata's wisdom, that very thing taught by the Tathāgata in the nature of causing realization is ultimately solely non-existent, because ultimately there is no going beyond. The word 'itself' should be viewed as placed after 'is not a perfection'. By this, it thoroughly shows how one should practice by positing it ultimately and entering into meditative equipoise in it.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By this, vastness is thoroughly taught. Examining from the thought of an objector who objects, "If those subtle particles are also solely unestablished because they are undifferentiated by distinctions of directional parts, how would those particles become many?", having asked, "Why is that?", here in reply he said, "Whatever particles of earth there are..." In order to clear away the apprehension of those many particles of earth as a singularity, whatever was taught in the nature of subtle particles is solely non-particles, because ultimately, like the nature of an emanation by illusion, subtle particles are solely non-existent and are of a nature thoroughly imputed by the mind. By this, it is taught merely as a means for those apprehending it as singular, but ultimately it is not so.
