Examining from the thought, "Since it is to be known individually by the Lord himself, it is unshared, and since it is ultimately unarisen, it cannot possibly be expressed by words," he asked, "Why is that?" and in reply he stated, "Subhūti, that which was taught by the Tathāgata as prajñāpāramitā..." Because ultimately it is to be known individually by oneself and is therefore unshared, and because ultimately all dharmas are utterly unarisen, it is indeed inappropriate to express it by words; nevertheless, one imputes externally onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and since that conceptualization is inherently mistaken, the aspect imputed by it is also false itself. Therefore, whatever prajñāpāramitā that has become a conceptual image was taught by the Tathāgata and made understood by words is itself not a perfection, but the Tathāgata's wisdom is not so, because in the true relative it has reached the beyond of the knowable. If it were not so, how would the Lord become omniscient? Because the cognizer is mistaken, it does not understand it and what has become a conceptual image as distinct. Therefore, it is said that in the nature of knowing, that very ultimate wisdom is taught by the Tathāgata. Thus, he intended: "There is no contradiction in teaching it like that." Alternatively, whatever is the Tathāgata's wisdom, that very thing taught by the Tathāgata in the nature of causing realization is ultimately solely non-existent, because ultimately there is no going beyond. The word 'itself' should be viewed as placed after 'is not a perfection'. By this, it thoroughly shows how one should practice by positing it ultimately and entering into meditative equipoise in it.

In order to teach that just as prajñāpāramitā is taught by the Lord by imputing externally solely onto the inherent nature of a conceptual image, and not otherwise, likewise all dharmas are also taught by the Tathāgata, he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" because ultimately all dharmas are unestablished. Even if they were established, because specific characteristics are unshared, conventions cannot be designated for them. Because general characteristics are imputed. Apart from specific characteristics and general characteristics, there is no other expressible thing, because those two have the characteristic of abiding in mutual exclusion.

Although it has thus been extensively taught that all dharmas are selfless, in order to free those beginners who think, "How should one meditate on all dharmas as selfless?" from a lack of skill in means for overcoming the signs of entities, concerning the tenth topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here it teaches that by realizing them to be free from the nature of one and many through two kinds of means, one should meditate on all dharmas as selfless. Among those, the two kinds of means are the means of attenuating and the means of making unapparent. Regarding that, by saying "however many particles of earth there are," it teaches that if one realizes it to be free from a singular nature, it is the means of attenuating. This world system is not logically singular, because it is endowed with distinct dharmas such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Therefore, if it is broken down into many, one should accept breaking it down into subtle particles. Therefore, it teaches that if one meditates on it as subtle particles, singularity itself will be abandoned.

translation: Therefore, saying "they are called particles of earth" is because they exist as logical conventionalities. If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. By this, it teaches that the means of realizing them to be free from a multiple nature is making them unapparent. Thus, because subsequently, having individually analyzed even the subtle particles by logic, one makes it apparent, one will realize world systems to be free from a multiple nature, and after that, one realizes them to be natureless.

[3-115] translation already produced for this document:
By this, vastness is thoroughly taught. Examining from the thought of an objector who objects, "If those subtle particles are also solely unestablished because they are undifferentiated by distinctions of directional parts, how would those particles become many?", having asked, "Why is that?", here in reply he said, "Whatever particles of earth there are..." In order to clear away the apprehension of those many particles of earth as a singularity, whatever was taught in the nature of subtle particles is solely non-particles, because ultimately, like the nature of an emanation by illusion, subtle particles are solely non-existent and are of a nature thoroughly imputed by the mind. By this, it is taught merely as a means for those apprehending it as singular, but ultimately it is not so.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Thus, having first expressed the receptacle world as solely natureless because it is free from a nature of one and many, in order to also express the world of sentient beings, he said, "Whatever world systems there are..." Here, "world systems" intends the world of sentient beings, because the other was already explained previously. He intended with the thought that saying "they are non-systems" is because they are free from a nature of one and many. Thus, first of all, whatever form aggregate there is from among them was explained by the receptacle world itself. How the remaining four aggregates are not endowed with a nature of one and many was already analyzed previously. Because it is not so, yogis see all dharmas as ultimately natureless, like an illusion. By this, profundity is also expressed. By implication, manifest adherence to the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings as entities ultimately is thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught; by thoroughly expressing a mere sign, saying "great trichiliocosm world system", it thoroughly teaches one to meditate on all entities as natureless. By saying "they are non-particles" and "they are non-systems," by this ultimate postulation, it thoroughly teaches how that is to be accomplished by entering into meditative equipoise in yoga.

[3-113] translation already produced for this document:
Although it has thus been extensively taught that all dharmas are selfless, in order to free those beginners who think, "How should one meditate on all dharmas as selfless?" from a lack of skill in means for overcoming the signs of entities, concerning the tenth topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here it teaches that by realizing them to be free from the nature of one and many through two kinds of means, one should meditate on all dharmas as selfless. Among those, the two kinds of means are the means of attenuating and the means of making unapparent. Regarding that, by saying "however many particles of earth there are," it teaches that if one realizes it to be free from a singular nature, it is the means of attenuating. This world system is not logically singular, because it is endowed with distinct dharmas such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Therefore, if it is broken down into many, one should accept breaking it down into subtle particles. Therefore, it teaches that if one meditates on it as subtle particles, singularity itself will be abandoned.

Examining from the thought of an objector who objects, "If those subtle particles are also solely unestablished because they are undifferentiated by distinctions of directional parts, how would those particles become many?", having asked, "Why is that?", here in reply he said, "Whatever particles of earth there are..." Therefore, saying "they are called particles of earth" is because they exist as logical conventionalities. If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. By this, it teaches that the means of realizing them to be free from a multiple nature is making them unapparent. Thus, because subsequently, having individually analyzed even the subtle particles by logic, one makes it apparent, one will realize world systems to be free from a multiple nature, and after that, one realizes them to be natureless.

Although it has thus been extensively taught that all dharmas are selfless, in order to free those beginners who think, "How should one meditate on all dharmas as selfless?" from a lack of skill in means for overcoming the signs of entities, concerning the tenth topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here it teaches that by realizing them to be free from the nature of one and many through two kinds of means, one should meditate on all dharmas as selfless. Among those, the two kinds of means are the means of attenuating and the means of making unapparent. Regarding that, by saying "however many particles of earth there are," it teaches that if one realizes it to be free from a singular nature, it is the means of attenuating. This world system is not logically singular, because it is endowed with distinct dharmas such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Therefore, if it is broken down into many, one should accept breaking it down into subtle particles. If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. By this, it teaches that the means of realizing them to be free from a multiple nature is making them unapparent. Thus, because subsequently, having individually analyzed even the subtle particles by logic, one makes it apparent, one will realize world systems to be free from a multiple nature, and after that, one realizes them to be natureless.

Although it has thus been extensively taught that all dharmas are selfless, in order to free those beginners who think, "How should one meditate on all dharmas as selfless?" from a lack of skill in means for overcoming the signs of entities, concerning the tenth topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here it teaches that by realizing them to be free from the nature of one and many through two kinds of means, one should meditate on all dharmas as selfless. Among those, the two kinds of means are the means of attenuating and the means of making unapparent. Regarding that, by saying "however many particles of earth there are," it teaches that if one realizes it to be free from a singular nature, it is the means of attenuating. This world system is not logically singular, because it is endowed with distinct dharmas such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Therefore, if it is broken down into many, one should accept breaking it down into subtle particles. Therefore, it teaches that if one meditates on it as subtle particles, singularity itself will be abandoned.

Examining from the thought of an objector who objects, "If those subtle particles are also solely unestablished because they are undifferentiated by distinctions of directional parts, how would those particles become many?", having asked, "Why is that?", here in reply he said, "Whatever particles of earth there are..." In order to clear away the apprehension of those many particles of earth as a singularity, whatever was taught in the nature of subtle particles is solely non-particles, because ultimately, like the nature of an emanation by illusion, subtle particles are solely non-existent and are of a nature thoroughly imputed by the mind. Therefore, saying "they are called particles of earth" is because they exist as logical conventionalities. If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. By this, it teaches that the means of realizing them to be free from a multiple nature is making them unapparent. Thus, because subsequently, having individually analyzed even the subtle particles by logic, one makes it apparent, one will realize world systems to be free from a multiple nature, and after that, one realizes them to be natureless.

Thus, having first expressed the receptacle world as solely natureless because it is free from a nature of one and many, in order to also express the world of sentient beings, he said, "Whatever world systems there are..." Here, "world systems" intends the world of sentient beings, because the other was already explained previously. He intended with the thought that saying "they are non-systems" is because they are free from a nature of one and many. Thus, first of all, whatever form aggregate there is from among them was explained by the receptacle world itself. How the remaining four aggregates are not endowed with a nature of one and many was already analyzed previously. Because it is not so, yogis see all dharmas as ultimately natureless, like an illusion. By this, profundity is also expressed. By implication, manifest adherence to the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings as entities ultimately is thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught; by thoroughly expressing a mere sign, saying "great trichiliocosm world system", it thoroughly teaches one to meditate on all entities as natureless. By saying "they are non-particles" and "they are non-systems," by this ultimate postulation, it thoroughly teaches how that is to be accomplished by entering into meditative equipoise in yoga.

translation: Therefore, in order to free them from not having accumulated the collections, concerning the eleventh topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here, the general summarized meaning is this: when making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, one does not view the Tathāgata through the perfection of marks; if one asks, "then how?", it is as ultimate dharmatā. The remaining explanation here accords with the topic of aspiring to attain the form body. Regarding this, one should also not suspect it of being a repetition of words, because previously it was taught to dismantle it at the time of aspiring to attain the form body, whereas now it is taught at the time of making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, so they are distinct. Here, by implication, manifest adherence to the form body as the Tathāgata is thoroughly taught as the discordant class, and in order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught. By expressing a mere sign, saying "the perfection of marks," the entire form body is thoroughly taught. Saying "they are non-marks" is the ultimate postulation. By "therefore" and so forth, it teaches the subduing of distraction.

Although it has thus been extensively taught that all dharmas are selfless, in order to free those beginners who think, "How should one meditate on all dharmas as selfless?" from a lack of skill in means for overcoming the signs of entities, concerning the tenth topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here it teaches that by realizing them to be free from the nature of one and many through two kinds of means, one should meditate on all dharmas as selfless. Among those, the two kinds of means are the means of attenuating and the means of making unapparent. Regarding that, by saying "however many particles of earth there are," it teaches that if one realizes it to be free from a singular nature, it is the means of attenuating. This world system is not logically singular, because it is endowed with distinct dharmas such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Therefore, if it is broken down into many, one should accept breaking it down into subtle particles. Therefore, it teaches that if one meditates on it as subtle particles, singularity itself will be abandoned.

If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. [3-117] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, having first expressed the receptacle world as solely natureless because it is free from a nature of one and many, in order to also express the world of sentient beings, he said, "Whatever world systems there are..." Here, "world systems" intends the world of sentient beings, because the other was already explained previously. He intended with the thought that saying "they are non-systems" is because they are free from a nature of one and many. Thus, first of all, whatever form aggregate there is from among them was explained by the receptacle world itself. How the remaining four aggregates are not endowed with a nature of one and many was already analyzed previously. Because it is not so, yogis see all dharmas as ultimately natureless, like an illusion. By this, profundity is also expressed. By implication, manifest adherence to the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings as entities ultimately is thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught; by thoroughly expressing a mere sign, saying "great trichiliocosm world system", it thoroughly teaches one to meditate on all entities as natureless. By saying "they are non-particles" and "they are non-systems," by this ultimate postulation, it thoroughly teaches how that is to be accomplished by entering into meditative equipoise in yoga.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Thus, although the means for realizing selflessness in all dharmas has already been taught, in order to free from attachment those who, attached to body and life and craving gain and honor, have become lazy and attached to gain, honor, and alms, concerning the twelfth topic he said, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." and so forth. By this, it thoroughly teaches: "Since you create an obstacle to whatever merit is not obtained even by thoroughly giving up this many bodies, out of attachment for the sake of a single body that is essenceless and the abode of many hundreds of thousands of sufferings, it is proper to exert yourselves in this with your whole being, with a mind that does not regard body and life." By this, by implication, laziness and so forth are thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, it also teaches aspiration and making wishing prayers for the sake of thoroughly retaining the holy Dharma and so forth. By expressing a mere sign, saying "from this dharma discourse," it makes one listen and so forth to the entire Mahāyāna. By saying "much more merit," it expresses extensiveness. Saying "by the force of the Dharma" means "by the force of faith in the Dharma." That the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of causing other lazy ones to generate immense faith by expressing the marvelous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, through the blessing of the Bhagavan.

[3-116] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, saying "they are called particles of earth" is because they exist as logical conventionalities. If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. By this, it teaches that the means of realizing them to be free from a multiple nature is making them unapparent. Thus, because subsequently, having individually analyzed even the subtle particles by logic, one makes it apparent, one will realize world systems to be free from a multiple nature, and after that, one realizes them to be natureless.

[3-117] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, having first expressed the receptacle world as solely natureless because it is free from a nature of one and many, in order to also express the world of sentient beings, he said, "Whatever world systems there are..." Here, "world systems" intends the world of sentient beings, because the other was already explained previously. He intended with the thought that saying "they are non-systems" is because they are free from a nature of one and many. Thus, first of all, whatever form aggregate there is from among them was explained by the receptacle world itself. How the remaining four aggregates are not endowed with a nature of one and many was already analyzed previously. Because it is not so, yogis see all dharmas as ultimately natureless, like an illusion. By this, profundity is also expressed. By implication, manifest adherence to the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings as entities ultimately is thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught; by thoroughly expressing a mere sign, saying "great trichiliocosm world system", it thoroughly teaches one to meditate on all entities as natureless. By saying "they are non-particles" and "they are non-systems," by this ultimate postulation, it thoroughly teaches how that is to be accomplished by entering into meditative equipoise in yoga.

Therefore, in order to free them from not having accumulated the collections, concerning the eleventh topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here, the general summarized meaning is this: when making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, one does not view the Tathāgata through the perfection of marks; if one asks, "then how?", it is as ultimate dharmatā. The remaining explanation here accords with the topic of aspiring to attain the form body. Regarding this, one should also not suspect it of being a repetition of words, because previously it was taught to dismantle it at the time of aspiring to attain the form body, whereas now it is taught at the time of making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, so they are distinct. Here, by implication, manifest adherence to the form body as the Tathāgata is thoroughly taught as the discordant class, and in order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught. By expressing a mere sign, saying "the perfection of marks," the entire form body is thoroughly taught. Saying "they are non-marks" is the ultimate postulation. By "therefore" and so forth, it teaches the subduing of distraction.

Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

དེས་ན་སའི་རྡུལ་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་རིགས་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ནི་བརྗོད་དུ་མི་རུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་བརྗོད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་པ་ཁོ་ནར་དགོངས་པའོ། །བརྗོད་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་དེ་བསྟན་པར་ཡང་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དེའི་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ནི་གཞན་ཡང་མི་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཐབས་ནི་སྣང་བ་མེད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །འདི་ལྟར་མཇུག་ཏུ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རིགས་པས་སོ་སོར་བཏགས་ནས་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་པས་ན། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བར་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་དོ། །
[3-116] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, saying "they are called particles of earth" is because they exist as logical conventionalities. If it were not so, he intended with the sole thought that they would not be expressed, because they do not exist ultimately and because specific characteristics are inexpressible. It is also illogical to teach them as expressible conventionalities, because their inherent nature does not appear otherwise. By this, it teaches that the means of realizing them to be free from a multiple nature is making them unapparent. Thus, because subsequently, having individually analyzed even the subtle particles by logic, one makes it apparent, one will realize world systems to be free from a multiple nature, and after that, one realizes them to be natureless.

[3-117] source:
དེ་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་སྣོད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བས་རང་བཞིན་ནི་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ནར་བརྗོད་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཡང་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་གང་ལགས་པ་དེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ནི་འདིར་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་དགོངས་པ་སྟེ། གཞན་ནི་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ཁམས་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པ་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་དེ་ལས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་སྣོད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བཤད་དོ། །ཕུང་པོ་ལྷག་མ་བཞི་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་མི་ལྡན་པར་སྔར་དཔྱད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་པས་ན་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྒྱུ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་དོན་དམ་པར་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མཐོང་ངོ་། །འདིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་ཡང་བརྗོད་དོ། །དོན་གྱིས་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་སྣོད་དང་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་དངོས་པོར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏེ། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པས་དངོས་པོ་མཐའ་དག་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་བསྒོམ་པར་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་རྡུལ་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་།ཁམས་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པ་འདིས་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-117] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, having first expressed the receptacle world as solely natureless because it is free from a nature of one and many, in order to also express the world of sentient beings, he said, "Whatever world systems there are..." Here, "world systems" intends the world of sentient beings, because the other was already explained previously. He intended with the thought that saying "they are non-systems" is because they are free from a nature of one and many. Thus, first of all, whatever form aggregate there is from among them was explained by the receptacle world itself. How the remaining four aggregates are not endowed with a nature of one and many was already analyzed previously. Because it is not so, yogis see all dharmas as ultimately natureless, like an illusion. By this, profundity is also expressed. By implication, manifest adherence to the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings as entities ultimately is thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught; by thoroughly expressing a mere sign, saying "great trichiliocosm world system", it thoroughly teaches one to meditate on all entities as natureless. By saying "they are non-particles" and "they are non-systems," by this ultimate postulation, it thoroughly teaches how that is to be accomplished by entering into meditative equipoise in yoga.

[3-118] source:
དེས་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་བཀག་ནས་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Therefore, by saying "they are called world systems," having refuted the extreme of deprecation, it teaches the subduing of distraction.

ད་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་དག་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕན་འདོགས་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་ན་དེའི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པར་མི་འཇིག་པ་དེ་དག་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཡང་དག་པ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་ལ་མ་ཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Now, whatever bodhisattvas, when making offerings to the Bhagavan due to the great benefit of accomplishing the collection of merit, do not dismantle his body, they will not thoroughly complete the collection of merit, because they have not engaged in correct mental attention.

[3-120] source:
དེ་བས་ན་དེ་དག་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བཅུ་གཅིག་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིར་སྤྱིར་བསྡུ་བའི་དོན་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་། རིམ་གྲོ་བྱེད་པ་ན་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མི་ལྟའི། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། དོན་དམ་པ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ལྷག་མའི་བཤད་པ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་གནས་དང་འདིར་མཐུན་ནོ། །འདི་ལ་ཚིག་ཟློས་པ་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པར་ཡང་མི་བྱ་སྟེ། སྔར་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དུས་ན་དེ་རྣམ་པར་གཞིག་པར་བསྟན། ད་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱ་བའི་དུས་ན་བསྟན་པས་ཐ་དད་དོ། །འདིར་དོན་གྱིས་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པར་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པ་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པའོ། །དེས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Therefore, in order to free them from not having accumulated the collections, concerning the eleventh topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here, the general summarized meaning is this: when making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, one does not view the Tathāgata through the perfection of marks; if one asks, "then how?", it is as ultimate dharmatā. The remaining explanation here accords with the topic of aspiring to attain the form body. Thus, although the means for realizing selflessness in all dharmas has already been taught, in order to free from attachment those who, attached to body and life and craving gain and honor, have become lazy and attached to gain, honor, and alms, concerning the twelfth topic he said, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." and so forth. By this, it thoroughly teaches: "Since you create an obstacle to whatever merit is not obtained even by thoroughly giving up this many bodies, out of attachment for the sake of a single body that is essenceless and the abode of many hundreds of thousands of sufferings, it is proper to exert yourselves in this with your whole being, with a mind that does not regard body and life." By this, by implication, laziness and so forth are thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, it also teaches aspiration and making wishing prayers for the sake of thoroughly retaining the holy Dharma and so forth. By expressing a mere sign, saying "from this dharma discourse," it makes one listen and so forth to the entire Mahāyāna. By saying "much more merit," it expresses extensiveness. Saying "by the force of the Dharma" means "by the force of faith in the Dharma." That the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of causing other lazy ones to generate immense faith by expressing the marvelous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, through the blessing of the Bhagavan.

translation: Thinking, "Why?", he said, "Ever since my exalted wisdom arose." Saying "ever since" means: "Starting from when the exalted wisdom whose domain is the noble truth arose, up until now, I have not previously heard a dharma discourse like this, which, as taught, has supreme merit as its result and which is not the domain of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas." By this, it expresses that it is difficult to find.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-118] source:
དེས་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་བཀག་ནས་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-118] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, by saying "they are called world systems," having refuted the extreme of deprecation, it teaches the subduing of distraction.

[3-119] source:
ད་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་དག་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕན་འདོགས་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་ན་དེའི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པར་མི་འཇིག་པ་དེ་དག་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཡང་དག་པ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་ལ་མ་ཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-119] translation already produced for this document:
Now, whatever bodhisattvas, when making offerings to the Bhagavan due to the great benefit of accomplishing the collection of merit, do not dismantle his body, they will not thoroughly complete the collection of merit, because they have not engaged in correct mental attention.

[3-120] source:
དེ་བས་ན་དེ་དག་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བཅུ་གཅིག་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིར་སྤྱིར་བསྡུ་བའི་དོན་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་། རིམ་གྲོ་བྱེད་པ་ན་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མི་ལྟའི། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། དོན་དམ་པ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ལྷག་མའི་བཤད་པ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་གནས་དང་འདིར་མཐུན་ནོ། །འདི་ལ་ཚིག་ཟློས་པ་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པར་ཡང་མི་བྱ་སྟེ། སྔར་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དུས་ན་དེ་རྣམ་པར་གཞིག་པར་བསྟན། ད་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱ་བའི་དུས་ན་བསྟན་པས་ཐ་དད་དོ། །འདིར་དོན་གྱིས་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པར་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པ་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པའོ། །དེས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-120] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, in order to free them from not having accumulated the collections, concerning the eleventh topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here, the general summarized meaning is this: when making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, one does not view the Tathāgata through the perfection of marks; if one asks, "then how?", it is as ultimate dharmatā. The remaining explanation here accords with the topic of aspiring to attain the form body. Regarding this, one should also not suspect it of being a repetition of words, because previously it was taught to dismantle it at the time of aspiring to attain the form body, whereas now it is taught at the time of making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, so they are distinct. Here, by implication, manifest adherence to the form body as the Tathāgata is thoroughly taught as the discordant class, and in order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught. By expressing a mere sign, saying "the perfection of marks," the entire form body is thoroughly taught. Saying "they are non-marks" is the ultimate postulation. By "therefore" and so forth, it teaches the subduing of distraction.

[3-121] source:
དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ལུས་དང་སྲོག་ལ་ཆགས་ཤིང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་ལ་གདུ་བ་གང་དག་ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལ་ཆགས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དག་དེ་ལ་ཆགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་སྐྱེས་པའམ་བུད་མེད་གང་གིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིས་ནི་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བརྒྱ་སྟོང་དུ་མའི་གནས་ལུས་གཅིག་གི་ཕྱིར་ཁྱེད་ལ་ཆགས་ནས་ལུས་འདི་སྙེད་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་བས་ཀྱང་མི་རྙེད་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་བར་ཆད་བྱེད་ཀྱིས། ལུས་དང་སྲོག་ལ་མི་ལྟ་བའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ཉིད་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་འདི་ལ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་བའི་རིགས་སོ་ཞེས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྱིས་ན་ལེ་ལོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་སྤང་པའི་ཕྱིར་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པ་ཡང་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལས་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་མཐའ་དག་ལ་ཉན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པར་མཛད་པའོ། །བསོད་ནམས་ཆེས་མང་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ལ་དད་པའི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་མཆི་མ་བྱུང་བ་དེ་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་ཀྱིས་ལེ་ལོ་ཅན་གཞན་དག་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བ་བརྗོད་པས་ཤིན་ཏུ་དད་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་དོན་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[3-121] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, although the means for realizing selflessness in all dharmas has already been taught, in order to free from attachment those who, attached to body and life and craving gain and honor, have become lazy and attached to gain, honor, and alms, concerning the twelfth topic he said, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." and so forth. By this, it thoroughly teaches: "Since you create an obstacle to whatever merit is not obtained even by thoroughly giving up this many bodies, out of attachment for the sake of a single body that is essenceless and the abode of many hundreds of thousands of sufferings, it is proper to exert yourselves in this with your whole being, with a mind that does not regard body and life." By this, by implication, laziness and so forth are thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, it also teaches aspiration and making wishing prayers for the sake of thoroughly retaining the holy Dharma and so forth. By expressing a mere sign, saying "from this dharma discourse," it makes one listen and so forth to the entire Mahāyāna. By saying "much more merit," it expresses extensiveness. Saying "by the force of the Dharma" means "by the force of faith in the Dharma." That the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of causing other lazy ones to generate immense faith by expressing the marvelous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, through the blessing of the Bhagavan.

[3-122] source:
དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལག་པས་མཆི་མ་ཕྱིས་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །
[3-122] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, having wiped away his tears with his hand, he spoke to the Bhagavan as follows.

[3-123] source:
ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པས་གསུངས་པ་ནི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ངོ་མཚར་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །ཇི་སྙེད་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མི་བྱེད་པའི་བྱེ་བྲག་སྟེ། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བར་འོས་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་གསུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །
[3-123] translation already produced for this document:
He said, "Bhagavan, it is wonderful that the Tathāgata has spoken this dharma discourse to whatever extent." Saying "to whatever extent" is a distinction of non-action; it means he spoke to the bodhisattvas by means of however many aspects are suitable to be explained.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Thus, having heard of that distinguished merit, in order to thoroughly abandon the fault of those who, having aroused joyous effort and engaged, will perceive this Dharma literally, he said this, "most wonderful": "Because they have conviction in such a generator of extensive merit that is difficult for base beings to have faith in, and because they have conviction in the extremely profound selflessness of persons and dharmas, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, more than those like myself who have realized the mere selflessness of persons." Saying "correct perception" refers to perceiving the unmistaken meaning, but it does not refer to perceiving by thinking, "this is correct," while manifestly adhering to it literally. This is because, here, all dharmas being without nature is taught with the ultimate in mind, whereas conventionally they are not without nature. Therefore, he intended that it does not contradict what is seen and so forth. If there were a correct perception, that which is to be perceived would also exist ultimately, because if there were nothing to be perceived, it would absurdly follow that there is also no perception.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-119] source:
ད་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་དག་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕན་འདོགས་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་ན་དེའི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པར་མི་འཇིག་པ་དེ་དག་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཡང་དག་པ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་ལ་མ་ཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-119] translation already produced for this document:
Now, whatever bodhisattvas, when making offerings to the Bhagavan due to the great benefit of accomplishing the collection of merit, do not dismantle his body, they will not thoroughly complete the collection of merit, because they have not engaged in correct mental attention.

[3-120] source:
དེ་བས་ན་དེ་དག་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བཅུ་གཅིག་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིར་སྤྱིར་བསྡུ་བའི་དོན་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་། རིམ་གྲོ་བྱེད་པ་ན་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མི་ལྟའི། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། དོན་དམ་པ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ལྷག་མའི་བཤད་པ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་གནས་དང་འདིར་མཐུན་ནོ། །འདི་ལ་ཚིག་ཟློས་པ་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པར་ཡང་མི་བྱ་སྟེ། སྔར་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དུས་ན་དེ་རྣམ་པར་གཞིག་པར་བསྟན། ད་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱ་བའི་དུས་ན་བསྟན་པས་ཐ་དད་དོ། །འདིར་དོན་གྱིས་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པར་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པ་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པའོ། །དེས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-120] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, in order to free them from not having accumulated the collections, concerning the eleventh topic he said, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Here, the general summarized meaning is this: when making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, one does not view the Tathāgata through the perfection of marks; if one asks, "then how?", it is as ultimate dharmatā. The remaining explanation here accords with the topic of aspiring to attain the form body. Regarding this, one should also not suspect it of being a repetition of words, because previously it was taught to dismantle it at the time of aspiring to attain the form body, whereas now it is taught at the time of making offerings and doing service to the Tathāgata, so they are distinct. Here, by implication, manifest adherence to the form body as the Tathāgata is thoroughly taught as the discordant class, and in order to abandon that, aspiration and making wishing prayers are also taught. By expressing a mere sign, saying "the perfection of marks," the entire form body is thoroughly taught. Saying "they are non-marks" is the ultimate postulation. By "therefore" and so forth, it teaches the subduing of distraction.

[3-121] source:
དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ལུས་དང་སྲོག་ལ་ཆགས་ཤིང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་ལ་གདུ་བ་གང་དག་ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལ་ཆགས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དག་དེ་ལ་ཆགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་སྐྱེས་པའམ་བུད་མེད་གང་གིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིས་ནི་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བརྒྱ་སྟོང་དུ་མའི་གནས་ལུས་གཅིག་གི་ཕྱིར་ཁྱེད་ལ་ཆགས་ནས་ལུས་འདི་སྙེད་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་བས་ཀྱང་མི་རྙེད་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་བར་ཆད་བྱེད་ཀྱིས། ལུས་དང་སྲོག་ལ་མི་ལྟ་བའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ཉིད་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་འདི་ལ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་བའི་རིགས་སོ་ཞེས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྱིས་ན་ལེ་ལོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་སྤང་པའི་ཕྱིར་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པ་ཡང་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལས་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་མཐའ་དག་ལ་ཉན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པར་མཛད་པའོ། །བསོད་ནམས་ཆེས་མང་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ལ་དད་པའི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་མཆི་མ་བྱུང་བ་དེ་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་ཀྱིས་ལེ་ལོ་ཅན་གཞན་དག་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བ་བརྗོད་པས་ཤིན་ཏུ་དད་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་དོན་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[3-121] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, although the means for realizing selflessness in all dharmas has already been taught, in order to free from attachment those who, attached to body and life and craving gain and honor, have become lazy and attached to gain, honor, and alms, concerning the twelfth topic he said, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." and so forth. By this, it thoroughly teaches: "Since you create an obstacle to whatever merit is not obtained even by thoroughly giving up this many bodies, out of attachment for the sake of a single body that is essenceless and the abode of many hundreds of thousands of sufferings, it is proper to exert yourselves in this with your whole being, with a mind that does not regard body and life." By this, by implication, laziness and so forth are thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, it also teaches aspiration and making wishing prayers for the sake of thoroughly retaining the holy Dharma and so forth. By expressing a mere sign, saying "from this dharma discourse," it makes one listen and so forth to the entire Mahāyāna. By saying "much more merit," it expresses extensiveness. Saying "by the force of the Dharma" means "by the force of faith in the Dharma." That the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of causing other lazy ones to generate immense faith by expressing the marvelous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, through the blessing of the Bhagavan.

[3-122] source:
དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལག་པས་མཆི་མ་ཕྱིས་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །
[3-122] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, having wiped away his tears with his hand, he spoke to the Bhagavan as follows.

[3-123] source:
ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པས་གསུངས་པ་ནི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ངོ་མཚར་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །ཇི་སྙེད་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མི་བྱེད་པའི་བྱེ་བྲག་སྟེ། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བར་འོས་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་གསུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །
[3-123] translation already produced for this document:
He said, "Bhagavan, it is wonderful that the Tathāgata has spoken this dharma discourse to whatever extent." Saying "to whatever extent" is a distinction of non-action; it means he spoke to the bodhisattvas by means of however many aspects are suitable to be explained.

[3-124] source:
ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་སྙམ་པ་ལ། བདག་གི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་ཚུན་ཆད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །ཚུན་ཆད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་གྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་པ་ནས་བཟུང་སྟེ། དེའི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཇི་སྐད་བསྟན་པ་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་སྔོན་ཆད་མ་ཐོས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྙེད་དཀའ་བར་བརྗོད་དོ། །
[3-124] translation already produced for this document:
Thinking, "Why?", he said, "Ever since my exalted wisdom arose." Saying "ever since" means: "Starting from when the exalted wisdom whose domain is the noble truth arose, up until now, I have not previously heard a dharma discourse like this, which, as taught, has supreme merit as its result and which is not the domain of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas." By this, it expresses that it is difficult to find.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Therefore, having considered the objection thinking, "How are all dharmas established as being ultimately without nature?", he asked, "Why is that?", and in response he said, "Bhagavan, whatever is a correct perception..." Because what is to be perceived does not exist whatsoever, and because it is free from the nature of one or many, ultimately that itself is a non-perception; therefore, it is taught that one should not perceive that correct perception as a correct perception.

Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Thus, although the means for realizing selflessness in all dharmas has already been taught, in order to free from attachment those who, attached to body and life and craving gain and honor, have become lazy and attached to gain, honor, and alms, concerning the twelfth topic he said, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." and so forth. By this, it thoroughly teaches: "Since you create an obstacle to whatever merit is not obtained even by thoroughly giving up this many bodies, out of attachment for the sake of a single body that is essenceless and the abode of many hundreds of thousands of sufferings, it is proper to exert yourselves in this with your whole being, with a mind that does not regard body and life." By this, by implication, laziness and so forth are thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, it also teaches aspiration and making wishing prayers for the sake of thoroughly retaining the holy Dharma and so forth. By expressing a mere sign, saying "from this dharma discourse," it makes one listen and so forth to the entire Mahāyāna. By saying "much more merit," it expresses extensiveness. Saying "by the force of the Dharma" means "by the force of faith in the Dharma." That the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of causing other lazy ones to generate immense faith by expressing the marvelous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, through the blessing of the Bhagavan.

[3-125] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, having heard of that distinguished merit, in order to thoroughly abandon the fault of those who, having aroused joyous effort and engaged, will perceive this Dharma literally, he said this, "most wonderful": "Because they have conviction in such a generator of extensive merit that is difficult for base beings to have faith in, and because they have conviction in the extremely profound selflessness of persons and dharmas, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, more than those like myself who have realized the mere selflessness of persons." Saying "correct perception" refers to perceiving the unmistaken meaning, but it does not refer to perceiving by thinking, "this is correct," while manifestly adhering to it literally. This is because, here, all dharmas being without nature is taught with the ultimate in mind, whereas conventionally they are not without nature. Therefore, he intended that it does not contradict what is seen and so forth. If there were a correct perception, that which is to be perceived would also exist ultimately, because if there were nothing to be perceived, it would absurdly follow that there is also no perception.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Because it exists as merely pleasing when unexamined, therefore the Tathāgata calls it "correct perception." If it were not so, he would not have spoken of it, because it would be non-existent in every way. By this, positing it ultimately, both how it is to be established by engaging in meditative equipoise and how distraction is to be eliminated are taught. It also expresses profundity. The extremes of superimposition and deprecation are also abandoned.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ལུས་དང་སྲོག་ལ་ཆགས་ཤིང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་ལ་གདུ་བ་གང་དག་ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལ་ཆགས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དག་དེ་ལ་ཆགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་སྐྱེས་པའམ་བུད་མེད་གང་གིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིས་ནི་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བརྒྱ་སྟོང་དུ་མའི་གནས་ལུས་གཅིག་གི་ཕྱིར་ཁྱེད་ལ་ཆགས་ནས་ལུས་འདི་སྙེད་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་བས་ཀྱང་མི་རྙེད་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་བར་ཆད་བྱེད་ཀྱིས། ལུས་དང་སྲོག་ལ་མི་ལྟ་བའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ཉིད་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་འདི་ལ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་བའི་རིགས་སོ་ཞེས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྱིས་ན་ལེ་ལོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་སྤང་པའི་ཕྱིར་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གདབ་པ་ཡང་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལས་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་མཐའ་དག་ལ་ཉན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པར་མཛད་པའོ། །བསོད་ནམས་ཆེས་མང་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ལ་དད་པའི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་མཆི་མ་བྱུང་བ་དེ་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་ཀྱིས་ལེ་ལོ་ཅན་གཞན་དག་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བ་བརྗོད་པས་ཤིན་ཏུ་དད་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་དོན་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[3-121] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, although the means for realizing selflessness in all dharmas has already been taught, in order to free from attachment those who, attached to body and life and craving gain and honor, have become lazy and attached to gain, honor, and alms, concerning the twelfth topic he said, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." and so forth. By this, it thoroughly teaches: "Since you create an obstacle to whatever merit is not obtained even by thoroughly giving up this many bodies, out of attachment for the sake of a single body that is essenceless and the abode of many hundreds of thousands of sufferings, it is proper to exert yourselves in this with your whole being, with a mind that does not regard body and life." By this, by implication, laziness and so forth are thoroughly taught as the discordant class. In order to abandon that, it also teaches aspiration and making wishing prayers for the sake of thoroughly retaining the holy Dharma and so forth. By expressing a mere sign, saying "from this dharma discourse," it makes one listen and so forth to the entire Mahāyāna. By saying "much more merit," it expresses extensiveness. Saying "by the force of the Dharma" means "by the force of faith in the Dharma." That the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of causing other lazy ones to generate immense faith by expressing the marvelous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, through the blessing of the Bhagavan.

[3-122] source:
དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལག་པས་མཆི་མ་ཕྱིས་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །

Therefore, having wiped away his tears with his hand, he spoke to the Bhagavan as follows.

[3-123] source:
ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པས་གསུངས་པ་ནི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ངོ་མཚར་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །ཇི་སྙེད་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མི་བྱེད་པའི་བྱེ་བྲག་སྟེ། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བར་འོས་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་གསུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །
[3-123] translation already produced for this document:
He said, "Bhagavan, it is wonderful that the Tathāgata has spoken this dharma discourse to whatever extent." Saying "to whatever extent" is a distinction of non-action; it means he spoke to the bodhisattvas by means of however many aspects are suitable to be explained.

[3-124] source:
ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་སྙམ་པ་ལ། བདག་གི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་ཚུན་ཆད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །ཚུན་ཆད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་གྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་པ་ནས་བཟུང་སྟེ། དེའི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཇི་སྐད་བསྟན་པ་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་སྔོན་ཆད་མ་ཐོས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྙེད་དཀའ་བར་བརྗོད་དོ། །
[3-124] translation already produced for this document:
Thinking, "Why?", he said, "Ever since my exalted wisdom arose." Saying "ever since" means: "Starting from when the exalted wisdom whose domain is the noble truth arose, up until now, I have not previously heard a dharma discourse like this, which, as taught, has supreme merit as its result and which is not the domain of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas." By this, it expresses that it is difficult to find.

[3-125] source:
དེ་ལྟར་བསོད་ནམས་ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་ཐོས་ནས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་བརྩམས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་གང་དག་ཆོས་འདི་ལ་སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་དག་གི་ཉེས་པ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་གསོལ་ཏེ། བསོད་ནམས་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་སྐྱེད་པ་སྐྱེ་བོ་མ་རབས་ཀྱིས་དད་པར་དཀའ་བ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་མོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་པ་ལ་མོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་ལྟ་བུ་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཙམ་རྟོགས་པ་དག་པས་དེ་དེ་དག་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་བྱའི་སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་འདི་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་ནི་མི་བྱའོ། །འདི་ལྟར་འདིར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་དོན་དམ་པ་ལ་དགོངས་ནས་བསྟན་གྱི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ནི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེས་ན་མཐོང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འགལ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡོད་པ་ན་འདུ་ཤེས་ཡོད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། འདུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བ་མེད་ན་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-125] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, having heard of that distinguished merit, in order to thoroughly abandon the fault of those who, having aroused joyous effort and engaged, will perceive this Dharma literally, he said this, "most wonderful": "Because they have conviction in such a generator of extensive merit that is difficult for base beings to have faith in, and because they have conviction in the extremely profound selflessness of persons and dharmas, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, more than those like myself who have realized the mere selflessness of persons." Saying "correct perception" refers to perceiving the unmistaken meaning, but it does not refer to perceiving by thinking, "this is correct," while manifestly adhering to it literally. This is because, here, all dharmas being without nature is taught with the ultimate in mind, whereas conventionally they are not without nature. Therefore, he intended that it does not contradict what is seen and so forth. If there were a correct perception, that which is to be perceived would also exist ultimately, because if there were nothing to be perceived, it would absurdly follow that there is also no perception.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In order to generate wonder in those lazy ones themselves, he said, "For me to understand and have conviction in this dharma discourse being explained is not wonderful to me, but, Bhagavan, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, whatever sentient beings take up, hold, and fully comprehend this dharma discourse, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities." The summarized meaning for this is this: "If, in the future, at the time when the true Dharma will be thoroughly destroyed, there will arise such bodhisattvas who will hold this dharma discourse and who will not apprehend a person and so forth, since you do not have such practice even at the time endowed with the festival of the true Dharma, this is an occasion of great shame for you." Here, saying "me" refers to having realized the selflessness of persons. Saying "this" refers to what completely teaches the selflessness of persons and dharmas. Saying "being explained" refers to being made clear directly by the Bhagavan. Saying "understand" is the aspect of pure faith, so it teaches pure faith. Saying "conviction" is the aspect of belief. Saying "those sentient beings" refers to those who will arise in the future time, separated from the Bhagavan. Whatever words are mentioned here, such as "taking up" and so forth, have already been explained earlier. This will be taught as follows: he intended, "It is not wonderful that I, having realized the mere selflessness of persons, have merely come to have faith and belief in such a Dharma that teaches the method of both kinds of selflessness by the power of having heard it directly from the Bhagavan; but whoever, when separated from the Bhagavan, realizes such a dharma discourse through the stages of holding it and so forth, and fully comprehends it, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, because when separated from the Bhagavan and there are many who abandon the Mahāyāna, it is extremely rare for faith in it to arise." By this, it is taught that, having abandoned laziness, one should abide with aspiration and prayers for holding the true Dharma and so forth. In order to teach that they will not only be endowed with mere scripture but also with the perfection of realization, he further said, "Moreover, Bhagavan..."

If there were a correct perception, that which is to be perceived would also exist ultimately, because if there were nothing to be perceived, it would absurdly follow that there is also no perception.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Mentioning "self" and so forth is an illustration; therefore, they will not engage in the perception of a dharma, because they realize both selflessnesses simultaneously. Regarding the thought thinking, "If selflessness and so forth exist, then at that time that perception would certainly also occur," having asked, "Why is that?", he said in response, "the perception of a self." By this, it teaches thus: "Leave aside for a moment a self and so forth as was just stated; if even this perception of a self thinking, 'this is me,' which is well known to all beings, is nothing whatsoever because it cannot bear the burden of analysis, what need is there to mention that the unexperienced entities of a self and so forth will not exist?" By this, engaging in meditative equipoise is taught.

Thus, having heard of that distinguished merit, in order to thoroughly abandon the fault of those who, having aroused joyous effort and engaged, will perceive this Dharma literally, he said this, "most wonderful": "Because they have conviction in such a generator of extensive merit that is difficult for base beings to have faith in, and because they have conviction in the extremely profound selflessness of persons and dharmas, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, more than those like myself who have realized the mere selflessness of persons." Saying "correct perception" refers to perceiving the unmistaken meaning, but it does not refer to perceiving by thinking, "this is correct," while manifestly adhering to it literally. This is because, here, all dharmas being without nature is taught with the ultimate in mind, whereas conventionally they are not without nature. Therefore, he intended that it does not contradict what is seen and so forth. If there were a correct perception, that which is to be perceived would also exist ultimately, because if there were nothing to be perceived, it would absurdly follow that there is also no perception.

In order to generate wonder in those lazy ones themselves, he said, "For me to understand and have conviction in this dharma discourse being explained is not wonderful to me, but, Bhagavan, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, whatever sentient beings take up, hold, and fully comprehend this dharma discourse, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities." The summarized meaning for this is this: "If, in the future, at the time when the true Dharma will be thoroughly destroyed, there will arise such bodhisattvas who will hold this dharma discourse and who will not apprehend a person and so forth, since you do not have such practice even at the time endowed with the festival of the true Dharma, this is an occasion of great shame for you." Here, saying "me" refers to having realized the selflessness of persons. Saying "this" refers to what completely teaches the selflessness of persons and dharmas. Saying "being explained" refers to being made clear directly by the Bhagavan. Saying "understand" is the aspect of pure faith, so it teaches pure faith. Saying "conviction" is the aspect of belief. Saying "those sentient beings" refers to those who will arise in the future time, separated from the Bhagavan. Whatever words are mentioned here, such as "taking up" and so forth, have already been explained earlier. This will be taught as follows: he intended, "It is not wonderful that I, having realized the mere selflessness of persons, have merely come to have faith and belief in such a Dharma that teaches the method of both kinds of selflessness by the power of having heard it directly from the Bhagavan; but whoever, when separated from the Bhagavan, realizes such a dharma discourse through the stages of holding it and so forth, and fully comprehends it, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, because when separated from the Bhagavan and there are many who abandon the Mahāyāna, it is extremely rare for faith in it to arise." By this, it is taught that, having abandoned laziness, one should abide with aspiration and prayers for holding the true Dharma and so forth. In order to teach that they will not only be endowed with mere scripture but also with the perfection of realization, he further said, "Moreover, Bhagavan..."

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Having considered the internally stated question thinking, "Even if a self and so forth do not exist, having become mistaken about them, what makes it evident that the perception of a self and so forth will not occur?", he asked, "Why is that?", and in response he said, "Because the Buddha Bhagavans are free from all perceptions." The meaning regarding this is this: because they have realized the reality of all entities without exception exactly as it is, they are called "Buddha Bhagavans." Because ultimately there is nothing whatsoever to be perceived, they do not engage in perception regarding anything whatsoever. If it were not so, they would become mistaken. Bodhisattvas engage because they train following the Buddhas.

In order to generate wonder in those lazy ones themselves, he said, "For me to understand and have conviction in this dharma discourse being explained is not wonderful to me, but, Bhagavan, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, whatever sentient beings take up, hold, and fully comprehend this dharma discourse, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities." The summarized meaning for this is this: "If, in the future, at the time when the true Dharma will be thoroughly destroyed, there will arise such bodhisattvas who will hold this dharma discourse and who will not apprehend a person and so forth, since you do not have such practice even at the time endowed with the festival of the true Dharma, this is an occasion of great shame for you." Here, saying "me" refers to having realized the selflessness of persons. Saying "this" refers to what completely teaches the selflessness of persons and dharmas. Saying "being explained" refers to being made clear directly by the Bhagavan. Saying "understand" is the aspect of pure faith, so it teaches pure faith. Saying "conviction" is the aspect of belief. Saying "those sentient beings" refers to those who will arise in the future time, separated from the Bhagavan. Whatever words are mentioned here, such as "taking up" and so forth, have already been explained earlier. This will be taught as follows: he intended, "It is not wonderful that I, having realized the mere selflessness of persons, have merely come to have faith and belief in such a Dharma that teaches the method of both kinds of selflessness by the power of having heard it directly from the Bhagavan; but whoever, when separated from the Bhagavan, realizes such a dharma discourse through the stages of holding it and so forth, and fully comprehends it, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, because when separated from the Bhagavan and there are many who abandon the Mahāyāna, it is extremely rare for faith in it to arise." By this, it is taught that, having abandoned laziness, one should abide with aspiration and prayers for holding the true Dharma and so forth. In order to teach that they will not only be endowed with mere scripture but also with the perfection of realization, he further said, "Moreover, Bhagavan..."

Mentioning "self" and so forth is an illustration; therefore, they will not engage in the perception of a dharma, because they realize both selflessnesses simultaneously. Regarding the thought thinking, "If selflessness and so forth exist, then at that time that perception would certainly also occur," having asked, "Why is that?", he said in response, "the perception of a self." By this, it teaches thus: "Leave aside for a moment a self and so forth as was just stated; if even this perception of a self thinking, 'this is me,' which is well known to all beings, is nothing whatsoever because it cannot bear the burden of analysis, what need is there to mention that the unexperienced entities of a self and so forth will not exist?" By this, engaging in meditative equipoise is taught.

translation: If it were not so, how would one attain their state? Therefore, just as the Buddha Bhagavans trained in being free from all perceptions, bodhisattvas should also train. Therefore, whatever bodhisattvas train following them will certainly not engage in the perception of a self and so forth. Saying "so it is" was spoken twice by the Bhagavan, acknowledging it, in order to bring certainty to those to be tamed. Up to this point, it was spoken with regard to turning away from joyous effort. Now, in order to separate those persons who, having heard this profound Dharma, become mentally terrified and do not initiate joyous effort from the very beginning, from that non-initiation of joyous effort, he said, "whatever sentient beings..." and so forth. If they are terrified, they will not initiate joyous effort. In the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Bhagavan taught, "This is merely dharmas; regarding this, a person is completely non-existent," and in the Mahāyāna, he taught, "Even those mere dharmas are false." Therefore, those with uncultivated bodies whose hearts are connected with the view of a self that is co-emergent from beginningless time, upon hearing the selflessness of persons, become terrified, thinking, "I do not exist." In order to refute that, he said "not terrified." Those who are strongly attached to mere dharmas become completely terrified at the time of hearing the teaching on the selflessness of dharmas. Because whatever mere dharmas there are also do not exist, they think, "Alas! I am undone!" and because there is no refuge even if they look in the ten directions, they become completely terrified; in order to refute that, he said "not completely frightened." At the time of thinking, because they are unable to apply themselves to the non-existence of both, they will become completely frightened. In order to refute becoming completely terrified from the very beginning, thinking, "How will we realize both selflessnesses?", he said "will not become completely frightened." Others say, "At that time, whatever terror there is from not having realized the two kinds of selflessness, the small, medium, and great degrees are taught respectively by the three phrases." Others say, "The three kinds of terror are at the times of hearing, thinking, and meditating."

[3-127] translation already produced for this document:
Because it exists as merely pleasing when unexamined, therefore the Tathāgata calls it "correct perception." If it were not so, he would not have spoken of it, because it would be non-existent in every way. By this, positing it ultimately, both how it is to be established by engaging in meditative equipoise and how distraction is to be eliminated are taught. It also expresses profundity. The extremes of superimposition and deprecation are also abandoned.

ལེ་ལོ་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ངོ་མཚར་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་བཤད་པ་ལ་རྟོག་ཅིང་མོས་པ་ནི་བདག་ལ་ངོ་མཚར་མ་ལགས་ཀྱི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སླད་མའི་ཚེ་སླད་མའི་དུས་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་པ་ཐ་མ་ལ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལེན་པ་དང་། འཛིན་པ་དང་། ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བགྱིད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །འདིའི་ཕྱིར་བསྡུ་བའི་དོན་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ་མ་འོངས་པ་ན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་དུས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་དག་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་འཛིན་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། དེ་དག་གང་ཟག་ལ་སོགས་པར་འཛིན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ཀྱང་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་ན། ཁྱེད་ཅག་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དགའ་སྟོན་དང་བཅས་པའི་དུས་ན་ཡང་སྒྲུབ་པ་དེ་འདྲ་བ་མེད་པས་ན་འདི་ནི་ཁྱེད་ཀྱི་ཤིན་ཏུ་ངོ་ཚ་བའི་གནས་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་ལ་བདག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའོ། །འདི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་པའོ། །བཤད་པ་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གསལ་བར་མཛད་པའོ། །རྟོག་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དང་བའི་རྣམ་པ་སྟེ་དང་བར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །མོས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡིད་ཆེས་པའི་རྣམ་པའོ། །སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བསྐལ་པ་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན་འབྱུང་བ་དག་གོ། །འདིར་ལེན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚིག་སྨོས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་སྔར་བཤད་པར་ཟད་དོ། །དེ་ནི་འདི་སྐད་དུ་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཙམ་རྟོགས་པ་བདག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་ཐོས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་དད་ཅིང་ཡིད་ཆེས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་གྱུར་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ངོ་མཚར་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། གང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བསྐལ་པ་ན་འདི་ལ་འཛིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རིམ་གྱིས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་རྟོགས་ནས་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དག་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དང་བསྐལ་པ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་སྤོང་བ་མང་བ་ན་དེ་ལ་དད་པ་སྐྱེས་པ་ནི་ཤིན་ཏུ་དཀོན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །འདིས་ནི་ལེ་ལོ་སྤངས་ཏེ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་གཟུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་དག་ལུང་འབའ་ཞིག་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་བར་མ་ཟད་ཀྱི་རྟོགས་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པར་ཡང་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །

In order to generate wonder in those lazy ones themselves, he said, "For me to understand and have conviction in this dharma discourse being explained is not wonderful to me, but, Bhagavan, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, whatever sentient beings take up, hold, and fully comprehend this dharma discourse, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities." The summarized meaning for this is this: "If, in the future, at the time when the true Dharma will be thoroughly destroyed, there will arise such bodhisattvas who will hold this dharma discourse and who will not apprehend a person and so forth, since you do not have such practice even at the time endowed with the festival of the true Dharma, this is an occasion of great shame for you." Here, saying "me" refers to having realized the selflessness of persons. Saying "this" refers to what completely teaches the selflessness of persons and dharmas. Saying "being explained" refers to being made clear directly by the Bhagavan. Saying "understand" is the aspect of pure faith, so it teaches pure faith. Saying "conviction" is the aspect of belief. Saying "those sentient beings" refers to those who will arise in the future time, separated from the Bhagavan. Whatever words are mentioned here, such as "taking up" and so forth, have already been explained earlier. This will be taught as follows: he intended, "It is not wonderful that I, having realized the mere selflessness of persons, have merely come to have faith and belief in such a Dharma that teaches the method of both kinds of selflessness by the power of having heard it directly from the Bhagavan; but whoever, when separated from the Bhagavan, realizes such a dharma discourse through the stages of holding it and so forth, and fully comprehends it, they will be endowed with the most wonderful qualities, because when separated from the Bhagavan and there are many who abandon the Mahāyāna, it is extremely rare for faith in it to arise." By this, it is taught that, having abandoned laziness, one should abide with aspiration and prayers for holding the true Dharma and so forth. In order to teach that they will not only be endowed with mere scripture but also with the perfection of realization, he further said, "Moreover, Bhagavan..."

[3-129] translation already produced for this document:
Mentioning "self" and so forth is an illustration; therefore, they will not engage in the perception of a dharma, because they realize both selflessnesses simultaneously. Regarding the thought thinking, "If selflessness and so forth exist, then at that time that perception would certainly also occur," having asked, "Why is that?", he said in response, "the perception of a self." By this, it teaches thus: "Leave aside for a moment a self and so forth as was just stated; if even this perception of a self thinking, 'this is me,' which is well known to all beings, is nothing whatsoever because it cannot bear the burden of analysis, what need is there to mention that the unexperienced entities of a self and so forth will not exist?" By this, engaging in meditative equipoise is taught.

Mentioning "self" and so forth is an illustration; therefore, they will not engage in the perception of a dharma, because they realize both selflessnesses simultaneously. Regarding the thought thinking, "If selflessness and so forth exist, then at that time that perception would certainly also occur," having asked, "Why is that?", he said in response, "the perception of a self." By this, it teaches thus: "Leave aside for a moment a self and so forth as was just stated; if even this perception of a self thinking, 'this is me,' which is well known to all beings, is nothing whatsoever because it cannot bear the burden of analysis, what need is there to mention that the unexperienced entities of a self and so forth will not exist?" By this, engaging in meditative equipoise is taught.
