By this, "for the sake of all sentient beings", its vastness is taught here. By all the rest, its profundity is taught. Having taught that for the time being it is proper to tolerate through reasoning, now, in order to teach that it is also proper through trust in the Tathāgata, he said, "speaking what is authentic" and so forth. The first is the teaching. The rest is the explanation. Alternatively, the four truths are taught. They should be correlated in order. Alternatively, "speaking what is authentic" teaches what is to be proven. "Tathāgata" teaches the reason: just as the blessed Buddhas have abandoned the obscurations of afflictions and to knowledge and are thus gone, since he too has gone and come in that way, he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, he speaks what is authentic, what is not mistaken; because he does not possess the obscuration that is the cause of teaching mistakenly, he proves it by the non-observation of a cause. Thinking, "How is it proven that he is exclusively a Tathāgata?", he said, "speaking the truth." That is whoever has the nature of speaking the truth, the characteristics of the four noble truths; therefore, he is determined to be called the Tathāgata. It is impossible to teach an extremely obscure meaning authentically in all aspects, as it was said: "What arises from method and its cause, being obscure, is extremely difficult to explain." Thinking, "How is it known to be true that he speaks the truth?", he said, "speaking suchness." Because he speaks the reality of entities, without mistake, just as they are, he speaks suchness.

translation: Furthermore, whatever thought wonders, 'What is the difference between one who gives gifts by observing the body and so forth and pursuing them, and one who does not pursue them because of not observing anything?'—the remedy for this third basis of intolerance is as follows: he said, 'For example...' and so forth. One who gives gifts having fallen into pursuing the entities that have the nature of body, existence, and resources, adhering to them exclusively as happiness, is like a person who has entered into darkness. Even though they have eyes, because they do not observe the reality of entities, they do not know the meaning of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; thus, they fall into mistaken entities, the state of all suffering. Therefore, the bodhisattva will completely fall away from the happiness of great resources. Because of not possessing that, being afflicted by suffering like the śrāvakas and so forth, they turn away from awakening. One gives gifts without falling into entities. One who gives gifts without observing entities of the body and so forth and without pursuing them is, for example, like a person possessing eyes who sees various forms because they exist, and having seen them, completely abandons what is to be abandoned and takes up what is to be adopted.

སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་འདིར་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ལྷག་མ་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་རིགས་པས་བཟོད་པར་རིགས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་ནས། ད་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་པས་ཀྱང་རིགས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུངས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དང་པོ་ནི་བསྟན་པའོ། །ལྷག་མ་ནི་བཤད་པའོ། །ཡང་ན་བདེན་པ་བཞི་བསྟན་པའོ། །གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་དུ་སྦྱར་རོ། །ཡང་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་གསུངས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཏན་ཚིགས་བསྟན་པ་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དག་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་སྤངས་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འདི་ཡང་གཤེགས་ཏེ་བྱོན་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་སྟེ། ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་སྟོན་པའི་རྒྱུ་སྒྲིབ་པ་མི་མངའ་བས་རྒྱུ་མི་དམིགས་པར་སྒྲུབ་པོ། །འདི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྲུབ་སྙམ་པ་དང་། བདེན་པ་གསུང་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །བདེན་པ་སྟེ་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་བཞིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་གསུང་བའི་ངང་ཚུལ་ཅན་གང་ཡིན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་ངེས་སོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་སྐོལ་བའི་དོན་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་དག་པར་སྟོན་མི་སྲིད་དེ། ཇི་སྐད་དུ། ཐབས་ལས་བྱུང་དང་དེ་ཡི་རྒྱུ། །ལྐོག་གྱུར་དེ་བཤད་ཤིན་ཏུ་དཀའ། །ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །འདི་བདེན་པ་གསུང་པ་བདེན་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་ཤེས་སྙམ་པ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་གསུང་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་དངོས་པོའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་གསུང་བས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་གསུང་པའོ། །

By this, "for the sake of all sentient beings", its vastness is taught here. By all the rest, its profundity is taught. Having taught that for the time being it is proper to tolerate through reasoning, now, in order to teach that it is also proper through trust in the Tathāgata, he said, "speaking what is authentic" and so forth. The first is the teaching. The rest is the explanation. Alternatively, the four truths are taught. They should be correlated in order. Alternatively, "speaking what is authentic" teaches what is to be proven. "Tathāgata" teaches the reason: just as the blessed Buddhas have abandoned the obscurations of afflictions and to knowledge and are thus gone, since he too has gone and come in that way, he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, he speaks what is authentic, what is not mistaken; because he does not possess the obscuration that is the cause of teaching mistakenly, he proves it by the non-observation of a cause. Thinking, "How is it proven that he is exclusively a Tathāgata?", he said, "speaking the truth." That is whoever has the nature of speaking the truth, the characteristics of the four noble truths; therefore, he is determined to be called the Tathāgata. It is impossible to teach an extremely obscure meaning authentically in all aspects, as it was said: "What arises from method and its cause, being obscure, is extremely difficult to explain." Thinking, "How is it known to be true that he speaks the truth?", he said, "speaking suchness." Because he speaks the reality of entities, without mistake, just as they are, he speaks suchness.

དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བ་དང་བླང་བར་བྱ་བའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཐབས་བཅས་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་གསུང་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་བདེན་པ་གསུང་བར་མི་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟར་གྱུར་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་དེས་བསྟན་པའི་བདེན་པ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གནས་པར་ཅི་མངོན་སྙམ་པ་ལ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་པའོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་མ་ལོག་པ་ཚད་མ་དང་ལྡན་པར་གསུང་གི་ཚད་མས་གནོད་པ་མི་གསུང་བ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་བདེན་པའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་འབྲས་བུའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཀྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཚད་མར་བསྒྲུབས་སོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། སྐྱོབ་ལས་ཡང་དག་བསྟན་མ་ལུས། །ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱི་མཁྱེན་པ་བསྒྲུབ། །ཅེས་བཤད་དོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་གཅིག་གྱང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པས། བདེན་པ་གཅིག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པར་དཀའ་ན་བདེན་པ་བཞིར་ལྟ་ག་ལ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། བདེན་པ་བཞི་བརྗོད་པས་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུང་བར་འགྱུར། འདི་ལྟར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་ན་དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་བདེན་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་བརྫུན་བའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཀུན་ཏུ་འབྱུང་བདག་འགོག་པ་དག་ཀྱང་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ལ་ནི་དེ་གཉིས་མི་སྲིད་དོ། །འགོག་པ་མེད་པས་དེར་འགྲོ་བའི་ལམ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དེ། བགྲོད་པར་བྱ་བ་མེད་ན་འགྲོ་བ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །འདི་སྐད་དུ།བྱང་ཆུབ་བཞགས་ནས་བདེན་པ་གཅིག་གྲུབ་པར། གཟིགས་པ་མེད་ན་བཞིར་ལྟ་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་བསྟན་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །དེ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་གང་དག་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུང་བ་ལ་སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་དེ་དག་གི་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་པའི་མཐའ་སྤང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བདེན་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་རང་བཞིན་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བརྫུན་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། བརྫུན་པ་ནི་བདེན་པ་རྣམ་པར་གཅོད་པར་གནས་པས་རྣམ་པར་གཅད་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གང་གིས་དེ་བརྫུན་པར་འགྱུར། ཡང་ན་བདེན་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་སྒྱུ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྫུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བརྫུན་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་ན་དགའ་བཙམ་དུ་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཐའ་གཉིས་བཀག་པ་འདིས་ནི་དབུ་མའི་ལམ་ཉིད་དུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་སྤང་བའི་ཕྱིར་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་ཆ་ཤས་ཀྱིས་བདེན་པ་བཞི་པོ་དག་བསྟན་གྱི། ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་མ་ཡིན་པས་འགལ་བ་མེད་དོ། །

Because he speaks the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the method, just as it abides, how could he not be speaking the truth? Thinking, "Even if that is so, what makes it evident that the four truths taught by him abide in that way?", he said, "not speaking falsely." The meaning is: because he speaks what is not false, possessing valid cognition, and does not speak what is invalidated by valid cognition, therefore it is the truth. By all this, the Blessed One is proven to be a valid authority by means of the reason of the result. For that very reason, it was said: "The entire authentic teaching of the Savior / proves his distinguished knowledge." Since ultimately not even one nature of an entity is established, if it is difficult to prove even one truth, how could there be four truths, such that by expressing four truths he would become one who speaks authentically? Thus, if the Blessed One taught that the five aggregates are like an illusion, how could their nature be the truth of suffering? Because suffering too is ultimately false, its origin and cessation also simply do not exist; for what is utterly non-existent like a rabbit's horn and so forth, those two are impossible. Since cessation does not exist, the path leading to it also ultimately does not exist; if there is nothing to be traversed to, there is no traversing. As it is taught: "Leaving aside awakening, if one sees not even one truth as established, how could there be four?" Having examined that, in order to abandon the extreme of exaggeration of those who adhere to "speaking authentically" according to the literal words, he also said, "Subhūti..." and so forth. "Neither true" is because ultimately no nature whatsoever is established. Regarding "nor false": because falsehood abides as the exclusion of truth, since that which is to be excluded does not exist, by what would it be false? Alternatively, "not true" is because the essence of how it is known is false like an illusion. "Nor false" is because it abides as merely pleasant when unexamined. By this negation of the two extremes, the middle path itself is taught. In order for the śrāvakas to abandon adherence to self, the four truths are taught by way of the aspect of mere selflessness of persons, but they are not for the sake of all, so there is no contradiction.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: To the thought, "Moreover, if the sun has risen, perhaps they might not see," he said, "when the sun has risen." To the thought, "Even if the sun has risen, if they are in a house or the like that is completely dark, they might not see," he said, "when day has dawned." The expression "when day has dawned" indicates [the dispelling of] darkness; therefore, the meaning is "in a place where there is no darkness." Having suspected the thought, "Even when those are assembled, a blind person would perhaps still not see," he said, "possessing eyes." That is how one should view a bodhisattva who has not fallen into entities. For them, the darkness of ignorance having dawned [i.e., cleared] and the sun of exalted wisdom having risen, they see various objects of knowledge exactly as they authentically are, and because the mistaken entities—the state of all suffering, the suffering which is to be abandoned—are false, they completely abandon them; and desiring the authentic state with the characteristics of unexcelled, completely perfect awakening—the state of all happiness, which is to be adopted—they begin to engage in it. Therefore, it is intended that bodhisattvas, having found the excellence of great resources, their bodies made steadfast by unexcelled happiness, will not turn back from awakening. For that very reason, they will not turn back. Previously, it was taught as "abiding" in that by mere observation. Here, it is "falling" into the characteristic of attachment to that, preceded by observation. Therefore, here "falling" is stated. In the former, "abiding" was stated. By all this, the thorough apprehension of the mind is taught.

དེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བ་དང་བླང་བར་བྱ་བའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཐབས་བཅས་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་གསུང་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་བདེན་པ་གསུང་བར་མི་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟར་གྱུར་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་དེས་བསྟན་པའི་བདེན་པ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གནས་པར་ཅི་མངོན་སྙམ་པ་ལ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་པའོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་མ་ལོག་པ་ཚད་མ་དང་ལྡན་པར་གསུང་གི་ཚད་མས་གནོད་པ་མི་གསུང་བ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་བདེན་པའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་འབྲས་བུའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཀྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཚད་མར་བསྒྲུབས་སོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། སྐྱོབ་ལས་ཡང་དག་བསྟན་མ་ལུས། །ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱི་མཁྱེན་པ་བསྒྲུབ། །ཅེས་བཤད་དོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་གཅིག་གྱང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པས། བདེན་པ་གཅིག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པར་དཀའ་ན་བདེན་པ་བཞིར་ལྟ་ག་ལ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། བདེན་པ་བཞི་བརྗོད་པས་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུང་བར་འགྱུར། འདི་ལྟར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་ན་དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་བདེན་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་བརྫུན་བའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཀུན་ཏུ་འབྱུང་བདག་འགོག་པ་དག་ཀྱང་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ལ་ནི་དེ་གཉིས་མི་སྲིད་དོ། །འགོག་པ་མེད་པས་དེར་འགྲོ་བའི་ལམ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དེ། བགྲོད་པར་བྱ་བ་མེད་ན་འགྲོ་བ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །འདི་སྐད་དུ།བྱང་ཆུབ་བཞགས་ནས་བདེན་པ་གཅིག་གྲུབ་པར། གཟིགས་པ་མེད་ན་བཞིར་ལྟ་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་བསྟན་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །དེ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་གང་དག་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུང་བ་ལ་སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་དེ་དག་གི་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་པའི་མཐའ་སྤང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བདེན་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་རང་བཞིན་གང་ཡང་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བརྫུན་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། བརྫུན་པ་ནི་བདེན་པ་རྣམ་པར་གཅོད་པར་གནས་པས་རྣམ་པར་གཅད་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གང་གིས་དེ་བརྫུན་པར་འགྱུར། ཡང་ན་བདེན་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་སྒྱུ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྫུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བརྫུན་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་ན་དགའ་བཙམ་དུ་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཐའ་གཉིས་བཀག་པ་འདིས་ནི་དབུ་མའི་ལམ་ཉིད་དུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་སྤང་བའི་ཕྱིར་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་ཆ་ཤས་ཀྱིས་བདེན་པ་བཞི་པོ་དག་བསྟན་གྱི། ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་མ་ཡིན་པས་འགལ་བ་མེད་དོ། །

Because he speaks the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the method, just as it abides, how could he not be speaking the truth? Thinking, "Even if that is so, what makes it evident that the four truths taught by him abide in that way?", he said, "not speaking falsely." The meaning is: because he speaks what is not false, possessing valid cognition, and does not speak what is invalidated by valid cognition, therefore it is the truth. By all this, the Blessed One is proven to be a valid authority by means of the reason of the result. For that very reason, it was said: "The entire authentic teaching of the Savior / proves his distinguished knowledge." Since ultimately not even one nature of an entity is established, if it is difficult to prove even one truth, how could there be four truths, such that by expressing four truths he would become one who speaks authentically? Thus, if the Blessed One taught that the five aggregates are like an illusion, how could their nature be the truth of suffering? Because suffering too is ultimately false, its origin and cessation also simply do not exist; for what is utterly non-existent like a rabbit's horn and so forth, those two are impossible. Since cessation does not exist, the path leading to it also ultimately does not exist; if there is nothing to be traversed to, there is no traversing. As it is taught: "Leaving aside awakening, if one sees not even one truth as established, how could there be four?" Having examined that, in order to abandon the extreme of exaggeration of those who adhere to "speaking authentically" according to the literal words, he also said, "Subhūti..." and so forth. "Neither true" is because ultimately no nature whatsoever is established. Regarding "nor false": because falsehood abides as the exclusion of truth, since that which is to be excluded does not exist, by what would it be false? Alternatively, "not true" is because the essence of how it is known is false like an illusion. "Nor false" is because it abides as merely pleasant when unexamined. By this negation of the two extremes, the middle path itself is taught. In order for the śrāvakas to abandon adherence to self, the four truths are taught by way of the aspect of mere selflessness of persons, but they are not for the sake of all, so there is no contradiction.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Even though they have been established in patience in this way, some taste the flavor of concentration, and becoming attached to it, they do not exert themselves in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the cause for completely fulfilling the accumulation of exalted wisdom. In order to separate them from being devoid of the accumulation of exalted wisdom, he spoke the words "Subhūti..." and so forth, in the context of the fourteenth basis. By this basis, in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, the excellence of the qualities of exerting oneself in the true Dharma is completely demonstrated through five aspects: being considered by the Tathāgata, completely gathering exceptionally noble merit, showing the Dharma and its accomplishment, being honored by gods and so forth, and complete purification of sins. Among these, being considered by the Tathāgata is what was stated as "The Tathāgata knows them..." and so forth. The explanation of the words "take up..." and so forth is like before.

To the thought, "Moreover, if the sun has risen, perhaps they might not see," he said, "when the sun has risen." To the thought, "Even if the sun has risen, if they are in a house or the like that is completely dark, they might not see," he said, "when day has dawned." The expression "when day has dawned" indicates [the dispelling of] darkness; therefore, the meaning is "in a place where there is no darkness." Having suspected the thought, "Even when those are assembled, a blind person would perhaps still not see," he said, "possessing eyes." That is how one should view a bodhisattva who has not fallen into entities. For them, the darkness of ignorance having dawned [i.e., cleared] and the sun of exalted wisdom having risen, they see various objects of knowledge exactly as they authentically are, and because the mistaken entities—the state of all suffering, the suffering which is to be abandoned—are false, they completely abandon them; and desiring the authentic state with the characteristics of unexcelled, completely perfect awakening—the state of all happiness, which is to be adopted—they begin to engage in it. Therefore, it is intended that bodhisattvas, having found the excellence of great resources, their bodies made steadfast by unexcelled happiness, will not turn back from awakening. For that very reason, they will not turn back. Previously, it was taught as "abiding" in that by mere observation. Here, it is "falling" into the characteristic of attachment to that, preceded by observation. Therefore, here "falling" is stated. In the former, "abiding" was stated. By all this, the thorough apprehension of the mind is taught.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Because the Bhagavan is omniscient, he knows all and sees all. Having examined the thought, "What is so wonderful about them in that?", in order to teach the excellence of completely gathering merit, he said, "all those sentient beings..." The meaning is that by generating an immeasurable aggregate of merit, he knows that they are fortunate.

Furthermore, whatever thought wonders, 'What is the difference between one who gives gifts by observing the body and so forth and pursuing them, and one who does not pursue them because of not observing anything?'—the remedy for this third basis of intolerance is as follows: he said, 'For example...' and so forth. One who gives gifts having fallen into pursuing the entities that have the nature of body, existence, and resources, adhering to them exclusively as happiness, is like a person who has entered into darkness. Even though they have eyes, because they do not observe the reality of entities, they do not know the meaning of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; thus, they fall into mistaken entities, the state of all suffering. Therefore, the bodhisattva will completely fall away from the happiness of great resources. Because of not possessing that, being afflicted by suffering like the śrāvakas and so forth, they turn away from awakening. One gives gifts without falling into entities. One who gives gifts without observing entities of the body and so forth and without pursuing them is, for example, like a person possessing eyes who sees various forms because they exist, and having seen them, completely abandons what is to be abandoned and takes up what is to be adopted.

To the thought, "Moreover, if the sun has risen, perhaps they might not see," he said, "when the sun has risen." To the thought, "Even if the sun has risen, if they are in a house or the like that is completely dark, they might not see," he said, "when day has dawned." The expression "when day has dawned" indicates [the dispelling of] darkness; therefore, the meaning is "in a place where there is no darkness." Having suspected the thought, "Even when those are assembled, a blind person would perhaps still not see," he said, "possessing eyes." That is how one should view a bodhisattva who has not fallen into entities. For them, the darkness of ignorance having dawned [i.e., cleared] and the sun of exalted wisdom having risen, they see various objects of knowledge exactly as they authentically are, and because the mistaken entities—the state of all suffering, the suffering which is to be abandoned—are false, they completely abandon them; and desiring the authentic state with the characteristics of unexcelled, completely perfect awakening—the state of all happiness, which is to be adopted—they begin to engage in it. Therefore, it is intended that bodhisattvas, having found the excellence of great resources, their bodies made steadfast by unexcelled happiness, will not turn back from awakening. For that very reason, they will not turn back. Previously, it was taught as "abiding" in that by mere observation. Here, it is "falling" into the characteristic of attachment to that, preceded by observation. Therefore, here "falling" is stated. In the former, "abiding" was stated. By all this, the thorough apprehension of the mind is taught.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Having examined the thought, "What excellence does that aggregate of merit have, by which it becomes immeasurable?", in order to teach the complete gathering of exceptionally noble merit, he again said, "Subhūti, whichever man or woman..." and so forth. Morning is a particular state of the sun, light, earth, water, and so forth; in order to teach that "time" is conceptually imputed only to such a particular state, and is not completely imputed by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it is particularized by being in common locus with the word "time". Were it not so, since it is a single essence, there would be no differentiation such as "this is morning". If one accepts that it is differentiated by the particulars of others, then if those very particulars are the cause for imputing conventions such as morning to particular states of the sun and so forth, he intended, "What is the point of conceptually imputing time which does not do anything at all and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by slow or fast intellects and so forth, because those slow intellects and so forth, even if arising from its cause, contradict arising gradually. That was indeed taught before. Since the valid cognition of refutation was taught previously in the context of refuting the self, there is no need for much more. Regarding that, in order to teach that the convention "time" is imputed to such particular states of living beings and so forth by the power of conventions generated by autonomous whim, and not by the power of conceptually imputing a connection between sound and meaning, it is particularized by the word "lifetime". If any one of them were stated, it would not teach the intention as it was taught, so all three words were stated. Because it is the object of convention, it is imputed to the word of convention and made into a common locus. Here this is stated in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, and since in the former passage giving and such an aspect of time were not taught, it does not become a repetition.

Furthermore, whatever thought wonders, 'What is the difference between one who gives gifts by observing the body and so forth and pursuing them, and one who does not pursue them because of not observing anything?'—the remedy for this third basis of intolerance is as follows: he said, 'For example...' and so forth. One who gives gifts having fallen into pursuing the entities that have the nature of body, existence, and resources, adhering to them exclusively as happiness, is like a person who has entered into darkness. Even though they have eyes, because they do not observe the reality of entities, they do not know the meaning of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; thus, they fall into mistaken entities, the state of all suffering. Therefore, the bodhisattva will completely fall away from the happiness of great resources. Because of not possessing that, being afflicted by suffering like the śrāvakas and so forth, they turn away from awakening. One gives gifts without falling into entities. One who gives gifts without observing entities of the body and so forth and without pursuing them is, for example, like a person possessing eyes who sees various forms because they exist, and having seen them, completely abandons what is to be abandoned and takes up what is to be adopted.

To the thought, "Moreover, if the sun has risen, perhaps they might not see," he said, "when the sun has risen." To the thought, "Even if the sun has risen, if they are in a house or the like that is completely dark, they might not see," he said, "when day has dawned." The expression "when day has dawned" indicates [the dispelling of] darkness; therefore, the meaning is "in a place where there is no darkness." Having suspected the thought, "Even when those are assembled, a blind person would perhaps still not see," he said, "possessing eyes." That is how one should view a bodhisattva who has not fallen into entities. For them, the darkness of ignorance having dawned [i.e., cleared] and the sun of exalted wisdom having risen, they see various objects of knowledge exactly as they authentically are, and because the mistaken entities—the state of all suffering, the suffering which is to be abandoned—are false, they completely abandon them; and desiring the authentic state with the characteristics of unexcelled, completely perfect awakening—the state of all happiness, which is to be adopted—they begin to engage in it. Therefore, it is intended that bodhisattvas, having found the excellence of great resources, their bodies made steadfast by unexcelled happiness, will not turn back from awakening. For that very reason, they will not turn back. Previously, it was taught as "abiding" in that by mere observation. Here, it is "falling" into the characteristic of attachment to that, preceded by observation. Therefore, here "falling" is stated. In the former, "abiding" was stated. By all this, the thorough apprehension of the mind is taught.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By the words, "Generates a much greater, incalculable, and immeasurable merit than that very basis," its vastness is completely demonstrated. This is because it outshines the merit arising from giving that is exceptionally noble in terms of the particulars of number, substance, and time. Thus, "as many as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā" teaches the particular of number. "Body" means difficult to fathom, which is the particular of substance. "Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons" is the particular of time. Those millions of eons are also billions. That is also hundreds of thousands - the words are combined thus. Regarding the thought, "How is that to be known?", in order to teach the excellence of praising the Dharma, he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth.

Even though they have been established in patience in this way, some taste the flavor of concentration, and becoming attached to it, they do not exert themselves in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the cause for completely fulfilling the accumulation of exalted wisdom. In order to separate them from being devoid of the accumulation of exalted wisdom, he spoke the words "Subhūti..." and so forth, in the context of the fourteenth basis. By this basis, in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, the excellence of the qualities of exerting oneself in the true Dharma is completely demonstrated through five aspects: being considered by the Tathāgata, completely gathering exceptionally noble merit, showing the Dharma and its accomplishment, being honored by gods and so forth, and complete purification of sins. Having examined the thought, "What excellence does that aggregate of merit have, by which it becomes immeasurable?", in order to teach the complete gathering of exceptionally noble merit, he again said, "Subhūti, whichever man or woman..." and so forth. Morning is a particular state of the sun, light, earth, water, and so forth; in order to teach that "time" is conceptually imputed only to such a particular state, and is not completely imputed by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it is particularized by being in common locus with the word "time". Were it not so, since it is a single essence, there would be no differentiation such as "this is morning". If one accepts that it is differentiated by the particulars of others, then if those very particulars are the cause for imputing conventions such as morning to particular states of the sun and so forth, he intended, "What is the point of conceptually imputing time which does not do anything at all and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by slow or fast intellects and so forth, because those slow intellects and so forth, even if arising from its cause, contradict arising gradually. That was indeed taught before. Since the valid cognition of refutation was taught previously in the context of refuting the self, there is no need for much more. Regarding that, in order to teach that the convention "time" is imputed to such particular states of living beings and so forth by the power of conventions generated by autonomous whim, and not by the power of conceptually imputing a connection between sound and meaning, it is particularized by the word "lifetime". If any one of them were stated, it would not teach the intention as it was taught, so all three words were stated. Because it is the object of convention, it is imputed to the word of convention and made into a common locus. Here this is stated in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, and since in the former passage giving and such an aspect of time were not taught, it does not become a repetition.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Because "this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable" teaches here the exceedingly profound characteristic that all dharmas lack an intrinsic nature, which is to be individually known by the Tathāgatas and cannot be conceived by others such as the śrāvakas and so forth. "Incomparable" is because such an aspect is not taught elsewhere, so there is nothing comparable to this or exceptionally nobler than it.

Even though they have been established in patience in this way, some taste the flavor of concentration, and becoming attached to it, they do not exert themselves in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the cause for completely fulfilling the accumulation of exalted wisdom. In order to separate them from being devoid of the accumulation of exalted wisdom, he spoke the words "Subhūti..." and so forth, in the context of the fourteenth basis. By this basis, in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, the excellence of the qualities of exerting oneself in the true Dharma is completely demonstrated through five aspects: being considered by the Tathāgata, completely gathering exceptionally noble merit, showing the Dharma and its accomplishment, being honored by gods and so forth, and complete purification of sins. Among these, being considered by the Tathāgata is what was stated as "The Tathāgata knows them..." and so forth. The explanation of the words "take up..." and so forth is like before.

Having examined the thought, "What excellence does that aggregate of merit have, by which it becomes immeasurable?", in order to teach the complete gathering of exceptionally noble merit, he again said, "Subhūti, whichever man or woman..." and so forth. Morning is a particular state of the sun, light, earth, water, and so forth; in order to teach that "time" is conceptually imputed only to such a particular state, and is not completely imputed by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it is particularized by being in common locus with the word "time". Were it not so, since it is a single essence, there would be no differentiation such as "this is morning". If one accepts that it is differentiated by the particulars of others, then if those very particulars are the cause for imputing conventions such as morning to particular states of the sun and so forth, he intended, "What is the point of conceptually imputing time which does not do anything at all and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by slow or fast intellects and so forth, because those slow intellects and so forth, even if arising from its cause, contradict arising gradually. That was indeed taught before. Since the valid cognition of refutation was taught previously in the context of refuting the self, there is no need for much more. Regarding that, in order to teach that the convention "time" is imputed to such particular states of living beings and so forth by the power of conventions generated by autonomous whim, and not by the power of conceptually imputing a connection between sound and meaning, it is particularized by the word "lifetime". If any one of them were stated, it would not teach the intention as it was taught, so all three words were stated. Because it is the object of convention, it is imputed to the word of convention and made into a common locus. Here this is stated in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, and since in the former passage giving and such an aspect of time were not taught, it does not become a repetition.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By this, because it has no equal and no superior, it teaches thus: "From an inconceivable cause, an inconceivable result itself arises." Regarding the thought, "How is it incomparable?", he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely beyond" is what is called "supreme"; thus he spoke the words, "this discourse on the Dharma of the śrāvakas and so forth..." "The highest vehicle" is grammatically analyzed as either the vehicle of the highest ones, or that it is both a vehicle and highest; those words are spoken to those who have perfectly entered into it. Similarly, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle" is also consistent, as those two belong to synonyms. The intention behind teaching synonyms is to benefit individuals to be trained, because some are transformed by one or another. Others say that it is "highest" in relation to vehicles other than this one. It is "supreme" because it completely purifies all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations. Alternatively, "highest" means excellent.

Even though they have been established in patience in this way, some taste the flavor of concentration, and becoming attached to it, they do not exert themselves in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the cause for completely fulfilling the accumulation of exalted wisdom. In order to separate them from being devoid of the accumulation of exalted wisdom, he spoke the words "Subhūti..." and so forth, in the context of the fourteenth basis. By this basis, in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, the excellence of the qualities of exerting oneself in the true Dharma is completely demonstrated through five aspects: being considered by the Tathāgata, completely gathering exceptionally noble merit, showing the Dharma and its accomplishment, being honored by gods and so forth, and complete purification of sins. Among these, being considered by the Tathāgata is what was stated as "The Tathāgata knows them..." and so forth. The explanation of the words "take up..." and so forth is like before.

Having examined the thought, "What excellence does that aggregate of merit have, by which it becomes immeasurable?", in order to teach the complete gathering of exceptionally noble merit, he again said, "Subhūti, whichever man or woman..." and so forth. Morning is a particular state of the sun, light, earth, water, and so forth; in order to teach that "time" is conceptually imputed only to such a particular state, and is not completely imputed by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it is particularized by being in common locus with the word "time". Were it not so, since it is a single essence, there would be no differentiation such as "this is morning". If one accepts that it is differentiated by the particulars of others, then if those very particulars are the cause for imputing conventions such as morning to particular states of the sun and so forth, he intended, "What is the point of conceptually imputing time which does not do anything at all and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by slow or fast intellects and so forth, because those slow intellects and so forth, even if arising from its cause, contradict arising gradually. That was indeed taught before. Since the valid cognition of refutation was taught previously in the context of refuting the self, there is no need for much more. Regarding that, in order to teach that the convention "time" is imputed to such particular states of living beings and so forth by the power of conventions generated by autonomous whim, and not by the power of conceptually imputing a connection between sound and meaning, it is particularized by the word "lifetime". If any one of them were stated, it would not teach the intention as it was taught, so all three words were stated. Because it is the object of convention, it is imputed to the word of convention and made into a common locus. Here this is stated in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, and since in the former passage giving and such an aspect of time were not taught, it does not become a repetition.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Regarding the thought that "even in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas there is excellence in relation to the vehicle of the śrāvakas," he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely to the utmost" is what is called "supreme"; since among the many vehicles of the śrāvakas and so forth this one has gone extremely to the utmost, the word "supreme" is stated here, and that is the Mahāyāna itself. Since the śrāvakas and so forth are not vessels for such a teaching of the Dharma, it was therefore spoken for the sake of the bodhisattvas. By that, it is established that "there is no comparison for this discourse on the Dharma." "Spoken by the Tathāgata" is because it is not the domain of others.

Even though they have been established in patience in this way, some taste the flavor of concentration, and becoming attached to it, they do not exert themselves in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the cause for completely fulfilling the accumulation of exalted wisdom. In order to separate them from being devoid of the accumulation of exalted wisdom, he spoke the words "Subhūti..." and so forth, in the context of the fourteenth basis. By this basis, in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, the excellence of the qualities of exerting oneself in the true Dharma is completely demonstrated through five aspects: being considered by the Tathāgata, completely gathering exceptionally noble merit, showing the Dharma and its accomplishment, being honored by gods and so forth, and complete purification of sins. Among these, being considered by the Tathāgata is what was stated as "The Tathāgata knows them..." and so forth. The explanation of the words "take up..." and so forth is like before.

Having examined the thought, "What excellence does that aggregate of merit have, by which it becomes immeasurable?", in order to teach the complete gathering of exceptionally noble merit, he again said, "Subhūti, whichever man or woman..." and so forth. Morning is a particular state of the sun, light, earth, water, and so forth; in order to teach that "time" is conceptually imputed only to such a particular state, and is not completely imputed by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it is particularized by being in common locus with the word "time". Were it not so, since it is a single essence, there would be no differentiation such as "this is morning". If one accepts that it is differentiated by the particulars of others, then if those very particulars are the cause for imputing conventions such as morning to particular states of the sun and so forth, he intended, "What is the point of conceptually imputing time which does not do anything at all and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by slow or fast intellects and so forth, because those slow intellects and so forth, even if arising from its cause, contradict arising gradually. That was indeed taught before. Since the valid cognition of refutation was taught previously in the context of refuting the self, there is no need for much more. Regarding that, in order to teach that the convention "time" is imputed to such particular states of living beings and so forth by the power of conventions generated by autonomous whim, and not by the power of conceptually imputing a connection between sound and meaning, it is particularized by the word "lifetime". If any one of them were stated, it would not teach the intention as it was taught, so all three words were stated. Because it is the object of convention, it is imputed to the word of convention and made into a common locus. Here this is stated in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, and since in the former passage giving and such an aspect of time were not taught, it does not become a repetition.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By the words, "this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth, having thoroughly established the meanings as they were explained, he concludes and teaches the excellence of praising those who accomplish it. Because this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and immeasurable, its ripening result is also inconceivable; therefore, the meaning is that "whoever holds this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth is established. "Immeasurable" is what is taught. The rest is the explanation.

Even though they have been established in patience in this way, some taste the flavor of concentration, and becoming attached to it, they do not exert themselves in the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the cause for completely fulfilling the accumulation of exalted wisdom. In order to separate them from being devoid of the accumulation of exalted wisdom, he spoke the words "Subhūti..." and so forth, in the context of the fourteenth basis. By this basis, in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, the excellence of the qualities of exerting oneself in the true Dharma is completely demonstrated through five aspects: being considered by the Tathāgata, completely gathering exceptionally noble merit, showing the Dharma and its accomplishment, being honored by gods and so forth, and complete purification of sins. Among these, being considered by the Tathāgata is what was stated as "The Tathāgata knows them..." and so forth. The explanation of the words "take up..." and so forth is like before.

Having examined the thought, "What excellence does that aggregate of merit have, by which it becomes immeasurable?", in order to teach the complete gathering of exceptionally noble merit, he again said, "Subhūti, whichever man or woman..." and so forth. Morning is a particular state of the sun, light, earth, water, and so forth; in order to teach that "time" is conceptually imputed only to such a particular state, and is not completely imputed by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it is particularized by being in common locus with the word "time". Were it not so, since it is a single essence, there would be no differentiation such as "this is morning". If one accepts that it is differentiated by the particulars of others, then if those very particulars are the cause for imputing conventions such as morning to particular states of the sun and so forth, he intended, "What is the point of conceptually imputing time which does not do anything at all and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by slow or fast intellects and so forth, because those slow intellects and so forth, even if arising from its cause, contradict arising gradually. That was indeed taught before. Since the valid cognition of refutation was taught previously in the context of refuting the self, there is no need for much more. Regarding that, in order to teach that the convention "time" is imputed to such particular states of living beings and so forth by the power of conventions generated by autonomous whim, and not by the power of conceptually imputing a connection between sound and meaning, it is particularized by the word "lifetime". If any one of them were stated, it would not teach the intention as it was taught, so all three words were stated. Because it is the object of convention, it is imputed to the word of convention and made into a common locus. Here this is stated in order to separate them from tasting the flavor of concentration, and since in the former passage giving and such an aspect of time were not taught, it does not become a repetition.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Here, "inconceivable" is taught because it transcends the object of thought, and because it cannot be inferred. "Incomparable" means without equal. "Immeasurable" is because it cannot be measured even if all sentient beings were assigned to do so. "Boundless" is because it is not suitable to be measured even by great regions and so forth, thus it is greater than even space. Alternatively, this and all of them belong to synonyms.

By the words, "Generates a much greater, incalculable, and immeasurable merit than that very basis," its vastness is completely demonstrated. This is because it outshines the merit arising from giving that is exceptionally noble in terms of the particulars of number, substance, and time. Thus, "as many as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā" teaches the particular of number. "Body" means difficult to fathom, which is the particular of substance. "Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons" is the particular of time. Those millions of eons are also billions. That is also hundreds of thousands - the words are combined thus. Regarding the thought, "How is that to be known?", in order to teach the excellence of praising the Dharma, he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth.

Because "this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable" teaches here the exceedingly profound characteristic that all dharmas lack an intrinsic nature, which is to be individually known by the Tathāgatas and cannot be conceived by others such as the śrāvakas and so forth. "Incomparable" is because such an aspect is not taught elsewhere, so there is nothing comparable to this or exceptionally nobler than it.

[3-153] translation already produced for this document:
By this, because it has no equal and no superior, it teaches thus: "From an inconceivable cause, an inconceivable result itself arises." Regarding the thought, "How is it incomparable?", he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely beyond" is what is called "supreme"; thus he spoke the words, "this discourse on the Dharma of the śrāvakas and so forth..." "The highest vehicle" is grammatically analyzed as either the vehicle of the highest ones, or that it is both a vehicle and highest; those words are spoken to those who have perfectly entered into it. Similarly, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle" is also consistent, as those two belong to synonyms. The intention behind teaching synonyms is to benefit individuals to be trained, because some are transformed by one or another. Others say that it is "highest" in relation to vehicles other than this one. It is "supreme" because it completely purifies all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations. Alternatively, "highest" means excellent.

[3-154] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought that "even in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas there is excellence in relation to the vehicle of the śrāvakas," he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely to the utmost" is what is called "supreme"; since among the many vehicles of the śrāvakas and so forth this one has gone extremely to the utmost, the word "supreme" is stated here, and that is the Mahāyāna itself. Since the śrāvakas and so forth are not vessels for such a teaching of the Dharma, it was therefore spoken for the sake of the bodhisattvas. By that, it is established that "there is no comparison for this discourse on the Dharma." "Spoken by the Tathāgata" is because it is not the domain of others.

By the words, "this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth, having thoroughly established the meanings as they were explained, he concludes and teaches the excellence of praising those who accomplish it. Because this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and immeasurable, its ripening result is also inconceivable; therefore, the meaning is that "whoever holds this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth is established. heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The words, "All those sentient beings will bear my awakening upon their shoulders," mean that by carrying the burden of awakening, it is like bearing it on the shoulder. By all of this, it is taught that having completely let go of tasting the joy of meditative concentration, one should abide through aspiration and prayer in the very retention of the Dharma and so forth, which is the cause for fulfilling the accumulation of pristine wisdom. "Why was it spoken by the Bhagavan for the sake of those who have perfectly entered the highest vehicle and not for others?"

[3-151] translation already produced for this document:
By the words, "Generates a much greater, incalculable, and immeasurable merit than that very basis," its vastness is completely demonstrated. This is because it outshines the merit arising from giving that is exceptionally noble in terms of the particulars of number, substance, and time. Thus, "as many as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā" teaches the particular of number. "Body" means difficult to fathom, which is the particular of substance. "Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons" is the particular of time. Those millions of eons are also billions. That is also hundreds of thousands - the words are combined thus. Regarding the thought, "How is that to be known?", in order to teach the excellence of praising the Dharma, he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth.

Because "this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable" teaches here the exceedingly profound characteristic that all dharmas lack an intrinsic nature, which is to be individually known by the Tathāgatas and cannot be conceived by others such as the śrāvakas and so forth. "Incomparable" is because such an aspect is not taught elsewhere, so there is nothing comparable to this or exceptionally nobler than it.

འདིས་ནི་མཉམ་པ་དང་ལྷག་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། རྒྱུ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ཉིད་འབྱུང་ངོ་ཞེས་དེ་སྐད་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཐེག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཆོག་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ཡིན་ནམ། དེ་ཐེག་པ་ཡང་ཡིན་ལ་མཆོག་ཀྱང་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་ཚིག་རྣམ་པར་སྦྱར་ཏེ། གང་དག་དེར་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་དག་ལ་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཐེག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡང་མཐུན་ཏེ། དེ་གཉིས་ནི་རྣམ་གྲངས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའོ། །རྣམ་གྲངས་བསྟན་པའི་དགོངས་པ་ནི་གདུལ་བའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པ་སྟེ། ལ་ལ་གང་གིས་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཞན་དག་ན་རེ་འདི་ལས་གཞན་པའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་མཆོག་གོ། །ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣམ་པར་དག་པས་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ་ཞེའོ། །ཡང་ན་མཆོག་ནི་དམ་པའོ། །
[3-153] translation already produced for this document:
By this, because it has no equal and no superior, it teaches thus: "From an inconceivable cause, an inconceivable result itself arises." Regarding the thought, "How is it incomparable?", he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely beyond" is what is called "supreme"; thus he spoke the words, "this discourse on the Dharma of the śrāvakas and so forth..." "The highest vehicle" is grammatically analyzed as either the vehicle of the highest ones, or that it is both a vehicle and highest; those words are spoken to those who have perfectly entered into it. Similarly, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle" is also consistent, as those two belong to synonyms. The intention behind teaching synonyms is to benefit individuals to be trained, because some are transformed by one or another. Others say that it is "highest" in relation to vehicles other than this one. It is "supreme" because it completely purifies all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations. Alternatively, "highest" means excellent.

རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་དམ་པ་ཡོད་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཐེག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཐེག་པ་མང་པོ་དག་གི་ནང་ན་འདི་ཤིན་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་འདིར་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྒྲ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དོ། །ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུའི་སྣོད་མ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལ་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བསྒྲུབས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-154] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought that "even in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas there is excellence in relation to the vehicle of the śrāvakas," he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely to the utmost" is what is called "supreme"; since among the many vehicles of the śrāvakas and so forth this one has gone extremely to the utmost, the word "supreme" is stated here, and that is the Mahāyāna itself. Since the śrāvakas and so forth are not vessels for such a teaching of the Dharma, it was therefore spoken for the sake of the bodhisattvas. By that, it is established that "there is no comparison for this discourse on the Dharma." "Spoken by the Tathāgata" is because it is not the domain of others.

ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་རྣམས་རབ་ཏུ་བསྒྲུབས་ནས་མཇུག་བསྡུ་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་བསྟོད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་ཅིང་གཞལ་དུ་མེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། དེའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་ཡང་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་གང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་འཛིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསྟན་པའོ། །ལྷག་མ་ནི་བཤད་པའོ། །
[3-155] translation already produced for this document:
By the words, "this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth, having thoroughly established the meanings as they were explained, he concludes and teaches the excellence of praising those who accomplish it. Because this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and immeasurable, its ripening result is also inconceivable; therefore, the meaning is that "whoever holds this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth is established. "Immeasurable" is what is taught. The rest is the explanation.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Thinking, "Does the Bhagavan also have hatred and desire?", he asked, "For what reason is that?" and in reply, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, those who are inclined toward the inferior..." and so forth. By this, it teaches thus: "Since the Bhagavan loves all sentient beings like an only child, he certainly does not possess hatred and desire; nevertheless, he teaches those who have become vessels at the time they become so, and not otherwise. If it were not so, since he is omniscient, the Bhagavan would become precisely non-omniscient." "By those inclined toward the inferior..." and so forth means by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. "By those who hold the view of a self..." and so forth means by the non-Buddhists. "There is no basis for that" means there is no occasion for that. The meaning is: "How could ordinary beings be able to hear what even the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to hear? How could they be able to take up and master what those ones are unable to hear? It is impossible." By this, they are introduced to meditative absorption in yoga. If one asks, "If so, how was the noble Subhūti able to hear this discourse on the Dharma?", it is by the blessing of the Bhagavan, so there is no fault. In order to teach the excellence of the veneration paid by gods and so forth, demonstrating that "out of all places, the single place where this sūtra is explained will be praised," he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth. Previously it was spoken in order to separate from attachment to outer treatises, whereas now it is spoken in order to separate from tasting the joy of meditative concentration, so there is no repetition; it should be known that there is no repetition because the meaning that summarizes everything is spoken precisely in different contexts. "Will be worthy of offerings" means with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

[3-151] translation already produced for this document:
By the words, "Generates a much greater, incalculable, and immeasurable merit than that very basis," its vastness is completely demonstrated. This is because it outshines the merit arising from giving that is exceptionally noble in terms of the particulars of number, substance, and time. Thus, "as many as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā" teaches the particular of number. "Body" means difficult to fathom, which is the particular of substance. "Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons" is the particular of time. Those millions of eons are also billions. That is also hundreds of thousands - the words are combined thus. Regarding the thought, "How is that to be known?", in order to teach the excellence of praising the Dharma, he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth.

[3-152] source:
ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ནི་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་པ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སོ་སོ་རང་གིས་རིག་པར་བྱ་བ་ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཞན་དག་གིས་བསམ་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་འདིར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚུངས་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་དུ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་མ་བསྟན་པས། འདི་དང་མཚུངས་པའམ། ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Because "this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable" teaches here the exceedingly profound characteristic that all dharmas lack an intrinsic nature, which is to be individually known by the Tathāgatas and cannot be conceived by others such as the śrāvakas and so forth. "Incomparable" is because such an aspect is not taught elsewhere, so there is nothing comparable to this or exceptionally nobler than it.

[3-153] source:
འདིས་ནི་མཉམ་པ་དང་ལྷག་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། རྒྱུ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ཉིད་འབྱུང་ངོ་ཞེས་དེ་སྐད་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཐེག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཆོག་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ཡིན་ནམ། དེ་ཐེག་པ་ཡང་ཡིན་ལ་མཆོག་ཀྱང་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་ཚིག་རྣམ་པར་སྦྱར་ཏེ། གང་དག་དེར་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་དག་ལ་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཐེག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡང་མཐུན་ཏེ། དེ་གཉིས་ནི་རྣམ་གྲངས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའོ། །རྣམ་གྲངས་བསྟན་པའི་དགོངས་པ་ནི་གདུལ་བའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པ་སྟེ། ལ་ལ་གང་གིས་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཞན་དག་ན་རེ་འདི་ལས་གཞན་པའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་མཆོག་གོ། །ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣམ་པར་དག་པས་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པའོ་ཞེའོ། །ཡང་ན་མཆོག་ནི་དམ་པའོ། །
[3-153] translation already produced for this document:
By this, because it has no equal and no superior, it teaches thus: "From an inconceivable cause, an inconceivable result itself arises." Regarding the thought, "How is it incomparable?", he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely beyond" is what is called "supreme"; thus he spoke the words, "this discourse on the Dharma of the śrāvakas and so forth..." "The highest vehicle" is grammatically analyzed as either the vehicle of the highest ones, or that it is both a vehicle and highest; those words are spoken to those who have perfectly entered into it. Similarly, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle" is also consistent, as those two belong to synonyms. The intention behind teaching synonyms is to benefit individuals to be trained, because some are transformed by one or another. Others say that it is "highest" in relation to vehicles other than this one. It is "supreme" because it completely purifies all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations. Alternatively, "highest" means excellent.

རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་དམ་པ་ཡོད་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཐེག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཐེག་པ་མང་པོ་དག་གི་ནང་ན་འདི་ཤིན་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པས་འདིར་ཕུལ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྒྲ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དོ། །ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུའི་སྣོད་མ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལ་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བསྒྲུབས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-154] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought that "even in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas there is excellence in relation to the vehicle of the śrāvakas," he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely to the utmost" is what is called "supreme"; since among the many vehicles of the śrāvakas and so forth this one has gone extremely to the utmost, the word "supreme" is stated here, and that is the Mahāyāna itself. Since the śrāvakas and so forth are not vessels for such a teaching of the Dharma, it was therefore spoken for the sake of the bodhisattvas. By that, it is established that "there is no comparison for this discourse on the Dharma." "Spoken by the Tathāgata" is because it is not the domain of others.

By the words, "this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth, having thoroughly established the meanings as they were explained, he concludes and teaches the excellence of praising those who accomplish it. Because this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and immeasurable, its ripening result is also inconceivable; therefore, the meaning is that "whoever holds this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth is established. "Immeasurable" is what is taught. The rest is the explanation.

[3-151] translation already produced for this document:
By the words, "Generates a much greater, incalculable, and immeasurable merit than that very basis," its vastness is completely demonstrated. This is because it outshines the merit arising from giving that is exceptionally noble in terms of the particulars of number, substance, and time. Thus, "as many as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā" teaches the particular of number. "Body" means difficult to fathom, which is the particular of substance. "Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons" is the particular of time. Those millions of eons are also billions. That is also hundreds of thousands - the words are combined thus. Regarding the thought, "How is that to be known?", in order to teach the excellence of praising the Dharma, he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth.

By this, because it has no equal and no superior, it teaches thus: "From an inconceivable cause, an inconceivable result itself arises." Regarding the thought, "How is it incomparable?", he spoke the words, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle." "Gone extremely beyond" is what is called "supreme"; thus he spoke the words, "this discourse on the Dharma of the śrāvakas and so forth..." "The highest vehicle" is grammatically analyzed as either the vehicle of the highest ones, or that it is both a vehicle and highest; those words are spoken to those who have perfectly entered into it. Similarly, "those who have perfectly entered the supreme vehicle" is also consistent, as those two belong to synonyms. The intention behind teaching synonyms is to benefit individuals to be trained, because some are transformed by one or another. Others say that it is "highest" in relation to vehicles other than this one. It is "supreme" because it completely purifies all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations. Alternatively, "highest" means excellent.

By the words, "this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth, having thoroughly established the meanings as they were explained, he concludes and teaches the excellence of praising those who accomplish it. Because this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and immeasurable, its ripening result is also inconceivable; therefore, the meaning is that "whoever holds this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth is established. "Immeasurable" is what is taught. The rest is the explanation.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Regarding the thought, "If, among those who strongly endeavor in such a discourse on the Dharma as this, some appear to be afflicted, how could this be?", in order to rely on the distinction of thoroughly purifying misdeeds, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whichever sons of noble family or daughters of noble family..." and so forth. "Will be afflicted" means harming by scolding, exposing faults, and so forth. "Will be thoroughly afflicted" means harming by killing, binding, and so forth. Regarding the thought, "How could such great beings be afflicted?", he asked, "For what reason is that?" and in reply, he spoke the words, "Thus, of those sentient beings..." and so forth. "Of previous lifetimes" means what was done in previous lifetimes. "In this very lifetime" means in the present lifetime.

By that, it is established that "there is no comparison for this discourse on the Dharma." "Spoken by the Tathāgata" is because it is not the domain of others.

[3-155] source:
ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་རྣམས་རབ་ཏུ་བསྒྲུབས་ནས་མཇུག་བསྡུ་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་བསྟོད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་ཅིང་གཞལ་དུ་མེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། དེའི་རྣམ་པར་སྨིན་པ་ཡང་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་གང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་འཛིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསྟན་པའོ། །ལྷག་མ་ནི་བཤད་པའོ། །
[3-155] translation already produced for this document:
By the words, "this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth, having thoroughly established the meanings as they were explained, he concludes and teaches the excellence of praising those who accomplish it. Because this discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable and immeasurable, its ripening result is also inconceivable; therefore, the meaning is that "whoever holds this discourse on the Dharma..." and so forth is established. "Immeasurable" is what is taught. The rest is the explanation.

[3-156] source:
དེ་ལ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསམ་པའི་ཡུལ་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར། རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །མཚུངས་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཟླ་མེད་པའོ། །གཞལ་དུ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྒོས་ཀྱང་གཞལ་དུ་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཚད་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡུལ་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ཀྱང་ཚད་དུ་མི་རུང་བས་ནམ་མཁའ་བས་ཀྱང་ལྷག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་ན་འདི་དང་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་རྣམ་གྲངས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའོ། །
[3-156] translation already produced for this document:
Here, "inconceivable" is taught because it transcends the object of thought, and because it cannot be inferred. "Incomparable" means without equal. "Immeasurable" is because it cannot be measured even if all sentient beings were assigned to do so. "Boundless" is because it is not suitable to be measured even by great regions and so forth, thus it is greater than even space. Alternatively, this and all of them belong to synonyms.

[3-157] source:
སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ངའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཕྲག་པར་ཐོགས་པ་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཁུར་ཁྱེར་བས་ཕྲག་ལ་ཁྱར་བ་དང་འདྲའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་བདེ་བའི་རོ་མྱང་བ་ཡོངས་སུ་བཏང་སྟེ། ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསྐང་བའི་རྒྱུ་ཆོས་ཡོངས་སུ་གཟུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་ཀྱི་གཞན་དག་ལ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-157] translation already produced for this document:
The words, "All those sentient beings will bear my awakening upon their shoulders," mean that by carrying the burden of awakening, it is like bearing it on the shoulder. By all of this, it is taught that having completely let go of tasting the joy of meditative concentration, one should abide through aspiration and prayer in the very retention of the Dharma and so forth, which is the cause for fulfilling the accumulation of pristine wisdom. "Why was it spoken by the Bhagavan for the sake of those who have perfectly entered the highest vehicle and not for others?"

[3-158] source:
ཅི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་ཡང་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་འདོད་པ་མངའ་འམ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཤིང་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་དམན་པ་ལ་མོས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིས་ནི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་བུ་གཅིག་པ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱམས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་འདོད་པ་མི་མངའ་མོད་ཀྱི་འོན་ཀྱང་གང་དག་གི་ཚེ་སྣོད་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དག་ལ་དེའི་ཚེ་སྟོན་ཏེ་གཞན་དུ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་དེ་སྐད་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དམན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །བདག་ལ་སོགས་པར་ལྟ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཕྱི་རོལ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །དེ་ནི་གནས་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་གོ་སྐབས་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའོ། །གང་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མཉན་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་དེ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནུས་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། གང་དེ་དག་གིས་མཉན་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་དེ་བླང་བ་དང་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱ་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་ནུས་ཏེ་མི་སྲིད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་ལ་འཛུད་དོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟར་ན་འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ཇི་ལྟར་མཉན་པར་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱི་རླབས་ཀྱིས་ཏེ་ཉེས་པ་མེད་དོ། །ས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་གང་དུ་མདོ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པུ་བསྔགས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པར་ལྷ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱེད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྔར་ནི་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པ་དང་དབྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་ལ། ད་ནི་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བ་དང་དབྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པས་ཚིག་ཟློས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའི་དོན་བརྗོད་པ་ཁོ་ནས་སྐབས་ཐ་དད་པར་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཟློས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བར་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །མཆོད་པར་འོས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གདུགས་དང་། རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་བ་དན་ལ་སོགས་པས་སོ། །
[3-158] translation already produced for this document:
Thinking, "Does the Bhagavan also have hatred and desire?", he asked, "For what reason is that?" and in reply, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, those who are inclined toward the inferior..." and so forth. By this, it teaches thus: "Since the Bhagavan loves all sentient beings like an only child, he certainly does not possess hatred and desire; nevertheless, he teaches those who have become vessels at the time they become so, and not otherwise. If it were not so, since he is omniscient, the Bhagavan would become precisely non-omniscient." "By those inclined toward the inferior..." and so forth means by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. "By those who hold the view of a self..." and so forth means by the non-Buddhists. "There is no basis for that" means there is no occasion for that. The meaning is: "How could ordinary beings be able to hear what even the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to hear? How could they be able to take up and master what those ones are unable to hear? It is impossible." By this, they are introduced to meditative absorption in yoga. If one asks, "If so, how was the noble Subhūti able to hear this discourse on the Dharma?", it is by the blessing of the Bhagavan, so there is no fault. In order to teach the excellence of the veneration paid by gods and so forth, demonstrating that "out of all places, the single place where this sūtra is explained will be praised," he also spoke the words, "Subhūti..." and so forth. Previously it was spoken in order to separate from attachment to outer treatises, whereas now it is spoken in order to separate from tasting the joy of meditative concentration, so there is no repetition; it should be known that there is no repetition because the meaning that summarizes everything is spoken precisely in different contexts. "Will be worthy of offerings" means with parasols, victory banners, pennants, and so forth.

[3-159] source:
ཕྱག་བྱ་བར་འོས་པ་ནི་འདུད་པར་བྱ་བའོ། །བསྐོར་བ་བྱ་བར་འོས་པ་ནི་བསྐོར་བར་བྱ་བའོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་མཆོད་པར་འོས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་དང་ལྡན་པས་མཆོད་རྟེན་ནོ། །
[3-159] translation already produced for this document:
"Worthy of homage" means to be bowed down to. "Worthy of circumambulation" means to be circumambulated. Therefore, because it is endowed with qualities such as being worthy of offerings and so forth, it is a caitya.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The words, "will also attain the awakening of a Buddha," mean that having thoroughly purified misdeeds, those who endeavor in meditation at another time will swiftly perfectly awaken to unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.
