[3-172] translation already produced for this document:
"If that dharma which the Tathāgata manifestly and completely awakened to as unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening does not exist, then how at that time could he be a Tathāgata? In this way, if one says 'Tathāgata' because, just as previous buddhas have gone to manifest and complete awakening, likewise he has gone here and manifestly and completely awakened, since there does not exist any dharma whatsoever to manifestly and completely awaken to, how could that be?" Regarding the thought of someone who thinks thus, the question "Why is that?" was asked, and in reply, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, 'Tathāgata'..." and so forth. "Suchness" refers to the unerring nature of dharmas; its essence is peaceful from the very beginning and so forth. Furthermore, since that is common to all dharmas, it is particularized by stating "right"; "right", with the meaning of unerring, refers to the pristine wisdom of the Tathāgata. Its suchness, the true nature which is ultimately unarisen, is called "Tathāgata", just as it was stated: "The always unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata." Moreover, since the true nature is ultimately not other than the phenomena, the essence of realizing the true nature of all dharmas being ultimately unarisen—which is pleasing only when unexamined, and is ultimately unarisen, but exists as thoroughly imputed in right conventional reality—this extremely superior pristine wisdom itself is called "Tathāgata"; this is the meaning. Furthermore, because it is ultimately unarisen, there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended or to apprehend, so ultimately there does not exist any dharma whatsoever that he manifestly and completely awakened to, but in reliance on right conventional reality, how that extraordinary pristine wisdom manifestly and completely awakened is merely called "Tathāgata"—this is the intended meaning.

"Why is that?" is connected to "does not speak truly". The rest is easy to understand, so it is not explained. "Well then, regarding the presentation that the Tathāgata manifestly and completely awakened conventionally, what is its true nature presented as?" Regarding this thought, he spoke the words, "Whatever dharma...". "Whatever" refers to the dharmas characterized as form and so forth. "In that there is no truth" means that its appearing aspect, like an illusion, does not arise with any strength when examined. Because it is utterly non-existent like a rabbit's horn. "There is also no falsehood", because in an unexamined essence it appears like an illusion. Alternatively, because ultimately whatever dharma it is is not established, "there is no truth". Because whatever truth to be analyzed is not established and all dharmas are unarisen, "there is also no falsehood". By this, having negated the extremes of superimposition and denigration, it establishes the middle way and induces entry into meditative equipoise upon that. "Therefore" means because thus ultimately all dharmas are unarisen, so there is neither truth nor falsehood. The Tathāgata is also differentiated by the completely pure true nature of being unarisen; therefore, because the unarisen true nature is common, the Tathāgata said, "All dharmas are the Buddha's dharmas," as in, "The always unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata. All dharmas are also like the Sugata. Those with childish minds who apprehend signs practice dharmas that do not exist in the world," and so forth.

Regarding the thought, "If these dharmas are exclusively unarisen, well then, how can they be called 'all dharmas'?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what is called 'all dharmas'..." and so forth. Here the meaning is this: this is not a convention designated because they exist ultimately, but rather, although form and so forth do not ultimately exist as dharmas, because they bear their own and general characteristics in reliance on the unexamined non-ultimate, they are therefore called "all dharmas." Ultimately they are not, because for one abiding in that, even though everything is seen, all conventions are non-existent. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught.

translation: The intended meaning is this: this clear realization of a bodhisattva is also merely differentiated by the arising of extremely superior pristine wisdom in reliance on right conventional reality, but in order to teach that ultimately there is nothing whatsoever that clearly realizes or is to be clearly realized, the noble Subhūti stated to the Bhagavān the words, "Bhagavān, a person possessed of a body [spoken of] by the Tathāgata..." and so forth. By this, in meaning, it thoroughly teaches [that this] is the discordant class of adhering to "possessed of a body" and "a great body". In order to abandon that, it teaches abiding by aspiration and prayer.

"If that dharma which the Tathāgata manifestly and completely awakened to as unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening does not exist, then how at that time could he be a Tathāgata? In this way, if one says 'Tathāgata' because, just as previous buddhas have gone to manifest and complete awakening, likewise he has gone here and manifestly and completely awakened, since there does not exist any dharma whatsoever to manifestly and completely awaken to, how could that be?" Regarding the thought of someone who thinks thus, the question "Why is that?" was asked, and in reply, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, 'Tathāgata'..." and so forth. "Suchness" refers to the unerring nature of dharmas; its essence is peaceful from the very beginning and so forth. Furthermore, since that is common to all dharmas, it is particularized by stating "right"; "right", with the meaning of unerring, refers to the pristine wisdom of the Tathāgata. Its suchness, the true nature which is ultimately unarisen, is called "Tathāgata", just as it was stated: "The always unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata." Moreover, since the true nature is ultimately not other than the phenomena, the essence of realizing the true nature of all dharmas being ultimately unarisen—which is pleasing only when unexamined, and is ultimately unarisen, but exists as thoroughly imputed in right conventional reality—this extremely superior pristine wisdom itself is called "Tathāgata"; this is the meaning. Furthermore, because it is ultimately unarisen, there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended or to apprehend, so ultimately there does not exist any dharma whatsoever that he manifestly and completely awakened to, but in reliance on right conventional reality, how that extraordinary pristine wisdom manifestly and completely awakened is merely called "Tathāgata"—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the thought, "Why is it not said that he manifestly and completely awakened in reliance on the ultimate?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, if anyone..." and so forth. "Why is that?" is connected to "does not speak truly". The rest is easy to understand, so it is not explained. "Well then, regarding the presentation that the Tathāgata manifestly and completely awakened conventionally, what is its true nature presented as?" Regarding this thought, he spoke the words, "Whatever dharma...". "Whatever" refers to the dharmas characterized as form and so forth. "In that there is no truth" means that its appearing aspect, like an illusion, does not arise with any strength when examined. Because it is utterly non-existent like a rabbit's horn. "There is also no falsehood", because in an unexamined essence it appears like an illusion. Alternatively, because ultimately whatever dharma it is is not established, "there is no truth". Because whatever truth to be analyzed is not established and all dharmas are unarisen, "there is also no falsehood". By this, having negated the extremes of superimposition and denigration, it establishes the middle way and induces entry into meditative equipoise upon that. "Therefore" means because thus ultimately all dharmas are unarisen, so there is neither truth nor falsehood. The Tathāgata is also differentiated by the completely pure true nature of being unarisen; therefore, because the unarisen true nature is common, the Tathāgata said, "All dharmas are the Buddha's dharmas," as in, "The always unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata. All dharmas are also like the Sugata. Those with childish minds who apprehend signs practice dharmas that do not exist in the world," and so forth.

Regarding the thought, "If these dharmas are exclusively unarisen, well then, how can they be called 'all dharmas'?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what is called 'all dharmas'..." and so forth. Here the meaning is this: this is not a convention designated because they exist ultimately, but rather, although form and so forth do not ultimately exist as dharmas, because they bear their own and general characteristics in reliance on the unexamined non-ultimate, they are therefore called "all dharmas." Ultimately they are not, because for one abiding in that, even though everything is seen, all conventions are non-existent. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By thoroughly expressing merely the sign "possessed of a body and a great body", it turns bodhisattvas away from adhering to all dharmas. It also establishes [them] in the ultimate, and also induces entry into meditative equipoise upon that. It also expresses profundity. It also abandons the extreme of superimposition. The previous one negated the extreme of denigration. "If the Tathāgata stated that that very body is non-existent, then at that time how could bodhisattvas who have attained clear realization think thus, 'I have attained the clear realization of a bodhisattva, so now I will liberate sentient beings'?" Regarding this concept of others, having analyzed the supreme, in order to teach clear realization through the absence of pride of superiority, he spoke the words, "Whatever bodhisattva...".

"If that dharma which the Tathāgata manifestly and completely awakened to as unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening does not exist, then how at that time could he be a Tathāgata? In this way, if one says 'Tathāgata' because, just as previous buddhas have gone to manifest and complete awakening, likewise he has gone here and manifestly and completely awakened, since there does not exist any dharma whatsoever to manifestly and completely awaken to, how could that be?" Regarding the thought of someone who thinks thus, the question "Why is that?" was asked, and in reply, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, 'Tathāgata'..." and so forth. "Suchness" refers to the unerring nature of dharmas; its essence is peaceful from the very beginning and so forth. Furthermore, since that is common to all dharmas, it is particularized by stating "right"; "right", with the meaning of unerring, refers to the pristine wisdom of the Tathāgata. Its suchness, the true nature which is ultimately unarisen, is called "Tathāgata", just as it was stated: "The always unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata." Moreover, since the true nature is ultimately not other than the phenomena, the essence of realizing the true nature of all dharmas being ultimately unarisen—which is pleasing only when unexamined, and is ultimately unarisen, but exists as thoroughly imputed in right conventional reality—this extremely superior pristine wisdom itself is called "Tathāgata"; this is the meaning. Furthermore, because it is ultimately unarisen, there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended or to apprehend, so ultimately there does not exist any dharma whatsoever that he manifestly and completely awakened to, but in reliance on right conventional reality, how that extraordinary pristine wisdom manifestly and completely awakened is merely called "Tathāgata"—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the thought, "Why is it not said that he manifestly and completely awakened in reliance on the ultimate?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, if anyone..." and so forth. "Why is that?" is connected to "does not speak truly". The rest is easy to understand, so it is not explained. "Well then, regarding the presentation that the Tathāgata manifestly and completely awakened conventionally, what is its true nature presented as?" Regarding this thought, he spoke the words, "Whatever dharma...". "Whatever" refers to the dharmas characterized as form and so forth. "In that there is no truth" means that its appearing aspect, like an illusion, does not arise with any strength when examined. Because it is utterly non-existent like a rabbit's horn. "There is also no falsehood", because in an unexamined essence it appears like an illusion. Alternatively, because ultimately whatever dharma it is is not established, "there is no truth". Because whatever truth to be analyzed is not established and all dharmas are unarisen, "there is also no falsehood". By this, having negated the extremes of superimposition and denigration, it establishes the middle way and induces entry into meditative equipoise upon that. "Therefore" means because thus ultimately all dharmas are unarisen, so there is neither truth nor falsehood. The Tathāgata is also differentiated by the completely pure true nature of being unarisen; therefore, because the unarisen true nature is common, the Tathāgata said, "All dharmas are the Buddha's dharmas," as in, "The always unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata. All dharmas are also like the Sugata. Those with childish minds who apprehend signs practice dharmas that do not exist in the world," and so forth.

[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If these dharmas are exclusively unarisen, well then, how can they be called 'all dharmas'?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what is called 'all dharmas'..." and so forth. Here the meaning is this: this is not a convention designated because they exist ultimately, but rather, although form and so forth do not ultimately exist as dharmas, because they bear their own and general characteristics in reliance on the unexamined non-ultimate, they are therefore called "all dharmas." Ultimately they are not, because for one abiding in that, even though everything is seen, all conventions are non-existent. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By this, it teaches that whoever thinks thus, "I will thoroughly lead sentient beings beyond sorrow," or thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," possesses the pride of superiority and in the genuine sense is not a bodhisattva. The words "Why is that?" are a thorough inquiry here into the logical reason that makes this known. What is called "dharma" is the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of persons and so forth. The noble Subhūti, because that dharma is not seen when analyzed by reasoning, stated the words, "that does not exist". Because that reasoning is common to all, the Bhagavān, in order to induce entry into both selflessnesses, spoke the words, "Therefore...". The words "No sentient being..." and so forth are illustrative; they should also be viewed as being without nature. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught. Clear realization has been explained.

[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If that dharma which the Bhagavān manifestly and completely awakened to does not exist at all, how could bodhisattvas, having actualized the taking up of the instructions, realize that selflessness of dharmas and persons?", having analyzed that, in order to teach clear realization he spoke the words, "Suppose, for example..." and so forth. This teaches clear realization through the attainment of pristine wisdom and the absence of pride of superiority. If one asks, "What is it like through the attainment of pristine wisdom?", it is in reliance on two types of pristine wisdom: the pristine wisdom that thoroughly apprehends the lineage and the pristine wisdom of equality. Therein, the pristine wisdom through the attainment of which one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata, and is certain in the lineage of the Buddha, is the pristine wisdom that thoroughly apprehends the lineage. Because that has arisen, one is "possessed of a body". "Possessed" means making it one's own; "body" is the body of the Tathāgata, so whoever has attained that is "possessed of a body". Regarding the thought, "How does one know that that pristine wisdom has been attained?", he spoke the words, "a great body". This teaches clear realization after having attained the pristine wisdom of equality through the equality of the selflessness of persons and dharmas; therefore, it teaches that it is "the pristine wisdom of the lineage". Through that pristine wisdom of equality, having realized all sentient beings as the selflessness of persons and dharmas, one subsumes them exclusively within oneself. Therefore, because one subsumes the bodies of all sentient beings into oneself, it is "a great body". It is not that this is not the literal meaning: thus, because all sentient beings are subsumed into oneself, it is called "body". Furthermore, since those are extremely numerous, it is a "great body", so it is not the literal meaning. This expresses the vastness of this topic.

heading: སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱ་ས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: From here on is the thorough seeking of the Buddha. Furthermore, that of the Buddha is thoroughly subsumed by seven excellences. The seven excellences are the excellence of the thoroughly pure field, the excellence of thoroughly pure unsurpassable seeing, the excellence of thoroughly pure unsurpassable knowing, the excellence of gaining mastery over the accumulation of merit, the excellence of body, the excellence of speech, and the excellence of mind.

[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If that dharma which the Bhagavān manifestly and completely awakened to does not exist at all, how could bodhisattvas, having actualized the taking up of the instructions, realize that selflessness of dharmas and persons?", having analyzed that, in order to teach clear realization he spoke the words, "Suppose, for example..." and so forth. This teaches clear realization through the attainment of pristine wisdom and the absence of pride of superiority. If one asks, "What is it like through the attainment of pristine wisdom?", it is in reliance on two types of pristine wisdom: the pristine wisdom that thoroughly apprehends the lineage and the pristine wisdom of equality. Therein, the pristine wisdom through the attainment of which one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata, and is certain in the lineage of the Buddha, is the pristine wisdom that thoroughly apprehends the lineage. Because that has arisen, one is "possessed of a body". "Possessed" means making it one's own; "body" is the body of the Tathāgata, so whoever has attained that is "possessed of a body". Regarding the thought, "How does one know that that pristine wisdom has been attained?", he spoke the words, "a great body". This teaches clear realization after having attained the pristine wisdom of equality through the equality of the selflessness of persons and dharmas; therefore, it teaches that it is "the pristine wisdom of the lineage". Through that pristine wisdom of equality, having realized all sentient beings as the selflessness of persons and dharmas, one subsumes them exclusively within oneself. Therefore, because one subsumes the bodies of all sentient beings into oneself, it is "a great body". It is not that this is not the literal meaning: thus, because all sentient beings are subsumed into oneself, it is called "body". Furthermore, since those are extremely numerous, it is a "great body", so it is not the literal meaning. This expresses the vastness of this topic.

By this, it teaches that whoever thinks thus, "I will thoroughly lead sentient beings beyond sorrow," or thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," possesses the pride of superiority and in the genuine sense is not a bodhisattva. The words "Why is that?" are a thorough inquiry here into the logical reason that makes this known. What is called "dharma" is the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of persons and so forth. The noble Subhūti, because that dharma is not seen when analyzed by reasoning, stated the words, "that does not exist". Because that reasoning is common to all, the Bhagavān, in order to induce entry into both selflessnesses, spoke the words, "Therefore...". The words "No sentient being..." and so forth are illustrative; they should also be viewed as being without nature. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught. Clear realization has been explained.

heading: ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Here, in order to clear away the doubt thinking, "If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, who will make effort in order to thoroughly accomplish a buddha-field?", having made it the context of the excellence of a thoroughly pure buddha-field, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Furthermore, the words "should also be expressed in that way" mean that because of possessing the pride of superiority, one should not say "he is a bodhisattva." This is because, without having realized the selflessness of persons and dharmas, they act with the pride of superiority, thinking, "I have realized [it]." Thus, by acting with the pride of superiority thinking "that is me", they have not realized the selflessness of persons. Because they act with the pride of superiority regarding that [even though] the arrays of fields do not exist, they have not realized the selflessness of dharmas. By this, how a bodhisattva should abide by resolving upon the arrays of fields as being like an illusion is taught. For those who think, "If ultimately those arrays of fields are non-existent, how did the Bhagavān state [them]?", he asked the words, "Why is that?" The explanation of this is like the previous one. This also does not become a repetition. The previous one is in order to clear away the conceptualization of a bodhisattva on the occasion of a bodhisattva abiding on the stage of action by resolve praying for a thoroughly pure bodhisattva field. Now, it was spoken in order to clear away the conceptualization of those who conceptualize thus, thinking "when bodhisattvas engage in order to accomplish a thoroughly pure buddha-field, they engage by adhering thus." At that time, because such other conceptualizations of some do not arise, it also does not become endless. By this, how a bodhisattva should practice upon this is taught.

འདིས་ནི་གང་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ། །བདག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་དེ་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་དུ་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མ་ཡིན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདིར་ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཡོངས་སུ་འདྲི་བའོ། །ཆོས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དམ་གང་ཟག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་དེ་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་མ་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ནི་མ་མཆིས་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏེ། །རིགས་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐུན་མོང་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉི་ག་ལ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་ཅན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཡང་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཡིང་བ་ཚར་གཅད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ།། །།
[3-178] translation already produced for this document:
By this, it teaches that whoever thinks thus, "I will thoroughly lead sentient beings beyond sorrow," or thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," possesses the pride of superiority and in the genuine sense is not a bodhisattva. The words "Why is that?" are a thorough inquiry here into the logical reason that makes this known. What is called "dharma" is the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of persons and so forth. The noble Subhūti, because that dharma is not seen when analyzed by reasoning, stated the words, "that does not exist". Because that reasoning is common to all, the Bhagavān, in order to induce entry into both selflessnesses, spoke the words, "Therefore...". The words "No sentient being..." and so forth are illustrative; they should also be viewed as being without nature. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught. Clear realization has been explained.

འདི་མན་ཆད་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཡང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་བདུན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྡུས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་བདུན་ནི། ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བརྙེས་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །
[3-179] translation already produced for this document:
From here on is the thorough seeking of the Buddha. Furthermore, that of the Buddha is thoroughly subsumed by seven excellences. The seven excellences are the excellence of the thoroughly pure field, the excellence of thoroughly pure unsurpassable seeing, the excellence of thoroughly pure unsurpassable knowing, the excellence of gaining mastery over the accumulation of merit, the excellence of body, the excellence of speech, and the excellence of mind.

heading: ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

[3-176] translation already produced for this document:
The intended meaning is this: this clear realization of a bodhisattva is also merely differentiated by the arising of extremely superior pristine wisdom in reliance on right conventional reality, but in order to teach that ultimately there is nothing whatsoever that clearly realizes or is to be clearly realized, the noble Subhūti stated to the Bhagavān the words, "Bhagavān, a person possessed of a body [spoken of] by the Tathāgata..." and so forth. By this, in meaning, it thoroughly teaches [that this] is the discordant class of adhering to "possessed of a body" and "a great body". In order to abandon that, it teaches abiding by aspiration and prayer.

By thoroughly expressing merely the sign "possessed of a body and a great body", it turns bodhisattvas away from adhering to all dharmas. It also establishes [them] in the ultimate, and also induces entry into meditative equipoise upon that. It also expresses profundity. It also abandons the extreme of superimposition. The previous one negated the extreme of denigration. "If the Tathāgata stated that that very body is non-existent, then at that time how could bodhisattvas who have attained clear realization think thus, 'I have attained the clear realization of a bodhisattva, so now I will liberate sentient beings'?" heading: གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, at that time the Tathāgata would be exclusively devoid of possessing thoroughly pure seeing and thoroughly pure knowing; because, since that arises from a bodhisattva, if that does not exist, how would that be fit to occur? That which is without a cause would become the meaning of existing eternally and so forth.

Here, in order to clear away the doubt thinking, "If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, who will make effort in order to thoroughly accomplish a buddha-field?", having made it the context of the excellence of a thoroughly pure buddha-field, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Furthermore, the words "should also be expressed in that way" mean that because of possessing the pride of superiority, one should not say "he is a bodhisattva." This is because, without having realized the selflessness of persons and dharmas, they act with the pride of superiority, thinking, "I have realized [it]." Thus, by acting with the pride of superiority thinking "that is me", they have not realized the selflessness of persons. Because they act with the pride of superiority regarding that [even though] the arrays of fields do not exist, they have not realized the selflessness of dharmas. By this, how a bodhisattva should abide by resolving upon the arrays of fields as being like an illusion is taught. For those who think, "If ultimately those arrays of fields are non-existent, how did the Bhagavān state [them]?", he asked the words, "Why is that?" The explanation of this is like the previous one. This also does not become a repetition. The previous one is in order to clear away the conceptualization of a bodhisattva on the occasion of a bodhisattva abiding on the stage of action by resolve praying for a thoroughly pure bodhisattva field. Now, it was spoken in order to clear away the conceptualization of those who conceptualize thus, thinking "when bodhisattvas engage in order to accomplish a thoroughly pure buddha-field, they engage by adhering thus." At that time, because such other conceptualizations of some do not arise, it also does not become endless. By this, how a bodhisattva should practice upon this is taught.

Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

heading: གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Therefore, for the sake of whoever in the gathered assembly conceptualizes thus, having made it the context of the two, unsurpassable thoroughly pure seeing and knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti also, having first grasped the intention of the Bhagavān, stated the words, "He possesses [it]." By this, [it is taught that] even though ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, conventionally there is the very existence of a bodhisattva whose nature is mere aggregates pleasant only when unexamined, who, having thoroughly fulfilled the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, becomes a Tathāgata of thoroughly pure knowing and seeing. Were it not so, if that did not exist even conventionally, then who would become a Tathāgata? Thus it teaches. Here, not saying that the Tathāgata possesses only the eye of prajñā teaches that he possesses the eyes in order to teach that thoroughly pure seeing is distinguished. Briefly, there are four kinds of eyes: apprehending form, apprehending ultimate truth, apprehending conventional truth, and apprehending the objects of knowledge in all aspects. Apprehending form is also of two kinds: the result of karma and the result of meditation. They are in accordance with the sequence of the five eyes. Here, because the object is coarse, apprehending form is taught first. By the power of the ultimate, conventional knowledge becomes thoroughly pure; therefore, apprehending the ultimate truth is taught first, and apprehending the conventional truth is explained later—this is the connection teaching the sequence.

འདིས་ནི་གང་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ། །བདག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་དེ་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་དུ་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མ་ཡིན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདིར་ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཡོངས་སུ་འདྲི་བའོ། །ཆོས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དམ་གང་ཟག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་དེ་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་མ་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ནི་མ་མཆིས་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏེ། །རིགས་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐུན་མོང་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉི་ག་ལ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་ཅན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཡང་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཡིང་བ་ཚར་གཅད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ།། །།
[3-178] translation already produced for this document:
By this, it teaches that whoever thinks thus, "I will thoroughly lead sentient beings beyond sorrow," or thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," possesses the pride of superiority and in the genuine sense is not a bodhisattva. The words "Why is that?" are a thorough inquiry here into the logical reason that makes this known. What is called "dharma" is the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of persons and so forth. The noble Subhūti, because that dharma is not seen when analyzed by reasoning, stated the words, "that does not exist". Because that reasoning is common to all, the Bhagavān, in order to induce entry into both selflessnesses, spoke the words, "Therefore...". The words "No sentient being..." and so forth are illustrative; they should also be viewed as being without nature. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught. Clear realization has been explained.

འདི་མན་ཆད་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཡང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་བདུན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྡུས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་བདུན་ནི། ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བརྙེས་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་། ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །

From here on is the thorough seeking of the Buddha. Furthermore, that of the Buddha is thoroughly subsumed by seven excellences. The seven excellences are the excellence of the thoroughly pure field, the excellence of thoroughly pure unsurpassable seeing, the excellence of thoroughly pure unsurpassable knowing, the excellence of gaining mastery over the accumulation of merit, the excellence of body, the excellence of speech, and the excellence of mind.

དེ་ལ་གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་ན་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འབད་པར་བྱེད་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྗོད་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའོ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་སྟེ། གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་མ་རྟོགས་པར་རྟོགས་སོ་སྙམ་དུ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ལྟར་དེའི་ངའོ་སྙམ་དུ་མངོན་པར་ང་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་པས་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་མ་རྟོགས་སོ། །ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་མེད་པར་དེ་ལ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་པས་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་མ་རྟོགས་སོ། །འདིས་ནི་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་མོས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཇི་ལྟར་གསུངས་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་ལ་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་ཏེ། འདིའི་བཤད་པ་ནི་སྔ་མ་བཞིན་ནོ། །འདི་ཚིག་ཟློས་པར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ།སྔ་མ་ནི་མོས་པས་སྤྱོད་པའི་ས་ལ་གནས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པར་སྨོན་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་སེལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ད་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་ འཇུག་པ་ན་དེ་ལྟར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་འཇུག་གོ་སྙམ་དུ་གང་དག་དེ་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་དེ་དག་གི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་དེ་བསལ་བར་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ཚེ་ཁ་ཅིག་གི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་གཞན་མི་འབྱུང་བས་ཐུག་པ་མེད་པར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Here, in order to clear away the doubt thinking, "If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, who will make effort in order to thoroughly accomplish a buddha-field?", having made it the context of the excellence of a thoroughly pure buddha-field, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Furthermore, the words "should also be expressed in that way" mean that because of possessing the pride of superiority, one should not say "he is a bodhisattva." This is because, without having realized the selflessness of persons and dharmas, they act with the pride of superiority, thinking, "I have realized [it]." Thus, by acting with the pride of superiority thinking "that is me", they have not realized the selflessness of persons. Because they act with the pride of superiority regarding that [even though] the arrays of fields do not exist, they have not realized the selflessness of dharmas. By this, how a bodhisattva should abide by resolving upon the arrays of fields as being like an illusion is taught. For those who think, "If ultimately those arrays of fields are non-existent, how did the Bhagavān state [them]?", he asked the words, "Why is that?" The explanation of this is like the previous one. This also does not become a repetition. The previous one is in order to clear away the conceptualization of a bodhisattva on the occasion of a bodhisattva abiding on the stage of action by resolve praying for a thoroughly pure bodhisattva field. Now, it was spoken in order to clear away the conceptualization of those who conceptualize thus, thinking "when bodhisattvas engage in order to accomplish a thoroughly pure buddha-field, they engage by adhering thus." At that time, because such other conceptualizations of some do not arise, it also does not become endless. By this, how a bodhisattva should practice upon this is taught.

Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

heading: གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

By this, it teaches that whoever thinks thus, "I will thoroughly lead sentient beings beyond sorrow," or thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," possesses the pride of superiority and in the genuine sense is not a bodhisattva. The words "Why is that?" are a thorough inquiry here into the logical reason that makes this known. What is called "dharma" is the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of persons and so forth. The noble Subhūti, because that dharma is not seen when analyzed by reasoning, stated the words, "that does not exist". Because that reasoning is common to all, the Bhagavān, in order to induce entry into both selflessnesses, spoke the words, "Therefore...". The words "No sentient being..." and so forth are illustrative; they should also be viewed as being without nature. By this, the suppression of distraction is taught. Clear realization has been explained.

Here, in order to clear away the doubt thinking, "If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, who will make effort in order to thoroughly accomplish a buddha-field?", having made it the context of the excellence of a thoroughly pure buddha-field, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Furthermore, the words "should also be expressed in that way" mean that because of possessing the pride of superiority, one should not say "he is a bodhisattva." This is because, without having realized the selflessness of persons and dharmas, they act with the pride of superiority, thinking, "I have realized [it]." Thus, by acting with the pride of superiority thinking "that is me", they have not realized the selflessness of persons. Because they act with the pride of superiority regarding that [even though] the arrays of fields do not exist, they have not realized the selflessness of dharmas. By this, how a bodhisattva should abide by resolving upon the arrays of fields as being like an illusion is taught. For those who think, "If ultimately those arrays of fields are non-existent, how did the Bhagavān state [them]?", he asked the words, "Why is that?" The explanation of this is like the previous one. This also does not become a repetition. The previous one is in order to clear away the conceptualization of a bodhisattva on the occasion of a bodhisattva abiding on the stage of action by resolve praying for a thoroughly pure bodhisattva field. Now, it was spoken in order to clear away the conceptualization of those who conceptualize thus, thinking "when bodhisattvas engage in order to accomplish a thoroughly pure buddha-field, they engage by adhering thus." At that time, because such other conceptualizations of some do not arise, it also does not become endless. By this, how a bodhisattva should practice upon this is taught.

Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: In order to express thoroughly pure knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The minds and mental factors of the three times are the stream of mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called 'knowing', not 'seeing'. Furthermore, it should be known as the various natures of affliction and purification, such as 'a mind with attachment' and 'a mind free of attachment'.

Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

[3-183] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, for the sake of whoever in the gathered assembly conceptualizes thus, having made it the context of the two, unsurpassable thoroughly pure seeing and knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti also, having first grasped the intention of the Bhagavān, stated the words, "He possesses [it]." By this, [it is taught that] even though ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, conventionally there is the very existence of a bodhisattva whose nature is mere aggregates pleasant only when unexamined, who, having thoroughly fulfilled the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, becomes a Tathāgata of thoroughly pure knowing and seeing. Were it not so, if that did not exist even conventionally, then who would become a Tathāgata? Thus it teaches. Here, not saying that the Tathāgata possesses only the eye of prajñā teaches that he possesses the eyes in order to teach that thoroughly pure seeing is distinguished. Briefly, there are four kinds of eyes: apprehending form, apprehending ultimate truth, apprehending conventional truth, and apprehending the objects of knowledge in all aspects. Apprehending form is also of two kinds: the result of karma and the result of meditation. They are in accordance with the sequence of the five eyes. Here, because the object is coarse, apprehending form is taught first. By the power of the ultimate, conventional knowledge becomes thoroughly pure; therefore, apprehending the ultimate truth is taught first, and apprehending the conventional truth is explained later—this is the connection teaching the sequence.

He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

translation: The words 'that many world systems' are an illustration, because he thoroughly knows the streams of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. Thus, conventionally the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye and so forth; therefore, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that. By this passage, both excellences are taught.

Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, at that time the Tathāgata would be exclusively devoid of possessing thoroughly pure seeing and thoroughly pure knowing; because, since that arises from a bodhisattva, if that does not exist, how would that be fit to occur? That which is without a cause would become the meaning of existing eternally and so forth.

[3-183] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, for the sake of whoever in the gathered assembly conceptualizes thus, having made it the context of the two, unsurpassable thoroughly pure seeing and knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti also, having first grasped the intention of the Bhagavān, stated the words, "He possesses [it]." By this, [it is taught that] even though ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, conventionally there is the very existence of a bodhisattva whose nature is mere aggregates pleasant only when unexamined, who, having thoroughly fulfilled the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, becomes a Tathāgata of thoroughly pure knowing and seeing. Were it not so, if that did not exist even conventionally, then who would become a Tathāgata? Thus it teaches. Here, not saying that the Tathāgata possesses only the eye of prajñā teaches that he possesses the eyes in order to teach that thoroughly pure seeing is distinguished. Briefly, there are four kinds of eyes: apprehending form, apprehending ultimate truth, apprehending conventional truth, and apprehending the objects of knowledge in all aspects. Apprehending form is also of two kinds: the result of karma and the result of meditation. They are in accordance with the sequence of the five eyes. Here, because the object is coarse, apprehending form is taught first. By the power of the ultimate, conventional knowledge becomes thoroughly pure; therefore, apprehending the ultimate truth is taught first, and apprehending the conventional truth is explained later—this is the connection teaching the sequence.

He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The fleshly eye and so forth are themselves unapprehendable when analyzed by the nature of one and many, and it is also unreasonable to apprehend them by consciousness as a different entity. Investigating the intention of one who thinks, 'If it is like what was analyzed before, how can the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye and so forth and thoroughly know the stream of mind?', the question, 'Why is that?' was asked. And in order to teach how a bodhisattva should accomplish that by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga on these two purities, he spoke the words, 'the stream of mind, the stream of mind' and so forth. The words 'there is no stream' are from the ultimate perspective.

Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, at that time the Tathāgata would be exclusively devoid of possessing thoroughly pure seeing and thoroughly pure knowing; because, since that arises from a bodhisattva, if that does not exist, how would that be fit to occur? That which is without a cause would become the meaning of existing eternally and so forth.

[3-183] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, for the sake of whoever in the gathered assembly conceptualizes thus, having made it the context of the two, unsurpassable thoroughly pure seeing and knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti also, having first grasped the intention of the Bhagavān, stated the words, "He possesses [it]." By this, [it is taught that] even though ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, conventionally there is the very existence of a bodhisattva whose nature is mere aggregates pleasant only when unexamined, who, having thoroughly fulfilled the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, becomes a Tathāgata of thoroughly pure knowing and seeing. Were it not so, if that did not exist even conventionally, then who would become a Tathāgata? Thus it teaches. Here, not saying that the Tathāgata possesses only the eye of prajñā teaches that he possesses the eyes in order to teach that thoroughly pure seeing is distinguished. Briefly, there are four kinds of eyes: apprehending form, apprehending ultimate truth, apprehending conventional truth, and apprehending the objects of knowledge in all aspects. Apprehending form is also of two kinds: the result of karma and the result of meditation. They are in accordance with the sequence of the five eyes. Here, because the object is coarse, apprehending form is taught first. By the power of the ultimate, conventional knowledge becomes thoroughly pure; therefore, apprehending the ultimate truth is taught first, and apprehending the conventional truth is explained later—this is the connection teaching the sequence.

གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པའི་ཡུལ་ལ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་མངའོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཆོས་ཙམ་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཉིད་དེ་གང་ཟག་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཞེས་གང་ཟག་སྟོང་སྟེ། ཆོས་ཙམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་ལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ནོ། །ཤེས་བྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་མཁྱེན་པ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། འདིས་ནི་ད་ལྟར་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པར་བཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་བསྟན་པས་ནི་གང་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །
[3-184] translation already produced for this document:
He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

ཅི་འདྲ་བ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་ཞེས་ལན་གཉིས་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདག་མེད་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་ལན་གཉིས་བརྗོད་པས་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་དེ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གཅིག་ནི་བཟླས་པའོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འོག་མ་ནི་ཚུལ་ལོ། །དེས་ན་ཇི་སྐད་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། སུ་དག་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པོ་སྙམ་དུ་གང་ཟག་ལ་སོགས་པར་འཛིན་པ་མེད་པ་དང་། ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་ཆོས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་ཡང་མེད་པ་དེ་དག་མེད་པ་གཉི་ག་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། འདིས་ནི་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །གནས་འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དེ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་དེ་ལ་མོས་པས་འཇུག་པར་བསྟན་པས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བརྗོད་དོ། །
[3-181] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "What sort of [person] is called a bodhisattva?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. Saying twice the words "dharmas are selfless" teaches that dharmas are selfless through the two kinds of selflessness. Saying twice the words "bodhisattva, being" teaches the realization of those very two kinds of selflessness. Alternatively, one [of the phrases] "he is a bodhisattva" is repeated. The latter, the words "is called a bodhisattva", is the method. If one asks, "Then what is being taught?", it teaches the words, "He is called a bodhisattva because of comprehending both of those non-existences: the absence of apprehending persons and so forth, thinking 'Who will accomplish [it]?', and also the absence of apprehending as dharmas the 'arrays of fields'." By this, thoroughly restraining the mind is taught. By this entire point, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas engage with it by resolving in order to accomplish that illusion-like buddha-field, extensiveness is expressed.

[3-182] source:
གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་ན་དེའི་ཚེ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་དང་། མཁྱེན་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ནར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའི་དེ་མེད་ན་དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་རུང་བར་འགྱུར། རྒྱུ་མེད་པ་ནི་རྟག་ཏུ་ཡོད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དོན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-182] translation already produced for this document:
If there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, at that time the Tathāgata would be exclusively devoid of possessing thoroughly pure seeing and thoroughly pure knowing; because, since that arises from a bodhisattva, if that does not exist, how would that be fit to occur? That which is without a cause would become the meaning of existing eternally and so forth.

[3-183] source:
དེ་བས་ན་འཁོར་འདུས་པ་གང་དེ་སྙམ་དུ་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེའི་ཆེད་དུ་གཟིགས་པ་དང་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་དགོངས་པ་སྔར་བཟུང་ནས་མངའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་གང་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྐངས་ནས་མཁྱེན་པ་དང་གཟིགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མ་བརྟགས་གཅིག་པུ་ན་དགའ་བ་ཕུང་པོ་ཙམ་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གལ་ཏེ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡང་དེ་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ན་དེའི་ཚེ་སུ་ཞིག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་དེ་སྐད་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཁོ་ན་མངའོ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྤྱན་མངའ་བར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །མདོར་བསྡུ་ན་སྤྱན་རྣམ་པ་བཞི་སྟེ། གཟུགས་འཛིན་པ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པ་དང་།རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཤེས་བྱ་འཛིན་པའོ། །གཟུགས་འཛིན་པ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། ལས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་དང་། བསྒོམས་པའི་འབྲས་བུའོ། །སྤྱན་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་དང་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལ་ཡུལ་རགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་པོར་གཟུགས་འཛིན་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དོན་དམ་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཤེས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེས་ན་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པ་ནི་སྔར་བསྟན་ལ། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཕྱིས་བཤད་དོ་ཞེས་གོ་རིམས་བསྟན་པའི་མཚམས་སྦྱར་བའོ། །

Therefore, for the sake of whoever in the gathered assembly conceptualizes thus, having made it the context of the two, unsurpassable thoroughly pure seeing and knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti also, having first grasped the intention of the Bhagavān, stated the words, "He possesses [it]." By this, [it is taught that] even though ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever called a bodhisattva, conventionally there is the very existence of a bodhisattva whose nature is mere aggregates pleasant only when unexamined, who, having thoroughly fulfilled the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, becomes a Tathāgata of thoroughly pure knowing and seeing. Were it not so, if that did not exist even conventionally, then who would become a Tathāgata? Thus it teaches. Here, not saying that the Tathāgata possesses only the eye of prajñā teaches that he possesses the eyes in order to teach that thoroughly pure seeing is distinguished. Briefly, there are four kinds of eyes: apprehending form, apprehending ultimate truth, apprehending conventional truth, and apprehending the objects of knowledge in all aspects. Apprehending form is also of two kinds: the result of karma and the result of meditation. They are in accordance with the sequence of the five eyes. Here, because the object is coarse, apprehending form is taught first. By the power of the ultimate, conventional knowledge becomes thoroughly pure; therefore, apprehending the ultimate truth is taught first, and apprehending the conventional truth is explained later—this is the connection teaching the sequence.

[3-184] source:
གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པའི་ཡུལ་ལ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་མངའོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཆོས་ཙམ་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཉིད་དེ་གང་ཟག་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཞེས་གང་ཟག་སྟོང་སྟེ། ཆོས་ཙམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་ལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ནོ། །ཤེས་བྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་མཁྱེན་པ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། འདིས་ནི་ད་ལྟར་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པར་བཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་བསྟན་པས་ནི་གང་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །

He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: If the minds of the three times do not exist, at that time the aggregate of merit would also not exist, because that depends on the mind.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-184] source:
གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པའི་ཡུལ་ལ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་མངའོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཆོས་ཙམ་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཉིད་དེ་གང་ཟག་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཞེས་གང་ཟག་སྟོང་སྟེ། ཆོས་ཙམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་ལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ནོ། །ཤེས་བྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་མཁྱེན་པ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། འདིས་ནི་ད་ལྟར་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པར་བཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་བསྟན་པས་ནི་གང་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །
[3-184] translation already produced for this document:
He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

[3-185] source:
མཁྱེན་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་རྣམས་ནི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ནོ། །དེ་བས་ན་དུས་གསུམ་ཡུལ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡུལ་དེ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་མཁྱེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའི་གཟིགས་པ་ཞེས་ནི་མི་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་དང་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་དབྲལ་བའི་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་བྱང་བའི་ངོ་བོ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-185] translation already produced for this document:
In order to express thoroughly pure knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The minds and mental factors of the three times are the stream of mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called 'knowing', not 'seeing'. Furthermore, it should be known as the various natures of affliction and purification, such as 'a mind with attachment' and 'a mind free of attachment'.

[3-186] source:
དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་མཐའ་ཡས་པར་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཡོངས་སུ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་མངའ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་དེས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་པར་བྱ་བའོ། །གཞུང་འདིས་ནི་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གཉི་ག་ཡང་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-186] translation already produced for this document:
The words 'that many world systems' are an illustration, because he thoroughly knows the streams of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. Thus, conventionally the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye and so forth; therefore, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that. By this passage, both excellences are taught.

[3-187] source:
ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་དཔྱད་ན་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཉིད་ལ། དོན་གཞན་ཤེས་པས་འཛིན་པར་ཡང་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། ཇི་ལྟར་སྔར་དཔྱད་པ་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་མངའ་བ་དང་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་རབ་ཏུ་མཁྱེན་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་འདི་གཉིས་ལ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར། སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་རོ། །
[3-187] translation already produced for this document:
The fleshly eye and so forth are themselves unapprehendable when analyzed by the nature of one and many, and it is also unreasonable to apprehend them by consciousness as a different entity. Investigating the intention of one who thinks, 'If it is like what was analyzed before, how can the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye and so forth and thoroughly know the stream of mind?', the question, 'Why is that?' was asked. And in order to teach how a bodhisattva should accomplish that by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga on these two purities, he spoke the words, 'the stream of mind, the stream of mind' and so forth. The words 'there is no stream' are from the ultimate perspective.

[3-188] source:
རང་བཞིན་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་བརྗོད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བརྗོད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་སྤྱན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་སྐབས་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་སུམ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཞུས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་དམིགས་ཀྱི། ཡོད་ཀྱང་འཛིན་པར་མི་འཐད་པས་མི་དམིགས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མི་དམིགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ནི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ནི་སྔར་ཡང་བཤད་དེ། སྟོན་པར་ཡང་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་ཤའི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །འདི་ལ་རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚིག་གིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ལྷག་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །
[3-188] translation already produced for this document:
Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Therefore, having investigated the thought, "How should a bodhisattva strive to accomplish the excellence of possessing the aggregate of merit of the Tathāgata?", addressing the excellence of possessing the aggregate of merit, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

[3-185] translation already produced for this document:
In order to express thoroughly pure knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The minds and mental factors of the three times are the stream of mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called 'knowing', not 'seeing'. Furthermore, it should be known as the various natures of affliction and purification, such as 'a mind with attachment' and 'a mind free of attachment'.

The words 'that many world systems' are an illustration, because he thoroughly knows the streams of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. Thus, conventionally the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye and so forth; therefore, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that. [3-187] translation already produced for this document:
The fleshly eye and so forth are themselves unapprehendable when analyzed by the nature of one and many, and it is also unreasonable to apprehend them by consciousness as a different entity. Investigating the intention of one who thinks, 'If it is like what was analyzed before, how can the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye and so forth and thoroughly know the stream of mind?', the question, 'Why is that?' was asked. And in order to teach how a bodhisattva should accomplish that by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga on these two purities, he spoke the words, 'the stream of mind, the stream of mind' and so forth. The words 'there is no stream' are from the ultimate perspective.

རང་བཞིན་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་བརྗོད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བརྗོད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་སྤྱན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་སྐབས་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་སུམ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཞུས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་དམིགས་ཀྱི། ཡོད་ཀྱང་འཛིན་པར་མི་འཐད་པས་མི་དམིགས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མི་དམིགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ནི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ནི་སྔར་ཡང་བཤད་དེ། སྟོན་པར་ཡང་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་ཤའི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །འདི་ལ་རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚིག་གིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ལྷག་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །
[3-188] translation already produced for this document:
Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: By this, he teaches thus: "If a son of noble family or daughter of noble family who gives away even outer entities such as jewels comes to possess a great aggregate of merit, why would the Tathāgata not possess the aggregate of merit by having habituated to many hundreds of hardships for immeasurable, innumerable eons?" Therefore, it is taught that although the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately, because it exists conventionally, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish mastery over it. This also expresses extensiveness.

He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

[3-185] translation already produced for this document:
In order to express thoroughly pure knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The minds and mental factors of the three times are the stream of mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called 'knowing', not 'seeing'. Furthermore, it should be known as the various natures of affliction and purification, such as 'a mind with attachment' and 'a mind free of attachment'.

The words 'that many world systems' are an illustration, because he thoroughly knows the streams of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. Thus, conventionally the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye and so forth; therefore, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that.
