[3-187] translation already produced for this document:
The fleshly eye and so forth are themselves unapprehendable when analyzed by the nature of one and many, and it is also unreasonable to apprehend them by consciousness as a different entity. Investigating the intention of one who thinks, 'If it is like what was analyzed before, how can the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye and so forth and thoroughly know the stream of mind?', the question, 'Why is that?' was asked. And in order to teach how a bodhisattva should accomplish that by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga on these two purities, he spoke the words, 'the stream of mind, the stream of mind' and so forth. The words 'there is no stream' are from the ultimate perspective.

རང་བཞིན་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་བརྗོད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བརྗོད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་སྤྱན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་སྐབས་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་སུམ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཞུས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་དམིགས་ཀྱི། ཡོད་ཀྱང་འཛིན་པར་མི་འཐད་པས་མི་དམིགས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མི་དམིགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ནི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ནི་སྔར་ཡང་བཤད་དེ། སྟོན་པར་ཡང་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་ཤའི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །འདི་ལ་རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚིག་གིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ལྷག་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །
[3-188] translation already produced for this document:
Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Having investigated the thought, "Why is the aggregate of merit not posited as existing ultimately?", in order to teach both how a bodhisattva should accomplish this and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, if" and so forth. The words "if" (gal te) are synonymous with "if" (ji ste).

[3-184] translation already produced for this document:
He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

[3-185] translation already produced for this document:
In order to express thoroughly pure knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The minds and mental factors of the three times are the stream of mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called 'knowing', not 'seeing'. Furthermore, it should be known as the various natures of affliction and purification, such as 'a mind with attachment' and 'a mind free of attachment'.

དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་མཐའ་ཡས་པར་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཡོངས་སུ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་མངའ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་དེས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་པར་བྱ་བའོ། །གཞུང་འདིས་ནི་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གཉི་ག་ཡང་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

The words 'that many world systems' are an illustration, because he thoroughly knows the streams of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. Thus, conventionally the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye and so forth; therefore, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that. [3-187] translation already produced for this document:
The fleshly eye and so forth are themselves unapprehendable when analyzed by the nature of one and many, and it is also unreasonable to apprehend them by consciousness as a different entity. Investigating the intention of one who thinks, 'If it is like what was analyzed before, how can the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye and so forth and thoroughly know the stream of mind?', the question, 'Why is that?' was asked. And in order to teach how a bodhisattva should accomplish that by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga on these two purities, he spoke the words, 'the stream of mind, the stream of mind' and so forth. The words 'there is no stream' are from the ultimate perspective.

[3-188] source:
རང་བཞིན་མེད་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་བརྗོད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བརྗོད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་སྤྱན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་སྐབས་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་སུམ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཞུས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་དམིགས་ཀྱི། ཡོད་ཀྱང་འཛིན་པར་མི་འཐད་པས་མི་དམིགས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མི་དམིགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ནི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ནི་སྔར་ཡང་བཤད་དེ། སྟོན་པར་ཡང་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་སྨོས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་ཤའི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་འདས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །འདི་ལ་རྒྱུན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚིག་གིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ལྷག་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །
[3-188] translation already produced for this document:
Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The words "the Tathāgata would not speak" are because ultimately expression does not apply; the intention is the thought, "Even without being taught, it would be renowned like that." How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. By this, both how a bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of possessing the Tathāgata's aggregate of merit should accomplish it by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga through not apprehending it ultimately, and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained by abandoning adherence to apprehending it ultimately, are taught; profundity is also expressed.

He possesses the eye of prajñā regarding the object that is the selflessness of persons and dharmas. The person is empty because conventionally it is merely appearing as dharmas but is not a person; regarding the object of mere dharmas is the eye of dharma. Knowing all objects of knowledge in all aspects is called the eye of the Buddha. By this, by teaching the five eyes in genuine conventionality because he dwells directly actualizing [them] now, thoroughly pure seeing is expressed.

[3-185] translation already produced for this document:
In order to express thoroughly pure knowing, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The minds and mental factors of the three times are the stream of mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called 'knowing', not 'seeing'. Furthermore, it should be known as the various natures of affliction and purification, such as 'a mind with attachment' and 'a mind free of attachment'.

[3-187] translation already produced for this document:
The fleshly eye and so forth are themselves unapprehendable when analyzed by the nature of one and many, and it is also unreasonable to apprehend them by consciousness as a different entity. Investigating the intention of one who thinks, 'If it is like what was analyzed before, how can the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye and so forth and thoroughly know the stream of mind?', the question, 'Why is that?' was asked. And in order to teach how a bodhisattva should accomplish that by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga on these two purities, he spoke the words, 'the stream of mind, the stream of mind' and so forth. The words 'there is no stream' are from the ultimate perspective.

[3-188] translation already produced for this document:
Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

translation: If the aggregate of merit were indeed non-existent, then at that time the two aspects of the excellence of the body of the Tathāgatas—the excellence of the body of minor marks and the excellence of the body of marks—which are asserted to be born from unsurpassed merit, would also not exist because they would be without a cause.

Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

By this, he teaches thus: "If a son of noble family or daughter of noble family who gives away even outer entities such as jewels comes to possess a great aggregate of merit, why would the Tathāgata not possess the aggregate of merit by having habituated to many hundreds of hardships for immeasurable, innumerable eons?" Therefore, it is taught that although the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately, because it exists conventionally, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish mastery over it. This also expresses extensiveness.

The words "the Tathāgata would not speak" are because ultimately expression does not apply; the intention is the thought, "Even without being taught, it would be renowned like that." How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. By this, both how a bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of possessing the Tathāgata's aggregate of merit should accomplish it by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga through not apprehending it ultimately, and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained by abandoning adherence to apprehending it ultimately, are taught; profundity is also expressed.

translation: Therefore, having investigated the thought, "How should a bodhisattva strive in order to thoroughly accomplish the two aspects of the excellence of the body of the Tathāgata?", for that sake, addressing the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgatas, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The words "form body" should be viewed as being the body of minor marks.

Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

The words "the Tathāgata would not speak" are because ultimately expression does not apply; the intention is the thought, "Even without being taught, it would be renowned like that." How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. By this, both how a bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of possessing the Tathāgata's aggregate of merit should accomplish it by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga through not apprehending it ultimately, and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained by abandoning adherence to apprehending it ultimately, are taught; profundity is also expressed.

heading: སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The body of marks will be explained below, in the manner of "cow and ox". From this, the thought of the noble Subhūti is this: "Just as the aggregate of merit is completely non-existent as an aggregate ultimately, likewise the form body is also completely unarisen; therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body ultimately." Conventionally, just like a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion, the form body does indeed exist; therefore, it is indeed suitable to arise from the aggregate of merit. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva, having belief in the form of a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion like that, should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish it. Here, it will also not be repetitive; because previously, at the time of aspiration to obtain the form body on the level of action through belief, and at the time of making offerings and serving the Tathāgata, adherence to it in that way is completely abandoned, whereas now, it is spoken in order to clear away the bad conceptualization of those in the retinue who say, "A bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata on the level of pure superior intention possesses adherence to form".

Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. heading: སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Thinking, "Then how is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?", he asked, "Why is that?", connecting to the words "one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body." This is unestablished; the form body is not established as having the nature of possessing limbs, or as having the nature of accumulated subtle atoms, just as it was analyzed previously. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it is taught. The word "therefore" means it exists thus conventionally; because it is not that it does not exist in all aspects like the horn of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of deprecation, how the mind should be thoroughly restrained is taught. By all these points, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should strive in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, extensiveness is also taught. Addressing the excellence of the body of marks, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth; all the explanation here is identical to the previous one.

[3-188] translation already produced for this document:
Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

By this, he teaches thus: "If a son of noble family or daughter of noble family who gives away even outer entities such as jewels comes to possess a great aggregate of merit, why would the Tathāgata not possess the aggregate of merit by having habituated to many hundreds of hardships for immeasurable, innumerable eons?" Therefore, it is taught that although the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately, because it exists conventionally, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish mastery over it. This also expresses extensiveness.

The words "the Tathāgata would not speak" are because ultimately expression does not apply; the intention is the thought, "Even without being taught, it would be renowned like that." How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. By this, both how a bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of possessing the Tathāgata's aggregate of merit should accomplish it by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga through not apprehending it ultimately, and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained by abandoning adherence to apprehending it ultimately, are taught; profundity is also expressed.

translation: If one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body, at that time the teaching of the Bhagavān would also not exist, because that is subsumed by the form body.

Even though they are without nature, it is spoken based on conventionality; for that very reason, he spoke the words, 'it is called the stream of mind'. The intention is the thought that, were it otherwise, ultimately it would not be expressed because it is beyond all spheres of expression. Mentioning 'stream of mind' is an illustration; this is the occasion to express the words 'the fleshly eye and so forth are also taught as lacking the nature of an eye', which is stated directly. In order to teach how the mind should be thoroughly restrained regarding this, the question 'Why is that?' was asked, connecting to the words, 'there is no stream'. Because the past mind and so forth are ultimately unarisen, they are unapprehendable, but it is not that they are unapprehendable because it is invalid to apprehend them even though they exist. If that were so, it would not be taught that there is no stream of mind, because merely being unapprehendable does not make entities lack a nature. How the minds of the three times do not exist ultimately has been explained before and will also be taught. Mentioning 'mind' is an illustration; therefore, the past and so forth of the fleshly eye and so forth are also unapprehendable. Here, by the words 'there is no stream' and so forth, profundity is expressed. By the remainder, extensiveness.

By this, he teaches thus: "If a son of noble family or daughter of noble family who gives away even outer entities such as jewels comes to possess a great aggregate of merit, why would the Tathāgata not possess the aggregate of merit by having habituated to many hundreds of hardships for immeasurable, innumerable eons?" Therefore, it is taught that although the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately, because it exists conventionally, a bodhisattva should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish mastery over it. This also expresses extensiveness.

The words "the Tathāgata would not speak" are because ultimately expression does not apply; the intention is the thought, "Even without being taught, it would be renowned like that." How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. By this, both how a bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of possessing the Tathāgata's aggregate of merit should accomplish it by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga through not apprehending it ultimately, and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained by abandoning adherence to apprehending it ultimately, are taught; profundity is also expressed.

[3-193] translation already produced for this document:
The words "the Tathāgata would not speak" are because ultimately expression does not apply; the intention is the thought, "Even without being taught, it would be renowned like that." How the aggregate of merit does not exist ultimately has already been taught previously. By this, both how a bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of possessing the Tathāgata's aggregate of merit should accomplish it by engaging in meditative equipoise in yoga through not apprehending it ultimately, and how the mind should be thoroughly restrained by abandoning adherence to apprehending it ultimately, are taught; profundity is also expressed.

[3-196] translation already produced for this document:
The body of marks will be explained below, in the manner of "cow and ox". From this, the thought of the noble Subhūti is this: "Just as the aggregate of merit is completely non-existent as an aggregate ultimately, likewise the form body is also completely unarisen; therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body ultimately." Conventionally, just like a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion, the form body does indeed exist; therefore, it is indeed suitable to arise from the aggregate of merit. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva, having belief in the form of a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion like that, should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish it. Here, it will also not be repetitive; because previously, at the time of aspiration to obtain the form body on the level of action through belief, and at the time of making offerings and serving the Tathāgata, adherence to it in that way is completely abandoned, whereas now, it is spoken in order to clear away the bad conceptualization of those in the retinue who say, "A bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata on the level of pure superior intention possesses adherence to form".

Thinking, "Then how is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?", he asked, "Why is that?", connecting to the words "one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body." This is unestablished; the form body is not established as having the nature of possessing limbs, or as having the nature of accumulated subtle atoms, just as it was analyzed previously. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it is taught. The word "therefore" means it exists thus conventionally; because it is not that it does not exist in all aspects like the horn of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of deprecation, how the mind should be thoroughly restrained is taught. By all these points, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should strive in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, extensiveness is also taught. Addressing the excellence of the body of marks, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth; all the explanation here is identical to the previous one.

གལ་ཏེ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲུབ་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱ་ན། དེའི་ཚེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པ་ཡང་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

heading: གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
source: དོན་དམ་པར་འཆད་པ་པོ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཤད་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་ངས་ཆོས་བསྟན་ཏོ་སྙམ་དུ་མི་དགོངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟར་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་འཆད་པ་པོ་སྟེ་བདག་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ཕྱི་ནང་གི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། བཤད་པ་སྟེ། བྱེད་པ་གཟུགས་སམ་སྒྲའི་བདག་ཉིད་མེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ནི་སྔར་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་ཟིན་ཏེ། དངོས་པོ་མཐའ་དག་ལ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཁྱབ་པར་སྔར་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་འཆད་པ་པོ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཤད་པ་མ་བརྟགས་ན་དགའ་བས་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཏུ་ཟད་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དངོས་པོའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཁ་ཅིག་མགོ་རྨོངས་ཏེ་དོན་དམ་པར་གསུམ་པོ་ཡོད་པར་སེམས་ན་དེའི་ཚེ་ཅིར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་སུ་ཞིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྐུར་པ་ནི་དོན་མེད་པར་གླེང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་མེད་པ་དེས་གླེང་བར་ནུས་སྙམ་པ་ལ། ལོག་པར་འཛིན་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་ལོག་པར་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྲག་ཅ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྟ་བུར་ཤེས་པས་འཇུག་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: Ultimately, because there is no teacher, no thing to be taught, and no teaching, the Tathāgata does not consider the thought, "I have taught the Dharma." If it were not so, because it would become a mistake, he would not become omniscient. How a teacher, such as a self and so forth, a thing to be taught, such as outer and inner entities, and a teaching, meaning an action of form or the nature of sound, do not exist, has already been extensively taught in that way previously, because it was previously established that emptiness pervades all entities. Conventionally, the teacher, the thing to be taught, and the teaching are merely imputations of convention that are pleasing when unexamined, but ultimately they are not. Thinking, "Even though the reality of entities has been taught like that, if some become bewildered and think that the three exist ultimately, then at that time what would happen?", he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whoever..." and so forth. "Deprecation" is because of speaking meaninglessly. Thinking, "How can that which is non-existent speak?", he spoke the words, "by wrong grasping", meaning that because it is wrongly grasped through mistaken adherence, that does not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should dwell is taught: "A bodhisattva who engages in the excellence of the speech of the Tathāgata should engage by knowing it to be like an echo and so forth".

[3-196] translation already produced for this document:
The body of marks will be explained below, in the manner of "cow and ox". From this, the thought of the noble Subhūti is this: "Just as the aggregate of merit is completely non-existent as an aggregate ultimately, likewise the form body is also completely unarisen; therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body ultimately." Conventionally, just like a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion, the form body does indeed exist; therefore, it is indeed suitable to arise from the aggregate of merit. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva, having belief in the form of a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion like that, should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish it. Here, it will also not be repetitive; because previously, at the time of aspiration to obtain the form body on the level of action through belief, and at the time of making offerings and serving the Tathāgata, adherence to it in that way is completely abandoned, whereas now, it is spoken in order to clear away the bad conceptualization of those in the retinue who say, "A bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata on the level of pure superior intention possesses adherence to form".

Thinking, "Then how is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?", he asked, "Why is that?", connecting to the words "one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body." This is unestablished; the form body is not established as having the nature of possessing limbs, or as having the nature of accumulated subtle atoms, just as it was analyzed previously. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it is taught. The word "therefore" means it exists thus conventionally; because it is not that it does not exist in all aspects like the horn of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of deprecation, how the mind should be thoroughly restrained is taught. By all these points, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should strive in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, extensiveness is also taught. Addressing the excellence of the body of marks, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth; all the explanation here is identical to the previous one.

source: གལ་ཏེ་བཤད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུམ་པོ་དེ་མེད་ན་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་ཚིག་དང་ངག་གི་ངོ་བོ་སྣ་ཚོགས་འདི་ཇི་ལྟར་གྲགས། དེ་ཡོད་ན་ནི་གང་དེས་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་ལ། གང་དེ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་འཆད་པ་པོ་དེ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ན་གསུམ་ཆར་ཡོད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་ལ་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། འདིར་ལན་དུ་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་ཏེ། ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་ན་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའམ། སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཞིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་གྲང་ན། རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་སྔར་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བར་གསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཉིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་མེད་ན་གནས་མེད་པས་ཅི་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྤྱི་དངོས་པོར་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཁོ་ནར་འདུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་གསལ་བས་དེ་ཡང་གསལ་བ་ཉིད་དོ། །གཞན་རྣམ་པར་གཅད་པས་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ནི་སྒྲོ་བརྟགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཞེས་རྟོག་ན་ནི་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་དོན་མེད་པས་གྲུབ་པ་སྒྲུབ་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེ་དོན་དམ་པར་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡོད་དུ་ཆུག་ན་ཡང་དེས་ཆོས་བསྟན་པར་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། སྒྲ་གསལ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བརྟག་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཚིག་ཏུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་ནི་རིམ་དང་རིམ་མ་ཡིན་པས་དོན་བྱེད་པར་འགལ་ཏེ། ནུས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བས་ཤེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ལ་ཡང་སྦྱོར་བ་མེད་དེ། ཅི་ཡང་མི་བྱེད་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་ཚིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་མི་རྟག་པ་ཡང་བརྡར་འདོགས་པའི་ཚེ་ན་མཐོང་བ་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པའི་ཚེ་ན་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་པས་ཚིག་ཏུ་མི་རིགས་སོ་བརྡར་འདོགས་པ་ཡང་གཞན་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་ཡང་གཞན་པར་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
translation: Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

[3-196] translation already produced for this document:
The body of marks will be explained below, in the manner of "cow and ox". From this, the thought of the noble Subhūti is this: "Just as the aggregate of merit is completely non-existent as an aggregate ultimately, likewise the form body is also completely unarisen; therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body ultimately." Conventionally, just like a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion, the form body does indeed exist; therefore, it is indeed suitable to arise from the aggregate of merit. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva, having belief in the form of a Buddha magically emanated by an illusion like that, should dwell in aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish it. Here, it will also not be repetitive; because previously, at the time of aspiration to obtain the form body on the level of action through belief, and at the time of making offerings and serving the Tathāgata, adherence to it in that way is completely abandoned, whereas now, it is spoken in order to clear away the bad conceptualization of those in the retinue who say, "A bodhisattva who has engaged in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata on the level of pure superior intention possesses adherence to form".

འོ་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྟན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཤིང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་ཏེ། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲུབ་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །འདི་ནི་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དེ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་ནམ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་བསགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་མ་གྲུབ་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་སྔར་དཔྱད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །འདིས་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དེས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདི་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡོད་དོ། རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་བཞིན་དུ་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་མེད་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་བཀག་ནས་ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །གནས་འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་འབད་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་པས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མཚན་གྱི་སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། འདིར་བཤད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་སྔ་མ་དང་འདྲའོ། །
[3-197] translation already produced for this document:
Thinking, "Then how is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?", he asked, "Why is that?", connecting to the words "one should not view the Tathāgata by the thorough establishment of a form body." This is unestablished; the form body is not established as having the nature of possessing limbs, or as having the nature of accumulated subtle atoms, just as it was analyzed previously. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it is taught. The word "therefore" means it exists thus conventionally; because it is not that it does not exist in all aspects like the horn of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of deprecation, how the mind should be thoroughly restrained is taught. By all these points, profundity is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should strive in order to accomplish the excellence of the form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, extensiveness is also taught. Addressing the excellence of the body of marks, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth; all the explanation here is identical to the previous one.

heading: གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Therefore, because there is no following along, it is also illogical for a specific characteristic to be expressed. If a general entity is also accepted as that which is to be expressed, because it becomes the nature of that which is to be expressed, because it is the nature of a specific characteristic, it indeed does not go to other objects. It is also illogical for a single thing to pervade many manifestations that are individually distinct regarding object, time, and so forth. Like this: if its entire identity is complete in one manifestation, at that time, through whatever thoroughly conceptualizes its nature in that one alone, there does not exist in it another nature related to other manifestations that would permeate others, because its singleness would be impaired. If it pervades by a part, it would result in the faults of possessing parts and of not being apprehended. Like that, if it is apprehended in accordance with positing that it pervades however many distinct manifestations by a part of it, although it might be suitable to apprehend it because apprehending in one manifestation is apprehending a part, in those individually distinct manifestations of age, object, time, and so forth, because apprehending from one manifestation is apprehending a part, since there is no simultaneous apprehension, it would indeed become devoid of conception. Therefore, that which is to be expressed and the expression are logical only as the nature of an imputed aspect, but ultimately they are not. Because of that very reason, the Bhagavān stated elsewhere: 'By whatever names, whatever phenomena are expressed, they do not exist in that; that is the reality of phenomena.' Because the teaching is also false, whatever taught the existence of the thing to be taught and the teacher from that approach is indeed cleared away because that too comes from that approach, so the Bhagavān did not state separately that both of them do not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it and how the mind should be thoroughly controlled is taught. By all this, the profound is taught.

Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

source: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཐ་དད་པ་བདུན་ཏེ། དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ་དང་། མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་དང་། ཆོས་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ་དང་། གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ་དང་། བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའོ། །
translation: The excellence of mind is seven distinct aspects: the close placement of mindfulness, manifest perfect awakening, designating the Dharma as having great meaning, designating the instruction as having great meaning, thoroughly apprehending the dharmakāya, not abiding in nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, and perfectly pure abiding.

Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

Therefore, because there is no following along, it is also illogical for a specific characteristic to be expressed. If a general entity is also accepted as that which is to be expressed, because it becomes the nature of that which is to be expressed, because it is the nature of a specific characteristic, it indeed does not go to other objects. It is also illogical for a single thing to pervade many manifestations that are individually distinct regarding object, time, and so forth. Like this: if its entire identity is complete in one manifestation, at that time, through whatever thoroughly conceptualizes its nature in that one alone, there does not exist in it another nature related to other manifestations that would permeate others, because its singleness would be impaired. If it pervades by a part, it would result in the faults of possessing parts and of not being apprehended. Like that, if it is apprehended in accordance with positing that it pervades however many distinct manifestations by a part of it, although it might be suitable to apprehend it because apprehending in one manifestation is apprehending a part, in those individually distinct manifestations of age, object, time, and so forth, because apprehending from one manifestation is apprehending a part, since there is no simultaneous apprehension, it would indeed become devoid of conception. Therefore, that which is to be expressed and the expression are logical only as the nature of an imputed aspect, but ultimately they are not. Because of that very reason, the Bhagavān stated elsewhere: 'By whatever names, whatever phenomena are expressed, they do not exist in that; that is the reality of phenomena.' Because the teaching is also false, whatever taught the existence of the thing to be taught and the teacher from that approach is indeed cleared away because that too comes from that approach, so the Bhagavān did not state separately that both of them do not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it and how the mind should be thoroughly controlled is taught. By all this, the profound is taught.

translation: Here, now, thinking, "In the future time, for those enveloped by the net of bad views, will such a profound Dharma be fruitful?", the retinue lacked confidence; in order to clear away the lack of confidence of whoever thinks like that, the noble Subhūti, with regard to the close placement of mindfulness out of the excellence of mind, asked, "Bhagavān," and so forth.

Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

Therefore, because there is no following along, it is also illogical for a specific characteristic to be expressed. If a general entity is also accepted as that which is to be expressed, because it becomes the nature of that which is to be expressed, because it is the nature of a specific characteristic, it indeed does not go to other objects. It is also illogical for a single thing to pervade many manifestations that are individually distinct regarding object, time, and so forth. Like this: if its entire identity is complete in one manifestation, at that time, through whatever thoroughly conceptualizes its nature in that one alone, there does not exist in it another nature related to other manifestations that would permeate others, because its singleness would be impaired. If it pervades by a part, it would result in the faults of possessing parts and of not being apprehended. Like that, if it is apprehended in accordance with positing that it pervades however many distinct manifestations by a part of it, although it might be suitable to apprehend it because apprehending in one manifestation is apprehending a part, in those individually distinct manifestations of age, object, time, and so forth, because apprehending from one manifestation is apprehending a part, since there is no simultaneous apprehension, it would indeed become devoid of conception. Therefore, that which is to be expressed and the expression are logical only as the nature of an imputed aspect, but ultimately they are not. Because of that very reason, the Bhagavān stated elsewhere: 'By whatever names, whatever phenomena are expressed, they do not exist in that; that is the reality of phenomena.' Because the teaching is also false, whatever taught the existence of the thing to be taught and the teacher from that approach is indeed cleared away because that too comes from that approach, so the Bhagavān did not state separately that both of them do not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it and how the mind should be thoroughly controlled is taught. By all this, the profound is taught.

The excellence of mind is seven distinct aspects: the close placement of mindfulness, manifest perfect awakening, designating the Dharma as having great meaning, designating the instruction as having great meaning, thoroughly apprehending the dharmakāya, not abiding in nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, and perfectly pure abiding.

heading: **དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ།**
translation: Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

[3-201] translation already produced for this document:
Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

Therefore, because there is no following along, it is also illogical for a specific characteristic to be expressed. If a general entity is also accepted as that which is to be expressed, because it becomes the nature of that which is to be expressed, because it is the nature of a specific characteristic, it indeed does not go to other objects. It is also illogical for a single thing to pervade many manifestations that are individually distinct regarding object, time, and so forth. Like this: if its entire identity is complete in one manifestation, at that time, through whatever thoroughly conceptualizes its nature in that one alone, there does not exist in it another nature related to other manifestations that would permeate others, because its singleness would be impaired. If it pervades by a part, it would result in the faults of possessing parts and of not being apprehended. Like that, if it is apprehended in accordance with positing that it pervades however many distinct manifestations by a part of it, although it might be suitable to apprehend it because apprehending in one manifestation is apprehending a part, in those individually distinct manifestations of age, object, time, and so forth, because apprehending from one manifestation is apprehending a part, since there is no simultaneous apprehension, it would indeed become devoid of conception. Therefore, that which is to be expressed and the expression are logical only as the nature of an imputed aspect, but ultimately they are not. Because of that very reason, the Bhagavān stated elsewhere: 'By whatever names, whatever phenomena are expressed, they do not exist in that; that is the reality of phenomena.' Because the teaching is also false, whatever taught the existence of the thing to be taught and the teacher from that approach is indeed cleared away because that too comes from that approach, so the Bhagavān did not state separately that both of them do not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it and how the mind should be thoroughly controlled is taught. By all this, the profound is taught.

གལ་ཏེ་བཤད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུམ་པོ་དེ་མེད་ན་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་ཚིག་དང་ངག་གི་ངོ་བོ་སྣ་ཚོགས་འདི་ཇི་ལྟར་གྲགས། དེ་ཡོད་ན་ནི་གང་དེས་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་ལ། གང་དེ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་འཆད་པ་པོ་དེ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ན་གསུམ་ཆར་ཡོད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་ལ་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། འདིར་ལན་དུ་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་ཏེ། ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་ན་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའམ། སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཞིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་གྲང་ན། རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་སྔར་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བར་གསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཉིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་མེད་ན་གནས་མེད་པས་ཅི་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྤྱི་དངོས་པོར་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཁོ་ནར་འདུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་གསལ་བས་དེ་ཡང་གསལ་བ་ཉིད་དོ། །གཞན་རྣམ་པར་གཅད་པས་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ནི་སྒྲོ་བརྟགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཞེས་རྟོག་ན་ནི་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་དོན་མེད་པས་གྲུབ་པ་སྒྲུབ་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེ་དོན་དམ་པར་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡོད་དུ་ཆུག་ན་ཡང་དེས་ཆོས་བསྟན་པར་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། སྒྲ་གསལ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བརྟག་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཚིག་ཏུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་ནི་རིམ་དང་རིམ་མ་ཡིན་པས་དོན་བྱེད་པར་འགལ་ཏེ། ནུས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བས་ཤེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ལ་ཡང་སྦྱོར་བ་མེད་དེ། ཅི་ཡང་མི་བྱེད་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་ཚིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་མི་རྟག་པ་ཡང་བརྡར་འདོགས་པའི་ཚེ་ན་མཐོང་བ་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པའི་ཚེ་ན་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་པས་ཚིག་ཏུ་མི་རིགས་སོ་བརྡར་འདོགས་པ་ཡང་གཞན་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་ཡང་གཞན་པར་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

དེ་བས་ན་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་པས་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱང་བརྗོད་པར་མི་རིགས་སོ། །སྤྱིའི་དངོས་པོ་ཡང་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བར་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་དེ་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་པས་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡུལ་གཞན་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །གཅིག་པུ་ནི་ཡུལ་དང་དུས་ལ་སོགས་པ་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་གསལ་བ་དུ་མ་ལ་ཁྱབ་པར་ཡང་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་བདག་ཉིད་ཐམས་ཅད་གསལ་བ་གཅིག་ལ་རྫོགས་ན་ནི་དེའི་ཚེ་གཅིག་ཁོ་ན་ལ་དེའི་རང་བཞིན་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་གང་གིས་ནི་གཞན་ལ་ཡང་ཆུབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གསལ་བ་གཞན་དང་འབྲེལ་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གཞན་ནི་དེ་ལ་མེད་དེ། གཅིག་པུ་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་གིས་ཁྱབ་ན་ནི་ཡན་ལག་དང་བཅས་པ་དང་མ་ཟིན་པའི་སྐྱོན་དུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་གསལ་བ་ཐ་དད་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་ལ་དེའི་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་གིས་ཁྱབ་པར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པར་དེ་སྙེད་འཛིན་ན་ནི་གསལ་བ་གཅིག་ལ་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་འཛིན་པས་དེ་ལ་འཛིན་པར་རུང་གྲང་ན། གསལ་བ་ཐ་དད་པ་ན་ཚོད་དང་ཡུལ་དང་། དུས་ལ་སོགས་པ་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་དེ་དག་ལ་གསལ་བ་གཅིག་ལས་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་འཛིན་པས་ཅིག་ཅར་འཛིན་པ་མེད་པས་རྟོག་པ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། རྗོད་པ་ནི་སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པའི་རྣམ་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཁོ་ནར་རིགས་ཀྱི་ཡང་དག་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གཞན་དག་ཏུ། མིང་ནི་གང་དང་གང་དག་གིས། །ཆོས་རྣམས་གང་དང་གང་བརྗོད་པ། །དེ་ལ་དེ་ནི་མེད་པ་སྟེ། །དེ་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བཤད་པ་ཡང་བརྫུན་པས་སྒོ་དེ་ནས་བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། འཆད་པ་པོ་ཡོད་པར་བསྟན་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡང་སྒོ་དེ་ནས་འོངས་པས་གསལ་བ་ཉིད་དེ། དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་མེད་པར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ལོགས་ཤིག་ཏུ་མ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིས་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Therefore, because there is no following along, it is also illogical for a specific characteristic to be expressed. If a general entity is also accepted as that which is to be expressed, because it becomes the nature of that which is to be expressed, because it is the nature of a specific characteristic, it indeed does not go to other objects. It is also illogical for a single thing to pervade many manifestations that are individually distinct regarding object, time, and so forth. Like this: if its entire identity is complete in one manifestation, at that time, through whatever thoroughly conceptualizes its nature in that one alone, there does not exist in it another nature related to other manifestations that would permeate others, because its singleness would be impaired. If it pervades by a part, it would result in the faults of possessing parts and of not being apprehended. Like that, if it is apprehended in accordance with positing that it pervades however many distinct manifestations by a part of it, although it might be suitable to apprehend it because apprehending in one manifestation is apprehending a part, in those individually distinct manifestations of age, object, time, and so forth, because apprehending from one manifestation is apprehending a part, since there is no simultaneous apprehension, it would indeed become devoid of conception. Therefore, that which is to be expressed and the expression are logical only as the nature of an imputed aspect, but ultimately they are not. Because of that very reason, the Bhagavān stated elsewhere: 'By whatever names, whatever phenomena are expressed, they do not exist in that; that is the reality of phenomena.' Because the teaching is also false, whatever taught the existence of the thing to be taught and the teacher from that approach is indeed cleared away because that too comes from that approach, so the Bhagavān did not state separately that both of them do not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it and how the mind should be thoroughly controlled is taught. By all this, the profound is taught.

The excellence of mind is seven distinct aspects: the close placement of mindfulness, manifest perfect awakening, designating the Dharma as having great meaning, designating the instruction as having great meaning, thoroughly apprehending the dharmakāya, not abiding in nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, and perfectly pure abiding.

heading: **དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ།**
translation: In reliance upon the existence of the nature of the aggregates abiding conventionally, they are stated; therefore, because they conventionally exist, they are called "sentient beings". If that were not so, if they did not exist even conventionally, they would not be spoken of. By this, thoroughly controlling the mind is taught. By all this, the profound is expressed. Because the Bhagavān taught the close placement of mindfulness as unobstructed towards all sentient beings, the extensive is taught.

Thinking, "If those three, the teaching and so forth, do not exist, how are these various natures of words and speech, the teaching of the Dharma by the Bhagavān, which teach the selflessness of persons and phenomena and so forth, known? If that exists, then what is taught by it, the thing to be taught, also indeed exists; and what teaches it, the teacher, also indeed exists, so by implication, all three exist," he asked, "Why is that?", and here in reply, he spoke the words "the teaching of Dharma". Having intended this thought: "If the teaching of Dharma ultimately exists, it would presumably be either the nature of a specific characteristic or the nature of a general characteristic. Firstly, it is not the first alternative, because all ultimate specific characteristics were previously extensively cleared away. It is not the second either, because if specific characteristics do not exist, since there is no basis, there is nothing at all. If a general characteristic is accepted as an entity, because it would be subsumed merely as a specific characteristic, by that being cleared away, that too is indeed cleared away. If one conceptualizes that a general characteristic is an imputed nature through the exclusion of the other, because the teaching of Dharma would lack reality, it would be establishing what is already established. Even if one were to allow that its specific characteristic ultimately exists, it is illogical for that to be the teaching of Dharma, because what is thoroughly imputed as words by others upon the conceptualized nature of manifested sounds and so forth contradicts performing a function sequentially or non-sequentially; because it is devoid of all potency, it has no connection to anything at all, such as consciousness and so forth. Without doing anything, how could it become words? And if a specific characteristic is impermanent, because what is seen at the time of imputing the designation does not follow along at the time of imputing the convention, it is illogical to be words. It is illogical for what is imputed with the designation to be other and what is imputed with the convention to be other, because it would result in absurd consequences."

Therefore, because there is no following along, it is also illogical for a specific characteristic to be expressed. If a general entity is also accepted as that which is to be expressed, because it becomes the nature of that which is to be expressed, because it is the nature of a specific characteristic, it indeed does not go to other objects. It is also illogical for a single thing to pervade many manifestations that are individually distinct regarding object, time, and so forth. Like this: if its entire identity is complete in one manifestation, at that time, through whatever thoroughly conceptualizes its nature in that one alone, there does not exist in it another nature related to other manifestations that would permeate others, because its singleness would be impaired. If it pervades by a part, it would result in the faults of possessing parts and of not being apprehended. Like that, if it is apprehended in accordance with positing that it pervades however many distinct manifestations by a part of it, although it might be suitable to apprehend it because apprehending in one manifestation is apprehending a part, in those individually distinct manifestations of age, object, time, and so forth, because apprehending from one manifestation is apprehending a part, since there is no simultaneous apprehension, it would indeed become devoid of conception. Therefore, that which is to be expressed and the expression are logical only as the nature of an imputed aspect, but ultimately they are not. Because of that very reason, the Bhagavān stated elsewhere: 'By whatever names, whatever phenomena are expressed, they do not exist in that; that is the reality of phenomena.' Because the teaching is also false, whatever taught the existence of the thing to be taught and the teacher from that approach is indeed cleared away because that too comes from that approach, so the Bhagavān did not state separately that both of them do not exist. By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish it and how the mind should be thoroughly controlled is taught. By all this, the profound is taught.

Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

If that were not so, if they did not exist even conventionally, they would not be spoken of. By this, thoroughly controlling the mind is taught. By all this, the profound is expressed. Because the Bhagavān taught the close placement of mindfulness as unobstructed towards all sentient beings, the extensive is taught.

heading: **མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ།**
translation: For the sake of those who think, "If one wishes to manifestly perfectly awaken to however many dharmas there are, then at that time there is also a teaching," with regard to manifest perfect awakening, he stated, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti, grasping the previous intention, replied, "There is not." He thinks like this: "Intending the ultimate, the Bhagavān refuted the teaching." Just as there is no Dharma taught whatsoever ultimately, there is also no manifest perfect awakening; that was taught previously. Conventionally, there is indeed the Dharma taught by the Bhagavān, perfect awakening, and the path which is its cause. Therefore, a bodhisattva should make effort in order to accomplish the correct conventional nature of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening; by this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught. Previously, at the time of thoroughly seeking instruction, the false imagination of a bodhisattva who thinks "manifest perfect awakening is ultimate" was removed, whereas now, at the time of thoroughly seeking the level of a Buddha, such false imaginations of others are removed, so it does not incur the fault of repetition. For one who thinks, "What is the unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening posited as the correct conventional like?", he stated, "Even the slightest..." and so forth.

Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

heading: **མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ།**
translation: The nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas without remainder, while the Bhagavān, when abiding in whichever exalted wisdom, does not observe even the subtle nature of dharmas whose characteristic is retaining their own characteristics, is unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening. Because it is supreme over whatever knowledges of outsiders, learners, and non-learners, it is "unexcelled". Because it is the nature of comprehending the suchness of all entities just as they are, it is called "perfectly complete awakening"; such is the meaning. Here, as the reason for not observing dharmas, "do not exist" was stated. Because they do not exist, therefore they are not observed; it is not that they are not observed despite existing, because if all dharmas existed, they would become the very things that make known the observation of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom. By this, the nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Now, in order to teach the nature of realizing the selflessness of persons, he stated, "Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.
