Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

heading: **མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ།**
translation: As for "there is no inequality whatsoever", it is because it is unmistaken in all respects, because manifest attachment to the entities of the continuum of apprehending a self is abandoned. The Bhagavān has abandoned apprehending a self along with its latencies; therefore, the perfect awakening that is the nature of his very realization of the selflessness of persons is called "unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening", and it does not belong to others. Regarding the thought, "In what way is that Dharma equal?", he stated, "without a sentient being" and so forth. By all this, what is to be accomplished by meditative absorption in yoga is taught.

Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

Did not the Bhagavān too previously state, "in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise," and so forth? Now, in order to teach not to be manifestly attached to them as exclusively existent and non-existent, he did not state that they exist, but in order to refute the two extremes, he stated "Subhūti, they are..." and so forth. Ultimately, because the existence of the nature of aggregates, persons, and so forth is not observed, "they are not sentient beings either"; by this, the extreme of imputation is refuted. Because they thoroughly abide as pleasant when unexamined, "nor are they non-sentient beings"; by this, the extreme of deprecation is refuted. By this, by teaching "they will arise", what the Bhagavān's unmistaken close placement of mindfulness towards sentient beings is like is taught, and it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer in that excellent close placement of mindfulness of the Bhagavān. By this "they are not sentient beings either", meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Having considered one who thinks, "If they are not sentient beings, then how did the Bhagavān state 'in the future time, those possessing moral discipline and possessing good qualities will arise' and so forth?", he asked, "Why is that?"

For the sake of those who think, "If one wishes to manifestly perfectly awaken to however many dharmas there are, then at that time there is also a teaching," with regard to manifest perfect awakening, he stated, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti, grasping the previous intention, replied, "There is not." He thinks like this: "Intending the ultimate, the Bhagavān refuted the teaching." Just as there is no Dharma taught whatsoever ultimately, there is also no manifest perfect awakening; that was taught previously. Conventionally, there is indeed the Dharma taught by the Bhagavān, perfect awakening, and the path which is its cause. Therefore, a bodhisattva should make effort in order to accomplish the correct conventional nature of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening; by this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught. Previously, at the time of thoroughly seeking instruction, the false imagination of a bodhisattva who thinks "manifest perfect awakening is ultimate" was removed, whereas now, at the time of thoroughly seeking the level of a Buddha, such false imaginations of others are removed, so it does not incur the fault of repetition. For one who thinks, "What is the unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening posited as the correct conventional like?", he stated, "Even the slightest..." and so forth.

Because it is the nature of comprehending the suchness of all entities just as they are, it is called "perfectly complete awakening"; such is the meaning. heading: **མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ།**
translation: Because they exist conventionally, he stated 'wholesome dharmas'; therefore, there is no fault in saying that one manifestly perfectly awakens by wholesome dharmas. By this, thoroughly holding the mind is taught, because it removes the distraction of apprehending the extremes of superimposition and deprecation. By all these points, the profound is taught. By thoroughly expressing the own nature of perfectly complete awakening, which is the nature of realizing the selflessness of persons and dharmas without remainder, the extensive is also taught.

For the sake of those who think, "If one wishes to manifestly perfectly awaken to however many dharmas there are, then at that time there is also a teaching," with regard to manifest perfect awakening, he stated, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti, grasping the previous intention, replied, "There is not." He thinks like this: "Intending the ultimate, the Bhagavān refuted the teaching." Just as there is no Dharma taught whatsoever ultimately, there is also no manifest perfect awakening; that was taught previously. Conventionally, there is indeed the Dharma taught by the Bhagavān, perfect awakening, and the path which is its cause. Therefore, a bodhisattva should make effort in order to accomplish the correct conventional nature of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening; by this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught. Previously, at the time of thoroughly seeking instruction, the false imagination of a bodhisattva who thinks "manifest perfect awakening is ultimate" was removed, whereas now, at the time of thoroughly seeking the level of a Buddha, such false imaginations of others are removed, so it does not incur the fault of repetition. For one who thinks, "What is the unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening posited as the correct conventional like?", he stated, "Even the slightest..." and so forth.

[3-210] translation already produced for this document:
The nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas without remainder, while the Bhagavān, when abiding in whichever exalted wisdom, does not observe even the subtle nature of dharmas whose characteristic is retaining their own characteristics, is unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening. Because it is supreme over whatever knowledges of outsiders, learners, and non-learners, it is "unexcelled". Because it is the nature of comprehending the suchness of all entities just as they are, it is called "perfectly complete awakening"; such is the meaning. Here, as the reason for not observing dharmas, "do not exist" was stated. Because they do not exist, therefore they are not observed; it is not that they are not observed despite existing, because if all dharmas existed, they would become the very things that make known the observation of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom. By this, the nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Now, in order to teach the nature of realizing the selflessness of persons, he stated, "Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.

[3-212] translation already produced for this document:
As for "there is no inequality whatsoever", it is because it is unmistaken in all respects, because manifest attachment to the entities of the continuum of apprehending a self is abandoned. The Bhagavān has abandoned apprehending a self along with its latencies; therefore, the perfect awakening that is the nature of his very realization of the selflessness of persons is called "unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening", and it does not belong to others. Regarding the thought, "In what way is that Dharma equal?", he stated, "without a sentient being" and so forth. By all this, what is to be accomplished by meditative absorption in yoga is taught.

[3-210] translation already produced for this document:
The nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas without remainder, while the Bhagavān, when abiding in whichever exalted wisdom, does not observe even the subtle nature of dharmas whose characteristic is retaining their own characteristics, is unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening. Because it is supreme over whatever knowledges of outsiders, learners, and non-learners, it is "unexcelled". Because it is the nature of comprehending the suchness of all entities just as they are, it is called "perfectly complete awakening"; such is the meaning. Here, as the reason for not observing dharmas, "do not exist" was stated. Because they do not exist, therefore they are not observed; it is not that they are not observed despite existing, because if all dharmas existed, they would become the very things that make known the observation of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom. By this, the nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Now, in order to teach the nature of realizing the selflessness of persons, he stated, "Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.

[3-212] translation already produced for this document:
As for "there is no inequality whatsoever", it is because it is unmistaken in all respects, because manifest attachment to the entities of the continuum of apprehending a self is abandoned. The Bhagavān has abandoned apprehending a self along with its latencies; therefore, the perfect awakening that is the nature of his very realization of the selflessness of persons is called "unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening", and it does not belong to others. Regarding the thought, "In what way is that Dharma equal?", he stated, "without a sentient being" and so forth. By all this, what is to be accomplished by meditative absorption in yoga is taught.

Because they exist conventionally, he stated 'wholesome dharmas'; therefore, there is no fault in saying that one manifestly perfectly awakens by wholesome dharmas. By this, thoroughly holding the mind is taught, because it removes the distraction of apprehending the extremes of superimposition and deprecation. By all these points, the profound is taught. By thoroughly expressing the own nature of perfectly complete awakening, which is the nature of realizing the selflessness of persons and dharmas without remainder, the extensive is also taught.

heading: **ཆོས་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: As for "Sumeru, king of mountains," it is an illustration; whatever merit there is from giving having completely filled infinite world systems with precious things, that too simply does not bear comparison. As for "from this prajñāpāramitā," because it does not thoroughly express merely a mark, it illustrates all dharmas of the Great Vehicle. The word "up to" includes "a thousandth part," "a hundred thousandth part," and "even as an example and cause." Thus, by the reason of designating the Dharma as having great meaning, the Bhagavān's consummate mind is known as the unexcelled nature of perfectly complete awakening, because without such a perfectly complete awakening, such a Dharma could not be explained. Therefore, in order to accomplish such a consummate mind through aspiration and prayer, one should abide; by all this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught, and by this very thing the extensive is also expressed. That perfect awakening is also to be viewed as the nature of the authentic conventional, but not ultimately, because it was explained previously. Although not stated directly, by implication, meditative absorption in yoga, thoroughly holding the mind, and the profound are also taught.

[3-210] translation already produced for this document:
The nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas without remainder, while the Bhagavān, when abiding in whichever exalted wisdom, does not observe even the subtle nature of dharmas whose characteristic is retaining their own characteristics, is unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening. Because it is supreme over whatever knowledges of outsiders, learners, and non-learners, it is "unexcelled". Because it is the nature of comprehending the suchness of all entities just as they are, it is called "perfectly complete awakening"; such is the meaning. Here, as the reason for not observing dharmas, "do not exist" was stated. Because they do not exist, therefore they are not observed; it is not that they are not observed despite existing, because if all dharmas existed, they would become the very things that make known the observation of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom. By this, the nature of realizing the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Now, in order to teach the nature of realizing the selflessness of persons, he stated, "Furthermore, Subhūti," and so forth.

Because they exist conventionally, he stated 'wholesome dharmas'; therefore, there is no fault in saying that one manifestly perfectly awakens by wholesome dharmas. By this, thoroughly holding the mind is taught, because it removes the distraction of apprehending the extremes of superimposition and deprecation. By all these points, the profound is taught. heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: When the Bhagavān abides in supramundane exalted wisdom, because he is extremely in meditative equipoise, the notion of sentient beings and so forth does not arise at all; that is not a great marvel. When bestowing the transmission of excellent liberation to sentient beings, during the time of not being in meditative equipoise, even when abiding in pure mundane exalted wisdom, the notion of sentient beings and so forth does not arise at all. Teaching that, by the reason of designating the instruction as having great meaning, in order to teach that the unexcelled consummate mind of the Bhagavān is known, having acted in the context of instructing the instruction having great meaning, he stated, "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" and so forth.

རིའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རི་རབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་དག་རིན་པོ་ཆེས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཀང་སྟེ་བྱིན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡང་དཔེར་མི་བཟོད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ལས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་བརྗོད་པས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་མཐའ་དག་མཚོན་ཏོ། །བར་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྒྲས་ནི་སྟོང་གི་ཆ་དང་། འབུམ་གྱི་ཆ་དང་། དཔེ་དང་རྒྱུར་ཡང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་དག་སྡུད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པའི་རྒྱུས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཤེས་ཏེ། ཡང་དག་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་བཤད་པར་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གནས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་ཏེ། འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཡང་བརྗོད་དོ། །རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ་ཡང་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའི་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ།སྔར་བཤད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དངོས་སུ་མ་གསུངས་ཀྱང་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་ན་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་དང་། ཟག་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-217] translation already produced for this document:
As for "Sumeru, king of mountains," it is an illustration; whatever merit there is from giving having completely filled infinite world systems with precious things, that too simply does not bear comparison. As for "from this prajñāpāramitā," because it does not thoroughly express merely a mark, it illustrates all dharmas of the Great Vehicle. The word "up to" includes "a thousandth part," "a hundred thousandth part," and "even as an example and cause." Thus, by the reason of designating the Dharma as having great meaning, the Bhagavān's consummate mind is known as the unexcelled nature of perfectly complete awakening, because without such a perfectly complete awakening, such a Dharma could not be explained. Therefore, in order to accomplish such a consummate mind through aspiration and prayer, one should abide; by all this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught, and by this very thing the extensive is also expressed. That perfect awakening is also to be viewed as the nature of the authentic conventional, but not ultimately, because it was explained previously. Although not stated directly, by implication, meditative absorption in yoga, thoroughly holding the mind, and the profound are also taught.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: Having asked, without waiting for an answer, as if having urgency, he himself stated, "Subhūti, do not view it like that," and so forth. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer regarding such a cause of the instruction having great meaning, the consummate mind of the Bhagavān.

[3-212] translation already produced for this document:
As for "there is no inequality whatsoever", it is because it is unmistaken in all respects, because manifest attachment to the entities of the continuum of apprehending a self is abandoned. The Bhagavān has abandoned apprehending a self along with its latencies; therefore, the perfect awakening that is the nature of his very realization of the selflessness of persons is called "unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening", and it does not belong to others. Regarding the thought, "In what way is that Dharma equal?", he stated, "without a sentient being" and so forth. By all this, what is to be accomplished by meditative absorption in yoga is taught.

[3-213] source:
དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་འཚང་རྒྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ། དགེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་བདག་ཉིད་དགེ་བའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་འཚང་རྒྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །

As for "Sumeru, king of mountains," it is an illustration; whatever merit there is from giving having completely filled infinite world systems with precious things, that too simply does not bear comparison. As for "from this prajñāpāramitā," because it does not thoroughly express merely a mark, it illustrates all dharmas of the Great Vehicle. The word "up to" includes "a thousandth part," "a hundred thousandth part," and "even as an example and cause." Thus, by the reason of designating the Dharma as having great meaning, the Bhagavān's consummate mind is known as the unexcelled nature of perfectly complete awakening, because without such a perfectly complete awakening, such a Dharma could not be explained. Therefore, in order to accomplish such a consummate mind through aspiration and prayer, one should abide; by all this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught, and by this very thing the extensive is also expressed. That perfect awakening is also to be viewed as the nature of the authentic conventional, but not ultimately, because it was explained previously. Although not stated directly, by implication, meditative absorption in yoga, thoroughly holding the mind, and the profound are also taught.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: Regarding the thought, "If sentient beings indeed exist, because they would become the cause of thorough affliction, does the Tathāgata not think that? Or is it because sentient beings are non-existent?" Having analyzed the thought of thinking this, it was asked, "Why is that?", and in order to teach that because any sentient being of the nature of the aggregates and a person is ultimately non-existent, it is not observed like that, he stated, "Because any sentient being released by the Tathāgata does not exist at all." By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Regarding the thought, "How does one know they are non-existent?", he stated, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom engages just as the object of knowledge is. If it were not so, because obscurations were not abandoned, how would one become a Tathāgata? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, at that time they would be completely seen by the Tathāgata, because he observes the self directly and therefore has no doubt. That itself would become a tight apprehension of a self for him. Therefore, the binding of the entire net of afflictions arisen from the cause of apprehending a self for him would become slight or extreme; because the obscurations of the extremely tight bindings of attachment and so forth were not abandoned at that time, the Bhagavān would not have attained the state of a Tathāgata. Since the Bhagavān has attained that state, therefore, he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning obscurations, all the mountains of apprehending a self are destroyed. Therefore, he does not know sentient beings to be non-existent.

As for "Sumeru, king of mountains," it is an illustration; whatever merit there is from giving having completely filled infinite world systems with precious things, that too simply does not bear comparison. As for "from this prajñāpāramitā," because it does not thoroughly express merely a mark, it illustrates all dharmas of the Great Vehicle. The word "up to" includes "a thousandth part," "a hundred thousandth part," and "even as an example and cause." Thus, by the reason of designating the Dharma as having great meaning, the Bhagavān's consummate mind is known as the unexcelled nature of perfectly complete awakening, because without such a perfectly complete awakening, such a Dharma could not be explained. Therefore, in order to accomplish such a consummate mind through aspiration and prayer, one should abide; by all this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught, and by this very thing the extensive is also expressed. That perfect awakening is also to be viewed as the nature of the authentic conventional, but not ultimately, because it was explained previously. Although not stated directly, by implication, meditative absorption in yoga, thoroughly holding the mind, and the profound are also taught.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: Regarding the thought, "Even though it is selfless, is there not the apprehension of a self, that is, the characteristic of the view of a self? How does the Bhagavān not perceive a self and so forth?", he stated, "Subhūti, as for what is called the apprehension of a self..." and so forth. If he were to apprehend any entity of a self and so forth, at that time the Bhagavān, who has abandoned obscurations, would have the apprehension of a self arise in him, but because there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended as a self, the Tathāgata stated it to be exactly non-apprehension. Regarding the thought, "Then what is it that is called the apprehension of a self?", he stated, "That too..." and so forth. They are "childish" because they do not have hearing and so forth, and do not clearly know what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. They are "ordinary beings" because, being without realization, they have become distinct from the noble ones. In order to exclude those ordinary beings who, having listened to authentic treatises and abiding in proper mental engagement, when resolving upon the selflessness of dharmas do not apprehend a self by adhering to it as true, he said "childish". If he had said only "childish", even such ordinary beings who are skilled in the aggregates and so forth are of a childish nature because the path of the noble ones has not arisen in them, so it is in order to teach a distinction of the childish. Even though that apprehension of a self is mistaken, because they are childish, it appears to them like an apprehension of a self; therefore, by the power of their intention, he teaches it as "the apprehension of a self."

[3-220] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If sentient beings indeed exist, because they would become the cause of thorough affliction, does the Tathāgata not think that? Or is it because sentient beings are non-existent?" Having analyzed the thought of thinking this, it was asked, "Why is that?", and in order to teach that because any sentient being of the nature of the aggregates and a person is ultimately non-existent, it is not observed like that, he stated, "Because any sentient being released by the Tathāgata does not exist at all." By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Regarding the thought, "How does one know they are non-existent?", he stated, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom engages just as the object of knowledge is. If it were not so, because obscurations were not abandoned, how would one become a Tathāgata? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, at that time they would be completely seen by the Tathāgata, because he observes the self directly and therefore has no doubt. That itself would become a tight apprehension of a self for him. Therefore, the binding of the entire net of afflictions arisen from the cause of apprehending a self for him would become slight or extreme; because the obscurations of the extremely tight bindings of attachment and so forth were not abandoned at that time, the Bhagavān would not have attained the state of a Tathāgata. Since the Bhagavān has attained that state, therefore, he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning obscurations, all the mountains of apprehending a self are destroyed. Therefore, he does not know sentient beings to be non-existent.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: It does not become true merely by that, but it would absurdly follow: why would one not apprehend a self and so forth as true even through the application of words like "selflessness"? Regarding the thought, "If there is no self, who is called 'ordinary beings'?", he stated, "Childish ordinary beings," and so forth. Ultimately, beings are completely non-existent; because it was stated relying on the conventional, there is no fault. By all this, because the extremes of exaggeration and deprecation are eliminated, thoroughly holding the mind is taught. By all this, the profound itself is expressed directly; teaching [this] as the cause of designating the instruction as having great meaning with respect to the entire realm of sentient beings also teaches the extensive consummate mind.

As for "Sumeru, king of mountains," it is an illustration; whatever merit there is from giving having completely filled infinite world systems with precious things, that too simply does not bear comparison. As for "from this prajñāpāramitā," because it does not thoroughly express merely a mark, it illustrates all dharmas of the Great Vehicle. The word "up to" includes "a thousandth part," "a hundred thousandth part," and "even as an example and cause." Thus, by the reason of designating the Dharma as having great meaning, the Bhagavān's consummate mind is known as the unexcelled nature of perfectly complete awakening, because without such a perfectly complete awakening, such a Dharma could not be explained. Therefore, in order to accomplish such a consummate mind through aspiration and prayer, one should abide; by all this, how a bodhisattva should abide is taught, and by this very thing the extensive is also expressed. That perfect awakening is also to be viewed as the nature of the authentic conventional, but not ultimately, because it was explained previously. Although not stated directly, by implication, meditative absorption in yoga, thoroughly holding the mind, and the profound are also taught.

[3-220] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought, "If sentient beings indeed exist, because they would become the cause of thorough affliction, does the Tathāgata not think that? Or is it because sentient beings are non-existent?" Having analyzed the thought of thinking this, it was asked, "Why is that?", and in order to teach that because any sentient being of the nature of the aggregates and a person is ultimately non-existent, it is not observed like that, he stated, "Because any sentient being released by the Tathāgata does not exist at all." By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Regarding the thought, "How does one know they are non-existent?", he stated, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom engages just as the object of knowledge is. If it were not so, because obscurations were not abandoned, how would one become a Tathāgata? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, at that time they would be completely seen by the Tathāgata, because he observes the self directly and therefore has no doubt. That itself would become a tight apprehension of a self for him. Therefore, the binding of the entire net of afflictions arisen from the cause of apprehending a self for him would become slight or extreme; because the obscurations of the extremely tight bindings of attachment and so forth were not abandoned at that time, the Bhagavān would not have attained the state of a Tathāgata. Since the Bhagavān has attained that state, therefore, he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning obscurations, all the mountains of apprehending a self are destroyed. Therefore, he does not know sentient beings to be non-existent.

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
translation: If childish ordinary beings do not exist, how could there be Tathāgatas, who have become consummate bodies adorned with marks and excellent signs? Regarding the thought, 'Having generated the mind of awakening arisen from the root of compassion, ordinary beings themselves apply themselves to the perfections and become consummate Tathāgata bodies adorned with marks and so forth, but if they do not exist, because there is no root, how could they become such consummate Tathāgata bodies?' — for the sake of those seated in the retinue who had accumulated no small realization but who, by adhering to form and so forth as entities, were thinking in this way, he stated, 'Subhūti, what do you think of this?' and so forth, doing so in terms of thoroughly grasping the dharmakāya. Earlier, a presentation as the dharmakāya was not made; because this was stated in order to present the dharmakāya, it does not become the fault of repetition. Knowing that if investigated ultimately, the consummate marks are unjustified as the nature of having parts or being an accumulation of subtle particles, grasping the very same earlier intention, the noble Subhūti requested, 'That is not so.' The Bhagavān stated another justification for this very point, 'Subhūti, if...' and so forth.

The intention here is this: the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom engages just as the object of knowledge is. If it were not so, because obscurations were not abandoned, how would one become a Tathāgata? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, at that time they would be completely seen by the Tathāgata, because he observes the self directly and therefore has no doubt. That itself would become a tight apprehension of a self for him. Therefore, the binding of the entire net of afflictions arisen from the cause of apprehending a self for him would become slight or extreme; because the obscurations of the extremely tight bindings of attachment and so forth were not abandoned at that time, the Bhagavān would not have attained the state of a Tathāgata. Since the Bhagavān has attained that state, therefore, he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning obscurations, all the mountains of apprehending a self are destroyed. Therefore, he does not know sentient beings to be non-existent.

Regarding the thought, "Even though it is selfless, is there not the apprehension of a self, that is, the characteristic of the view of a self? How does the Bhagavān not perceive a self and so forth?", he stated, "Subhūti, as for what is called the apprehension of a self..." and so forth. If he were to apprehend any entity of a self and so forth, at that time the Bhagavān, who has abandoned obscurations, would have the apprehension of a self arise in him, but because there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended as a self, the Tathāgata stated it to be exactly non-apprehension. Regarding the thought, "Then what is it that is called the apprehension of a self?", he stated, "That too..." and so forth. They are "childish" because they do not have hearing and so forth, and do not clearly know what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. They are "ordinary beings" because, being without realization, they have become distinct from the noble ones. In order to exclude those ordinary beings who, having listened to authentic treatises and abiding in proper mental engagement, when resolving upon the selflessness of dharmas do not apprehend a self by adhering to it as true, he said "childish". If he had said only "childish", even such ordinary beings who are skilled in the aggregates and so forth are of a childish nature because the path of the noble ones has not arisen in them, so it is in order to teach a distinction of the childish. Even though that apprehension of a self is mistaken, because they are childish, it appears to them like an apprehension of a self; therefore, by the power of their intention, he teaches it as "the apprehension of a self."

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
translation: If the Tathāgata were differentiated merely by consummate marks, since the reason for expression is the same, at that time why would a wheel-turning king not also become a Tathāgata? If one says, 'But due to abiding in their places, being clear, and being complete, the consummate marks of the Bhagavān are particular, whereas those of a wheel-turning king are not, so therefore he is not called a Tathāgata,' that is also incorrect: even the particulars of abiding in their places and so forth have no difference whatsoever in being of the nature of insentient matter. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were differentiated by dharmas such as marks of the nature of insentient matter, at that time a wheel-turning king would also become a Tathāgata, but that is not so. Therefore, the intention is that the Tathāgata is differentiated merely by having realized the nature of all entities just as they are. By this, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer regarding such an aspect of the body which has the exalted wisdom of the Tathāgata as its cause. Now, in order to teach that ultimately one should not adhere even to that exalted wisdom of the Tathāgata, he presents the dharmakāya, and teaches how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga through two verses.

Regarding the thought, "If sentient beings indeed exist, because they would become the cause of thorough affliction, does the Tathāgata not think that? Or is it because sentient beings are non-existent?" Having analyzed the thought of thinking this, it was asked, "Why is that?", and in order to teach that because any sentient being of the nature of the aggregates and a person is ultimately non-existent, it is not observed like that, he stated, "Because any sentient being released by the Tathāgata does not exist at all." By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Regarding the thought, "How does one know they are non-existent?", he stated, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom engages just as the object of knowledge is. If it were not so, because obscurations were not abandoned, how would one become a Tathāgata? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, at that time they would be completely seen by the Tathāgata, because he observes the self directly and therefore has no doubt. That itself would become a tight apprehension of a self for him. Therefore, the binding of the entire net of afflictions arisen from the cause of apprehending a self for him would become slight or extreme; because the obscurations of the extremely tight bindings of attachment and so forth were not abandoned at that time, the Bhagavān would not have attained the state of a Tathāgata. Since the Bhagavān has attained that state, therefore, he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning obscurations, all the mountains of apprehending a self are destroyed. Therefore, he does not know sentient beings to be non-existent.

Regarding the thought, "Even though it is selfless, is there not the apprehension of a self, that is, the characteristic of the view of a self? How does the Bhagavān not perceive a self and so forth?", he stated, "Subhūti, as for what is called the apprehension of a self..." and so forth. If he were to apprehend any entity of a self and so forth, at that time the Bhagavān, who has abandoned obscurations, would have the apprehension of a self arise in him, but because there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended as a self, the Tathāgata stated it to be exactly non-apprehension. Regarding the thought, "Then what is it that is called the apprehension of a self?", he stated, "That too..." and so forth. They are "childish" because they do not have hearing and so forth, and do not clearly know what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. They are "ordinary beings" because, being without realization, they have become distinct from the noble ones. In order to exclude those ordinary beings who, having listened to authentic treatises and abiding in proper mental engagement, when resolving upon the selflessness of dharmas do not apprehend a self by adhering to it as true, he said "childish". If he had said only "childish", even such ordinary beings who are skilled in the aggregates and so forth are of a childish nature because the path of the noble ones has not arisen in them, so it is in order to teach a distinction of the childish. Even though that apprehension of a self is mistaken, because they are childish, it appears to them like an apprehension of a self; therefore, by the power of their intention, he teaches it as "the apprehension of a self."

Regarding the thought, "If sentient beings indeed exist, because they would become the cause of thorough affliction, does the Tathāgata not think that? Or is it because sentient beings are non-existent?" Having analyzed the thought of thinking this, it was asked, "Why is that?", and in order to teach that because any sentient being of the nature of the aggregates and a person is ultimately non-existent, it is not observed like that, he stated, "Because any sentient being released by the Tathāgata does not exist at all." By this, how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga is taught. Regarding the thought, "How does one know they are non-existent?", he stated, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom engages just as the object of knowledge is. If it were not so, because obscurations were not abandoned, how would one become a Tathāgata? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, at that time they would be completely seen by the Tathāgata, because he observes the self directly and therefore has no doubt. That itself would become a tight apprehension of a self for him. Therefore, the binding of the entire net of afflictions arisen from the cause of apprehending a self for him would become slight or extreme; because the obscurations of the extremely tight bindings of attachment and so forth were not abandoned at that time, the Bhagavān would not have attained the state of a Tathāgata. Since the Bhagavān has attained that state, therefore, he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning obscurations, all the mountains of apprehending a self are destroyed. Therefore, he does not know sentient beings to be non-existent.

Regarding the thought, "Even though it is selfless, is there not the apprehension of a self, that is, the characteristic of the view of a self? How does the Bhagavān not perceive a self and so forth?", he stated, "Subhūti, as for what is called the apprehension of a self..." and so forth. If he were to apprehend any entity of a self and so forth, at that time the Bhagavān, who has abandoned obscurations, would have the apprehension of a self arise in him, but because there is nothing whatsoever to be apprehended as a self, the Tathāgata stated it to be exactly non-apprehension. Regarding the thought, "Then what is it that is called the apprehension of a self?", he stated, "That too..." and so forth. They are "childish" because they do not have hearing and so forth, and do not clearly know what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. They are "ordinary beings" because, being without realization, they have become distinct from the noble ones. In order to exclude those ordinary beings who, having listened to authentic treatises and abiding in proper mental engagement, when resolving upon the selflessness of dharmas do not apprehend a self by adhering to it as true, he said "childish". If he had said only "childish", even such ordinary beings who are skilled in the aggregates and so forth are of a childish nature because the path of the noble ones has not arisen in them, so it is in order to teach a distinction of the childish. Even though that apprehension of a self is mistaken, because they are childish, it appears to them like an apprehension of a self; therefore, by the power of their intention, he teaches it as "the apprehension of a self."

source: ཇི་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། མཐོང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་དག་ཏུའོ། །སུ་དག་གིས་མི་མཐོང་ཞེ་ན། ལོག་པས་སྤོང་བར་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །གཟུགས་སུ་མཐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་གང་ཟག་གཟུགས་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ།དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་ལ་སོགས་པས་བརྒྱན་པ་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་གི་གཟུགས་ཅན་དུ་མཐོང་བར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྒྲར་ཤེས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བདག་གིས་སྒྲ་ལས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དེ་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་འདི་འདྲ་བ་ཞིག་གོ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་ཐོས་པར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་འདི་གཉིས་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ནི་བྱེ་བྲག་ཕྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་བསྡུའོ། །སྐྱེ་བོ་ལོག་པས་སྤོང་བར་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་ལམ་ལོག་པར་ཞུགས་པས་ང་ཡང་དག་པར་མི་མཐོང་ངོ་། །འདིས་སྤོང་བས་ན་སྤོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ་ལམ་ལ་བྱའོ། །དེ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པས་ལོག་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་བའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འོ་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཇི་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ལྟ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་གཤའ་མ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་རིགས་པ་དང་ལུང་གིས་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཟོད་མ་ནས་ཞི་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་དང་། ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ་དང་། མཚན་མ་མེད་པ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རྣམ་གྲངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པའོ། །
translation: If one asks, 'How should he not be viewed?' In conventional designations by seeing and so forth. If one asks, 'By whom is he not seen?' By those who have engaged in abandoning through what is wrong. By this saying, 'see in form,' it is taught that a person who adheres to form conventionally designates seeing what is adorned with marks and so forth as possessing the form of dharmas and persons ultimately. 'Know through sound' means 'I know from sound that the Tathāgata is like this, like that' — this is the meaning of the words. By this, conventional designation as hearing is taught. These two conventional designations are illustrations; by them, differentiating and cognizing are also subsumed. Those beings who have engaged in abandoning through what is wrong do not see me perfectly because they have engaged in a wrong path. Because one abandons by this, it is what makes one abandon; this refers to the path. Because it has become inverted, it is wrong; that also is the cause of not seeing. Regarding the thought, 'Well then, how should a Buddha be viewed?' he stated, 'see the dharmatā,' and so forth. Whatever is the genuine nature of dharmas is called dharmatā; because it is established by reasoning and scripture, it is of the nature of being primordially peaceful and so forth. That itself is expressed by synonyms such as tathatā, dharmadhātu, the authentic limit, the signless, and the ultimate.

[3-224] translation already produced for this document:
If the Tathāgata were differentiated merely by consummate marks, since the reason for expression is the same, at that time why would a wheel-turning king not also become a Tathāgata? If one says, 'But due to abiding in their places, being clear, and being complete, the consummate marks of the Bhagavān are particular, whereas those of a wheel-turning king are not, so therefore he is not called a Tathāgata,' that is also incorrect: even the particulars of abiding in their places and so forth have no difference whatsoever in being of the nature of insentient matter. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were differentiated by dharmas such as marks of the nature of insentient matter, at that time a wheel-turning king would also become a Tathāgata, but that is not so. Therefore, the intention is that the Tathāgata is differentiated merely by having realized the nature of all entities just as they are. By this, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer regarding such an aspect of the body which has the exalted wisdom of the Tathāgata as its cause. Now, in order to teach that ultimately one should not adhere even to that exalted wisdom of the Tathāgata, he presents the dharmakāya, and teaches how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga through two verses.

source: དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་ན་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོད་པས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དོ། །དེ་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་སྟེ། དེ་དག་གི་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་སོ། །ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པས་ཡང་དག་པ་སྟེ། དེའི་མཐར་གྱུར་པས་ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ་འོ། །དེ་ལ་སྔོན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་པས་མཚན་མ་མེད་པའོ། །ཡེ་ཤེས་དམ་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཡིན་པས་དོན་དམ་པའོ། །ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྐུའི་སྒྲ་ནི་རང་བཞིན་ལ་བྱའོ། །དེས་ན་དོན་འདིར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། གང་དག་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་གྱི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་དེ་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཏེ། གང་དག་གང་གི་རང་བཞིན་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་དེའི་ངོ་བོར་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། གཞན་ལ་གཞན་གྱི་ངོ་བོར་བལྟ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་ནི་སྣང་བའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དེས་མཚོན་པ་དེ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་སྙམ་པ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས། ཆོས་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཅི་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་རིག་གམ། འོན་ཏེ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་ན་ཉེས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རམ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་མི་ནུས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཆོས་ཅན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་གྲུབ་ན་ནི་དེའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པར་ནུས་པ་ཞིག་ན་གང་གི་ཚེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཅན་རང་གི་ངོ་བོར་གྲུབ་པ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་འབའ་ཞིག་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་ནུས་ཏེ། དེ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དགོངས་པའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཆོས་ཅན་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པས་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ཉེས་པ་མེད་དེ། གང་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའོ། །ཆོས་ཉིད་ནི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་པས་དེ་ནི་དེ་དང་མི་མཐུན་པ་སྐྱེ་བ་འཛིན་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུང་། བུམ་པ་འཛིན་པས་ནི་དེའི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་འཛིན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་བ་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་དེ་སྐད་སྟོན་ཏོ། །
translation: Because it exists thus at all times, it is tathatā. Because, focusing on it, all the qualities of a Buddha arise, and because it has become their cause, it is the dharmadhātu. Because it is un-inverted, it is authentic; because it has become the limit of that, it is the authentic limit. Because it lacks all signs of entities, such as blue and so forth, it is the signless. Because it is the domain of supreme exalted wisdom, it is the ultimate. Regarding the thought, 'Why should he be viewed as the dharmatā?', he stated, 'dharmakāya.' The word 'kāya' (body) refers to nature. Therefore, the meaning becomes this: those presented as Tathāgatas having authentic exalted wisdom as their cause are ultimately of the nature of dharmas; whatever are the nature of something, those should be viewed as the essence of that; one should not view something as the essence of something else. Regarding the thought, 'If so, the dharmatā would become of the nature of appearance. If not, having investigated, how could one be able to see those things illustrated by it?', he stated, 'dharmatā' and so forth. Regarding the thought, 'Is it not cognized because one is unable, or because if it were thoroughly known, it would be accompanied by a fault?', he stated, 'unable' and so forth. The intention is: 'If the nature of the dharma-possessor were established, one would be able to cognize its dharmatā; but when ultimately there is no dharma-possessor whatsoever established in its own essence, at that time how could one be able to cognize only that dharmatā in its own continuum? It does not exist merely alone.' If one asks, 'If so, since the dharma-possessor Buddhas of the essence of authentic exalted wisdom are also not established ultimately and therefore there is no seeing them, how should they be viewed as the dharmatā?', there is no fault in that: the very fact that one ultimately does not see all dharma-possessors is itself seeing the dharmatā. Since the dharmatā is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is discordant with it? By grasping at a vase, one will not grasp its non-arising. By this, it is taught: 'The Tathāgata should not be viewed as the form body; he should be viewed as the dharmakāya.'

It does not become true merely by that, but it would absurdly follow: why would one not apprehend a self and so forth as true even through the application of words like "selflessness"? Regarding the thought, "If there is no self, who is called 'ordinary beings'?", he stated, "Childish ordinary beings," and so forth. Ultimately, beings are completely non-existent; because it was stated relying on the conventional, there is no fault. By all this, because the extremes of exaggeration and deprecation are eliminated, thoroughly holding the mind is taught. If the Tathāgata were differentiated merely by consummate marks, since the reason for expression is the same, at that time why would a wheel-turning king not also become a Tathāgata? If one says, 'But due to abiding in their places, being clear, and being complete, the consummate marks of the Bhagavān are particular, whereas those of a wheel-turning king are not, so therefore he is not called a Tathāgata,' that is also incorrect: even the particulars of abiding in their places and so forth have no difference whatsoever in being of the nature of insentient matter. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were differentiated by dharmas such as marks of the nature of insentient matter, at that time a wheel-turning king would also become a Tathāgata, but that is not so. Therefore, the intention is that the Tathāgata is differentiated merely by having realized the nature of all entities just as they are. By this, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide by aspiration and prayer regarding such an aspect of the body which has the exalted wisdom of the Tathāgata as its cause. Now, in order to teach that ultimately one should not adhere even to that exalted wisdom of the Tathāgata, he presents the dharmakāya, and teaches how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by meditative absorption in yoga through two verses.

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
translation: To abandon the doubt of whoever thinks, 'Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of perfect marks, it is logical that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening arises from the cause of perfect marks, because thus, when he had become a bodhisattva, sign-readers, having seen him as possessing perfect marks, prophesied that the Bhagavān would attain unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening,' he stated, 'Subhūti, what do you think about this?' and so forth. The intention is: 'If perfect marks were to become the cause of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening, then at that time a wheel-turning monarch would also become so.' Sign-readers, having seen such a kind of mark, prophesied it, but it is not the cause, so there is no fault. By this, thoroughly apprehending the mind is taught. By all these points, profoundness itself is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom conventionally realizing the nature of all entities without exception, extensiveness is also taught.

If one asks, 'How should he not be viewed?' In conventional designations by seeing and so forth. If one asks, 'By whom is he not seen?' By those who have engaged in abandoning through what is wrong. By this saying, 'see in form,' it is taught that a person who adheres to form conventionally designates seeing what is adorned with marks and so forth as possessing the form of dharmas and persons ultimately. 'Know through sound' means 'I know from sound that the Tathāgata is like this, like that' — this is the meaning of the words. By this, conventional designation as hearing is taught. These two conventional designations are illustrations; by them, differentiating and cognizing are also subsumed. Those beings who have engaged in abandoning through what is wrong do not see me perfectly because they have engaged in a wrong path. Because one abandons by this, it is what makes one abandon; this refers to the path. Because it has become inverted, it is wrong; that also is the cause of not seeing. Regarding the thought, 'Well then, how should a Buddha be viewed?' he stated, 'see the dharmatā,' and so forth. Whatever is the genuine nature of dharmas is called dharmatā; because it is established by reasoning and scripture, it is of the nature of being primordially peaceful and so forth. That itself is expressed by synonyms such as tathatā, dharmadhātu, the authentic limit, the signless, and the ultimate.

Because it exists thus at all times, it is tathatā. Because, focusing on it, all the qualities of a Buddha arise, and because it has become their cause, it is the dharmadhātu. Because it is un-inverted, it is authentic; because it has become the limit of that, it is the authentic limit. Because it lacks all signs of entities, such as blue and so forth, it is the signless. Because it is the domain of supreme exalted wisdom, it is the ultimate. Regarding the thought, 'Why should he be viewed as the dharmatā?', he stated, 'dharmakāya.' The word 'kāya' (body) refers to nature. Therefore, the meaning becomes this: those presented as Tathāgatas having authentic exalted wisdom as their cause are ultimately of the nature of dharmas; whatever are the nature of something, those should be viewed as the essence of that; one should not view something as the essence of something else. Regarding the thought, 'If so, the dharmatā would become of the nature of appearance. If not, having investigated, how could one be able to see those things illustrated by it?', he stated, 'dharmatā' and so forth. Regarding the thought, 'Is it not cognized because one is unable, or because if it were thoroughly known, it would be accompanied by a fault?', he stated, 'unable' and so forth. The intention is: 'If the nature of the dharma-possessor were established, one would be able to cognize its dharmatā; but when ultimately there is no dharma-possessor whatsoever established in its own essence, at that time how could one be able to cognize only that dharmatā in its own continuum? It does not exist merely alone.' If one asks, 'If so, since the dharma-possessor Buddhas of the essence of authentic exalted wisdom are also not established ultimately and therefore there is no seeing them, how should they be viewed as the dharmatā?', there is no fault in that: the very fact that one ultimately does not see all dharma-possessors is itself seeing the dharmatā. Since the dharmatā is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is discordant with it? By grasping at a vase, one will not grasp its non-arising. By this, it is taught: 'The Tathāgata should not be viewed as the form body; he should be viewed as the dharmakāya.'

Because it exists thus at all times, it is tathatā. Because, focusing on it, all the qualities of a Buddha arise, and because it has become their cause, it is the dharmadhātu. Because it is un-inverted, it is authentic; because it has become the limit of that, it is the authentic limit. Because it lacks all signs of entities, such as blue and so forth, it is the signless. Because it is the domain of supreme exalted wisdom, it is the ultimate. Regarding the thought, 'Why should he be viewed as the dharmatā?', he stated, 'dharmakāya.' The word 'kāya' (body) refers to nature. Therefore, the meaning becomes this: those presented as Tathāgatas having authentic exalted wisdom as their cause are ultimately of the nature of dharmas; whatever are the nature of something, those should be viewed as the essence of that; one should not view something as the essence of something else. Regarding the thought, 'If so, the dharmatā would become of the nature of appearance. If not, having investigated, how could one be able to see those things illustrated by it?', he stated, 'dharmatā' and so forth. Regarding the thought, 'Is it not cognized because one is unable, or because if it were thoroughly known, it would be accompanied by a fault?', he stated, 'unable' and so forth. The intention is: 'If the nature of the dharma-possessor were established, one would be able to cognize its dharmatā; but when ultimately there is no dharma-possessor whatsoever established in its own essence, at that time how could one be able to cognize only that dharmatā in its own continuum? It does not exist merely alone.' If one asks, 'If so, since the dharma-possessor Buddhas of the essence of authentic exalted wisdom are also not established ultimately and therefore there is no seeing them, how should they be viewed as the dharmatā?', there is no fault in that: the very fact that one ultimately does not see all dharma-possessors is itself seeing the dharmatā. Since the dharmatā is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is discordant with it? By grasping at a vase, one will not grasp its non-arising. By this, it is taught: 'The Tathāgata should not be viewed as the form body; he should be viewed as the dharmakāya.'

To abandon the doubt of whoever thinks, 'Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of perfect marks, it is logical that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening arises from the cause of perfect marks, because thus, when he had become a bodhisattva, sign-readers, having seen him as possessing perfect marks, prophesied that the Bhagavān would attain unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening,' he stated, 'Subhūti, what do you think about this?' and so forth. The intention is: 'If perfect marks were to become the cause of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening, then at that time a wheel-turning monarch would also become so.' Sign-readers, having seen such a kind of mark, prophesied it, but it is not the cause, so there is no fault. By this, thoroughly apprehending the mind is taught. By all these points, profoundness itself is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom conventionally realizing the nature of all entities without exception, extensiveness is also taught.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: Therefore, for the sake of whoever doubts, thinking, 'Because the Tathāgata also does not exist, non-abiding nirvāṇa is also not established,' with respect to not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he stated, 'Subhūti, do you think thus, that those who have authentically entered the bodhisattva vehicle' and so forth. Also, there is no conceptualization that what has arisen is destroyed, because one realizes the dharmatā just as it abides. Therefore, it is explained: 'Here there is nothing whatsoever to be removed, and nothing whatsoever to be posited. One looks authentically at the authentic. Seeing authentically, one is completely liberated.' Also, there is no conceptualization of annihilation by obstructing the arising of future dharmas, because the dharmatā is taught just as it abides. Because all dharmas are accepted as arising in accordance with conditions, being pleasant when unanalyzed, and because the Buddha Bhagavān, the essence of the authentic conventional, who has attained mastery over emanations and so forth by the power of great compassion, is accepted as not cutting off the continuum of engaging in saṃsāra by teaching methods in accordance with those to be tamed, by this, the Bhagavān's not abiding in nirvāṇa is taught; and that one should abide with aspiration and prayer for such a body of the Bhagavān is also taught. Regarding the thought, 'If thus the Bhagavān is accepted as engaging in saṃsāra, he would become of the very nature of saṃsāra,' having investigated it, in order to teach his very non-abiding in saṃsāra, he stated, 'Moreover, Subhūti' and so forth.

Because it exists thus at all times, it is tathatā. Because, focusing on it, all the qualities of a Buddha arise, and because it has become their cause, it is the dharmadhātu. Because it is un-inverted, it is authentic; because it has become the limit of that, it is the authentic limit. Because it lacks all signs of entities, such as blue and so forth, it is the signless. Because it is the domain of supreme exalted wisdom, it is the ultimate. Regarding the thought, 'Why should he be viewed as the dharmatā?', he stated, 'dharmakāya.' The word 'kāya' (body) refers to nature. Therefore, the meaning becomes this: those presented as Tathāgatas having authentic exalted wisdom as their cause are ultimately of the nature of dharmas; whatever are the nature of something, those should be viewed as the essence of that; one should not view something as the essence of something else. Regarding the thought, 'If so, the dharmatā would become of the nature of appearance. If not, having investigated, how could one be able to see those things illustrated by it?', he stated, 'dharmatā' and so forth. Regarding the thought, 'Is it not cognized because one is unable, or because if it were thoroughly known, it would be accompanied by a fault?', he stated, 'unable' and so forth. The intention is: 'If the nature of the dharma-possessor were established, one would be able to cognize its dharmatā; but when ultimately there is no dharma-possessor whatsoever established in its own essence, at that time how could one be able to cognize only that dharmatā in its own continuum? It does not exist merely alone.' If one asks, 'If so, since the dharma-possessor Buddhas of the essence of authentic exalted wisdom are also not established ultimately and therefore there is no seeing them, how should they be viewed as the dharmatā?', there is no fault in that: the very fact that one ultimately does not see all dharma-possessors is itself seeing the dharmatā. Since the dharmatā is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is discordant with it? By grasping at a vase, one will not grasp its non-arising. By this, it is taught: 'The Tathāgata should not be viewed as the form body; he should be viewed as the dharmakāya.'

To abandon the doubt of whoever thinks, 'Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of perfect marks, it is logical that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening arises from the cause of perfect marks, because thus, when he had become a bodhisattva, sign-readers, having seen him as possessing perfect marks, prophesied that the Bhagavān would attain unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening,' he stated, 'Subhūti, what do you think about this?' and so forth. The intention is: 'If perfect marks were to become the cause of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening, then at that time a wheel-turning monarch would also become so.' Sign-readers, having seen such a kind of mark, prophesied it, but it is not the cause, so there is no fault. By this, thoroughly apprehending the mind is taught. By all these points, profoundness itself is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom conventionally realizing the nature of all entities without exception, extensiveness is also taught.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: 'Selfless' is because they are under the power of others, like an illusion. They are not of the nature of a self by themselves, because a permanent thing contradicts being a cause since it is neither sequential nor non-sequential, and because what is not a cause does not do anything, making it impossible to be an empowerer. There is also no self empowered by another. Therefore, in both ways, all those dharmas are selfless; just as it is stated, 'Monks, childish ones who lack learning impute and engage with "I" and "mine", but here there is no "I" and "mine".' By this, the patience regarding the selflessness of persons in all dharmas is taught. By 'non-arising', the patience regarding the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Thus, if entities were to arise, would they arise causelessly or from a cause? Furthermore, if from a cause, one might conceptualize whether they arise from a permanent cause or an impermanent cause. In that regard, since entities appear occasionally, the first conceptualization is unsuitable: because that which has no reliance has no distinctions anywhere, it would become either permanently existent or non-existent, just like the times of existence and non-existence. Therefore, precisely because they arise occasionally, the second alternative is also unsuitable: since the capacity of permanent things cannot be differentiated by other assisting factors, and since they do not rely on anything, how could they produce effects sequentially and not simultaneously? It is illogical for an effect whose causes are not incomplete to occasionally not appear; by what reason would it arise sequentially? Those who propound an intrinsic nature as the cause of entities also effectively accept non-existence: thus, what is established by intrinsic nature would become a cause, but what is unestablished would not, because it has the defining characteristic of being devoid of all capacities.

[3-227] translation already produced for this document:
Because it exists thus at all times, it is tathatā. Because, focusing on it, all the qualities of a Buddha arise, and because it has become their cause, it is the dharmadhātu. Because it is un-inverted, it is authentic; because it has become the limit of that, it is the authentic limit. Because it lacks all signs of entities, such as blue and so forth, it is the signless. Because it is the domain of supreme exalted wisdom, it is the ultimate. Regarding the thought, 'Why should he be viewed as the dharmatā?', he stated, 'dharmakāya.' The word 'kāya' (body) refers to nature. Therefore, the meaning becomes this: those presented as Tathāgatas having authentic exalted wisdom as their cause are ultimately of the nature of dharmas; whatever are the nature of something, those should be viewed as the essence of that; one should not view something as the essence of something else. Regarding the thought, 'If so, the dharmatā would become of the nature of appearance. If not, having investigated, how could one be able to see those things illustrated by it?', he stated, 'dharmatā' and so forth. Regarding the thought, 'Is it not cognized because one is unable, or because if it were thoroughly known, it would be accompanied by a fault?', he stated, 'unable' and so forth. The intention is: 'If the nature of the dharma-possessor were established, one would be able to cognize its dharmatā; but when ultimately there is no dharma-possessor whatsoever established in its own essence, at that time how could one be able to cognize only that dharmatā in its own continuum? It does not exist merely alone.' If one asks, 'If so, since the dharma-possessor Buddhas of the essence of authentic exalted wisdom are also not established ultimately and therefore there is no seeing them, how should they be viewed as the dharmatā?', there is no fault in that: the very fact that one ultimately does not see all dharma-possessors is itself seeing the dharmatā. Since the dharmatā is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is discordant with it? By grasping at a vase, one will not grasp its non-arising. By this, it is taught: 'The Tathāgata should not be viewed as the form body; he should be viewed as the dharmakāya.'

To abandon the doubt of whoever thinks, 'Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of perfect marks, it is logical that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening arises from the cause of perfect marks, because thus, when he had become a bodhisattva, sign-readers, having seen him as possessing perfect marks, prophesied that the Bhagavān would attain unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening,' he stated, 'Subhūti, what do you think about this?' and so forth. The intention is: 'If perfect marks were to become the cause of unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening, then at that time a wheel-turning monarch would also become so.' Sign-readers, having seen such a kind of mark, prophesied it, but it is not the cause, so there is no fault. By this, thoroughly apprehending the mind is taught. By all these points, profoundness itself is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's exalted wisdom conventionally realizing the nature of all entities without exception, extensiveness is also taught.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: If that intrinsic nature of entities is established, it is accepted as being established precisely without a cause; if another cause, distinct from it, is not asserted, how could it not be causeless? Because entities are not other than their intrinsic nature, when that is established, they are established, so they would be causeless. If that were not the case, since they would not be established when that [intrinsic nature] is established, how could they become of a nature that is not distinct from it? Therefore, whatever destroys the position that propounds causelessness applies equally here. Since being simultaneous or non-simultaneous contradicts being a cause, the third alternative is also unsuitable. Thus, if it were to become a cause, it would either be simultaneous with the effect or at a different time. It is not from being simultaneous, because that which has not attained its own identity is empty of all capacities and thus has no engagement with any effect. Its own identity, just like its nature, is precisely the essence of the entity that attains it simultaneously with the effect, so it does not engage with that effect. Furthermore, if they are at different times, it would occur having been separated by another time, for example, just as the Vaibhāṣikas assert the cause of ripening as a cause; or it would occur through meeting, for example, just as the Sautrāntikas say that the destruction and arising of the cause and effect are simultaneous like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. In that regard, if the effect arises having been separated by another time, it would be accepted as having arisen precisely from what is destroyed, but since that is devoid of all capacities, what is destroyed is illogical as a causal entity.

Therefore, for the sake of whoever doubts, thinking, 'Because the Tathāgata also does not exist, non-abiding nirvāṇa is also not established,' with respect to not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he stated, 'Subhūti, do you think thus, that those who have authentically entered the bodhisattva vehicle' and so forth. Also, there is no conceptualization that what has arisen is destroyed, because one realizes the dharmatā just as it abides. Therefore, it is explained: 'Here there is nothing whatsoever to be removed, and nothing whatsoever to be posited. One looks authentically at the authentic. Seeing authentically, one is completely liberated.' Also, there is no conceptualization of annihilation by obstructing the arising of future dharmas, because the dharmatā is taught just as it abides. Because all dharmas are accepted as arising in accordance with conditions, being pleasant when unanalyzed, and because the Buddha Bhagavān, the essence of the authentic conventional, who has attained mastery over emanations and so forth by the power of great compassion, is accepted as not cutting off the continuum of engaging in saṃsāra by teaching methods in accordance with those to be tamed, by this, the Bhagavān's not abiding in nirvāṇa is taught; and that one should abide with aspiration and prayer for such a body of the Bhagavān is also taught. Regarding the thought, 'If thus the Bhagavān is accepted as engaging in saṃsāra, he would become of the very nature of saṃsāra,' having investigated it, in order to teach his very non-abiding in saṃsāra, he stated, 'Moreover, Subhūti' and so forth.

[3-231] translation already produced for this document:
'Selfless' is because they are under the power of others, like an illusion. They are not of the nature of a self by themselves, because a permanent thing contradicts being a cause since it is neither sequential nor non-sequential, and because what is not a cause does not do anything, making it impossible to be an empowerer. There is also no self empowered by another. Therefore, in both ways, all those dharmas are selfless; just as it is stated, 'Monks, childish ones who lack learning impute and engage with "I" and "mine", but here there is no "I" and "mine".' By this, the patience regarding the selflessness of persons in all dharmas is taught. By 'non-arising', the patience regarding the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Thus, if entities were to arise, would they arise causelessly or from a cause? Furthermore, if from a cause, one might conceptualize whether they arise from a permanent cause or an impermanent cause. In that regard, since entities appear occasionally, the first conceptualization is unsuitable: because that which has no reliance has no distinctions anywhere, it would become either permanently existent or non-existent, just like the times of existence and non-existence. Therefore, precisely because they arise occasionally, the second alternative is also unsuitable: since the capacity of permanent things cannot be differentiated by other assisting factors, and since they do not rely on anything, how could they produce effects sequentially and not simultaneously? It is illogical for an effect whose causes are not incomplete to occasionally not appear; by what reason would it arise sequentially? Those who propound an intrinsic nature as the cause of entities also effectively accept non-existence: thus, what is established by intrinsic nature would become a cause, but what is unestablished would not, because it has the defining characteristic of being devoid of all capacities.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: If that were not so, how could a destroyed entity that is not an agent become destroyed? As for the position of meeting, if they meet with their entire nature, then at that time they would become simultaneous; if two partless entities meet with their entire nature, there is no other outcome except that they become a single time. Therefore, just as when subtle atoms meet with their entire nature, a mass would become just the size of a subtle atom, similarly it would be difficult to avoid that an eon would become just a single instant. If they meet by one part, they would become possessed of parts. Therefore, all entities are ultimately unarisen; they merely appear as if arising due to being false and pleasant when unanalyzed, similar to the nature of what appears to a mistaken consciousness. Since mere renown is not a valid cognition, how could it be logical for someone to say, 'Because the cause and effect of entities are renowned even up to cowherds, it is illogical to destroy them'? This is because renowned forms and so forth are destroyed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the valid cognitions of the eyes and so forth in the Samādhirāja Sūtra: 'The eyes, ears, and nose are also not valid cognitions. The tongue, body, and mind are also not valid cognitions. If these faculties were valid cognitions, what would the noble path do for anyone?'
