[3-230] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, for the sake of whoever doubts, thinking, 'Because the Tathāgata also does not exist, non-abiding nirvāṇa is also not established,' with respect to not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he stated, 'Subhūti, do you think thus, that those who have authentically entered the bodhisattva vehicle' and so forth. Also, there is no conceptualization that what has arisen is destroyed, because one realizes the dharmatā just as it abides. Therefore, it is explained: 'Here there is nothing whatsoever to be removed, and nothing whatsoever to be posited. One looks authentically at the authentic. Seeing authentically, one is completely liberated.' Also, there is no conceptualization of annihilation by obstructing the arising of future dharmas, because the dharmatā is taught just as it abides. Because all dharmas are accepted as arising in accordance with conditions, being pleasant when unanalyzed, and because the Buddha Bhagavān, the essence of the authentic conventional, who has attained mastery over emanations and so forth by the power of great compassion, is accepted as not cutting off the continuum of engaging in saṃsāra by teaching methods in accordance with those to be tamed, by this, the Bhagavān's not abiding in nirvāṇa is taught; and that one should abide with aspiration and prayer for such a body of the Bhagavān is also taught. Regarding the thought, 'If thus the Bhagavān is accepted as engaging in saṃsāra, he would become of the very nature of saṃsāra,' having investigated it, in order to teach his very non-abiding in saṃsāra, he stated, 'Moreover, Subhūti' and so forth.

བདག་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་གཞན་གྱི་དབང་གི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རང་གིས་བདག་གི་རང་བཞིན་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྟག་པ་ནི་རིམ་དང་རིམ་མ་ཡིན་པས་རྒྱུར་འགལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ལ། རྒྱུ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ནི་ཅི་ཡང་མི་བྱེད་པས་བྱིན་གྱིས་རློབ་པ་པོར་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བདག་གཞན་གྱིས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པ་ཡང་མེད་དེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་དེ་དག་སྟེ། ཇི་སྐད་དུ། དགེ་སློང་དག་བྱིས་པ་ཐོས་པ་དང་མི་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་བདག་དང་བདག་གི་ཞེས་འདོགས་ཤིང་འཇུག་གི་འདི་ལ་ནི་བདག་དང་བདག་གི་མེད་དེ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །འདིས་ནི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་གང་ཟག་ལ་བདག་མེད་པའི་བཟོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པའི་བཟོད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདི་ལྟར་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་ན་ནི་རྒྱུ་མེད་པའམ་རྒྱུ་དང་བཅས་པ་ལས་འགྱུར་གྲང་། རྒྱུ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཡང་རྒྱུ་རྟག་པའམ། རྒྱུ་མི་རྟག་པ་ལས་འགྱུར་བར་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་གྲང་ན། དེ་ལ་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་རེས་འགའ་སྣང་བས་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་དང་པོ་ལྟར་ནི་མི་རུང་སྟེ། ལྟོས་པ་མེད་པ་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་བྱེ་བྲག་མེད་པས་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པའི་དུས་བཞིན་དུ་རྟག་པར་ཡོད་པའམ་མེད་པ་ཞིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རེས་འགའ་བྱུང་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་གཉིས་པ་ལྟར་ཡང་མི་རུང་སྟེ། རྟག་པ་དག་གི་ནུས་པ་གྲོགས་བྱེད་པ་གཞན་དག་གིས་བྱེ་བྲག་ཏུ་བྱར་མེད་པ་ན་སུ་ལ་ཡང་ལྟོས་པ་མེད་ན་གང་གིས་འབྲས་བུ་རིམ་གྱིས་སྐྱེད་པ་ཅིག་ཅར་མ་ཡིན། རྒྱུ་མ་ཚང་པ་མེད་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་རེས་འགའ་མི་སྣང་བ་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། གང་གིས་ན་རིམ་གྱིས་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར། གང་དག་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུར་སྨྲ་བ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་དོན་དུ་ན་མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཁས་བླངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་གྲུབ་པ་ནི་རྒྱུར་འགྱུར་གྱི། མ་གྲུབ་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་ནུས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-231] translation already produced for this document:
'Selfless' is because they are under the power of others, like an illusion. They are not of the nature of a self by themselves, because a permanent thing contradicts being a cause since it is neither sequential nor non-sequential, and because what is not a cause does not do anything, making it impossible to be an empowerer. There is also no self empowered by another. Therefore, in both ways, all those dharmas are selfless; just as it is stated, 'Monks, childish ones who lack learning impute and engage with "I" and "mine", but here there is no "I" and "mine".' By this, the patience regarding the selflessness of persons in all dharmas is taught. By 'non-arising', the patience regarding the selflessness of dharmas is taught. Thus, if entities were to arise, would they arise causelessly or from a cause? Furthermore, if from a cause, one might conceptualize whether they arise from a permanent cause or an impermanent cause. In that regard, since entities appear occasionally, the first conceptualization is unsuitable: because that which has no reliance has no distinctions anywhere, it would become either permanently existent or non-existent, just like the times of existence and non-existence. Therefore, precisely because they arise occasionally, the second alternative is also unsuitable: since the capacity of permanent things cannot be differentiated by other assisting factors, and since they do not rely on anything, how could they produce effects sequentially and not simultaneously? It is illogical for an effect whose causes are not incomplete to occasionally not appear; by what reason would it arise sequentially? Those who propound an intrinsic nature as the cause of entities also effectively accept non-existence: thus, what is established by intrinsic nature would become a cause, but what is unestablished would not, because it has the defining characteristic of being devoid of all capacities.

source: འདི་ལྟར་དབང་པོ་འདི་དག་ཆད་མིན་ཏེ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བེམས་པོ་ལུང་མ་བསྟན། །དེ་ཕྱིར་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པའི་ལམ་འདོད་གང་། །དེས་ནི་འཕགས་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་བྱོས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སློབ་དཔོན་དག་གིས་མངོན་སུམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་གསུངས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་མངོན་སུམ་སྟེ། དོན་དམ་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ནི་མཐུན་པར་བརྒལ་ཞིང་བརྟག་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་དེ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་བརྟག་མི་བཟོད་པའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སཱ་ལུ་ལྗང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་བདག་དང་གཞན་ལས་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་བ་བཀག་གོ། །དེ་སྐད་དུ། འཕགས་པ་ལང་ཀར་གཤེགས་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བློ་གྲོས་ཆེན་པོ་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་ལས་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་མ་སྐྱེས་པའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་གསུངས་པ།རབ་འབྱོར་ཆོས་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མ་སྐྱེས་པ་དེ་ནི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའོ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་སྐད་དུ། དཀོན་མཆོག་འབྱུང་གནས་ཀྱི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། གང་ལ་རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །རང་བཞིན་མེད་པས་གཞན་རྐྱེན་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། །རང་བཞིན་མེད་པས་གཞན་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྐྱེད། །རྒྱུ་དེ་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པས་རབ་ཏུ་བསྟན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡང་། དངོས་པོ་སྐྱེ་བ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ། །
translation: 'Thus, these faculties are not valid cognitions; by their intrinsic nature, they are inert and unspecified. Therefore, whoever desires the path of nirvāṇa should perform the activities of the noble path,' so it is said. Whatever characteristics of direct perception the masters have spoken of, they too are direct perception conventionally; they should be seen as engaging with the ultimate. Conventionally, they are not analyzed and debated accordingly; therefore, because they are taught conventionally, they cannot withstand analysis. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the arising of entities from self and from other in the Śālistamba and so forth. Accordingly, it is also said in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: 'Mahāmati, because they do not arise from existence or non-existence, all phenomena are unarisen.' It is said in the Great Prajñāpāramitā: 'Subhūti, that no phenomenon whatsoever is arisen is called non-arising.' Regarding that, whatever is wisdom is called patience with unarisen phenomena. Accordingly, it is also said in the Ratnākara Sūtra: 'That which has no nature, because it has no nature, how could there be other conditions? Because it has no nature, how could it generate others? [3-232] translation already produced for this document:
If that intrinsic nature of entities is established, it is accepted as being established precisely without a cause; if another cause, distinct from it, is not asserted, how could it not be causeless? Because entities are not other than their intrinsic nature, when that is established, they are established, so they would be causeless. If that were not the case, since they would not be established when that [intrinsic nature] is established, how could they become of a nature that is not distinct from it? Therefore, whatever destroys the position that propounds causelessness applies equally here. Since being simultaneous or non-simultaneous contradicts being a cause, the third alternative is also unsuitable. Thus, if it were to become a cause, it would either be simultaneous with the effect or at a different time. It is not from being simultaneous, because that which has not attained its own identity is empty of all capacities and thus has no engagement with any effect. Its own identity, just like its nature, is precisely the essence of the entity that attains it simultaneously with the effect, so it does not engage with that effect. Furthermore, if they are at different times, it would occur having been separated by another time, for example, just as the Vaibhāṣikas assert the cause of ripening as a cause; or it would occur through meeting, for example, just as the Sautrāntikas say that the destruction and arising of the cause and effect are simultaneous like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. In that regard, if the effect arises having been separated by another time, it would be accepted as having arisen precisely from what is destroyed, but since that is devoid of all capacities, what is destroyed is illogical as a causal entity.

If that were not so, how could a destroyed entity that is not an agent become destroyed? As for the position of meeting, if they meet with their entire nature, then at that time they would become simultaneous; if two partless entities meet with their entire nature, there is no other outcome except that they become a single time. Therefore, just as when subtle atoms meet with their entire nature, a mass would become just the size of a subtle atom, similarly it would be difficult to avoid that an eon would become just a single instant. If they meet by one part, they would become possessed of parts. Therefore, all entities are ultimately unarisen; they merely appear as if arising due to being false and pleasant when unanalyzed, similar to the nature of what appears to a mistaken consciousness. Since mere renown is not a valid cognition, how could it be logical for someone to say, 'Because the cause and effect of entities are renowned even up to cowherds, it is illogical to destroy them'? This is because renowned forms and so forth are destroyed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the valid cognitions of the eyes and so forth in the Samādhirāja Sūtra: 'The eyes, ears, and nose are also not valid cognitions. The tongue, body, and mind are also not valid cognitions. If these faculties were valid cognitions, what would the noble path do for anyone?'

translation: ultimately, they have no nature,' so it is also said. If one says, 'All these are spoken with regard to the imagined intrinsic nature,' it is not so, because all intrinsic natures have already been eliminated by valid cognition. By this, it is taught: if even others who possess small roots of virtue do not experience the suffering of saṃsāra, how could a bodhisattva in whom the great light of pristine wisdom has arisen because of having obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, and who has obtained the generation of an unsurpassable heap of merit, experience the suffering of saṃsāra? Thus, one experiences suffering in saṃsāra in two ways: they have the characteristics of physical and mental discomfort. Among those, the former is the effect of non-virtuous karma. The latter is born from ignorance; it is born from wrong understanding. Regarding that, because they have obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, bodhisattvas have neither non-virtue nor ignorance, the causes of suffering. Because the causes are absent, it is impossible for them to be touched by the slightest trace of suffering. By this, how bodhisattvas should practice is taught. Even if they have generated an extremely large heap of merit, would they not simply remain in saṃsāra like sentient beings of the form realm and so forth? To address the doubt of thinking, 'How is it taught that merely by having generated a large heap of merit they do not abide in saṃsāra?', it also says, 'Subhūti,' and so forth.

[3-232] translation already produced for this document:
If that intrinsic nature of entities is established, it is accepted as being established precisely without a cause; if another cause, distinct from it, is not asserted, how could it not be causeless? Because entities are not other than their intrinsic nature, when that is established, they are established, so they would be causeless. If that were not the case, since they would not be established when that [intrinsic nature] is established, how could they become of a nature that is not distinct from it? Therefore, whatever destroys the position that propounds causelessness applies equally here. Since being simultaneous or non-simultaneous contradicts being a cause, the third alternative is also unsuitable. Thus, if it were to become a cause, it would either be simultaneous with the effect or at a different time. It is not from being simultaneous, because that which has not attained its own identity is empty of all capacities and thus has no engagement with any effect. Its own identity, just like its nature, is precisely the essence of the entity that attains it simultaneously with the effect, so it does not engage with that effect. Furthermore, if they are at different times, it would occur having been separated by another time, for example, just as the Vaibhāṣikas assert the cause of ripening as a cause; or it would occur through meeting, for example, just as the Sautrāntikas say that the destruction and arising of the cause and effect are simultaneous like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. In that regard, if the effect arises having been separated by another time, it would be accepted as having arisen precisely from what is destroyed, but since that is devoid of all capacities, what is destroyed is illogical as a causal entity.

If that were not so, how could a destroyed entity that is not an agent become destroyed? As for the position of meeting, if they meet with their entire nature, then at that time they would become simultaneous; if two partless entities meet with their entire nature, there is no other outcome except that they become a single time. Therefore, just as when subtle atoms meet with their entire nature, a mass would become just the size of a subtle atom, similarly it would be difficult to avoid that an eon would become just a single instant. If they meet by one part, they would become possessed of parts. Therefore, all entities are ultimately unarisen; they merely appear as if arising due to being false and pleasant when unanalyzed, similar to the nature of what appears to a mistaken consciousness. Since mere renown is not a valid cognition, how could it be logical for someone to say, 'Because the cause and effect of entities are renowned even up to cowherds, it is illogical to destroy them'? This is because renowned forms and so forth are destroyed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the valid cognitions of the eyes and so forth in the Samādhirāja Sūtra: 'The eyes, ears, and nose are also not valid cognitions. The tongue, body, and mind are also not valid cognitions. If these faculties were valid cognitions, what would the noble path do for anyone?'

translation: By this, whoever, even though having generated a heap of merit, apprehends the heap of merit through adhering to it in an inverted way, since they have not abandoned the inversions which are the root of all those afflictions, even if they attain a special migration, they are posited as a saṃsāric being. A bodhisattva, having obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, has no adherence to the heap of merit as being true; therefore, because they have abandoned deep ignorance which is the root of all those afflictions, they do not abide in saṃsāra,' thus it is taught.

If that intrinsic nature of entities is established, it is accepted as being established precisely without a cause; if another cause, distinct from it, is not asserted, how could it not be causeless? Because entities are not other than their intrinsic nature, when that is established, they are established, so they would be causeless. If that were not the case, since they would not be established when that [intrinsic nature] is established, how could they become of a nature that is not distinct from it? Therefore, whatever destroys the position that propounds causelessness applies equally here. Since being simultaneous or non-simultaneous contradicts being a cause, the third alternative is also unsuitable. Thus, if it were to become a cause, it would either be simultaneous with the effect or at a different time. It is not from being simultaneous, because that which has not attained its own identity is empty of all capacities and thus has no engagement with any effect. Its own identity, just like its nature, is precisely the essence of the entity that attains it simultaneously with the effect, so it does not engage with that effect. Furthermore, if they are at different times, it would occur having been separated by another time, for example, just as the Vaibhāṣikas assert the cause of ripening as a cause; or it would occur through meeting, for example, just as the Sautrāntikas say that the destruction and arising of the cause and effect are simultaneous like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. In that regard, if the effect arises having been separated by another time, it would be accepted as having arisen precisely from what is destroyed, but since that is devoid of all capacities, what is destroyed is illogical as a causal entity.

If that were not so, how could a destroyed entity that is not an agent become destroyed? As for the position of meeting, if they meet with their entire nature, then at that time they would become simultaneous; if two partless entities meet with their entire nature, there is no other outcome except that they become a single time. Therefore, just as when subtle atoms meet with their entire nature, a mass would become just the size of a subtle atom, similarly it would be difficult to avoid that an eon would become just a single instant. If they meet by one part, they would become possessed of parts. Therefore, all entities are ultimately unarisen; they merely appear as if arising due to being false and pleasant when unanalyzed, similar to the nature of what appears to a mistaken consciousness. Since mere renown is not a valid cognition, how could it be logical for someone to say, 'Because the cause and effect of entities are renowned even up to cowherds, it is illogical to destroy them'? This is because renowned forms and so forth are destroyed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the valid cognitions of the eyes and so forth in the Samādhirāja Sūtra: 'The eyes, ears, and nose are also not valid cognitions. The tongue, body, and mind are also not valid cognitions. If these faculties were valid cognitions, what would the noble path do for anyone?'

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

'Thus, these faculties are not valid cognitions; by their intrinsic nature, they are inert and unspecified. Therefore, whoever desires the path of nirvāṇa should perform the activities of the noble path,' so it is said. Whatever characteristics of direct perception the masters have spoken of, they too are direct perception conventionally; they should be seen as engaging with the ultimate. Conventionally, they are not analyzed and debated accordingly; therefore, because they are taught conventionally, they cannot withstand analysis. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the arising of entities from self and from other in the Śālistamba and so forth. Accordingly, it is also said in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: 'Mahāmati, because they do not arise from existence or non-existence, all phenomena are unarisen.' It is said in the Great Prajñāpāramitā: 'Subhūti, that no phenomenon whatsoever is arisen is called non-arising.' Regarding that, whatever is wisdom is called patience with unarisen phenomena. Accordingly, it is also said in the Ratnākara Sūtra: 'That which has no nature, because it has no nature, how could there be other conditions? Because it has no nature, how could it generate others? ultimately, they have no nature,' so it is also said. If one says, 'All these are spoken with regard to the imagined intrinsic nature,' it is not so, because all intrinsic natures have already been eliminated by valid cognition. By this, it is taught: if even others who possess small roots of virtue do not experience the suffering of saṃsāra, how could a bodhisattva in whom the great light of pristine wisdom has arisen because of having obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, and who has obtained the generation of an unsurpassable heap of merit, experience the suffering of saṃsāra? Thus, one experiences suffering in saṃsāra in two ways: they have the characteristics of physical and mental discomfort. Among those, the former is the effect of non-virtuous karma. The latter is born from ignorance; it is born from wrong understanding. Regarding that, because they have obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, bodhisattvas have neither non-virtue nor ignorance, the causes of suffering. Because the causes are absent, it is impossible for them to be touched by the slightest trace of suffering. By this, how bodhisattvas should practice is taught. Even if they have generated an extremely large heap of merit, would they not simply remain in saṃsāra like sentient beings of the form realm and so forth? To address the doubt of thinking, 'How is it taught that merely by having generated a large heap of merit they do not abide in saṃsāra?', it also says, 'Subhūti,' and so forth.

'Thus, these faculties are not valid cognitions; by their intrinsic nature, they are inert and unspecified. Therefore, whoever desires the path of nirvāṇa should perform the activities of the noble path,' so it is said. Whatever characteristics of direct perception the masters have spoken of, they too are direct perception conventionally; they should be seen as engaging with the ultimate. Conventionally, they are not analyzed and debated accordingly; therefore, because they are taught conventionally, they cannot withstand analysis. Therefore, the Bhagavān negated the arising of entities from self and from other in the Śālistamba and so forth. Accordingly, it is also said in the noble Laṅkāvatāra: 'Mahāmati, because they do not arise from existence or non-existence, all phenomena are unarisen.' It is said in the Great Prajñāpāramitā: 'Subhūti, that no phenomenon whatsoever is arisen is called non-arising.' Regarding that, whatever is wisdom is called patience with unarisen phenomena. Accordingly, it is also said in the Ratnākara Sūtra: 'That which has no nature, because it has no nature, how could there be other conditions? Because it has no nature, how could it generate others? By this, it is taught: if even others who possess small roots of virtue do not experience the suffering of saṃsāra, how could a bodhisattva in whom the great light of pristine wisdom has arisen because of having obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, and who has obtained the generation of an unsurpassable heap of merit, experience the suffering of saṃsāra? Thus, one experiences suffering in saṃsāra in two ways: they have the characteristics of physical and mental discomfort. Among those, the former is the effect of non-virtuous karma. The latter is born from ignorance; it is born from wrong understanding. Regarding that, because they have obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, bodhisattvas have neither non-virtue nor ignorance, the causes of suffering. Because the causes are absent, it is impossible for them to be touched by the slightest trace of suffering. By this, how bodhisattvas should practice is taught. Even if they have generated an extremely large heap of merit, would they not simply remain in saṃsāra like sentient beings of the form realm and so forth? To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Regarding that, if the Buddha is to be seen as the dharmakāya and not as the rūpakāya, then how would this not contradict what is well-known from scripture regarding the Bhagavān's four deportments, taking birth, going forth, and so forth? For the sake of those who think thus, having made reference to abiding through deportment, which is the excellence of abiding, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone...', and so forth. By the two terms 'goes' or 'comes', walking is taught. The remaining ones teach the deportments of standing and so forth in their respective order. The teaching of deportments is merely an illustration; therefore, taking birth and so forth are also to be seen as taught here. Whoever adheres entirely literally to what is fully expressed in the scriptures regarding the Bhagavān's deportments and so forth, because of adhering in an inverted way, does not know the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Bhagavān is not differentiated by the form body; he is completely pure pristine wisdom. Because that pristine wisdom is bodiless, going and so forth are impossible for it even conventionally. Because going and so forth are differentiated by the specific states of the aggregate of form, those are spoken of in dependence on the emanation body of the Bhagavān; they are not in dependence on the body of pristine wisdom, because going and so forth are impossible for it conventionally and ultimately. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an excellence of abiding through deportment. Having considered the thought of those who think, 'If going and so forth are not present in the Tathāgata, how is the term "Tathāgata" taught as if differentiated by going?', it says, 'Why is that?', which should be connected with the statement, 'They do not know the meaning of what I have explained.'

ultimately, they have no nature,' so it is also said. If one says, 'All these are spoken with regard to the imagined intrinsic nature,' it is not so, because all intrinsic natures have already been eliminated by valid cognition. By this, it is taught: if even others who possess small roots of virtue do not experience the suffering of saṃsāra, how could a bodhisattva in whom the great light of pristine wisdom has arisen because of having obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, and who has obtained the generation of an unsurpassable heap of merit, experience the suffering of saṃsāra? Thus, one experiences suffering in saṃsāra in two ways: they have the characteristics of physical and mental discomfort. Among those, the former is the effect of non-virtuous karma. The latter is born from ignorance; it is born from wrong understanding. Regarding that, because they have obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, bodhisattvas have neither non-virtue nor ignorance, the causes of suffering. Because the causes are absent, it is impossible for them to be touched by the slightest trace of suffering. By this, how bodhisattvas should practice is taught. Even if they have generated an extremely large heap of merit, would they not simply remain in saṃsāra like sentient beings of the form realm and so forth? To address the doubt of thinking, 'How is it taught that merely by having generated a large heap of merit they do not abide in saṃsāra?', it also says, 'Subhūti,' and so forth.

To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

By this, whoever, even though having generated a heap of merit, apprehends the heap of merit through adhering to it in an inverted way, since they have not abandoned the inversions which are the root of all those afflictions, even if they attain a special migration, they are posited as a saṃsāric being. A bodhisattva, having obtained patience with unarisen phenomena, has no adherence to the heap of merit as being true; therefore, because they have abandoned deep ignorance which is the root of all those afflictions, they do not abide in saṃsāra,' thus it is taught.

[3-237] translation already produced for this document:
To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

[3-239] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding that, if the Buddha is to be seen as the dharmakāya and not as the rūpakāya, then how would this not contradict what is well-known from scripture regarding the Bhagavān's four deportments, taking birth, going forth, and so forth? For the sake of those who think thus, having made reference to abiding through deportment, which is the excellence of abiding, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone...', and so forth. By the two terms 'goes' or 'comes', walking is taught. The remaining ones teach the deportments of standing and so forth in their respective order. The teaching of deportments is merely an illustration; therefore, taking birth and so forth are also to be seen as taught here. Whoever adheres entirely literally to what is fully expressed in the scriptures regarding the Bhagavān's deportments and so forth, because of adhering in an inverted way, does not know the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Bhagavān is not differentiated by the form body; he is completely pure pristine wisdom. Because that pristine wisdom is bodiless, going and so forth are impossible for it even conventionally. Because going and so forth are differentiated by the specific states of the aggregate of form, those are spoken of in dependence on the emanation body of the Bhagavān; they are not in dependence on the body of pristine wisdom, because going and so forth are impossible for it conventionally and ultimately. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an excellence of abiding through deportment. Having considered the thought of those who think, 'If going and so forth are not present in the Tathāgata, how is the term "Tathāgata" taught as if differentiated by going?', it says, 'Why is that?', which should be connected with the statement, 'They do not know the meaning of what I have explained.'

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Because he has perfectly and completely understood, he is called a perfectly and completely awakened Buddha. If it were not so, because the form body is of the nature of insentient matter, he would not be called that; such is the intention. By this, entering evenly into yoga and the thorough holding of the mind are taught. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that, conventionally, in dependence on the emanation body of the Tathāgata, going and so forth are unobstructed in infinite world realms, the extensive is also taught. To teach that whatever is the emanation form body of the Tathāgata and whatever is the mental-nature body are also devoid of the nature of one and many, and thus are false just like a magically emanated Buddha, having made reference to abiding by dismantling the world of the vessel and sentient beings, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti...', and so forth. Previously, it was taught that a bodhisattva on the level of action through zealous application dismantles that, whereas now, by teaching the abiding of the Bhagavān on the level of a Buddha, it does not become repetitious. Here, too, by realizing through two methods that it is devoid of the nature of one and many, selflessness is taught.

To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

Regarding that, if the Buddha is to be seen as the dharmakāya and not as the rūpakāya, then how would this not contradict what is well-known from scripture regarding the Bhagavān's four deportments, taking birth, going forth, and so forth? For the sake of those who think thus, having made reference to abiding through deportment, which is the excellence of abiding, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone...', and so forth. By the two terms 'goes' or 'comes', walking is taught. The remaining ones teach the deportments of standing and so forth in their respective order. The teaching of deportments is merely an illustration; therefore, taking birth and so forth are also to be seen as taught here. Whoever adheres entirely literally to what is fully expressed in the scriptures regarding the Bhagavān's deportments and so forth, because of adhering in an inverted way, does not know the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Bhagavān is not differentiated by the form body; he is completely pure pristine wisdom. Because that pristine wisdom is bodiless, going and so forth are impossible for it even conventionally. Because going and so forth are differentiated by the specific states of the aggregate of form, those are spoken of in dependence on the emanation body of the Bhagavān; they are not in dependence on the body of pristine wisdom, because going and so forth are impossible for it conventionally and ultimately. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an excellence of abiding through deportment. Having considered the thought of those who think, 'If going and so forth are not present in the Tathāgata, how is the term "Tathāgata" taught as if differentiated by going?', it says, 'Why is that?', which should be connected with the statement, 'They do not know the meaning of what I have explained.'

Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

Regarding that, if the Buddha is to be seen as the dharmakāya and not as the rūpakāya, then how would this not contradict what is well-known from scripture regarding the Bhagavān's four deportments, taking birth, going forth, and so forth? For the sake of those who think thus, having made reference to abiding through deportment, which is the excellence of abiding, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone...', and so forth. By the two terms 'goes' or 'comes', walking is taught. The remaining ones teach the deportments of standing and so forth in their respective order. The teaching of deportments is merely an illustration; therefore, taking birth and so forth are also to be seen as taught here. Whoever adheres entirely literally to what is fully expressed in the scriptures regarding the Bhagavān's deportments and so forth, because of adhering in an inverted way, does not know the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Bhagavān is not differentiated by the form body; he is completely pure pristine wisdom. Because that pristine wisdom is bodiless, going and so forth are impossible for it even conventionally. Because going and so forth are differentiated by the specific states of the aggregate of form, those are spoken of in dependence on the emanation body of the Bhagavān; they are not in dependence on the body of pristine wisdom, because going and so forth are impossible for it conventionally and ultimately. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an excellence of abiding through deportment. Having considered the thought of those who think, 'If going and so forth are not present in the Tathāgata, how is the term "Tathāgata" taught as if differentiated by going?', it says, 'Why is that?', which should be connected with the statement, 'They do not know the meaning of what I have explained.'

Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: To someone who thinks, 'Since infinitesimal particles have different directional parts, are they not unestablished? How could they become a collection?', it is asked, 'For what reason?', and in response, 'Bhagavān, if...' is stated. Thinking thus: 'That collection which is analytically divided into infinitesimal particles merely as a method for reversing the apprehension of it as singular, was spoken of by the Bhagavān, but it is not that it ultimately abides. If it were not so, since a collection of infinitesimal particles would be manifestly well-known to everyone, the Bhagavān would therefore not have declared "a collection of infinitesimal particles"; because even without his speaking, it would be well-known as such.' By this, it is taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an abiding by dismantling the form of the Tathāgata.

To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

Regarding that, if the Buddha is to be seen as the dharmakāya and not as the rūpakāya, then how would this not contradict what is well-known from scripture regarding the Bhagavān's four deportments, taking birth, going forth, and so forth? For the sake of those who think thus, having made reference to abiding through deportment, which is the excellence of abiding, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone...', and so forth. By the two terms 'goes' or 'comes', walking is taught. The remaining ones teach the deportments of standing and so forth in their respective order. The teaching of deportments is merely an illustration; therefore, taking birth and so forth are also to be seen as taught here. Whoever adheres entirely literally to what is fully expressed in the scriptures regarding the Bhagavān's deportments and so forth, because of adhering in an inverted way, does not know the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Bhagavān is not differentiated by the form body; he is completely pure pristine wisdom. Because that pristine wisdom is bodiless, going and so forth are impossible for it even conventionally. Because going and so forth are differentiated by the specific states of the aggregate of form, those are spoken of in dependence on the emanation body of the Bhagavān; they are not in dependence on the body of pristine wisdom, because going and so forth are impossible for it conventionally and ultimately. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an excellence of abiding through deportment. Having considered the thought of those who think, 'If going and so forth are not present in the Tathāgata, how is the term "Tathāgata" taught as if differentiated by going?', it says, 'Why is that?', which should be connected with the statement, 'They do not know the meaning of what I have explained.'

Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Having considered the thought of someone who thinks, 'If the collection does not exist, why did the Bhagavān ask, "Would that collection of infinitesimal particles be large?"', he stated, 'Why is that?'. The words 'that is not a collection' mean that since those infinitesimal particles which abide through the analytical division of directions such as east and north are not established by nature, in reality they are not suitable to be a collection.

To dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti, as if not having grasped the intention, expresses a contradiction, saying, 'Should it not be grasped?' His thought is this: 'The Bhagavān has said in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should grasp the heap of merit. If here he says it is not to be grasped, how would it not be a contradiction?' To teach the intention by which both were spoken, the Bhagavān also said, 'It is indeed to be grasped.' Whatever was spoken of as 'grasped' is the way of grasping characterized by accomplishment. Here, the characteristic of wrong apprehension is eliminated, so there is no contradiction. Wrong apprehension is apprehending the wrong path. By this, abandoning that conceptualization teaches the thorough holding of the mind. Furthermore, beginning with 'Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family...', the extensive is taught. By the rest of the preceding, the profound was taught. By all these points, having negated the extremes of permanence and annihilation, the middle path is expressed. Not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has been explained.

Regarding that, if the Buddha is to be seen as the dharmakāya and not as the rūpakāya, then how would this not contradict what is well-known from scripture regarding the Bhagavān's four deportments, taking birth, going forth, and so forth? For the sake of those who think thus, having made reference to abiding through deportment, which is the excellence of abiding, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone...', and so forth. By the two terms 'goes' or 'comes', walking is taught. The remaining ones teach the deportments of standing and so forth in their respective order. The teaching of deportments is merely an illustration; therefore, taking birth and so forth are also to be seen as taught here. Whoever adheres entirely literally to what is fully expressed in the scriptures regarding the Bhagavān's deportments and so forth, because of adhering in an inverted way, does not know the meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Bhagavān is not differentiated by the form body; he is completely pure pristine wisdom. Because that pristine wisdom is bodiless, going and so forth are impossible for it even conventionally. Because going and so forth are differentiated by the specific states of the aggregate of form, those are spoken of in dependence on the emanation body of the Bhagavān; they are not in dependence on the body of pristine wisdom, because going and so forth are impossible for it conventionally and ultimately. Therefore, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an excellence of abiding through deportment. Having considered the thought of those who think, 'If going and so forth are not present in the Tathāgata, how is the term "Tathāgata" taught as if differentiated by going?', it says, 'Why is that?', which should be connected with the statement, 'They do not know the meaning of what I have explained.'

Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

source: གཅིག་པུར་འཛིན་པ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་དེ། དེ་བས་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པ་མེད་ན་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ལ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུ་རོལ་དང་། སྟེང་དང་འོག་དང་། ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པ་ནས་བསྐོར་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རྒྱས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆ་ཉིད་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དུ་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དེར་ཡང་དཔྱད་པ་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་གྱུར་ཀྱང་ཐུགས་མེད་དོ་ཞེ་ན། མི་རུང་སྟེ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་ཅི་ཞིག་གྲུབ། ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ནི་དངོས་པོར་མི་འགྲུབ་སྟེ། དེ་བས་ན་ངེད་ཀྱི་འདོད་པ་ཉིད་གྲུབ་པོ། །ངེད་ནི་འདོད་རྒྱལ་དུ་རྡུལ་རྣམ་པ་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་སྨྲ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐུག་པ་མེད་ན་གང་གིས་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བརྗོད། ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཆ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཐ་དད་པ་ན་གནས་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པས་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཡན་ལག་དང་བཅས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐལ་བར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་དག་གིས་གཅིག་ཏུ་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ལུས་མེད་པས་ཕྱོགས་ན་མི་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱིས་གནས་པ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་བས་ན། དེ་ནི་མིག་མིན་གཟུགས་ལ་མིན། །དེ་གཉིས་བར་ན་མི་གནས་ཏེ། །དེ་ནི་གང་ན་གནས་གྱུར་པ། །དེ་ནི་ཡོད་མིན་མེད་པ་མིན། །ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏེ་ཐལ་བས་ནི་ཆོག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ནས་སྣང་བ་མེད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་བསྟན་པས་རྣམ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དེ་མང་བ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ལྷག་མས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: It is merely spoken in order to dispel the apprehension of it as singular; therefore, it is called a collection of infinitesimal particles. If they do not have different directional parts, infinitesimal particles would not be surrounded by other infinitesimal particles from different directions, such as beyond and near, and above and below. Therefore, they would not become extensive, just like mind and mental factors and so forth. It is not suitable to state that the parts themselves become infinitesimal particles, because the analysis applies equally to them. If you say, 'Even if they do, there is no end,' it is not suitable: if infinitesimal particles become of an endless nature, what have you established? An endless nature is not established as an entity; therefore, our own assertion is established. Since we do not arbitrarily assert the nature of multiple aspects of particles, we state, 'If infinitesimal particles have no end, by what are they established?' Since you accept that whatever you posit as the partless nature of infinitesimal particles abides in different directions such as east and north, you have accepted that they have different directional parts, and therefore, it absurdly follows that they have parts. Therefore, in order to prove the absurd consequence, the basis of the reason is unestablished. It is not that it is inconclusive due to mind and mental factors either, because since they are bodiless they do not abide in directions; they do not abide by directions such as east and north. Therefore, it is taught, 'It is not the eye, it is not in form, nor does it abide between those two; wherever it abides, it is neither existent nor non-existent,' and so enough with absurd consequences. By this, because it teaches the method of making it unapparent having understood that it is devoid of a multiple nature, entering evenly into yoga and the thorough holding of the mind are taught. By the statement, 'That collection of infinitesimal particles would be large', the extensive is taught. By the rest, the profound is taught.

Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

Because he has perfectly and completely understood, he is called a perfectly and completely awakened Buddha. If it were not so, because the form body is of the nature of insentient matter, he would not be called that; such is the intention. By this, entering evenly into yoga and the thorough holding of the mind are taught. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that, conventionally, in dependence on the emanation body of the Tathāgata, going and so forth are unobstructed in infinite world realms, the extensive is also taught. To teach that whatever is the emanation form body of the Tathāgata and whatever is the mental-nature body are also devoid of the nature of one and many, and thus are false just like a magically emanated Buddha, having made reference to abiding by dismantling the world of the vessel and sentient beings, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti...', and so forth. Previously, it was taught that a bodhisattva on the level of action through zealous application dismantles that, whereas now, by teaching the abiding of the Bhagavān on the level of a Buddha, it does not become repetitious. Here, too, by realizing through two methods that it is devoid of the nature of one and many, selflessness is taught.

To someone who thinks, 'Since infinitesimal particles have different directional parts, are they not unestablished? How could they become a collection?', it is asked, 'For what reason?', and in response, 'Bhagavān, if...' is stated. Thinking thus: 'That collection which is analytically divided into infinitesimal particles merely as a method for reversing the apprehension of it as singular, was spoken of by the Bhagavān, but it is not that it ultimately abides. If it were not so, since a collection of infinitesimal particles would be manifestly well-known to everyone, the Bhagavān would therefore not have declared "a collection of infinitesimal particles"; because even without his speaking, it would be well-known as such.' By this, it is taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an abiding by dismantling the form of the Tathāgata.

Having considered the thought of someone who thinks, 'If the collection does not exist, why did the Bhagavān ask, "Would that collection of infinitesimal particles be large?"', he stated, 'Why is that?'. The words 'that is not a collection' mean that since those infinitesimal particles which abide through the analytical division of directions such as east and north are not established by nature, in reality they are not suitable to be a collection.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Now, making reference to abiding by dismantling the world of sentient beings, he stated, 'that which was spoken of as the trichiliocosm, the great chiliocosm,' and so forth. Since the world of the vessel has already been explained previously, here 'world realm' is asserted to be the world of sentient beings. The mention of 'trichiliocosm, the great chiliocosm' for both indicates infinite world realms. Therefore, the statement, 'the Tathāgata spoke of that as not a realm', is explained just as before, because that world of sentient beings, the nature of the five aggregates, is also devoid of the nature of one and many. By this, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an abiding by dismantling the Tathāgata's world of sentient beings. By making it unapparent, how this entering evenly into yoga is to be accomplished is also taught. Now, in order to teach how the mind is to be thoroughly held, it is asked, 'Why is that?', which connects with 'the Tathāgata spoke of that as not a realm'.

Here, in response, it is said, 'Tathāgata,' and so forth. Thinking thus, this expression is not differentiated by going, but is differentiated by realization, because the word 'going' has the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of entities just as they abide, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, because he too has known and understood the suchness of entities just as the previous Buddhas understood it un-invertedly, he is the Tathāgata. Moreover, in correct relative truth it is suitable as the very body of pristine wisdom, because there is no conceptualization regarding anything else. Because that, too, is bodiless, going anywhere and so forth is impossible even conventionally. Ultimately, because it is unarisen, it is utterly impossible. Therefore, because he has understood the nature of entities, he becomes the foremost of the entire world, and being worthy of offerings, he is called an arhat.

Because he has perfectly and completely understood, he is called a perfectly and completely awakened Buddha. If it were not so, because the form body is of the nature of insentient matter, he would not be called that; such is the intention. By this, entering evenly into yoga and the thorough holding of the mind are taught. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that, conventionally, in dependence on the emanation body of the Tathāgata, going and so forth are unobstructed in infinite world realms, the extensive is also taught. To teach that whatever is the emanation form body of the Tathāgata and whatever is the mental-nature body are also devoid of the nature of one and many, and thus are false just like a magically emanated Buddha, having made reference to abiding by dismantling the world of the vessel and sentient beings, it is said, 'Furthermore, Subhūti...', and so forth. Previously, it was taught that a bodhisattva on the level of action through zealous application dismantles that, whereas now, by teaching the abiding of the Bhagavān on the level of a Buddha, it does not become repetitious. Here, too, by realizing through two methods that it is devoid of the nature of one and many, selflessness is taught.

To someone who thinks, 'Since infinitesimal particles have different directional parts, are they not unestablished? How could they become a collection?', it is asked, 'For what reason?', and in response, 'Bhagavān, if...' is stated. Thinking thus: 'That collection which is analytically divided into infinitesimal particles merely as a method for reversing the apprehension of it as singular, was spoken of by the Bhagavān, but it is not that it ultimately abides. If it were not so, since a collection of infinitesimal particles would be manifestly well-known to everyone, the Bhagavān would therefore not have declared "a collection of infinitesimal particles"; because even without his speaking, it would be well-known as such.' By this, it is taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an abiding by dismantling the form of the Tathāgata.

Having considered the thought of someone who thinks, 'If the collection does not exist, why did the Bhagavān ask, "Would that collection of infinitesimal particles be large?"', he stated, 'Why is that?'. The words 'that is not a collection' mean that since those infinitesimal particles which abide through the analytical division of directions such as east and north are not established by nature, in reality they are not suitable to be a collection.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: In response, he stated, 'Bhagavān, if...' and so forth. If the world of sentient beings, just as it is well-known, were ultimately to become the nature of a single coarse entity, then, since the Tathāgata realizes the reality of entities just as they abide, he would apprehend that very thing as a mass. Therefore, since the cause of apprehending a self is merely the apprehension of the nature of the aggregates as a mass, that very thing would become a firm apprehension as a mass for the Tathāgata, implying that he has not abandoned it. But it is not so. Therefore, that apprehension as a mass which the Bhagavān spoke of elsewhere to childish ordinary beings as the cause of apprehending a self ultimately does not exist as an apprehension, because the apprehended mass has no nature whatsoever of either one or many.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (An Extensive Commentary on “The Perfection of Wisdom”), author: ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

[3-243] source:
རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནམ། དེ་དག་ཚོགས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་ལ་དེའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་གལ་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། གཅིག་པུར་འཛིན་པ་བཟློག་པའི་ཐབས་ཙམ་དུ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དབྱེ་བར་ཚོགས་པ་དེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་པའི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གྲགས་པར་གྱུར་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བཀའ་མི་སྩོལ་ཏེ། མ་གསུངས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་གྲགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་རྣམ་པར་གཞིག་པར་བཞུགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-243] translation already produced for this document:
To someone who thinks, 'Since infinitesimal particles have different directional parts, are they not unestablished? How could they become a collection?', it is asked, 'For what reason?', and in response, 'Bhagavān, if...' is stated. Thinking thus: 'That collection which is analytically divided into infinitesimal particles merely as a method for reversing the apprehension of it as singular, was spoken of by the Bhagavān, but it is not that it ultimately abides. If it were not so, since a collection of infinitesimal particles would be manifestly well-known to everyone, the Bhagavān would therefore not have declared "a collection of infinitesimal particles"; because even without his speaking, it would be well-known as such.' By this, it is taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an abiding by dismantling the form of the Tathāgata.

[3-244] source:
གལ་ཏེ་ཚོགས་མེད་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དེ་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བཀའ་སྩལ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ཚོགས་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་དབྱེ་བས་གནས་པ་དེ་དག་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པས་ཡང་དག་པར་ན་ཚོགས་སུ་མི་རིགས་སོ། །
[3-244] translation already produced for this document:
Having considered the thought of someone who thinks, 'If the collection does not exist, why did the Bhagavān ask, "Would that collection of infinitesimal particles be large?"', he stated, 'Why is that?'. The words 'that is not a collection' mean that since those infinitesimal particles which abide through the analytical division of directions such as east and north are not established by nature, in reality they are not suitable to be a collection.

[3-245] source:
གཅིག་པུར་འཛིན་པ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་དེ། དེ་བས་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པ་མེད་ན་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ལ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུ་རོལ་དང་། སྟེང་དང་འོག་དང་། ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པ་ནས་བསྐོར་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རྒྱས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆ་ཉིད་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དུ་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དེར་ཡང་དཔྱད་པ་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་གྱུར་ཀྱང་ཐུགས་མེད་དོ་ཞེ་ན། མི་རུང་སྟེ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་ཅི་ཞིག་གྲུབ། ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ནི་དངོས་པོར་མི་འགྲུབ་སྟེ། དེ་བས་ན་ངེད་ཀྱི་འདོད་པ་ཉིད་གྲུབ་པོ། །ངེད་ནི་འདོད་རྒྱལ་དུ་རྡུལ་རྣམ་པ་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་སྨྲ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐུག་པ་མེད་ན་གང་གིས་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བརྗོད། ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཆ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཐ་དད་པ་ན་གནས་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པས་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཡན་ལག་དང་བཅས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐལ་བར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་དག་གིས་གཅིག་ཏུ་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ལུས་མེད་པས་ཕྱོགས་ན་མི་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱིས་གནས་པ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་བས་ན། དེ་ནི་མིག་མིན་གཟུགས་ལ་མིན། །དེ་གཉིས་བར་ན་མི་གནས་ཏེ། །དེ་ནི་གང་ན་གནས་གྱུར་པ། །དེ་ནི་ཡོད་མིན་མེད་པ་མིན། །ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏེ་ཐལ་བས་ནི་ཆོག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ནས་སྣང་བ་མེད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་བསྟན་པས་རྣམ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དེ་མང་བ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ལྷག་མས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-245] translation already produced for this document:
It is merely spoken in order to dispel the apprehension of it as singular; therefore, it is called a collection of infinitesimal particles. If they do not have different directional parts, infinitesimal particles would not be surrounded by other infinitesimal particles from different directions, such as beyond and near, and above and below. Therefore, they would not become extensive, just like mind and mental factors and so forth. It is not suitable to state that the parts themselves become infinitesimal particles, because the analysis applies equally to them. If you say, 'Even if they do, there is no end,' it is not suitable: if infinitesimal particles become of an endless nature, what have you established? An endless nature is not established as an entity; therefore, our own assertion is established. Since we do not arbitrarily assert the nature of multiple aspects of particles, we state, 'If infinitesimal particles have no end, by what are they established?' Since you accept that whatever you posit as the partless nature of infinitesimal particles abides in different directions such as east and north, you have accepted that they have different directional parts, and therefore, it absurdly follows that they have parts. Therefore, in order to prove the absurd consequence, the basis of the reason is unestablished. It is not that it is inconclusive due to mind and mental factors either, because since they are bodiless they do not abide in directions; they do not abide by directions such as east and north. Therefore, it is taught, 'It is not the eye, it is not in form, nor does it abide between those two; wherever it abides, it is neither existent nor non-existent,' and so enough with absurd consequences. By this, because it teaches the method of making it unapparent having understood that it is devoid of a multiple nature, entering evenly into yoga and the thorough holding of the mind are taught. By the statement, 'That collection of infinitesimal particles would be large', the extensive is taught. By the rest, the profound is taught.

Now, making reference to abiding by dismantling the world of sentient beings, he stated, 'that which was spoken of as the trichiliocosm, the great chiliocosm,' and so forth. Since the world of the vessel has already been explained previously, here 'world realm' is asserted to be the world of sentient beings. The mention of 'trichiliocosm, the great chiliocosm' for both indicates infinite world realms. Therefore, the statement, 'the Tathāgata spoke of that as not a realm', is explained just as before, because that world of sentient beings, the nature of the five aggregates, is also devoid of the nature of one and many. By this, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer toward such an abiding by dismantling the Tathāgata's world of sentient beings. By making it unapparent, how this entering evenly into yoga is to be accomplished is also taught. Now, in order to teach how the mind is to be thoroughly held, it is asked, 'Why is that?', which connects with 'the Tathāgata spoke of that as not a realm'.

[3-245] translation already produced for this document:
It is merely spoken in order to dispel the apprehension of it as singular; therefore, it is called a collection of infinitesimal particles. If they do not have different directional parts, infinitesimal particles would not be surrounded by other infinitesimal particles from different directions, such as beyond and near, and above and below. Therefore, they would not become extensive, just like mind and mental factors and so forth. It is not suitable to state that the parts themselves become infinitesimal particles, because the analysis applies equally to them. If you say, 'Even if they do, there is no end,' it is not suitable: if infinitesimal particles become of an endless nature, what have you established? An endless nature is not established as an entity; therefore, our own assertion is established. Since we do not arbitrarily assert the nature of multiple aspects of particles, we state, 'If infinitesimal particles have no end, by what are they established?' Since you accept that whatever you posit as the partless nature of infinitesimal particles abides in different directions such as east and north, you have accepted that they have different directional parts, and therefore, it absurdly follows that they have parts. Therefore, in order to prove the absurd consequence, the basis of the reason is unestablished. It is not that it is inconclusive due to mind and mental factors either, because since they are bodiless they do not abide in directions; they do not abide by directions such as east and north. Therefore, it is taught, 'It is not the eye, it is not in form, nor does it abide between those two; wherever it abides, it is neither existent nor non-existent,' and so enough with absurd consequences. By this, because it teaches the method of making it unapparent having understood that it is devoid of a multiple nature, entering evenly into yoga and the thorough holding of the mind are taught. By the statement, 'That collection of infinitesimal particles would be large', the extensive is taught. By the rest, the profound is taught.

In response, he stated, 'Bhagavān, if...' and so forth. If the world of sentient beings, just as it is well-known, were ultimately to become the nature of a single coarse entity, then, since the Tathāgata realizes the reality of entities just as they abide, he would apprehend that very thing as a mass. Therefore, since the cause of apprehending a self is merely the apprehension of the nature of the aggregates as a mass, that very thing would become a firm apprehension as a mass for the Tathāgata, implying that he has not abandoned it. But it is not so. Therefore, that apprehension as a mass which the Bhagavān spoke of elsewhere to childish ordinary beings as the cause of apprehending a self ultimately does not exist as an apprehension, because the apprehended mass has no nature whatsoever of either one or many.
